articles.title: Donald Trump gets a warm welcome in the Philippines
articles.deck: But he almost skipped about the only country that still adores him

paragraphs.text: DONALD TRUMP had planned to give Manila a miss on his swing through Asia this week. When the Philippines first announced its East Asia Summit (where South-East Asian leaders meet interested others), it was set for five days before he was due in China for the higher-profile APEC. That was awkward timing. So the Philippines pushed back the date , offering Mr Trump a 24-hour layover in the capital, where he landed on November 17th. Invitations to the leaders of China, Japan and India, sent months earlier, were updated. The accommodation is a reflection of a long-standing security alliance between America and the Philippines, which has remained surprisingly unscathed during Mr Trump’s second term. Joint military exercises have grown in scale under Mr Trump. After the Trump administration gutted USAID in early 2025, the Philippines was among the first countries to receive new development assistance.

Mr Trump encountered some protests in Manila; more than 200 who took to the streets were detained. But the overall welcome was warm. Since Mr Trump had missed all the formal summitry, the Philippine president, Ferdinand Marcos junior, convened a special meeting in his honour. Mr Trump reciprocated by saying Mr Marcos had inherited “good genetics” from his parents—brutal kleptocrats who led the Philippines for two decades last century. The 97-year-old Imelda Marcos, who partied with Mr Trump in New York in the 1990s, was pushed out in a wheelchair to greet her old friend. America and the Philippines, Mr Trump said, have never been closer than they are now.

This is not just talk. A survey published in June found that 68% of Filipino respondents had confidence in Mr Trump to do the right thing, the highest level among 36 countries polled. This is partly a response to the Philippines’ clashes with China in the South China Sea. Mr Marcos has staked his foreign policy on having America’s support in these disputes. Since his election in 2022, he has opened four more Philippine military bases to American troops and allowed the Americans to bring in a Typhon missile system with the range to strike China.

Not everyone approves. Some believe Mr Marcos has unnecessarily drawn the Philippines into the rivalry between America and China. Others say he is foolish to trust America. Mr Marcos’s predecessor, Rodrigo Duterte, was an erratic authoritarian who preferred China to America. His daughter, the front-runner to succeed Mr Marcos in 2028, has criticised Mr Marcos’s foreign policy as unbalanced.

To insure against problems in a second Duterte presidency, boosters of the alliance are trying to deepen non-military ties. The Philippines in April said it would join America’s Pax Silica initiative, its effort to build tech supply chains without Chinese content. But the initiative has so far produced nothing concrete for the Philippines. Mr Trump said before departing that the two countries had concluded a “very big trade deal”. Similar deals heralded by Mr Trump, however, have not included much detail. Even if it was light in substance, a congenial visit is a win for the Philippines. As America’s other allies can attest, it could have been a lot worse.

articles.title: India feeds the world, but its methane emissions are heating it
articles.deck: Rice farming and cattle are both to blame

paragraphs.text: INDIA’S 53M HECTARES of rice paddy are picturesque and bountiful. Last year they produced 154m tonnes of rice, 28% of the global total, overtaking China and making India for the first time the world’s largest producer. Around 22m tonnes of that were shipped abroad, some 40% of global exports. The paddies also generated millions of tonnes of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. When paddy fields flood, the soil is starved of oxygen, letting anaerobic organisms called methanogens thrive. The bugs gobble up plant detritus and manure, converting it into energy with methane as a by-product. Rice paddies produce 8-12% of global methane emissions each year. India’s are responsible for 16.5% of that, second only to China’s.

Reducing methane emissions is a good way to slow the pace of global warming. Tonne for tonne, methane is a far more powerful warming gas than carbon dioxide, and it degrades rapidly in the atmosphere, disappearing in around 12 years. So cutting methane emissions can quickly slow the pile-up of greenhouse gases. Carbon dioxide, by contrast, stays aloft for anything from centuries to millennia, which is why climate wonks argue that it should be actively taken out of the atmosphere.

In many countries, particularly heavily industrialised ones, cutting methane emissions mostly means plugging leaks in fossil-fuel infrastructure—good for producers and the atmosphere alike. In India, just under half of methane emissions come from agricultural activities, primarily rice and cattle farming. That creates special challenges for reducing them.

Various approaches are being tried. The solution for rice paddies largely involves using less water for irrigation. Alternate wetting and drying, for instance, means periodically draining the paddies. That lowers water use by roughly a third and also inhibits the methanogens by allowing oxygen into the soil. Studies suggest that as a result emissions can drop by between 30% and 70%. Another method is to use varieties of rice that can be directly seeded in dry soil, rather than being germinated in nurseries and then transplanted into flooded paddies. This saves labour as well as water, and can reduce methane emissions by anything from 30% to 98%.

The picture for livestock is different. Cattle foster methanogens in their stomachs’ first chamber, where they help to break down grass and other food; and India is home to nearly 200m cattle, more than anywhere else except Brazil. The burps from those cows and buffalo account for roughly one-third of India’s agricultural methane emissions.

Mixing more digestible green feeds in with dry fodder reduces the methane load in the burps. Additives can have the same result. Seaweed can reduce methane by 30-80%. The supplement is thought to inhibit an enzyme that the methanogens use to produce methane. Microbes in manure generate methane when it is wet or moist; to reduce these emissions it can be spread out in the sun and left to dry.

Unfortunately, none of this appears to be a priority. India’s climate targets do not single out methane reduction; nor did the government sign up to a 2021 pledge to cut emissions by at least 30% below 2020 levels by 2030. Moreover, much of Indian agriculture is on small-scale subsistence farms, so proposals to change the way they have operated for generations are hard to implement. For low-emissions programmes to take off, they need to give farmers clear incentives, in the shape of increased yields or lower labour or water costs.

Even then, change is difficult. Farmers often worry that experiments and unfamiliar practices are risky, says Prakashan Veettil, an economist at the International Rice Research Institute. He works closely with rice farmers. He says labour shortages during the covid-19 pandemic made “direct-seeded” rice popular in Punjab and Haryana, two states, but the practice was abandoned as labour markets recovered.

Farmers, he says, see continuous flooding as a form of insurance against the vagaries of the weather and water availability, particularly as climate change wreaks havoc on seasonal rains, and a long history of pumping groundwater has caused those supplies to deplete. So farmers consider it a dangerous gamble to drain their fields, despite evidence that yields can be maintained and costs lowered.

India’s farmers need to adjust their practices, and not just to adapt better to the changing climate. Dairy cattle are numerous, but they produce less milk per head than cattle elsewhere. And the country is producing more rice than it can consume, store for food security or export. The government is keen for its farmers to diversify. For smallholders and subsistence farmers who operate season by season, however, making such changes will not seem worthwhile without more protection against failure.

articles.title: Thailand’s fertility rate is collapsing
articles.deck: As with China, it is at levels elsewhere seen only in much richer ones

paragraphs.text: WITH ITS golden beaches and cheap beer, Thailand has long been popular among backpackers and partygoers. But in recent years it has attracted a new type of tourist. Prospective parents from around the world are flooding in for fertility treatments, drawn by low costs and high-quality care. Yet even as local baby-making businesses are booming, Thailand itself is in the midst of a baby bust.

In 2025 the country of 66m people registered a mere 417,000 births, the fewest for 75 years and 10% less than in 2024; it is expected to fall again this year. Estimates for Thailand’s total fertility rate (TFR), the number of births a typical woman has over her lifetime, are varied, but all are alarmingly low. Demographers at Mahidol University near Bangkok put the latest figure at 0.86, well under half the replacement rate of 2.1 (and below the UN’s projection, for 2025, of 1.2). That is also lower than the latest reliable estimates for China (1.0) and Japan (1.1), two Asian countries associated with fertility crises (though Taiwan and South Korea are even lower).

What makes Thailand’s demographic slide remarkable is its speed. In 1970 the average Thai woman had more than five children, compared with 4.5 in South Korea and around two in Japan. As countries grow richer, people tend to have fewer offspring. But Thailand’s ultra-low fertility has come at unusually low income levels: its GDP per person, of $8,100 in 2025, was less than half of Japan’s and South Korea’s, even adjusted for the cost of living (see chart). That has made Thailand the only country in South-East Asia where the population has already peaked. Like China, it is an extreme example of a predicament now confronting much of the developing world: getting old before getting rich.

Many of the forces driving the global fertility decline are shaping outcomes in Thailand. Economic development, expanding education and urbanisation have changed the nature of work and transformed the role of women. Nearly 60% of Thai women have formal jobs. The share of Thais of reproductive age who are single rose from 35.7% in 2017 to 40.5% in 2023, according to the national planning agency.

But despite these trends, most Thais still want children, points out Manasigan Kanchanachitra of Mahidol. A UN survey this year found that they wanted, on average, around two. Cost is the main problem. As Thais have grown richer, their aspirations for their kids have also surged. They increasingly see expensive private schools as the only way to ensure their children’s success, says Dr Manasigan. Adding to the burden is filial duty: young Thais are expected to take care of their parents. In September the World Bank predicted that Thailand would, by 2033, become a “super-aged” society, with more than 20% of the population aged over 65.

During elections this year, every big party promised to tackle the issue, with policy ideas that included giving more generous cash transfers for newborns, though the evidence suggests most such schemes have little impact. Fulfilling any of these promises, in any case, requires a degree of continuity and co-ordination often absent in Thai governance. The country has had four prime ministers in the past five years—almost as many as Britain.

articles.title: China is kicking up a fuss over a Japanese spy show
articles.deck: Even though its own tellies are full of anti-Japanese content

paragraphs.text: IN A REMOTE village near Azerbaijan Chinese spies are torturing captured Japanese agents from beppan, a fictional secret unit, in the basement of a castle. An intrepid Japanese team is planning a rescue. But first they must convince the villagers, who are living under Chinese domination, to co-operate. “Don’t you want to take back your own dignity?” one of them asks the village head, who decides he has had enough of being pushed around and agrees to help. Meanwhile the Chinese are thuggishly chopping off the fingers of their prisoners. The brave Japanese do not give in.

Such is the plot of “Vivant”, a drama that has just aired its second season on TBS, one of Japan’s main TV channels. It is Japan’s biggest hit this season. But it has also provoked a backlash from Chinese officials and state media amid a diplomatic stand-off between Japan and China. Chinese state media complain that the show “distorts history” by portraying Chinese villains doing the brutal things that Japanese soldiers did to Chinese people in the past. The outcry has pushed Sanrio, the firm that makes the Hello Kitty brand and had produced Vivant-themed merchandise, to apologise and cut ties with the show.

Within Japan, the show was not controversial until China made it so. Before the hullabaloo Takaichi Sanae, Japan’s prime minister, said that she was planning to binge-watch the series over the holidays. Koizumi Shinjiro, the defence minister, was asked whether beppan exists in real life—a timely question given that Japan recently launched its first post-war centralised intelligence agency. Mr Koizumi’s answer was that beppan has not, nor has it ever, existed, though he “does like the drama”.

Chinese critics may be projecting their own experiences onto Japan when they accuse the Japanese government of cognitive warfare, says Yi Wang, an expert on memory politics at the University of Birmingham. In China the state dictates a narrative that directors, producers and screenwriters must follow, he says: “Japanese invasion, bad Japanese, the great Chinese resistance.” Shows that add too much nuance are censored.

Japan’s entertainment industry is more commercially driven than China’s and usually apolitical, says Griseldis Kirsch, of SOAS University of London. “Vivant” has a more patriotic narrative than most, but that reflects a conservative streak among its audience, not the state trying to guide opinion. “It’s not deep. It’s just entertainment,” reckons Li Hao, a political scientist at the University of Tokyo. The show is “patriotic porn”, similar to dramas Chinese viewers watch to feel their country is strong.

articles.title: China’s efforts to strengthen its safety net fuel public anger
articles.deck: People don’t want to pay into an unequal system they don’t trust

paragraphs.text: Pan Kexin is a 25-year-old barista in the central city of Wuhan. Every month she reluctantly pays one-sixth of her 6,000 yuan ($900) salary into the state’s social-security scheme, which covers five types of insurance: old-age (pension), medical, unemployment, work injury and maternity. “Young people today don’t have much faith in the credibility of these institutions,” Ms Pan reckons. Her friends are mostly gig workers who have not enrolled. “The way they’re now forcing people to pay for social security basically means the government is running out of money,” she says.

For many people, China’s social-security system is meagre at best. The government wants to improve it, but is facing huge challenges. Businesses routinely skimp on their contributions by underreporting, or failing to report, employees’ salaries. People in informal work often make none. The population is ageing rapidly, which places an ever greater burden on the scheme: by the end of 2025 there were more than 320m aged 60 or over, or 23% of the population—up from 16% a decade earlier. And there are fewer people available to make payments: the working-age population fell by 60m in the same period. In the past decade the government has tried to cope by more than doubling fiscal subsidies for social security. But it has also tried to curb the cost of benefits by slowing their annual rise, while pursuing potential contributors more aggressively. Workers and employers alike are grumbling.

Ms Pan is formally employed, so she has to contribute. Employees pay at least 10% of their salary, while employers have to hand over the equivalent of about 25% of each worker’s pay cheque. But many people in smaller firms collude with their bosses to evade payments. An employer will not register with the scheme, or underdeclare salaries to reduce both the firm’s social-security bill and deductions from employees’ wages. The difference is paid to employees as cash under the table.

The government is getting impatient with foot-draggers. It wants a stronger social-security system in part to revitalise the economy. Consumer spending is weak because people are saving a lot for medical emergencies and retirement: a better safety net would encourage them to open their wallets and thereby stimulate growth. On October 11th the government vowed to use “every possible means” to ensure that firms fully report the pay of all staff and submit the correct contributions. Since November 1st it has imposed standard fines (up to three times the amount owed) on violators.

These moves have stirred anger online. On social media many complain their wages are so low that higher payments would be unaffordable. They express doubt that the government will fulfil its pension obligations. Hashtags such as “young people don’t want to pay social security” have spread: censors have blocked some of them. Bosses are squirming, too. In many industries overcapacity is forcing firms to make savings so they can fight price wars. Stricter enforcement of social-security rules could push up their costs, or prompt them to lay off formal employees and turn to gig workers instead.

Even if the government succeeds in boosting compliance by firms, it will struggle among gig workers. By some estimates there are about 320m of them, double the number in 2019. For gig workers enrolment is voluntary; but those who do sign up have to pay all their contributions themselves. Some delivery firms have offered to shoulder part of that cost, but few workers have opted in. A survey of delivery drivers in one district of Beijing found that 40% preferred extra payments in cash.

The far better deals enjoyed by people on the state’s payroll have deepened resentment of the government’s pressure. In September a netizen’s back-of-the-envelope calculation of payments received by Wuhan University’s retired staff set off a national discussion about stark inequality in welfare benefits. Urban public-sector workers get far more generous pensions than most people in China.

Older workers tend to put more trust in the system. Ms Pan’s parents, for example, are self-employed, so are not obliged to enroll. But they do make payments, believing they are worthwhile. Young Chinese are the biggest grumblers. They fume online about funding the generous packages of retired civil servants, when they themselves have a hard time finding jobs: youth unemployment is nearly 20%. The authorities have been fighting back. People’s Daily, the Communist Party’s main mouthpiece, recently attacked those who “question the fairness and sustainability” of the government’s pension provisions. It called for “vigilance” against those “propagating narratives such as ‘the system is on the verge of collapse’ or ‘young people can no longer afford to support the elderly.’”

Resentment will grow unless more people see rewards from compliance. “If policymakers really wanted to prioritise boosting consumption, then raising the level of benefits would be more effective in the near term than broadening coverage and enforcing contributions,” wrote Gavekal Dragonomics, a research firm, in a recent bulletin. But the party is hesitant. “We must resolutely avoid falling into the trap of welfarism that breeds idlers,” said China’s leader, Xi Jinping, in 2021.

Many people still rely on their families. Liu Jie, a delivery driver, criss-crosses Wuhan 12 hours a day to earn enough to save for his parents, who are construction workers. They are not in the social-security scheme. “When they are too old and can no longer work, my brother and I will take care of them,” he says. “If I paid social security, I wouldn’t be able to save.”

articles.title: China’s Buddhists are releasing animals where they do not belong
articles.deck: It is ruffling feathers in the Communist Party

paragraphs.text: On a drizzly Saturday night this month, someone released dozens of exotic birds near the ancient Longhua Temple in Shanghai. Alas, the city gets chilly at this time of year: tiger parrots and zebra finches prefer the tropics. Most quickly died from the cold, or at the claws of cats. The temple said it did not know who freed the birds. But it was probably a Buddhist conducting a ritual known as fang sheng. Some believers reckon that giving captive animals their freedom is a way to earn spiritual merit. The increasingly popular practice, however, is worrying officials and environmentalists.

During Mao’s Cultural Revolution, the enthusiastically atheist Communist Party banned fang sheng as a “feudal superstition” (and, in hard times, a waste of protein). Officials filled in temple ponds that were once reserved for freed fish. Since Mao’s death in 1976, Buddhism has seen a revival. Relatively few people formally identify with the religion. But surveys suggest that perhaps a third of Chinese people engage in some of the practices associated with it, from burning incense at temples to fang sheng. China’s abundance of markets selling live animals for the dinner table makes it easy for the devout, with money, to acquire religious merit.

In the past most fang sheng ceremonies might have just involved saving a fish or two from the chopping block and slipping them into a nearby river. But in recent decades believers have become both wealthier and more inventive. Some focus on quantity: last year around 400 cats were released near a reservoir in southern China (several drowned); fish are sometimes poured into waterways by the thousand, to the delight of local anglers. Others go for quality, in the form of exotic species (in 2012 a South American piranha turned up in a Chinese river). Technology is enabling new ways of performing fang sheng. Earlier this year a fang sheng ceremony was live-streamed from a riverbank in south-west China; those watching online could earn merit by sending money to the streamer, who would then take a baby turtle from a box and pop it in the water.

All this fuels illegal trade in wildlife. Many animals are captured or bred simply to be sold to Buddhists. Bird traders, for instance, set up shop outside temples to attract the sympathy of worshippers. And foreign species, if they do not perish, can also wreak havoc on China’s ecosystems. One of the worst offenders is the red-eared slider turtle, a native of North America that can outbreed local reptiles and spread infections. Beijing’s canals are infested with them.

Over the past decade officials have been trying harder to protect the environment. This has included efforts to regulate fang sheng more tightly. Since 2021 releasing invasive species has been a criminal offence. To avoid hefty fines, people are now supposed only to free approved species in designated spots, and register releases in advance with the government. In 2023 a woman in the eastern province of Jiangsu was fined some 90,000 yuan ($13,500) after dumping 12.5 tonnes of catfish in a lake. The state-affiliated Buddhist Association of China has denounced those who profit from fang sheng and has called for the practice to become more “scientific and reasonable”. Public opinion may be shifting, too. The release of the unlucky birds in Shanghai was greeted by squawks of disapproval on social media.

Still, investigations by state media suggest few people are telling the government about their activities (“I’m doing a good deed, why should I have to report it?” complained one Buddhist to reporters). And the practice is hard to police. Mr Gao, a 35-year-old in Shanghai who works in finance, has been releasing fish regularly for years, but has never sought government permission. At first he had hoped that fang sheng might make his work go more smoothly. Then he started to enjoy simply watching the fish swim away. He only releases a few at a time, and picks local species. Mr Gao admits that not every Buddhist is so careful. “It is easy to have good intentions but do bad things,” he says.

articles.title: China’s prison for the elite is massively expanding
articles.deck: Its list of inmates past and present is a Who’s Who of Chinese politics

paragraphs.text: Qincheng Prison has a fearsome reputation. It lies at the foot of a mountain range on the outskirts of northern Beijing. Since it was built in the 1950s under Chairman Mao it has held China’s most sensitive political prisoners, including many fallen officials. Student leaders of the Tiananmen Square protests were sent to Qincheng in 1989, where they had to endure solitary confinement and sleep on wooden planks. A former inmate described it as “a place where you come to realise you are not a human being”.

Satellite images analysed by The Economist show that China’s most famous prison is expanding faster than at any time since the 1960s during the Cultural Revolution. Construction that began early this year will probably add at least 300 cells: an increase of 50%. Details about the facility are treated as state secrets. But the growth coincides with a widening purge of senior officials that is being carried out by China’s ruler, Xi Jinping (105 minister-level officials had been imprisoned or punished in other ways as of September, more than one and a half times the number in the whole of 2025, see chart). It may suggest the prison has returned to the crowded conditions seen in bygone eras of political and social tumult.

Qincheng is the only prison operated by the Ministry of Public Security, which oversees China’s police forces (their duty includes hunting down critics of the Communist Party). Zhou Yongkang, who was once in charge of the ministry, is now imprisoned there. Jiang Qing, Mao’s wife, helped purge so many high officials during the Cultural Revolution that Qincheng had to be expanded in 1968. Jiang was herself imprisoned there after Mao’s death—she occupied the cell where her interrogator had been confined a few years earlier.

Life in Qincheng is bleak. Renovations have added new roofless, high-walled pens in which lucky prisoners get occasional fresh air. Solitary confinement is common—one inmate was kept this way for 20 years. Others are typically kept in cells with up to half a dozen other people, and a squat toilet. Some go insane. The food is bland, says a former detainee, and at times is simply poured into inmates’ hands. He recalls showers only once every two weeks.

Not all prisoners have it so rough. Well-connected ones fare better. Bao Tong, an official locked up after the Tiananmen Square unrest, got a mattress and an egg at breakfast—but only after his wife complained to Jiang Zemin, who was then China’s leader. Mr Zhou, the former security chief, is said to tend to a vegetable patch. Bo Xilai, once Mr Xi’s rival for the job of party leader and now serving a life sentence, reportedly wears a Western suit instead of a drab prison uniform (his father, Bo Yibo, also did a stint in Qincheng).

Disgraced cadres and sensitive political prisoners are put in Qincheng to keep them apart from ordinary criminals. People are sent there “not because of rank, but because of what they know”, said a former Ministry of Justice official in 2018. The facility’s high security prevents escape or unauthorised contact with the outside world that could threaten regime stability, says Ling Li of the University of Vienna. But it is not the kind of banishment errant officials suffered in imperial days: Qincheng is only an hour by car from the city centre.

In 2021 work began on a vast barracks on the western side of the compound, likely for police (this was first reported by Youshu, a Substack blog whose author is anonymous). It is the size of ten football pitches and has four dormitories, an athletics track, a parade ground and probably an armoury. In 2022 a north-east cell block was refurbished and exercise pens added.

Qincheng last received a new cell block in 2016. This year’s building work has involved demolishing two blocks to make way for a bigger complex, possibly six storeys tall. One of the former blocks, number 203, is where the Panchen Lama, a Tibetan religious leader, was sent in 1968 and Liu Xiaobo in 1989 (he later became China’s only Nobel peace-prize winner and died in custody). The prison administration has also expanded. Cranes are working on the eastern side of the compound, where staff live. Two other structures are hard to identify, but one is inside the prison’s internal walls, meaning it may also house inmates.

There has been no mention of the construction in China’s media. “Nobody’s talking. But that’s partly because nobody’s leaving,” says John Gerson, a former British diplomat. Indeed, the number of inmates is almost certainly rising, for now. The prison tends to get emptier when there is political change in the party, but Mr Xi shows every sign of being a lifer at the top.

articles.title: A lone protester highlights the pain from China’s property bust
articles.deck: “Excavator man” will not spark a popular movement, but his actions expose a deep malaise

paragraphs.text: The most famous protester in modern Chinese history is “tank man”, the anonymous pedestrian who stared down a line of tanks next to Tiananmen Square in 1989. Last week a new protester captivated audiences beyond China: excavator man. On November 9th he drove a yellow construction digger up to a large government building in western China and started to rip at its façade—all caught on bystanders’ mobile phones. Part of the fascination with the story lay in the desperation of his act. The building, like the government itself, was at no risk of being toppled; the only certain outcome was that the man would be locked up.

Four days after videos of his protest spread across social media, Chaguan visited the site in Fengdong New City, just west of the historic capital of Xi’an. Dozens of police stood in front of the building—a service centre for the public. Hoardings already covered the walls struck by the man, who was identified by officials only as Mr Hu, aged 47. Workers drilled and hammered as they repaired the damage. Inside, people paid taxes and registered companies as usual. With police there, no one tarried to take photos.

But in the streets nearby, seemingly everyone knew about the protest. “It was a spectacle. We were all gawping,” said a shopkeeper. Officials have given no motive. Two versions have circulated online. One is that Mr Hu was owed money for construction work; the other that he was aggrieved over compensation for his demolished farm. A longtime resident on his way out of the service centre blamed the sprawling development across the street, where a village had been razed to make way for a thicket of office buildings and housing blocks. One thing, he said, was clear. “The government doesn’t have the money to pay what it owes. Even a clever cook can’t make a meal without rice.”

Whichever version is true, the saga in Fengdong is an extreme case of a grim reality for many: a property bust has drained local coffers, and ordinary people are last in line to be paid. Some are being pushed to the brink—and, as in the case of excavator man, over it. Chinese provinces and cities used to rely on land sales to generate nearly half their revenue. When the property sector went cold, land sales came to a halt, leaving local governments struggling to pay bills. Richer coastal cities are building new high-tech industries and broader tax bases. Places inland like Fengdong have had no such luck. They were in the midst of massive building sprees as the music stopped, and have little share of China’s new tech-driven economy.

The area around Mr Hu’s protest bears the scars of the property crash. Across the street from the building he attacked is the concrete core of a skyscraper that was supposed to reach 100 storeys, making it the tallest tower in north-western China, but it remains incomplete. Work stopped two years ago. Around it are other half-finished buildings; completed ones have padlocked doors, shattered glass and to-let signs. The troubles have reached the local government’s balance-sheet. In May the state-owned group that oversees development of the Xixian New Area, which includes Fengdong, disclosed that it had nearly 3.7bn yuan ($550m) in overdue debt.

Signs of progress are few and faint. A nearby industrial park has attracted a genomics firm and a software developer. One forlorn building was repurposed a few months ago as a hub for “one-person companies”. These are intended to be small startups powered by artificial intelligence. Walking through empty corridors, a visitor would more readily call them “zero-person companies”. Even if some do eventually help the economy to grow, they will produce nothing like the windfall a decade ago from selling vast tracts of land. The government “can’t sell more land”, said the longtime resident, exaggerating only slightly.

Many places around China are in similar difficulty. In the first half of 2026 more than two-thirds of local-government financing vehicles—state-owned firms that turned land into property developments—did not earn enough to cover their interest payments, according to S&P, a credit-rating agency. Payments to suppliers are chronically late. Money owed to construction workers or to villagers as compensation easily slides to the bottom of the pile of bills. “There is nothing you can do. Suing them is pointless,” said a former road-construction contractor. In Fengdong, villagers showed up at the service centre every day for a month to demand payment, all to no avail, said the shopkeeper. “Officials delay and delay until they are transferred elsewhere,” he added.

One of Xi Jinping’s solutions has been to create a system of lifetime responsibility for debt. A party secretary or mayor who makes a mess like the one in Fengdong will, in theory, be on the hook many years later. That makes sense, but it has added to the chill: who wants to take risks that could haunt them forever? Pretty much the only construction in central Fengdong was the renovation of the building damaged by Mr Hu.

Do his actions signify that more people are beginning to vent their discontent in public? The contractor said a lesson from China’s long history is that it takes just one person to light a fire. On social media, the vast majority of comments were sympathetic. “Ordinary people have suffered too much,” read a typical one.

Yet there is scant evidence that Mr Hu’s lone act promises a popular movement. For potential copycats, the consequences are too frightening and the benefits too negligible. As a delivery driver in Fengdong put it, the important thing now is to get used to lower expectations. He can still put food on the table, so the situation is tolerable. That is hardly a ringing endorsement of his life. But as far as officials are concerned, what matters is that it is not a stinging denunciation. They can live with one excavator man.

articles.title: What is causing America’s recent outages
articles.deck: Frenzied preparations for cyber-attacks are creating their own risks

paragraphs.text: “Once is happenstance. Twice is coincidence,” observes Goldfinger, the eponymous villain of Ian Fleming’s novel, to James Bond. “The third time it’s enemy action.” That has been the conclusion of many Americans, too, as they watch the digital world seemingly crumble around them in recent days. On November 12th Microsoft services experienced a global outage, leaving office workers adrift. The next day a glitch in air-traffic control communications caused the longest flight stoppage since the attacks on September 11th, 2001. On November 16th technical problems afflicted several big banks. And on November 17th the National Security Agency (NSA), America’s signals-intelligence service, was hit by disruption to its own classified communication system.

The explanations from America’s officials have not inspired confidence. Markwayne Mullin, Donald Trump’s homeland security secretary, suggested on November 16th that the spate of outages might have been caused by “self-fixing” AI that was rewriting its own code too quickly, a theory he had gleaned from speaking to “one guy that’s very smart with tech”. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said that a faulty router was to blame for the problems with air-traffic control. Josh Hawley, a Republican senator, is among the Americans who don’t buy it. “The full Senate ought to be briefed on what exactly is going on,” he demanded on November 17th. “If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.”

America’s week of digital mayhem is indeed unusual. But it is not necessarily suspicious. There is little evidence that malicious hackers or wayward AI are to blame. Rather, some of the recent chaos could be a symptom of efforts to make America’s digital infrastructure more secure. Tinkering with such old and complex systems has always been fraught. But companies are now using AI to discover vulnerabilities and moving more quickly to repair them. Paradoxically, that defensive activity seems to be creating new short-term risks.

On the face of it, each of this month’s mishaps has a prosaic explanation. The FAA says its initial investigation found that a new router installed at a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, led to problems at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, flooding the system with “excessive data”. The work was part of routine upgrades from old copper wires to fibre-optic cables, rather than anything to do with newfangled AI systems. Sean Duffy, the transport secretary, demanded that Congress pony up $50bn for upgrades.

In Microsoft’s case, its issues stemmed from a patch to software rolled out in July. The patch had worked for four months, but contained a hidden bug that only cropped up later when data from two different systems inadvertently piled up on one network at the same time as server capacity was down. The result was a cascading failure, causing more than 80% of servers to keel over. Notably, JPMorganChase, a big bank, and NSA sources both say that the problems with their systems were also linked to software updates.

“I don’t think the events themselves are connected in any real meaningful or material way,” argues Chris Krebs, who led America’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency from 2018 to 2020. But there are commonalities. Each of these cases involves an effort to make a system more secure. The outages at Microsoft, the big banks and the NSA might have an additional link, to AI, though not for the reasons given by Mr Mullin.

Mark Warner, the vice-chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, offered a more thorough explanation on November 17th. “AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed,” he wrote on X, “creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change.”

In April Anthropic, an AI firm, announced Mythos, a model which turned out to be extremely good at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities in software. Firms and organisations granted special access to Mythos through a programme known as Glasswing, and have been using it to “tear down their existing code to discover vulnerabilities and patch them before bad guys can use their own tools to find them”, says Mr Krebs.

The sheer “volume and velocity” of that effort can cause issues, he notes, overwhelming the teams that deal with vulnerabilities and patches. Microsoft is an example of this. Between 2022 and 2025 the firm fixed about 4,000 “common vulnerabilities and exposures”, or CVEs in cyber-parlance, a security flaw in software that is catalogued with a unique number. In 2026 alone—assisted by Mythos and other models—the firm published more than 5,000, a staggering tally that is still growing (see chart). Ciaran Martin, who ran Britain’s cyber-security agency from 2016 to 2020, says it is plausible, though not yet proven, that AI-related layoffs might also have “stripped organisations bare of people who understand how their networks work”. That would make mistakes more likely.

In the short term, the result looks like digital bedlam. “Every incident…conjures fears of a cyber-attack,” observes Colin Clarke of the Soufan Centre, an intelligence and security research group. “Iran, Russia, and China live in Americans’ heads rent-free.” Those anxieties are compounded by Americans’ lack of trust in their government, he adds. It doesn’t help that real cyber-attacks continue. In October hackers linked to North Korea stole a whopping $6.3bn from Binance, a crypto firm.

In the long term, the process of frenetic AI-driven patching is good news, argues Mr Krebs. Many vulnerabilities will have been “swept out” in the coming months and years, he says, resulting in code that is “safer and more secure”. But Americans may take scant comfort in the prospect of more outages now and ever-more sophisticated attacks later.

articles.title: A fight over chips is roiling Donald Trump’s cabinet
articles.deck: Will Howard Lutnick be offered up as a sacrificial lamb?

paragraphs.text: The 18-hour flight carrying Donald Trump from Maryland to Manila, via Alaska, on November 16th might have been awkward for Scott Bessent and Howard Lutnick. In previous days Mr Bessent, the treasury secretary, had assailed Mr Lutnick, the commerce secretary, for lax enforcement of export controls on semiconductors, an issue thrust into public view by a scandal at Nvidia, America’s top chipmaker. Mr Trump initially appeared to side with Mr Lutnick. “One wants to be friendly with China,” the president quipped, “and one wants to have a blow-up with China.” But as they flew west, Mr Bessent seemed to gain the upper hand, forcing his rival into a remarkable U-turn on chip policy.

White House infighting over chips had simmered for months, but erupted after Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s boss, resigned on November 11th. Among his sins was an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm that had bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and enabled their remote use by Chinese customers through servers in Malaysia and Indonesia. Other chips may have been illegally diverted to China. A memo overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, had warned administration officials about Ms Huang’s suspected ties to Chinese intelligence, according to press reports.

In theory, it is the Commerce Department’s job to monitor chip exports. But Mr Lutnick and Jeff Kessler, a top deputy, are thought to have had an unusually close relationship with Nvidia. Mr Bessent complained publicly that other parts of the government, including the Treasury, had favoured adding Megaspeed to the list of firms subject to American trade restrictions. The Commerce Department, which maintains the list, had demurred.

Congress smells blood. Jamie Raskin and Gregory Meeks, two Democratic lawmakers, have pressed Mr Lutnick on whether his decisions were influenced by the financial interests of Cantor Fitzgerald. Mr Lutnick formerly ran the financial firm, now led by his sons. Tim Scott, the Republican chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has asked Mr Lutnick to testify on December 10th. Nvidia says that it placed Megaspeed on its “block list” in 2025 and sought permission from Mr Kessler’s Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, before sending replacement parts to the firm.

On November 16th Mr Trump said that he did not plan to fire Mr Lutnick. But the commerce secretary was forced that day into a humiliating retreat. BIS released a 117-page memo curbing remote access to American chips from several countries, closing a loophole long exploited by China. The press release made it clear that Mr Lutnick’s arm had been twisted: the rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council”, it said.

The new rule is not watertight. A new licence requirement applies only to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. Would-be smugglers could target other countries or Chinese firms could simply rent computing power in America. Congress is therefore likely to press ahead with efforts to include stricter rules in a defence-authorisation bill. These range from tighter oversight of chip sales to China to restrictions on renting chips through the cloud and measures to prevent smuggling.

The proposals were crafted months ago, but the Nvidia scandal has given them fresh momentum. And because they are attached to a must-pass defence bill, they are less likely to be vetoed by Mr Trump. “We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” insists the president. If America chokes off access to chips, that may change.

articles.title: The return of measles in America
articles.deck: Reversing an absurd, unnecessary failure will be expensive and slow

paragraphs.text: The failure is as monumental as it was predictable. For years, misinformation had helped depress America’s vaccination rates. The covid-19 pandemic made things worse by disrupting routine vaccinations and deepening distrust of jabs. At the start of his second term, Donald Trump appointed Robert Kennedy junior, a vaccine sceptic, as the country’s top health official. Mr Kennedy’s contributions since then have included urging West Virginia to offer religious exemptions to schools’ vaccine requirements and an executive order encouraging drugmakers to split the combined jab protecting against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR). Mr Trump claimed, with no evidence, that together “there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal.”

So it was little surprise when, on November 17th, an arm of the World Health Organisation declared that endemic transmission of measles has been re-established in America for the first time since 1999. It is nonetheless a stunning step backward for the country. This year has seen cases reported in 45 states and 11 measles-related deaths, compared with just three from 2000 to 2025. Fighting measles now will be costly and painful, for the Americans sickened by it and the health system once able to fend it off.

Measles is highly contagious, an airborne pathogen that takes up residence in a patient’s nose and throat before symptoms appear. In most cases those symptoms include a fever and rash. But among children under five who contract measles, one in six are hospitalised with complications such as brain inflammation or pneumonia; the rate for adults is almost as high. Even mild cases cast a long shadow. Measles causes “immune amnesia”, a loss of antibodies developed against common viruses, which can lead to more frequent illness for several years. One in 600 children infected before their first birthday will eventually develop a fatal brain condition.

After a vaccine was developed in the 1960s, vaccination efforts proceeded fitfully until the early 1990s, when Congress authorised free jabs for children. By the end of the century measles was no longer spreading and occasional outbreaks were easily contained.

That era is over. Two-thirds of counties in Pennsylvania and nearly a third of counties in Wisconsin have reported measles cases in 2026. Transmission in Utah and Arizona have been traced to an outbreak in Texas that began over a year ago.

Stopping this will be harder than it was the first time around, says Joseph Kanter of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials, a non-profit group in Virginia. In the 1990s vaccines could focus on children, because most adults had either contracted the disease in childhood or been vaccinated in a previous drive. Now adults account for about 40% of cases.

Muddled health policy will make the task more difficult, too. Since August the White House has directed an additional $100m to fight measles and vaccine-preventable diseases, but that may not be enough. To contain an outbreak, public-health workers must trace the contacts of infected people, ask them to isolate if they are not immune, and organise vaccination drives, often going door-to-door to make the case for the jab. That makes containment costly—an average of $43,000 per measles case—and complicated, even when the health system is trusted and fully staffed. It isn’t.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has lost 30% of its staff since March 2025, according to the American Federation of Government Employees, a federal workers’ union, so is less equipped to help local efforts. “Everybody is trying to pick up the pieces” of what the CDC normally does, says Jeanne Marrazzo of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, a group of doctors and scientists. State health departments are issuing their own guidelines on treating measles, as most doctors have never seen a child with the disease, let alone an adult. Professional societies are running webinars featuring doctors from outbreak hotspots, a practice that emerged in the early days of covid-19. On November 17th Mr Kennedy posted on X that he recommended MMR vaccination and that America would “work to regain U.S. measles elimination status”. The country may eventually succeed. But think of the time, treasure and lives wasted.

articles.title: America’s most respected jurist was never on the Supreme Court
articles.deck: Richard Posner was a different kind of conservative judge

paragraphs.text: IT MAY SEEM obvious that courts should weigh the practical consequences of their decisions. But this was a radical idea when first espoused by Richard Posner, the influential legal scholar and judge who died on November 10th.

Mr Posner’s pragmatism made him a giant of American law without ever joining its highest court. It also set him apart from a legal world that has become increasingly dominated by ideology. “He didn’t care about political arguments,” says Eric Segall, a law professor and friend of Mr Posner. Instead, he sought to follow a maxim set out by one of his heroes, Oliver Wendell Holmes, a 20th-century Supreme Court justice, that “the life of the law has not been logic: it has been experience”.

Mr Posner came to prominence in the 1970s as part of a group of scholars who sought to use the tools of economics to study law. Surveying centuries of decisions in areas such as contracts and criminal law, Mr Posner argued that judges had developed doctrines that approximated economically efficient outcomes. He went on to venture far beyond law and economics, writing more than 500 articles, 50 books and 3,300 judicial opinions on everything from the law and sex to how judges think. A 2021 study in the University of Chicago Law Review ranked him as the most cited American legal scholar of all time, comfortably ahead of his nearest rival.

Compared with the left-leaning legal academy of the 1960s and 1970s, he was conservative. That helps explain why in 1981 Ronald Reagan, then president, nominated Mr Posner to the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals. But although he was market-oriented, he was not motivated by ideology or arcane legal debates.

Take an opinion he wrote in 2014, striking down bans on gay marriage in Wisconsin and Indiana, the year before the Supreme Court did the same. Mr Posner argued that the bans should be judged simply on whether their benefits outweighed their harm to gay couples and their children. He concluded that they did not. He had previously opposed the idea of a constitutional right to gay marriage. But despite his forceful style, he was willing to admit being wrong. “Law is not a science,” he wrote, explaining his change of mind. “The notion that the 21st century can be ruled by documents authored in the 18th and mid-19th centuries is nonsense.”

In the last decades of his career, such views put him out of step with the conservative legal world’s love affair with originalism, a philosophy that attempts to decide cases based on the presumed intentions of the law’s authors. He was particularly critical of its greatest exponent on the Supreme Court, Antonin Scalia. In a review of the justice’s book, he criticised originalists for denying their political motivations and hiding behind semantics.

Mr Posner’s judicial doctrine was simpler, if less predictable. In 2016 he wrote that it came from a favourite poet, William Butler Yeats: “And I grew weary of the sun / Until my thoughts cleared up again, / Remembering that the best I have done / Was done to make it plain.” His decisions fill law-school casebooks, not least because they are so easy to read. “His writing was always clear and careful. It was elegant, but didn’t go for the clever quip,” says Guido Calabresi, a federal judge.

His willingness to be frank may be why he was never nominated to the Supreme Court. The contrast between his style and the justices’ was made clear during a 2019 oral argument. The case at hand concerned whether Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 covered discrimination based on sexual orientation in addition to gender. Mr Posner had concluded that it did for practical reasons: deciding otherwise would put “the entire burden of updating old statutes on the legislative branch”. The court reached the same result, but through more convoluted means.

Mr Posner may prove more influential than many Supreme Court justices. “We pay attention to the justices because their opinions matter, but very few of them have anything interesting or original to offer,” says Larry Kramer of the London School of Economics. “Dick Posner did.”

articles.title: A layered fight over a marginal commodity
articles.deck: Free-market purists want to legalise onion-futures trading

paragraphs.text: It was a financial scandal to make you cry. In the autumn of 1955, Vincent Kosuga and Sam Siegel set out to make a fortune from onions. The two men bought onions futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) and began hoarding vast quantities of the vegetable in warehouses in and around the city. The pair told a group of farmers that they would flood the market unless the farmers bought some of their onions at a healthy price. Meanwhile, the duo quietly accumulated a giant short position on the futures market. In early 1956, when the onions were soon to rot, they sold them en masse. Kosuga and Siegel made out like bandits.

Two years later future President Gerald Ford, then a congressman representing an onion-rich region of Michigan, sponsored the Onion Futures Act of 1958, to ban the trading of onion-futures contracts. Farmers had no way to hedge against price swings. The CME suddenly had a fifth of its business abolished—it turned to trading contracts for other goods, from pork bellies to frozen orange juice concentrate.

Now, however, an improbable campaign is trying to overturn the ban—an effort led by (who else) undergraduates at the University of Chicago, a temple of free-market economics. Their demonstrations feature adapted protest songs with titles such as “Which Side Are You Onion?”, and are perhaps the first-ever gatherings where someone shouts “We love free markets” through a megaphone. A recent event at the university was even attended by two women, one holding a sign that read “Hot girls hedge onions”.

The students’ complaint is simple. Siegel and Kosuga were able to hoard such a large share of onions in the 1950s because the market was smaller and much of the vegetables’ supply moved through Chicago anyway, by rail. They also built up a short position in secret. Now onions travel around the country in a more dispersed manner, by truck, and traders must report their positions. That makes the ban pointless, argues Adam Ash, a third-year economics student who led the singing. In 2026, being able to trade futures would help farmers hedge volatility, rather than expose them to shady financiers.

Mr Ash acknowledges that onions are not a pressing problem, but insists the students’ effort is entirely serious. “We care about it because it is small,” he says. If America’s democracy can’t change a silly law from the 1950s, what can it do? They have caught the attention of at least one congressman, Sean Casten, who represents some of Chicago’s southern suburbs. As the market for entry-level jobs changes quickly, the students may hope to catch the attention of bemused employers, too.

articles.title: Barack Obama’s acolytes are coming to power
articles.deck: As Democrats consider their next steps, a new cohort offers post-partisan rhetoric and populist policy

paragraphs.text: ROUGHLY 18 YEARS ago Democrats gathered in Denver to anoint Barack Obama, a first-term senator from Illinois, as their presidential nominee. The mood was giddy, helped, perhaps, by copious amounts of alcohol at high altitude. “We meet at one of those defining moments,” Mr Obama said. “A moment when our nation is at war, our economy is in turmoil and the American promise has been threatened once more.” From November 12th to 14th, still relishing their victories in the midterm elections, Democrats again travelled to the Mile High City for a mini-convention thrown by Majority Democrats, a centre-left group. The party’s new leaders pledged to end an unpopular war in the Middle East, lower prices and restore the American dream. Mr Obama was not there, but his influence was hard to miss.

Mr Obama’s 2008 campaign was notable for many things; high on the list is the number of young people it inspired. Not since George McGovern’s failed run for president in 1972 had a campaign nurtured such youthful idealism on the left. College students used their winter breaks to knock on doors for him in Dubuque and Davenport ahead of the Iowa caucuses. Twenty-somethings quit their jobs and moved to Chicago to join his fledgling campaign.

This network of Millennials and young Gen Xers persists—and their power is growing. Like Mr Obama in 2008, they are unwilling to defer to their elders. Former Obama volunteers are leading big cities, including Denver, and writing laws in statehouses. In the midterm elections they won a Senate seat in Texas (James Talarico) and the governor’s mansion in Iowa (Rob Sand, pictured). At least one Obama acolyte, Pete Buttigieg, is about to run for president, again. They share Mr Obama’s sensibility, his impatience for change and optimism about America’s ability to move beyond partisanship. But when it comes to substance, they also show how much Mr Obama’s party has changed.

Across the heartland in 2026, it was hard to ignore the echoes of Mr Obama’s most famous line, delivered in 2004, that America was not a collection of “red states and blue states”, but “one people, all of us pledging allegiance to the stars and stripes”. It’s a pitch that proved helpful to Democrats trying to woo red-state voters. In 2008 Mr Talarico worked to register fellow university students to vote. In Denver he bemoaned “politics as blood sport; politics as trolling and owning and name-calling”. After winning the Senate seat in November, he paraphrased Mr Obama’s line by telling the Texans who didn’t vote for him that “I will be your senator, too.”

Mr Sand, who caucused for Mr Obama in Iowa in 2008, evoked an Obama-like unity by having the crowds at his town halls sing “America the Beautiful”. By the end of the song, Mr Sand told Democrats in Denver, someone in the audience was usually crying. “It’s the first time that they can remember that they’ve been invited to know that they disagree with people, love them anyway, and work with them in person.”

Some politicians go further. Josh Shapiro, now the governor of Pennsylvania, was serving as a state representative in 2007 when he became the rare politician to endorse Mr Obama early, over Hillary Clinton. Mr Shapiro’s speeches often borrow not simply Mr Obama’s post-partisan message but his cadence, too. Jon Ossoff, a senator from Georgia, did not volunteer for Mr Obama, but adopts his signature camera shot from 2008: a three-quarter angle from below, with Mr Ossoff gazing toward some presumably bright future.

If the vibe is vintage Obama, however, the policies often are not. McGovern campaigners—including Tom Daschle, who would later become Senate majority leader, and Bill and Hillary Clinton—were shaped by his loss to Richard Nixon. Mr Obama’s acolytes have been hardened by the Trump era. Tech optimism has been replaced by an abhorrence of data centres and fear of an AI jobs apocalypse. Though Mr Obama campaigned in 2008 on a promise of universal health care—and, as president, passed Obamacare—some Democrats now advocate “Medicare for All” plans that go further. (Mr Talarico prefers “Medicare for Y’all”, a public option.) Mr Buttigieg is among those who call for abolishing the electoral college.

Mr Obama has changed, too. As the party’s elder statesman he has embraced young left-wingers like New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and Michigan’s senator-elect, Abdul El-Sayed. In his 2006 book, “The Audacity of Hope”, he rejected calls by party activists to “match the Republican right in stridency and hardball tactics”. Yet last year Mr Obama campaigned for Proposition 50, California’s ballot measure that allowed mid-decade partisan gerrymandering, as a response to a similar provocation by Republicans in Texas. “The cynics have been on the march for ten years now,” explains David Axelrod, Mr Obama’s longtime adviser. “I think the edge and the anger that he sometimes expresses is over that cynicism.”

Presidents’ legacies are usually measured by wars started or ended, policies passed, economic booms or busts—and, in Donald Trump’s case, by ballrooms built. But part of Mr Obama’s legacy is the people he inspired. Buffy Wicks, a lawmaker in California who was “employee number 32” on Mr Obama’s 2008 campaign, recalls the farewell speech he gave to supporters and staff in Chicago at the end of his administration, just before Mr Trump took office. “If you’re disappointed by your elected officials,” he said, “grab a clipboard, get some signatures and run for office yourself.” Many of them did.

Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief, our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance, a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters.

articles.title: Donald Trump’s love of “conquest” is more self-defeating than ever
articles.deck: Yet Marco Rubio and others continue to celebrate it

paragraphs.text: Among Roman generals, Pompey was a prodigy, if something of a rake. (Plutarch records that “Flora the courtesan” loved to recount that she never left his embraces “without bearing the marks of his teeth”.) He was in his early 20s when he was dispatched to Sicily in 82BC to suppress opponents of a Roman leader. He treated them all with kindness, Plutarch writes, except one group that sought safety in Roman law from the soldiers. Pompey mocked them. He executed two Roman citizens after treating them with “unnatural” cruelty, violating ancient custom by putting at least one to death without a trial.

Pompey’s contempt for the law sped the cycle of violence that ultimately put a bloody end to his own life, and Julius Caesar’s, and the republic itself. So it seemed strange when, on November 13th, the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, a lawyer, told a room full of lawyers that the Trump administration’s response to anyone invoking international law would probably be the same as Pompey’s: “He said, ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’” Stranger still, in speaking to the conservative Federalist Society, Mr Rubio drew a parallel between the International Criminal Court (ICC) and “activist courts” at home. Both were “alien to who we are”. And who is that? Americans, he said, have always shared “a hunger to expand, to grow, to explore, to conquer”.

Is it possible, at least, to be shocked that in less than two years such extremism from an American administration has lost its capacity to shock? That America’s chief diplomat would celebrate threats of violence rather than respect for law, and conquest as an American virtue, may be as unsurprising as discovering that Donald Trump and his men with swords are not chastened by the midterm elections. Still, the administration’s Pompeian contempt seems more self-defeating than ever, politically and strategically.

Last month a Gallup poll found Americans trusted Democrats to protect them from military threats more than Republicans for the first time since 2007. Three years ago, Republicans led by 22 points. Moreover, Mr Trump, as he jetted off to a summit in Asia, hoped to negotiate a nuclear accord with China and Russia. Why would any foreign power sign an agreement with Americans who believe rules are for sissies or suckers? Mr Trump has a pattern of tearing up not only agreements reached by past administrations, but those he signed himself. Such scorn for international rules is particularly dangerous when a new weapon, artificial intelligence, is loose in the world, and becoming more potent by the day.

It is possible, of course, that Mr Rubio, who trimmed his internationalism to fit Mr Trump’s America-first agenda, does not mean everything he says. Mr Trump’s swordsmen are starting to knife each other. Both Mr Rubio and J.D. Vance, the vice-president, are potential candidates to succeed Mr Trump. Mr Rubio has said he will not run if Mr Vance does, but after the midterms darkened the vice-president’s prospects a draft-Rubio movement has gathered momentum among Republicans on Capitol Hill. On November 12th Mr Trump abruptly declared that Mr Vance should abandon his efforts to negotiate peace with Iran. That came after Mr Vance posted on social media that Republicans lost the midterms because of the Iran war without—as Mr Trump later noted—saying whether he thought the war was a good idea. By contrast, when Mr Rubio spoke to the Federalist Society, he defended the war as necessary to stop Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. He did not explain why Mr Trump was wise to break America’s previous nuclear deal with Iran, or to wage war without any allies besides Israel, let alone the backing of the United Nations.

American administrations have always interpreted international law with a generous eye to the national interest. But past administrations identified that interest with supporting the rules-based order that America championed, after two world wars, to provide global stability. The cornerstone of this structure was the United Nations, with its foundational principle of sovereign equality and prohibition against using force against another state’s territorial integrity. Mr Trump regards such rules as not protecting sovereignty but assaulting it. “To the victor belong the spoils,” he informed the UN General Assembly in September, referring to the oil rights he claimed after invading Venezuela to capture its president, Nicolás Maduro. The day before the midterms, he boasted of America’s “conquest of Venezuela”.

Whatever their mistakes, all of America’s presidents have defended its sovereignty. No administration has supported acceding to the ICC, for example, for fear it would engage in political prosecution of American soldiers or citizens. Mr Rubio was condemning a straw man when he told the Federalist Society past presidents abandoned America’s interests to global governance. More important, in arguing America should “impose ourselves upon the world”, he did not explain why Americans will be safer when other countries claim the same right. Mr Trump's advisers never explain why American conquest will not legitimise more Russian or Chinese conquest. They do not explain why killing alleged smugglers at sea, without showing any proof, will not put American sailors at risk. Americans are not the only ones with swords.

Small wonder that Mr Rubio skips the 20th century and ransacks antiquity. In a speech last month in Athens he identified thumos—what he called “the fire of passion, strength, courage, pride”—as a core value of ancient Greece, and the one the Trump administration was demonstrating in its “unapologetic pursuit of national power”. Mr Rubio failed to contend with the Greeks’ tragic tales of leaders who neglected another virtue, reason, in chasing conquest. This administration is not teaching the lessons of his-tory, ancient or modern, but ignoring them.

articles.title: Latin America would like to be the next data-centre frontier
articles.deck: Chinese and American firms are scouting out the best spots

paragraphs.text: THE GREY monolith is quiet inside. Machines hum, cold air wafts and technicians glide through the corridors like ghosts. Yet outside Latin America’s biggest data centre—a modest 61 megawatt (MW) campus at Vinhedo in south-eastern Brazil—the compound bustles with activity. Another building is under construction; two more might be on the way. To Ascenty, the firm that leases them out, these projects are a $1.2bn bet on the region becoming a global hub for computing power. “We’re preparing for a boom,” says Chris Torto, Ascenty’s boss.

Latin America has long punched beneath its weight when it comes to digital infrastructure. The region has fewer than 600 data centres, totalling only about 1.5 gigawatts (GW) of capacity. That is less than you can find in Britain. But businesspeople and politicians are convinced that they can attract many more of the whirring warehouses. They point to surging data use at home, as well as a desire among both Chinese and American tech giants to plonk more data centres outside their domestic jurisdictions. To take full advantage, countries in the region will have to persuade tech firms that they are reliable partners, and ensure local populations stay supportive. They will also have to navigate the heated rivalry between the world’s technological superpowers.

Growing local demand is the primary driver. Most of Latin America’s data is still stored and processed in the United States. That was tolerable when few people were online. Yet internet adoption in the region is now near 80%, higher than in China. Brazilians spend more than nine hours per day on the internet, compared with fewer than seven hours for Americans, according to a report by Atlántico, a consultancy. This causes lags. Content from North Virginia, a global hub, takes 150 milliseconds to reach São Paulo. Content from Vinhedo takes two. Many companies see value in paying to narrow the gap, says Raimundo Diaz of Vistra, an accounting firm.

Yet that is not the only play. Some big tech companies view locations in Latin America as important nodes in networks they are creating to serve users all around the world. ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, is investing up to $39bn in a huge data-centre campus in north-east Brazil, apparently enticed in part by undersea cables that run from there to Europe, Africa and points elsewhere. Some companies are scouting for sites that are suitable for training AI models (for which proximity to the ultimate end-user is not crucial). In that kind of business Latin America will find itself competing for capital “against Canada, the Nordic countries, the Middle East and South-East Asia”, says David Dias of EY, a consultancy.

Latin American countries are busily talking up their advantages—over each other, and over hubs farther afield. Many can offer cut-price energy, which is also green (see chart). Lots of hydropower means 85% of Brazil’s electricity is renewable. In Chile, which has acres of solar panels, 68% is. Having plenty of affordable electricity can also reduce water consumption in data centres (by permitting the use of water-efficient cooling systems, which come with the downside of being power-hungry). Construction is generally affordable, too. Building data centres in Silicon Valley costs $14 per watt, according to a study by Turner & Townsend, a consultancy. Latin American rates range from $11.5 per watt in Mexico to $9 in Bogotá, the capital of Colombia.

Brazil has around 700MW of data-centre capacity, close to half the total in Latin America. By 2030 that could rise to as much as 5GW, predicts Alessandro Lombardi, the head of Elea Data Centres, one of the companies building them. The country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is keen; before the presidential election in October he ushered through a reform slashing an exorbitant import duty that Brazil has been imposing on IT equipment. “Bring the data centres here,” demanded Lula, as the president is known, during his victory speech.

Factories in Mexico have recently made a killing assembling servers destined for data centres in the United States (where, because of local opposition, it is becoming much harder to build new ones). The country would now like to add to its own 300MW of data-centre capacity, much of it clustered in the arid central state of Querétaro, north of the capital.

Chile can offer investor-friendly rules modelled on Singapore’s, says Natalia López of Chile Data Centres, a trade group; Colombia is touting the world’s first free-trade zone for hyperscalers. Paraguay does moonshots, such as a $12bn plan for an American plant near the thunderous Iguazú Falls. Even Argentina, a fiscal basket-case, has seen interest in the southern province of Patagonia, which is sparsely populated and contains Vaca Muerta, a huge patch of shale gas.

Yet to succeed Latin American countries will have to clear away a heap of obstacles. Some of these are technical. The sites with the best internet connectivity are often not the same as those in which electricity is most abundant. Even when energy is plentiful, spotty transmission can lead to blackouts, says Tomás Ocampo of Unblock energy, an Argentine startup that uses gas that would otherwise be flared to power data centres. Permitting can be cumbersome, with long waiting times to connect to the grid.

Technology firms worry that, although the region’s governments have been lining up to promise tax breaks, they can often sound flaky on crucial matters such as intellectual-property rights. Though Latin Americans are much less averse to data centres than peers in the United States, public opinion could shift as investment ramps up. Sporadic protests against new projects in the region have already begun to take place. “There’s a growing sense of worry,” says Fabro Steibel of ITS-Rio, a Brazilian think-tank.

In the background looms geopolitics. That came to the fore suddenly on November 16th when the US Commerce Department declared that Brazilian data centres would need a licence from them to import the most advanced semiconductors. This reflects a worry that they will become a way for China to bypass America’s export controls, by letting Chinese companies remotely train AI models using the latest kit. President Donald Trump has long demanded that Latin America curb Chinese investment in critical infrastructure, notes Bruna Santos of the Inter-American Dialogue, a Washington-based think-tank. Mr Trump could well begin insisting they turn away Chinese money for data centres too. And no one very much likes the idea of pulling that plug.
