articles.title: The whole world wants Colombians to have their babies
articles.deck: Lawmakers are struggling to regulate a boom in international surrogacy

paragraphs.text: IN 2019 MARK and his husband were ready to become fathers. But commercial surrogacy is not available in Ireland, where they lived. Going to America was too expensive; cheaper options such as Ukraine and Georgia excluded gay couples. Another couple suggested a less conventional destination: their son had been born in Colombia. So in the end they travelled to Bogotá, the capital, where an agency arranged an egg donor, IVF treatment, a surrogate and legal services.

A growing number of foreigners are turning to Colombia to help them start families. Mark Semple, who runs ReproVida, a medical group, recalls that the industry was “tiny” when he set up there in 2018. It exploded in the following years as gay couples in particular began arriving “largely through word of mouth”. A second wave followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which disrupted what had been sizeable surrogacy industries in both of those countries. That cataclysm had the effect of pushing lots of heterosexual couples towards Colombia, too.

Perhaps as many as 2,100 arrangements took place in Colombia in 2025, up from 1,600 in 2021. That makes it one of the world’s main destinations for international commercial surrogacy, reckons William Houghton of Sensible Surrogacy, a consultancy. The country’s advantages include relatively sophisticated fertility clinics, particularly in the capital, combined with low costs. A typical surrogacy programme costs around $65,000 in Colombia, compared with $110,000 in Mexico (Latin America’s other big surrogacy hub) and roughly $200,000 in the United States, estimates Mr Houghton. That the country has an ethnically diverse population is another draw: it means that in cases in which egg donation is required, parents can more easily find a local donor who shares their own physical characteristics.

In much of Latin America legal restrictions have prevented international surrogacy industries from taking root. Colombia is different: the industry there was engendered by a 2009 ruling of the Constitutional Court, which established that there were no laws prohibiting the practice. At the time, the justices recommended that surrogates should not provide their own eggs, and that arrangements should not be motivated by profit—though those strictures were never actually written into the statute books.

The lack of regulation is both a help and a hindrance to the industry—and to those who are relying on it to create their families. Judges struggling to apply existing family laws have sometimes reached conflicting conclusions in disputes over surrogacy, says Santiago Martínez, a lawyer at Martínez Díaz & Asociados, which advises on such cases. In one recent incident a surrogate in the city of Medellín declined to hand a baby over to its biological father. She initially won custody, only for an appeals court to overturn that decision this year.

Many clinics and agencies select surrogates carefully. One Colombian lawyer estimates that only one in ten applicants are accepted at the clinics he works with. But growing demand is making suitable candidates more difficult to find. A few years ago it would take about four months for agencies to match parents with a suitable surrogate; now some end up waiting as long as a year. The shortage is increasing the incentive for unscrupulous operators to cut corners, for example by accepting women who fail medical or psychological screening, or not screening them at all.

Weak oversight has left women vulnerable to exploitation, particularly those from poorer areas such as Cúcuta, near the Venezuelan border. Alejandra Vera of Corporación Mujer Denuncia y Muévete, a women’s-rights organisation, says some clinics recruit women in desperate financial situations through social media. Some Venezuelan migrants in Colombia say they were asked to sign surrogacy contracts in English that they could not understand. Some contracts have reportedly restricted women’s movements, diets or sexual relationships, or sought to deny them the right to an abortion, which is protected under Colombia’s constitution.

Such stories have intensified calls for tighter restrictions. In July Congress passed a law adding “reproductive exploitation” to the forms of exploitation covered by human-trafficking legislation (without clearly defining the term). A draft bill introduced in August seeks to ban surrogacy altogether. Opposition comes from both feminists on the left, who argue that surrogacy commodifies women’s bodies and exploits poorer women, and religious conservatives on the right, who believe it undermines the traditional family.

A ban looks improbable, all the same. Congress has long struggled to settle divisive moral questions, says Mr Martínez. Over a dozen bills attempting to regulate surrogacy in Colombia have failed over the past two decades. So the most likely scenario is that the business continues muddling along as at present. As a result, parents will continue to be open to the risk of lengthy legal battles, while too many surrogates will be left without firm protections. Colombia’s courts helped make the country a pioneer in reproductive freedom. Its lawmakers have yet to catch up.

articles.title: What a robot Olympiad reveals about Latin America’s future
articles.deck: Reasons to be hopeful about a region with too many lousy schools

paragraphs.text: Parents in Latin America can be gloomy about their children’s futures. Many more people there think that artificial intelligence will destroy jobs than believe it will create them. Worse, the region’s kids did dismally in recent international school tests—not the best starting-point for weathering an era that might bring astonishing change.

Talk to children themselves, however, and the mood is different. Many are thrilled about the possibilities presented by new technologies of all kinds. Happily, Latin America’s school systems host pockets of excellence from which reformers could easily build out broader enthusiasm.

For a glimpse of the opportunities, head to Uruguay’s robot Olympiad, which takes place annually in the country’s biggest indoor arena. Children cheer wildly and thump traditional candombe drums as robots that they have built and programmed in their schools whizz around courses. Some youngsters race drones through hoops and around obstacles. “Awesome, awesome,” beams Enrique Núñez, a 12-year-old with purple hair, when asked about the experience of building a robot and competing. When a band plays, the youngsters break into dance (the robot one, naturally). Even your correspondent cannot resist waggling an elbow.

The venue is better known for hosting massive pop concerts (a giant image of Jennifer Lopez looms over the budding engineers). The space is needed: the event now attracts 8,500 Uruguayan pupils, the number of teams taking part having increased about 20-fold since 2015. Even Uruguay’s president, Yamandú Orsi, stops by to applaud the kids. It also involves a competition that uses “micro:bit”, a pocket-sized computer with flashing LEDs that children as young as eight can program.

Competitions such as this are drawing in children across Latin America. Ones in Brazil and Mexico have begun attracting hundreds of teams. Winners of national competitions travel to international robotics contests such as the FIRST Championship in Houston, which boasts some 50,000 attendees from about 60 countries. Last year’s victors in Uruguay—a team of three girls from a remote, rural school—recently competed at a global robotics shindig in South Korea.

The event in Uruguay is organised by Ceibal, a state-funded body. Ceibal was created in 2007 to give every Uruguayan child a laptop, a world first. That improved access to computers but did not improve reading or maths scores. The focus on robotics may achieve more. Ceibal provides robotics kits, drones and 3D printers to hundreds of schools. But it also arranges classes, via video-link, with remote instructors who teach computational thinking and artificial intelligence.

These kinds of goings-on can help spark passions and heighten ambitions. A ten-year study by the organisers of the FIRST Championship in the United States found that participants, especially women, were much more likely than classmates who did not take part to do STEM subjects at university. Pollsters find young people in much of Latin America are far less concerned about the rise of AI in daily life than people over 50 are. Perhaps gloomy parents should listen to their children more.

articles.title: Climate change is making some African deserts greener
articles.deck: That could help farmers but will also bring dangerous floods

paragraphs.text: For decades Lake Chad seemed to be a terrifying portent of climate collapse. It had been among the world’s largest lakes, on which tens of millions of people depended in Chad, Cameroon, Niger and Nigeria, the four countries that share it. Yet years of droughts, compounded by diversion for irrigation, between the 1960s and 1990s helped shrink it by as much as 90%. With the planet warming and the Sahara desert apparently advancing, Lake Chad seemed destined to disappear. The famines that ravaged the surrounding Sahel in the 1980s looked like a grim preview of Africa’s hotter, drier future.

Instead the opposite happened. Today Lake Chad (pictured below) has more water than it has had for decades. A new study by the World Bank and the International Water Management Institute finds that its open-water area more than doubled in little more than a decade after 2012, reaching over 8,300 square kilometres in 2025. Elsewhere, too, waters are rising. Four of Africa’s biggest water bodies—Victoria, Malawi, Tanganyika and Turkana, the world’s largest permanent desert lake—have risen sharply in recent years. So has Africa’s biggest wetland, the Sudd marshes, which have swollen so much since 2020 that South Sudan’s landscape may have been altered for good.

Each case, like Africa’s 54 countries, is different. Yet rising waters in seemingly unlikely places such as Lake Chad hint at two important aspects of the continent’s climatic future. First, much of Africa may turn out to be wetter than many expect, especially those who recall the Sahelian droughts of the 1970s and 1980s. Second, exactly how climate change will play out across much of the continent is deeply uncertain, arguably more so than elsewhere. Helping Africans adapt to shifts that will be severe but hard to predict is a priority for the continent’s delegates at COP31, the UN’s annual climate summit that ends in Turkey on November 20th.

Plenty about Africa’s changing climate is clear-cut. Its few glaciers are vanishing. The seas along its coasts are rising. Heatwaves are growing longer, more frequent and more intense. A new study by the African Climate & Development Initiative at the University of Cape Town finds that since 2010 hot spells in South Africa have been nearly three times more “extreme”—a measure that combines duration, temperature and the area affected—than in the previous three decades. The World Meteorological Organisation says every African sub-region has grown hotter since 1961.

Parts of eastern and southern Africa appear to be drying. But in the Sahel, a vast semi-arid belt stretching from Senegal to Sudan, rainfall has for years been increasing (see map). The clearest sign is Lake Chad, which acts like a “giant rain gauge”, says Richard Washington of Oxford University. Another is the Sahel’s storms, which bring most of its rain. Extreme ones have become roughly three times as frequent since the early 1980s. Many climate scientists expect these trends to continue, as warming in the Sahara and the North Atlantic fuels the west African monsoon and draws more moisture into the Sahel.

In some places, that change brings the promise of better harvests. Satellite imagery shows that much of the Sahel is turning greener as once-parched lands revive. Richard Taylor of the University of Toronto says that a recent expansion in groundwater storage could, in theory, expand access to drinking water and one day even feed irrigated farms.

But more rain also means more floods. Rainfall in the Sahel in mid-2024 was between 120% to 600% above the seasonal average for the previous three decades, sweeping away villages, forcing hundreds of thousands from their homes and leaving parts of Niamey, Niger’s capital, under water. In 2025, more than 230 people were killed in flash floods in Nigeria.

All this challenges a long and widely held belief in Africa’s relentless “desertification”. The idea of the Sahara, the world’s largest hot desert, pushing southwards into the Sahelian savannah dates back to the colonial era. A study commissioned by the UN in the 1970s claimed it was expanding in Sudan by as many as six kilometres each year. “At that stage it did indeed look as though the Sahel and west Africa as a whole was getting drier and drier in some kind of inexorable process,” says Camilla Toulmin, a British drylands expert. Based on that premise, the African Union launched the “Great Green Wall”, an initiative involving at least 22 countries in tackling soil degradation and desertification, in part by planting trees.

In future, successful adaptation may have to look very different. It will require closer attention to what Stella Shumba, a Zimbabwean climate scientist, calls the “local expressions” of climate change in Africa. By some estimates, the continent will need $30bn-50bn (0.7-1.2% of GDP) a year for adaptation by 2030. Preparing for a future that is at once wetter and drier is both harder and more expensive.

In the first place, adapting means gathering more and better data, so that “we understand what is changing, how it is changing, where and when”, says Joyce Kimutai of Imperial College London and Kenya’s meteorological agency. Rainfall projections are especially tricky. In east Africa the “long rains” of March to May dwindled from the mid-1980s to around 2010, even as climate models predicted a wetter region in the future—a mismatch scientists dubbed the “eastern African paradox”.

More recently the rains have recovered somewhat, and the short rains between October and December have increased, which helps explain the dramatic rise of Lake Victoria and the lakes of Kenya’s Rift Valley. But projections for the region remain unusually unsettled, particularly for the long rains, says Caroline Wainwright of the University of Leeds. “It’s not just that we don’t know the magnitude of the future change; the direction of change is also uncertain.”

Tropical weather, especially rain, is generally much harder to simulate than the mid-latitude kind. A dearth of observations makes it harder still to test existing climate models and build better ones. Africa covers about a fifth of the world’s land, yet is estimated to host only about a tenth of its weather-monitoring stations, and perhaps half of those fail to record reliable data. The networks have thinned in recent decades. Cuts to Western aid budgets, which have long helped pay for African climate research, could hasten their decline.

The perils and promise can be seen on the shores of Lake Baringo in Kenya’s Rift Valley. The lake’s waters have been rising since 2010, engulfing schools, churches, homes and hotels. Nearby, some farmers are growing tomatoes on newly irrigated fields. The last rains failed. But in the coming weeks El Niño, a recurring climatic pattern that disrupts global weather, is expected to bring floods. Nobody knows for sure if the lake will continue to rise. But locals are preparing as though it will.

articles.title: The hunt for Sudan’s looted heritage
articles.deck: Priceless antiquities stolen in the war could take decades to recover

paragraphs.text: Two Nubian kings stand watch over a fire-scorched courtyard, empty but for the lions carved from sandstone guarding the entrance. When Rihab Khider, a Sudanese archaeologist, returned to Sudan’s national museum last year, the first time since the civil war began in 2023, almost everything she found had been damaged or destroyed. Ancient artefacts, some thousands of years old, lay strewn across the overgrown garden and on the busy road outside. “It was a very hard time for me,” she recalls. All she could do was to start picking up the pieces.

More than a year later, the museum in Khartoum, Sudan’s capital, remains a shell. Only a few artefacts survive (pictured on next page). The cabinets inside the main exhibition hall have nothing to display. For nearly two years the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group fighting Sudan’s army, occupied the city, ruining large swathes of it. Tens of thousands of people were killed. Like many other buildings, the museum was turned into a military encampment. By the time the RSF was driven out in 2025, an estimated 4,000 or more of the museum’s most precious possessions had vanished; even mummies, embalmed as long ago as 2,500BC, were stolen. The plunder recalled the looting of heritage in Syria and Iraq by Islamic State.

Recovering the loot could take decades. Much may be lost for ever. Before the war the national museum housed more than 100,000 artefacts, including 2,000 gold objects from the Kingdom of Kush, an ancient civilisation that at its height ruled swathes of Sudan and Egypt. These had been stored in a secure room; the RSF blew the door open and made off with the lot. Accounting for other items is harder. The museum had no complete inventory before the war. Of the documentation that did exist, much has been damaged or lost.

The national museum is not the only one that has suffered. The country has eight provincial museums, including three in Darfur, a vast region in the west largely controlled by the RSF, where some of the most important artefacts were held. “The entire timeline of Sudan was in the regional museums,” says Ali Nour of Blue Shield Sudan, a heritage-protection body established in 2024. Many are thought to have been ransacked. Yet sending teams to inspect them would be perilous. The curator of the museum in el-Geneina, in west Darfur, was killed inside the building along with his family. The curators of the museums in el-Fasher and Nyala are missing.

Some antiquities have found their way home. Sudanese police recovered an undamaged gilded statue of an archer, a masterpiece of Meroitic art dating from the second or third century BC, in Khartoum. In January the authorities announced the return of 570 stolen objects, including funerary statues of Kushite kings, apparently recovered elsewhere in the country.

But much of the loot is likely to have crossed Sudan’s borders, into Ethiopia, South Sudan and Chad. Ikhlass Abdelatif, who chairs Sudan’s antiquities-repatriation committee, says the RSF contacted the museum earlier this year hoping to sell back some of the artefacts, but then fell silent. She suspects that much of the plunder has ended up in the United Arab Emirates, an important ally of the RSF and a hub for laundering antiquities stolen across the Middle East and north Africa.

To hasten their recovery, Sudan’s government has offered rewards for information about the objects’ whereabouts and issued a global alert via Interpol. A government unit that tries to stymie the trafficking of cultural property is working with the British Museum and other international institutions to help police and officials in other countries know how to identify Sudanese artefacts. A team of archaeologists is racing to build a comprehensive inventory and put it online.

It will not be easy. No object stolen during the war has yet surfaced on the international art market, be it in auction houses or online marketplaces such as eBay. “With museum thefts we are often talking about decades” for objects to show up, says Olivia Whitting of the Art Loss Register, a London-based art-recovery firm. And Sudan is not yet a party to the UN convention against the illicit trade in cultural property, making it harder to secure the return of those that do.

For now, the guardians of Sudan’s heritage are focused on preserving what has not been stolen. Nearly four years in, Sudan’s war shows no sign of letting up; today even cultural sites far from the battlefield can be struck by drones. “Our priority is to protect what we already have,” says Mahmoud Suleiman, boss of Sudan’s National Corporation for Antiquities and Museums. Nothing, and no one, will be safe so long as Sudan remains at war.

articles.title: Iran is functioning without a supreme leader
articles.deck: Six men from a council of generals and bureaucrats now dominate decision making

paragraphs.text: “Yeki bood, yeki nabood,” Persian stories begin: “There was one, and there was no one.” Just such a fairy tale has taken over political life in Iran. For four decades there was a micromanaging supreme leader. Now there is no one. Mojtaba Khamenei, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s son, is said to have survived the Israeli strike that killed much of his family on the first day of the war. He formally rules in his father’s place. But he has neither been seen nor heard since. Iranians are discovering life without a meddlesome cleric at the helm.

Until the Islamic revolution in 1979, Shiism had been led by a hidden imam for more than a millennium. Today, Iranian officials and Western intelligence agencies insist Mojtaba remains alive. He is said to remain underground because of a reasonable fear of assassination. Some regime hands say he is controlling affairs behind the scenes, but his silence is deafening.

Even if he were active in politics, Mojtaba would need time to consolidate power, given lingering opposition to dynastic succession and his limited religious credentials. In his absence the Islamic Republic’s clerical imprint has grown visibly lighter. Iranians returning from abroad since the war include a pop star sentenced in absentia for incorporating Koranic verses into his songs. Even the daughters of some officials uncover their hair. Some smarter restaurants in Tehran now serve French wine.

The most important shift is in how the regime wields power. “What’s principally changed is that there’s no clear, final arbiter,” says Sanam Vakil of Chatham House, a think-tank in London. Appointments to the state broadcaster, government ministries and the judiciary were once subject to approval by the supreme leader’s 44,000-man court; today the executive has a freer hand. “Israel did Iranians a favour getting rid of Khamenei,” quipped an Iranian academic recently in Tehran. “You don’t need to wait any longer for his legitimation [or approval]. It’s more efficient.”

Instead, six men, all from the ranks of the Supreme National Security Council, a 13-man body of generals and bureaucrats, dominate decision-making. They are believed to include Masoud Pezeshkian, the president; Major General Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran’s principal military force; Mohsen Rezaei, the council’s secretary and a former IRGC chief; Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, the speaker of parliament and a former IRGC brigadier general; Ali Abdollahi, the chief of the general staff of the armed forces; and Abbas Araghchi, the foreign minister, the only other civilian among them.

The biggest decisions require the collective’s consent. These include matters such as talks about ending or restarting the war with America or nuclear policy. But they each also have a degree of autonomy. Mr Rezaei has been a stalwart of the system since becoming IRGC chief during the Iran-Iraq war in the 1980s. Mr Vahidi keeps order in the ranks of the IRGC; and Mr Qalibaf runs parliament’s affairs.

Mr Pezeshkian has largely been left to manage a war-induced depression and a currency in near free fall. The economy was down by 10% in the second quarter of this year compared with the same period in 2025. Unemployment has swelled by half a million since the war began, even as the labour force shrinks and over half of all jobs are now informal. And yet Mr Pezeshkian seems to be managing the fallout from war better than many had expected. He has kept the lights on, despite oil refineries and power plants being bombed.

Mr Pezeshkian has tried to open Iran’s borders to trade since the war began. Overland trade has increased. Some tankers are reportedly paying the tolls Iran demands for passage via the Strait of Hormuz. But Iran is struggling to evade America’s blockade on the export of oil from the southern ports. America’s armada cannot hermetically seal all 2,800km of Iran’s coastline, but estimates of exports in September averaged 260,000 barrels per day, or only around one-sixth of the pre-war flow.

Not all senior officials neatly fit under the six-man committee’s command, however. Domestic control remains largely in the hands of Hossein Taeb, an IRGC hard-man, former intelligence chief and clerical ideologue. He is said to have strong-armed clerics into electing Mojtaba, a longtime confidant, and has long been disliked by some within the establishment for his enthusiasm for a hereditary dynasty. His current role as head of the Basij, a vast paramilitary force, gives him a powerful base.

Since the war began his henchmen and -women have staged nightly rallies in squares across Iran, where anti-regime protesters might otherwise gather. They have distributed rifles to loyalists. In a further effort to intimidate would-be dissidents, Mr Taeb has overseen nearly 700 executions this year. In January the regime crushed nationwide demonstrations with massacres. The war has also helped suppress unrest. Patriotic sentiment has grown as the country’s infrastructure came under American and Israeli attack. Domestic unrest has slipped.

On questions of war and peace, the six-man council has set aside ideological differences. Where the supreme leader once dithered, it moves decisively. The council’s latest diplomatic initiative suggests inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency could return to Iran within two days of America accepting Iran’s proposal. That implies a slightly more flexible position than Iran offered in June. According to one Iranian official, Iran might waive its demand for tolls in Hormuz. And this time, says the official, Iran would not walk away from talks even if Israel continued bombing Lebanon.

Yet the leadership council is also willing to break the deadlock by force. Khamenei senior refrained from disrupting trade through Hormuz; Iran’s new leaders have tolerated its closure for months. In September they set seven “non-negotiable” conditions for ending the stand-off. They have hinted at reviving Iran’s nuclear programme if the blockade continues. “We will not allow even a single particle of enriched nuclear material to leave Iran,” Mr Rezaei said on November 11th. Confrontation with America has also pushed Iran to tighten its ties to Russia and China.

Donald Trump’s Damocles sword, the threat of resuming full-scale war, remains the biggest danger. But Mr Rezaei and his officials have met bombast with bombast and project confidence in their ability to deal with it. “Like for like,” says an official when asked how Iran will respond to attacks on shipping in the Caspian Sea, power infrastructure or its gasfields.

If fighting resumes, Iran’s leaders expect that they would determine its end. The Democrats’ control of Congress may complicate Mr Trump’s freedom to carry out military action. Iran faces no equivalent political deadline. A devolved chain of command would ensure that missiles keep flying even if senior commanders are killed. The regime’s new leaders are counting on outlasting Mr Trump.

articles.title: Neither America nor Iran has the means to end the war
articles.deck: From fridges to tankers, both sides are reduced to pinpricks

paragraphs.text: SINCE february 28TH Iran has targeted infrastructure across the Middle East and Europe, from airports and military bases to refineries and pipelines. Last month it may have struck another key national asset: France’s cheese supply. Authorities there blame Iran for a cyber-attack that turned refrigerators into ovens at hundreds of supermarkets, spoiling millions of euros’ worth of food (Iran denies it was involved). A similar hack hit other European countries on November 2nd.

After nearly nine months, the war between America and Iran is in limbo. They trade occasional strikes and try to inflict economic pain by disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Each side insists it is prepared for a long conflict, when in fact neither side wants one. America and Iran have a similar strategic dilemma: they would prefer to break the stalemate, but they lack the means to do so. Instead the campaign has settled into one of harassment—like attacking refrigerators.

Donald Trump airs his dilemma in public. In the run-up to the midterm elections he threatened a new round of fighting. But a few days of air strikes on Iranian infrastructure, as his generals have proposed, are unlikely to bring the regime to its knees. On November 9th, after talks with Qatar’s prime minister, Mr Trump seemed to retreat, saying escalation “doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing”.

A few days later he ordered J.D. Vance, his vice-president, to step back from negotiations. “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he wrote on social media. The Iranian regime has shown a degree of flexibility in talks but it still wants a lopsided deal. For now, then, Mr Trump seems content to hope that economic pressure will break it. But that comes at a steep cost—aircraft-carriers tied down away from the Pacific, Gulf allies pushed into a recession—and it means continuing a war that has become a millstone around his Republican party.

In public, Iranian officials are defiant: they are willing to make a deal on their own terms, or to keep fighting. But a long war will be painful. America’s naval blockade has hugely reduced Iran’s crude exports. One official says Iran is drafting a budget for the next fiscal year that assumes oil revenue will be zero (it normally makes up about one-third of the take). Yet the regime has no good options to break the impasse.

Its war strategy has gone through three phases. The first, in March and April, saw it launch thousands of missiles and drones at Gulf states. Over the summer it focused its fire on American bases in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan. Since September it has escalated attacks on commercial shipping.

Some hawks in Tehran are now urging a fourth, more destructive phase. “They’re arguing that they should be more like the Israelis,” carrying out assassinations and sabotage abroad, says an Iranian academic. But the regime has a poor record of executing such operations in America. When it attempted to kill the Saudi ambassador in Washington in 2011, it hired a used-car salesman who tried to arrange the hit with an undercover informant.

CNN reported on November 16th, citing American officials, that Iran was “developing plans” to detonate a dirty bomb in Washington. Most Iran-watchers in the capital were quick to dismiss the claim. Irradiating Washington would not compel Mr Trump to end the war; quite the opposite. Nor would other, less catastrophic acts, such as resuming large-scale attacks on Gulf states or trying to sink an American aircraft-carrier in the region (of which there are now three).

For Iran, as for Mr Trump, that leaves the status quo. Occasional attacks on bases, like the three drone strikes on Bahrain over the past week, yield only marginal benefits. Iran can impose costs on America, not drive it out of the region. Even the Hormuz weapon has lost some of its potency. Iran attacked at least 37 vessels in October, up from 14 in September and the highest monthly tally since the war began.

Yet oil flows through the strait remained high. Vortexa, a data firm, puts Gulf exports at 17.1m barrels per day last month, down slightly from September but still around three-quarters of pre-war levels. The International Energy Agency says the oil market is returning to surplus. At a conference in Houston this month, some executives mused about a possible glut of crude in 2027.

Markets are hardly back to normal. Diesel and jet-fuel prices are sky-high. So are shipping rates. Chartering an oil tanker from America’s Gulf coast to China costs more than launching a Falcon 9 rocket into space. But none of this seems to sway Mr Trump. With the midterms behind him, he may be even less responsive to oil prices.

So the stalemate grinds on. America will keep tightening its blockade. Iran might try more cyber-attacks. Recent computer outages disrupted American banks, email services and air-traffic control. Officials in Washington say these were unconnected malfunctions, and that there is no evidence of Iranian involvement. Still, they highlight vulnerabilities. Neither side can end the war, but both can keep it on ice.

articles.title: Israel claims its “dual-use” policy is a necessary protection
articles.deck: To Gazans it feels very much like collective punishment

paragraphs.text: Heavy rain in Gaza in early November caused flooding of thousands of tents and temporary dwellings, and deaths from landslides and exposure. The scenes of watery misery in the war-torn enclave prompted admonishments from Western governments and the American-backed Board of Peace, urging Israel to allow in more winter supplies. Then the sun came out and, once again, nothing happened.

A ceasefire in Gaza officially began over a year ago. Its 2.1m people are still huddled in the third of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops. And they have yet to see any sign of reconstruction, despite promises to rebuild the 80% of homes and civilian infrastructure damaged or destroyed over two years of war. Israel and Hamas, the Islamists who still control parts of Gaza, both officially committed to Donald Trump’s 20-point plan which includes reconstruction, Hamas disarming and a gradual Israeli withdrawal. But despite the president’s lofty promises, none of these is happening.

This is the second winter of the ceasefire and as one diplomat involved in the interminable talks says: “We’re starting to measure progress in years. It doesn’t look like it’s going to happen at a faster pace.” The Gazan technocratic government is stuck in Cairo, Hamas is entrenched and any talk of it giving up its arsenal has stalled. Meanwhile, no change in Israeli policy seems imminent. Israel is in a twilight zone between governments after elections on October 27th.

Life in Gaza, when the Israel Defence Forces isn’t carrying out strikes on what it claims are Hamas commanders, is dictated by Hamas, the weather and an Israeli blockade whose guiding principle is “dual-use”. In international trade, the term refers to technology, chemicals and industrial machinery that have both military and civilian uses. In Gaza, however, it can be applied to practically everything. Israel restricts anything once used by Hamas to transform Gaza into the military stronghold from which it launched its attacks on October 7th 2023 and which could conceivably be used again for that purpose.

The most basic building materials, such as cement, are not allowed because Hamas used these for years to construct its network of tunnels and weapons workshops beneath the strip. Likewise portable generators, essential for a population living largely in tents and makeshift shelters, are allowed in only for specific authorised projects and have to be regularly accounted for by aid organisations. Some tents may go in, but not the sturdier ones which have strong metal or wooden poles which could be used to shore up tunnels—or perhaps help the tents to withstand storms.

The Israeli authorities no longer publish an official list of dual-use items. Restrictions are communicated to aid groups mostly verbally. Every consignment involves a complex security bureaucracy. “Even when we’ve had projects authorised by the Israelis,” says an employee in a big aid organisation, “we then had to start getting them to agree to every component we needed to bring. It takes months.”

The requirements are onerous. To keep Gaza’s creaking fleet of supply trucks running, every spare part let into the strip has to be destined for a specific vehicle. When crucial items such as generators and water-pumps are authorised, the organisations have to continue providing proof they are being used for their original purpose to preserve their accreditation.

That is not possible for all aid groups. Since the beginning of this year Israel has banned ngos that refuse to disclose details of their Gazan employees for vetting by Israeli intelligence, to ensure they do not include members of Hamas. “We work now through Israeli ngos, whose employees served in the military co-ordination units and know how to navigate the system,” said the head of one charity which has sent emergency winter supplies to Gaza.

Whoever forms a government in Israel, rebuilding Gaza will not be a priority. Without international pressure, Israel will continue to restrict basic supplies on the basis of its “dual-use” explanation and blame Hamas for not disarming. For Gazans, it will feel like further punishment.

articles.title: The next stop for Europe’s failed asylum-seekers: Rwanda
articles.deck: The plan is the latest sign of hardening migration policy across the continent

paragraphs.text: “ATRULY HISTORIC paradigm shift”. “A game-changer”. “One big milestone”. If officials are cautious about overselling Europe’s asylum deal with Rwanda, no one told the politicians from five European governments who unveiled it in Vienna on November 16th. “This is the first real answer anyone has put on the table to solve the deep problems with the current system,” said Mette Frederiksen, Denmark’s prime minister.

Under the plan, which is promised to take effect next year, migrants in the five countries—Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands—whose asylum bids have been rejected may be transferred to a “return hub” in Rwanda. They will be able to integrate into local communities, return home or move to another country ready to accept them, said Vincent Biruta, Rwanda’s interior minister, speaking with European ministers whom his government had assiduously courted. Officials say Rwanda will now sign bilateral agreements with all five governments.

The Rwanda plan is a new element of Europe’s migration “turnaround”. Thanks partly to calmer conditions near its borders, irregular arrivals have plummeted (see chart 1). Last month saw the fewest asylum claims in Germany since October 2011. An “asylum pact” that took effect in June helps. But it is hard to deport asylum-seekers whose bids have failed. Lacking documentation, or coming from countries that do not co-operate, many fall into the shadows. The EU issues far more return orders than it carries out (see chart 2 ).

Politicians want to show they can do things previously seen as impossible, says Raphael Bossong from the German Institute for International and Security Affairs in Berlin. But where populist-right ones demand “remigration”, the mainstream seeks a more orderly approach. In October the EU passed a law allowing the creation of return hubs, with human-rights and monitoring safeguards. That, say officials, puts the scheme on a sounder legal footing than other efforts. Britain’s ill-fated 2022 deal, which unlike the European scheme would have sent migrants to Rwanda to process their asylum claims, cost taxpayers £715m ($910m) before being abandoned.

Details are scant and questions remain. The first is effectiveness. The few hundred migrants at most who could be sent to Rwanda next year will not make a dent in the stock of failed asylum-seekers in Europe. Germany alone has over 250,000 migrants served with return orders. The “bigger number”, Ms Frederiksen said, would be migrants who, hearing of the Rwanda scheme, might decide not to travel to Europe. But would minds really be changed by the remote possibility of being sent to Rwanda? “Evidence of a deterrent effect is highly uncertain,” said a British official of his country’s scheme, which had a more credible claim to deterrence since it would have applied to more migrants.

Second, what would actually happen to those sent to Rwanda, one of Africa’s poorer and most densely populated countries? Human-rights groups fear, once migrants are beyond Europe’s gaze, they could face mistreatment or further deportation, including refoulement into danger. “This is a hugely repressive regime,” says Tineke Strik, a Dutch Green member of the European Parliament. But such concerns rarely trouble European officials attacked by critics they see as naive do-gooders. “Unless you put a hub in Liechtenstein you’ll run out of options,” sniffs one. The new deal has a role for United Nations migration and refugee agencies in offering advice, monitoring conditions and aiding integration. Rwanda already hosts EU-funded centres for refugees who have been evacuated from Libya. Even so, legal challenges to the new plan are certain.

Others worry what the deal may mean for relations with Rwanda, which has supported a murderous militia in the Democratic Republic of Congo and persecutes dissidents (one was recently found beheaded in Uganda). “It is deeply troubling that European governments are considering sending rejected asylum-seekers to Rwanda,” says Rémy Amahirwa, a Sweden-based Rwandan whose mother, an opposition figure, has been imprisoned by Paul Kagame’s government. Last year the German government cancelled talks with Rwanda because of its actions in Congo. Europeans want to distinguish Rwanda’s treatment of migrants from its broader human-rights record. Yet some envoys say they already detect signs of diplomatic reticence from European governments.

Beyond diplomatic cover, what is in it for Mr Kagame? Mr Biruta said Rwanda was just doing its bit to manage the problem of irregular immigration. In reality it hopes for cash, aid projects and a reputation as a reliable partner. It also wants to select who comes, with a preference for professionals who can integrate into labour markets and boost the local economy. “They feel bruised from the UK arrangements, so there is a real interest to make this work,” says one European official.

Not everyone in Europe is on board. In Germany doubts among Social Democrats, the junior ruling coalition partner, extend into the cabinet. France and Spain, among others, remain sceptical. Yet both countries may elect right-wing governments during the next six months. Europe’s rightward march on migration policy is likely to continue.

Other EU countries, notably Italy, are clamouring to join the return-hub plan—even Britain may be interested—and European governments are reportedly negotiating with other potential return-hub hosts. Meanwhile, plans are being drawn up to avoid a repeat of the scenes earlier this year, when tens of thousands of Moroccans swarmed into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Frontex, Europe’s border-guard agency, may have its mandate expanded; it may also help with deportations to Rwanda. Ultimately some governments aspire to externalise the entire asylum process. One official says it is vital for centrist politicians to take action now to see off something nastier from right-wing populists: “It’s important we get this right, otherwise we’ll be in deep shit in a few years.”
Correction (November 17th): In earlier version of this story, chart 1 was inaccurately labelled as showing “monthly arrivals”, rather than “annual arrivals”.

articles.title: A scandal causes problems for Recep Tayyip Erdogan
articles.deck: It’s inching closer to the Turkish president’s inner circle

paragraphs.text: IN “BURNING DAYS”, a political thriller that made waves in Turkey a few years ago, enormous sinkholes appear near a fictitious town in the country’s heartland. When a prosecutor arrives to investigate, he uncovers widespread corruption. Threats and pressure ensue.

This autumn a new sinkhole, in the form of a sprawling financial scandal, has opened, swallowing senior bureaucrats, finance executives and politicians. The latest casualty, Sahap Kavcioglu, head of the bank regulator and a former central-bank governor, resigned on November 11th. Earlier victims include an ex-adviser to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a former head of the stock exchange, and Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, a deputy chair of the ruling Justice and Development (AK) party, who have all been arrested. The chairs of Turkey’s capital markets and auditing watchdogs and a deputy finance minister have lost their jobs.

The turmoil began in September, when regulators ordered the liquidation of 131 investment funds, after some failed to meet redemption requests. Some funds were hoovering up shares in small, often obscure companies, driving their valuations to gravity-defying levels. Investors hungry for easy money poured in. By the time the scheme had unravelled, leading to a stock-market rout, the funds held more than $20bn in assets and had attracted over 450,000 investors.

With elections pencilled in for early 2028, but expected to be brought forward, Mr Erdogan and AK are desperate to put the scandal behind them. Turkey’s leader had hoped vainly that the arrests of executives accused of running the scheme and the decision to wind up the funds would be enough. But the scale of the operation, the failure of the authorities to act earlier and new revelations have only invited more scrutiny. A charitable interpretation is that regulators were too slow to act on warning signs that began flashing in late 2025. A less generous but increasingly prevalent one is that some were complicit.

Mr Erdogan and his justice minister, Akin Gurlek, have vowed that the investigation will spare nobody. But the crisis has been inching closer to the president’s inner circle. Prosecutors are investigating how Ms Kaya, a former cabinet minister, and her husband made 2bn lira ($40m) by buying 163m lira-worth of shares in a company in which one fund, Tera, held a commanding stake, and selling them for 2.17bn lira before the fund was dissolved. Ms Kaya denies wrongdoing or receiving inside information. Rumours that other politicians, as well as officials inside the presidential administration, were in on the scheme continue to swirl around Ankara. More heads may yet roll.

The government is going to new lengths to ensure reporting on the financial scandal is neutered. In the past two months the authorities have blocked access to T24, an independent news website, and taken over Halk TV and Sozcu TV, two of the country’s most popular pro-opposition channels. Tensions are also mounting within AK. Another party deputy chairman, Hayati Yazici, has faced heat from colleagues after reports that a relative of his wife netted 2.4bn lira from one fund. Some worry that suspicion now hangs over the entire party. “As long as the list is not disclosed,” Abdulhamit Gul, a senior AK figure, has said, referring to the names of those under investigation, “there’s the impression that everyone is guilty.”

The stock-market fall has eased off, but not before $150bn in market value was wiped out between late August and late October. The political repercussions may haunt Mr Erdogan and his party allies for some time to come.

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine are bombing bridges. Who’s winning?
articles.deck: A setback for Russia in Crimea, but damage in Kyiv may matter more

paragraphs.text: THIS WAS the week when the war in Ukraine became a battle of bridges. Four crossings in all, 725km apart. Two systems of fighting: one creative and carefully orchestrated, the other blunt but just as effective. The headlines focused on Ukraine’s partial destruction of the bridge at Kerch, a $3.6bn monument to Russia’s annexation of Crimea. That wounded both Vladimir Putin’s vanity and his logistics. But Russia’s ballistic strikes on Kyiv’s river bridges, which damaged two vital crossings, could count for more.

The scale of destruction at Kerch emerged in early dawn. Images released by the Ukrainians showed the road bridge’s suspension arch and navigation span lying in the water, blocking Russia’s shipping channel to the Azov sea. The rail bridge was damaged enough to limit its use to a single track. It was not the only good news for Ukraine. Farther north, its forces severed a crossing on the road linking Russia to Crimea, a vital artery for resupply to Russia’s southern military grouping.

The strikes were like two claws closing on the peninsula. Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, called them the finale of a “seven-stage operation”. Those involved say they show how good the Ukrainians have become at combined cruise-missile and drone operations. Their forces meticulously peeled away air defences in Crimea, including the security system around the bridge, before launching waves of night attacks. “Our pilots have become so good, so exact, that you don’t even see a leaf fall from a nearby tree when they impact,” says one Ukrainian commander.

In Kyiv the method was cruder. Seven Russian ballistic missiles cut through starved air defences to partially destroy two bridges joining the western and eastern banks of the city. Road and metro links were severed, and some suspension cables were torn loose. The morning commute turned grim for hundreds of thousands, with traffic jams stretching for kilometres and pedestrians stumbling across what remained of the bridges in the rain. Russia had struck before, with both drones and missiles. But these attacks were the most damaging so far.

Ukrainian air defences face a losing battle this winter, with interceptors running low and what appears to be a deliberate American policy to hold back deliveries. But there is one area where they seem to be winning. In the summer a new generation of Russian remote-controlled drones threatened to bring the capital to a standstill by targeting infrastructure with pinpoint accuracy. Today, they have been blunted by a system of f16 fighters, drone interceptors and what has been called a protective “dome” over Kyiv.

The dome, a network of jammers designed to confuse signals from drones and the communications networks they work on, was installed over the capital in September. It is part of a broader system, making its contribution hard to assess. But December One, a firm that made most of the jammers, says the results speak for themselves. “Like everyone else in Kyiv I was thinking about moving my family in September,” says Illia Kabachynsky, a company official. “Now, pinpoint jet-drone hits have practically disappeared.”

The success of Kyiv’s anti-drone system has pushed Russia to double down on its ballistic missiles. It has hundreds of these in reserve, and a steady production rate. That has led some to question the wisdom of the decision to attack one of Mr Putin’s most sensitive projects, given the risk of him lashing out in response.

Captain Dmitry Pletenchuk, spokesman for the navy, which helped attack the Kerch bridge, dismisses any idea of tit-for-tat provocation. “We cannot keep looking over our shoulder to think what the enemy might think of us,” he says. Russia was already attacking civilian ships, blocking Ukraine’s vital shipping lanes. Much of its campaign was co-ordinated from Crimea. Hitting the Kerch bridge just before the winter also makes quick repairs impossible. “It will be spring before they manage a fix,” he predicts. Less clear is how many of Kyiv’s bridges will still be standing then.

articles.title: Andrej Babis tries to curtail public broadcasting
articles.deck: Hundreds of thousands protested in the biggest demonstration since the fall of communism

paragraphs.text: It was the biggest demonstration in Prague since the Velvet Revolution, the non-violent protests that toppled communism in 1989. On a sunny November 15th, as many as 400,000 Czechs gathered on Letna plain next to Prague Castle to protest against proposed changes to the funding of public-service broadcasters. They waved Czech, European and Ukrainian flags and held signs saying “We refuse the Slovak scenario”. Many wore triangular paper hats similar to Vecernícek, a character from a children’s show on public television, who has become a symbol of the fight for independent public broadcasting.

The demonstration was the latest and biggest in a series held in 21 Czech towns, following a strike of public-service television and radio staff on November 3rd. The protests began when the government of Andrej Babis, the prime minister, rushed through a draft bill in an overnight parliamentary session in late October to scrap mandatory licence fees (which amount to 205 koruna or $9 a month for radio and TV) and replace them with funding from the public budget. But they have turned into something bigger, an expression of deep discontent with Mr Babis, the Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) and the Motorists, his populist-right coalition partners. “For the first time since the Velvet Revolution Czechs are really worried about their democracy,” says Erik Tabery, the editor-in-chief of Respekt, a weekly.

Mr Babis had already chipped away at the independence of public-service broadcasters during his first term in office between 2017 and 2021. He accused in particular Czech Television (CT) of bias against him. In 2020 lawmakers from ANO (“Yes”), his party, elected several outspoken critics of CT to the Czech Television Council, which is responsible for appointing the broadcaster’s director-general and overseeing its budget. “This is a continuation of what he did then”, says Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies in Frankfurt an der Oder.

Although Mr Babis has not fulfilled campaign promises of cheaper energy and a lower pension age, ANO is still the biggest party, polling around 30%. Yet fringe parties in his coalition, whose leaders are seen as arrogant and incompetent, are viscerally disliked, says Mr Stetka. At recent elections for the Senate the ruling coalition failed to win a single seat, a result Mr Babis called “catastrophic”.

Mr Babis is likely to retain his draft bill but may agree to changes. The issue is whether that will be enough to satisfy protesters who worry that the Czech Republic may be following Slovakia,where in 2023, just before Robert Fico, the authoritarian prime minister, returned to power, the licence fee was replaced with stingier state-budget funding. In 2024 Radio and Television of Slovakia (RTVS), was renamed Slovak Television and Radio (STVR), with a board appointed by the government. Popular programmes were cut and critical journalists fired. Today Slovak public broadcasting is a shadow of its former self. In the 2026 World Press Freedom Index by Reporters without Borders, Slovakia ranks 37th. The Czech Republic still ranks 11th.

The pro-Russian Mr Fico faces elections in September next year. He is looking more vulnerable after losing his majority in parliament following the defection of an independent lawmaker in early November. Mr Babis, however, is determined to serve out his full term until 2029. One reason is that he enjoys being shielded by parliamentary immunity from standing trial in a long-running case involving alleged abuse of European Union subsidies. Morover, he is not term-limited. The 72-year-old wants to stick around and could yet choose to run again in 2029 or later, he has said on Sorry jako, his video podcast.

Two days after the big protest on Letna plain, Czechs celebrated the anniversary of the Velvet Revolution. Mr Babis skipped the festivities in favour of a working trip to Israel. He risked being booed had he stayed at home. In December protesters will take to the streets again. The bill must still go through its second and third readings in the Chamber of Deputies.

articles.title: Why French politicians write so many books
articles.deck: In a country of keen readers, books offer a good way to keep people talking about you

paragraphs.text: Jordan Bardella, a French populist-right leader, has just published his third book—at the age of 31. François Hollande, a Socialist former president, has brought out a dozen. On November 6th Jean-Luc Mélenchon, from the populist-left, published his 21st. It shot to the top of the bestseller list, and in its first week sold more copies than the winner of this year’s prix Goncourt, the most prestigious literary award. In literary France, which treats writers as national treasures, any self-respecting politician must put plume to paper and publish. A book is a mark of seriousness, a measure of appeal—and a way to keep people talking about you.

The French are unusually voracious readers. As many as 83% say they enjoy reading, and on average they get through a staggering 18 books a year. France has won 16 Nobel prizes for literature, more than any other country. The prix Goncourt, first awarded in 1903, is older than America’s Pulitzer (1917) and Britain’s Booker prize (1969). Yet overall book sales have been declining, from a peak of 486m in 2021 to 420m in 2025. One of the few categories to have seen an increase in market share is current affairs and political essays.

Politicians’ contributions to the literary canon vary. Nicolas Sarkozy, another former president, served up “Diary of a prisoner”: a meditation on 20 days he spent behind bars in 2025. Bruno Le Maire, a former finance minister with over a dozen titles to his name, once wrote a novel with a sex scene featuring a female protagonist which included such delights as the “brown bulge of her anus”. Most politicians stick to politics or themselves. Until this summer, when a court of appeal lifted a ban on his boss, Marine Le Pen, Mr Bardella thought he would be running for the presidency in 2027. In his latest work, he confesses that “it may have shaken me.” Mr Mélenchon, a revolutionary firebrand and rival presidential candidate, has the virtue of consistency: he argued for “permanent insurrection” in a book in 1991.

Some political books become real blockbusters. Mr Sarkozy’s account of life inside sold 280,000 copies. Mr Bardella’s first book sold over 230,000 copies. This is more than twice the average for a book that makes it into the New York Times bestseller lists. Many more works, though, end up in cardboard boxes in the publisher’s back room. Nor is literary triumph a guarantor of electoral success. If nothing else a book is an entrance ticket to one of the country’s many talk shows. In a pre-election year, this makes them a valuable promotional tool. As Descartes might have said: “I publish, therefore I am.”

articles.title: How Ukraine brought out the EU’s stubborn streak
articles.deck: Europe is proving remarkably hard to exhaust

paragraphs.text: Aesop’s tortoise would have felt at home in Brussels. Slow-moving, deliberative and apparently untroubled by the spectacle of nimbler creatures racing ahead, the plodding reptile shares many qualities with the European Union. The ancient fable has the hare dashing off showily before losing interest in the race. Ukraine’s struggle against Russian revanchism has offered a modern retelling. America originally sprinted ahead as Europe dithered; politicians in Washington were on hand to deliver missiles to Ukraine even as those in Berlin were offering to send helmets.

Yet for all its military prowess America’s enthusiasm has proved erratic, to put it mildly. Europe, by contrast, has spent four years inching forward. Yes, it has squabbled over many decisions and sometimes seemed incapable of getting out of its own way. But in its own unflashy manner the European tortoise has kept moving, powered by a determination seemingly greater than its public disagreements. What it lacks in agility, the EU has made up for in staying power.

The remarkable thing is not how slowly Europe has moved, but that it has kept moving at all. The continent’s endurance in supporting Ukraine has surprised even its supporters. For years suspicions have abounded that “war fatigue” was about to sap the continent’s resolve. (Ukrainians, plenty fatigued, do not alas have the luxury of deciding they have had enough.) And yet look who keeps showing up to help, even as America has at times seemed to put more pressure on Ukraine than Russia. Just this week the process of unlocking a further €45bn ($49bn) in EU financial support to Ukraine has begun, no matter the strained public finances of many member states. The bloc is embarking on a 22nd round of sanctions, undeterred by the fractious haggling that was a feature of the 21 previous rounds. Talks with Ukraine about joining the EU—or at least closely integrating it into the club pending full membership further down the line—are ongoing. Nearly five years into the fighting, millions of Ukrainians enjoy refugee-like protection (and generous welfare provisions) wherever in Europe they might choose to settle. Fatigued, moi?

Granted, EU decision-making about Ukraine sometimes makes tortoises look dynamic. The most recent squabbling has concerned who might represent Europe at peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. For years now the continent has been asked to come up with preferably a single person to represent its interests at the negotiating table. Jared Kushner, the presidential son-in-law who serves as one of America’s envoys, recently quipped that getting Europe to agree on just one interlocutor was harder than getting Russia to accept having them at the negotiating table at all. As if to prove his point, at a summit on November 13th the Europeans put forward a team of no fewer than seven representatives to speak for them—one each from Germany, France, Britain, Italy, Poland, the EU institutions and NATO. (No Luxembourg?) It may seem absurd to have more Europeans at the table than every other party combined. But the truly mad feature of the talks is that America is sitting in the chair of mediator, seemingly neutral between the Ukrainian victim and the Russian aggressor. For its part, Europe is unambiguously on the side of Ukraine.

Unity of purpose is perhaps unsurprising among EU countries fearful that they might be next on President Vladimir Putin’s menu if Ukraine loses (and many of which already face nebulous “hybrid attacks” steered from the Kremlin). Some disagreements have been unedifying. Greece recently wangled an exemption from EU sanctions so its shipping fleet could keep ferrying Russian gas. Belgium has stood in the way of Europe seizing frozen Russian assets that many would like to see handed over to Ukraine. Promising Ukraine will join the EU is laudable, and could one day be a large carrot to get Ukrainians to accept a painful peace involving territorial losses to Russia. Yet in Brussels diplomatic circles the prospect is thought to be at least a decade away. If that might justifiably come as a disappointment to Ukrainians, who once hoped to join by 2027, they could be reminded that America suddenly eased sanctions on Russia ahead of midterm elections earlier this month. Better a plodding friend than a fickle one.

Slow-and-steady as the Europeans have been, there is always a risk that their resolve will reach its limits. Notably, a slew of forthcoming elections could shift the calculus of solidarity. At least three of the five European countries in the negotiating group will go to the polls in 2027. Populists in Italy and Poland are pro-Ukraine, but might need support from Kyiv-bashing allies to form coalitions. The biggest risk is the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidency. Although her tone on Ukraine has softened—and her xenophobic National Rally party is no longer financed by a Russian bank—she says France cannot afford to send more money to the cause. Somewhat in anticipation, European leaders are seeing if they might hurriedly sign off on a long-term EU budget that includes an additional €100bn in funding for Ukraine, locking in support before the political winds change.

Europe’s plodding yet purposeful approach has worked well enough so long as the job has been merely to keep Ukraine supplied with money, weapons and prospects for the future. Peace negotiations may demand something different. Alas, for now substantive talks seem a distant prospect. Russia continues to issue impossible demands as a precondition for bringing its war of aggression to an end, including NATO troops being pulled out of central Europe. Mr Putin seems to be betting that another winter of fighting will wear down Ukrainian resistance. Should a deal come within reach, Europe may need to move faster than it is used to. Until then, the tortoise has little reason to envy the hare.

articles.title: The Royal Navy’s big bet on uncrewed vessels
articles.deck: Costly, exquisite destroyers are out; cheap, semi-autonomous ships are in

paragraphs.text: On November 5th, at a ceremony in Portsmouth, the Royal Navy brought the 1st Autonomous Squadron into service. The squadron’s 20 uncrewed speedboats will monitor the seas for threats such as drones. More importantly, they mark the birth of Britain’s new “hybrid navy”.

Armed forces often prepare for the last war rather than the next. Here, however, Britain is going all-in on a revolutionary idea. Its hybrid navy will combine crewed ships with submarines and uncrewed vessels carrying missiles, sensors and radars. The first sea lord, General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, describes the guiding principle as “crewed where necessary, uncrewed wherever possible, and integrated always”.

Critics say a lack of cash is forcing the navy to place a huge bet on unproven technology. Advocates compare it to when, in 1906, Sir Gwyn’s predecessor “Jackie” Fisher launched the first Dreadnaught battleship and transformed naval warfare. Jake Rigby of BMT, a maritime consultancy, says: “The transition…represents a doctrinal, organisational and technological shift on a scale not seen since Fisher’s reforms.”

The navy sees no alternative. It has two crucial tasks: to maintain Britain’s submarine-based nuclear deterrent and to keep lines of communication in the North Atlantic and High North open, while defending critical undersea infrastructure. That means meeting a growing threat from Russia’s fleet along the Kola Peninsula. Above all, Russian submarines must not slip through the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap.

Sidharth Kaushal of RUSI, a think-tank, says the navy had either to rely on a shrinking number of “exquisite” conventional platforms, or risk doing something radically different. In that context, the “all-in bet is entirely rational”.

In June the government’s Defence Investment Plan (DIP) scrapped proposals for eight air-defence destroyers, which would have cost £2.5bn ($3.3bn) each. A senior navy source says Sir Gwyn realised “what we would have ended up with is bigger, more expensive, but fewer hulls and with ships that were outdated before the first steel was even cut.” John Healey, then defence secretary and now chancellor, backed Sir Gwyn to change course. “That was the only way to generate the mass and lethality the Royal Navy needed.”

So instead it has ordered six Common Combat Vessels (CCVs) for about £200m each—half the cost of a general-purpose Type 31 frigate, and less than a quarter that of a high-end Type 26. The aim is for all the CCVs to be operational by the mid-2030s.

The CCVs will be manned by command-and-control teams and engineers, who will operate fleets of semi-autonomous, uncrewed vessels. Type 91s are missile-carriers equipped for both attack and defence; Type 92s are “sloops” which will conduct undersea surveillance; Type 93s are underwater vehicles for tracking and destroying hostile submarines; Type 94s are radar and sensor platforms to serve as picket ships. The idea is to split the functions of complex, conventional warships—sensing, decision-making and use of weapons—across many specialised platforms.

Ukraine’s use of one-way attack vessels against Russia has influenced the navy. But while it is merely denying Russia access to the relatively calm Black Sea, Britain seeks control of the seas in the much harsher North Atlantic. So the Type 9X platforms are much bigger: up to 110 metres long. These are not “throw away” drones, says Mr Kaushal, but can take more risk than costly warships full of sailors.

They should also be far cheaper and easier to build. Just how much will depend on decisions over the Type 9Xs' durability. But the hope is that their modular hulls can be built by many commercial shipyards rather than just the two biggest naval yards in Scotland, making it easier to scale up production. Competition should help, too. Naval sources expect a unit of a CCV and uncrewed platforms, operating as part of a carrier group, to be more capable and cheaper than a single destroyer.

In theory, the Type 9X platforms should also have twice the availability of crewed vessels, which typically spend only a third of their service lives on operations. Uncrewed vessels do not need leave, training or new crew members after maintenance.

So what makes this such a gamble? First, nobody has done it before. The American and Chinese navies can afford to hedge their bets, adding uncrewed systems gradually to much larger surface fleets. Smaller European navies like those of Norway and Denmark, which work with the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force, can wait to see how the Royal Navy gets on.

Second, uncrewed vessels must function dozens of miles from their CCVs. So the technological links binding them together must work seamlessly and resist enemy jamming, spoofing and even an electromagnetic pulse triggered by a nuclear blast. “Disaggregation makes communication the weakest link,” says Mr Rigby.

Steve Prest, once the navy’s first robotics officer and now affiliated with RUSI, argues that the acid test will be whether, in a contested environment, real-time data can reach the Type 91 missile platform with the low latency needed for air defence of the fleet. The priority, he says, is to build the right “cognitive architecture” and “engineering ecosystem”. The navy insists its AI-supported “Maritime Fighting Web” will provide the right “digital glue”.

Maintenance is another hurdle. On crewed warships it is conducted 24/7, but the uncrewed Type 9Xs are to remain at sea for up to 120 days with only weekly maintenance from the CCVs. The navy’s solution is to rely on simpler propulsion systems and to move from “Formula One-style maintenance to that of the family car”. And safety is a worry, too, relying on flawless navigation and transmission of targeting data. The navy aims to get an uncrewed vessel longer than 24 metres afloat next year to test the myriad remaining issues.

The final problem is money. Nick Childs of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, another think-tank, points out that though the DIP allocated the navy £18bn for the next four years, only £1.5bn was for the transition to uncrewed warfare. The Ministry of Defence thinks it will need £32bn more between 2030 and 2035 to make the hybrid navy a reality.
Sir Gwyn’s vision is bold and logical. But even Fisher, his exemplar, made mistakes. A lot is riding on whether the Royal Navy’s all-in bet pays off.

articles.title: Welcome to Plymouth, Britain’s naval-drone factory
articles.deck: For the port city, greater defence spending heralds a jobs boom

paragraphs.text: Testing autonomous vessels in calm waters doesn’t prove much, says Commander Mark Butcher of the Royal Navy. It is only out in the choppy English Channel that you can see what they are made of. And so off the coast of Plymouth, a pointed craft with no crew slips gracefully over the waves. One piloted by a human—carrying naval officers, the bosses of two maritime-drone firms and your correspondent—bumps sickeningly along behind.

The drone was made by ZeroUSV; its software by MarineAI, a sister firm. During the trial, it drops three smaller vessels made by a third firm, Oshen. The navy wants to see that these metre-long “C-Stars”, which Oshen likens to a network of CCTV cameras, can be deployed in triangle formation and detect an undersea signal.

Cutting-edge technology has long helped the Royal Navy meet new threats. Now, thanks to collaboration between the government, academia and industry, Plymouth has become one of Britain’s most impressive factories for such technology.

If Plymouth owes part of its success to its location, it is also giving innovative firms what they want. Oshen, MarineAI and ZeroUSV are based at Turnchapel Wharf, a waterside industrial estate that opened in 2014 and is devoted to maritime tech. Tenants can easily test their equipment in different water conditions—rough, calm, shallow or deep. A cluster of minnows sits alongside leviathans such as Thales, a leading French defence firm. They make everything from autonomous submarines to surface drones and sensors.

Then there is the navy. Plymouth has been synonymous with it since Francis Drake sailed from there to confront the Spanish armada. (In those days, uncrewed vessels meant “fire ships” sent burning towards the enemy.) Today the city is home to HMNB Devonport, western Europe’s biggest naval base, which the government has pledged to upgrade with an investment of £7.1bn ($9.4bn). For the navy’s suppliers, having their biggest customer nearby helps projects move faster.

The Devonport cash, plus a £50m government investment in marine-tech defence firms, will revivify Plymouth. Local officials think it will spark a jobs boom, and so plan to build more green spaces, schools and public transport. Amanda Ratsey of Plymouth City Council, who is married to ZeroUSV’s boss, says Plymouth will need more, and better, housing to attract gifted techies. It aims to build 10,000 new homes over the next 20-30 years.

Businesses’ one gripe is red tape. Dylan Kalis, boss of the firm that owns Turnchapel Wharf, is trying to develop another site in Plymouth for similar purposes. He complains that his attempts have been slowed by the “box-ticking gnomes” he must appeal to for planning permission.

What is not lacking is demand. Back on dry land, naval officers quiz Oshen and ZeroUSV about how their technology could be taken further. Could an advanced version be made to relay data even when the enemy has jammed communications? As Britain’s navy attempts to transform the nature of sea power, it looks like it will transform Plymouth as well.

articles.title: Britain’s corporate register gets tough on financial crime
articles.deck: Companies House hopes a more assertive approach can reduce fraud

paragraphs.text: A garbage-strewn corporate register shows how ripe Britain is for financial shenanigans. Since it was set up in 1844 officials have seldom probed the information submitted. For a piddling sum you could incorporate a company with almost no questions asked. In 2022 a Labour peer showed the absurdity of this by asking what steps Companies House, the agency running the register, had made to verify the identity of a company secretary called Adolf Tooth Fairy Hitler.

The National Crime Agency (NCA) has estimated that more than £100bn ($132bn) is laundered through Britain or British corporate structures each year. Russian cash has grabbed the most headlines, and the 2022 invasion of Ukraine jolted Parliament into action. The following year it passed the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act, giving Companies House powers to fight shady behaviour.

It started by weeding out the Nazi tooth fairies. Companies House says it verified the identities of 7.3m directors in a year-long process that ran to November 17th, and is pushing to prosecute the worst offenders. It has also raised the fee for digital incorporation from £12 to £100 since 2024. This is modest by global standards, but has helped pay for the crackdown.

No one imagines this will eliminate fraud. Tom Keatinge of RUSI, a think-tank, says that ensuring people named on the register exist is just getting to the starting line. The real test will be whether Companies House enforces the new rules well.

That is what it says it is now doing. Martin Swain, Companies House’s head of intelligence and law enforcement, says that three years ago the intelligence team numbered a handful of people. Now a group of around 110, many drawn from the police and intelligence agencies, can investigate and challenge filings.

Since growing a backbone it has helped tackle fraudulent high-street shops. Companies House has assisted the NCA on Operation Machinise, its effort to tackle cash-based businesses that may be evading taxes and serving as fronts for money-launderers. Companies House can interrogate its data for patterns to link seemingly unconnected corporate vehicles that sit behind these vape stores, sweet shops and hairdressers, which can help track down the real owners. Besides the register, users of Companies House leave digital footprints—an IP address, payment data, email addresses. All provide clues.

Illicit Kurdish barbershops, alas, may prove to be softer targets than the global gangs and kleptocrats who launder their money in Britain. Going after such criminals demands manpower and tech to keep up with them.

The agency has also flexed its muscles against rogue company-formation agents. These set up British corporate entities on behalf of clients without going through proper anti-money-laundering checks—and so are magnets for criminals. Over the past year Companies House has worked with the Insolvency Service to shut down unregulated British companies that between them had set up more than 12,000 firms on the corporate register on behalf of foreign customers. From late 2027 this practice will be restricted to “authorised corporate service providers” regulated by anti-money-laundering bodies.

The reforms are not perfect. Transparency International, an anti-corruption campaign group, has said that identity verification cannot say whether those verified are mere nominees put forward by others, obscuring beneficial ownership. And verification is yet to cover limited partnerships, a corporate structure open to abuse because of the privacy it lends partners. In October the government “paused” a plan to make small firms file profit-and-loss statements, after business groups complained that it was too burdensome. This could have helped root out those paying too little tax—reckoned to have cost the taxman £4.5bn in 2022-23 (0.2% of GDP).

Graham Barrow, an expert on financial crime, says the reforms are welcome, but that it is hard to be optimistic about efforts to fight money-laundering, given its scale. Even so, he says, “You have to try.”
