articles.title: Lessons from Britain’s beleaguered statistics office
articles.deck: Its weaknesses are those of the British state at large

paragraphs.text: Go to a theme park and you might ride the teacups, spinning ever faster until you lose all sense of direction. The sensation has become familiar to students of the British economy. In 2024 the Labour Force Survey (LFS) suggested employment was rising, contradicting more accurate tax data which said it was falling. In 2023 the Office for National Statistics (ONS) put net migration to Britain in 2022 at 606,000; its latest estimate for that year is 891,000. And for ages Britons were castigated for some of the worst productivity growth in the rich world. It now looks like they were in the front half of the pack all along.

Plenty blame the ONS for this dizzy feeling. Not all of the criticism is fair: the migration figures were revised because it switched to a better methodology. But it has blundered in several crucial areas, especially the LFS, and been slow to respond in others. Its failures resemble the shortcomings of the country at large. Britain does cutting-edge things well (like scientific research) but struggles to get basics like housing right. The ONS has similarly excelled at innovation (in measuring infection rates during the pandemic, for example) but has failed in its main job of compiling accurate core statistics.

The nadir came in 2023, when the ONS stopped publishing employment figures because its survey was so shoddy. The response rate had fallen to 18%, from 47% in 2019. This made it harder to correct for the fact that some groups were less likely to respond than others. Results became wildly inaccurate. The Resolution Foundation, a think-tank, made its own measure based on tax data, finding that, at its worst, the LFS undercounted the employed by nearly 1m (see chart 1). This had big knock-on effects—such as making it impossible to gauge productivity accurately.

Failure at the ONS resulted from three weaknesses that are endemic in the British state. The first is trying to do too much at once. An independent report found that the ONS’s top brass missed errors because they were distracted by shiny new projects, like using administrative data to replace the census. Their distraction, plus a reluctance to hear bad news, left the core surveys lacking both funding and proper scrutiny. Andy Burnham should take note. Britain’s prime minister wants to launch a National Care Service even as existing parts of the state, such as prisons, crumble.

Some also blame the ONS’s problems on its move from London to Newport, a Welsh city, in the 2000s. More than 90% of the office’s London staff quit rather than relocating. James Benford, a senior civil servant at the ONS, “hates” this argument, saying that its troubles since 2020 cannot be put down to a move made 19 years ago.

Yet uncompetitive pay, Mr Benford admits, makes recruitment and retention a struggle. With AI firms and the City of London gobbling up the best talent, the stinginess of public-sector pay is a shortcoming for the government as a whole. A London-based software engineer working for Anthropic can easily earn £260,000 ($340,000) a year; in the civil service you would count yourself lucky if you got more than £70,000. And it is not just tech talent—experienced policymakers also leave to become fat-cat lobbyists.

The final weakness is Britons’ reluctance to share personal data. Although response rates for surveys have fallen around the world, things are especially bad in Britain. Successful surveys rely on people’s trust and willingness to give up time; in Britain, both are lacking. Many European countries make it compulsory to fill in government questionnaires, but Britain’s are voluntary. Other states including the Netherlands rely less on surveys because they have population registers, in which a person’s real-time data are linked to an ID number.

In Britain, however, Mr Burnham has cancelled a scheme to introduce digital IDs amid a backlash around privacy concerns. In 2026 the ONS stopped trying to link different departments’ datasets after it also ran into trouble over data privacy. All this makes Britain’s statistics worse, and means policy is often made in the dark.

Despite these weaknesses, the ONS is slowly recovering. Mr Benford says the office is focusing on “quality over quantity”, having cut statistical output by 10% this year while improving core surveys. It has hired 60% more interviewers over the past three years, for instance, and response rates have started to rise (see chart 2). The office is looking into whether to make surveys mandatory. Headline employment numbers are now much more in line with the tax data. For Ed Humpherson, who runs the ONS’s regulator, the most important thing is that the organisation is now much more “open and humble” about mistakes.

Further gremlins could yet emerge. But for now, the ONS’s efforts to fix Britain’s statistics point to an underappreciated strength of its state: it is surprisingly good at bouncing back. The country’s initial response to covid-19 was shambolic, but by 2021 it was garnering praise for a speedy vaccine roll-out. In 2022 Britons moaned about long delays at the passport office; by 2023 new passports were arriving within days of an application. It would be a relief for disorientated economists if the ONS could follow suit. Statistics are not supposed to remind you of a fairground.

articles.title: The world’s oldest travel retailer has hit turbulence
articles.deck: WHSmith hopes a new boss and a streamlined strategy will see it through

paragraphs.text: It started selling newspapers in London in 1792, the year revolutionary France declared war on Austria. Business boomed. Soon WHSmith (as it now styles itself) was peddling news of Napoleon’s conquests to the provinces by stagecoach; then books to Victorians travelling on Britain’s expanding railways. When Heathrow airport opened in 1946, the newsagent was the first shop to set up beside the runway.

Yet by the 2000s the world’s first travel retailer made most of its revenue selling pens and DVDs in tatty high-street stores. As shoppers moved online, sales on the high street fell—by half in real terms between 2016 and 2024. Meanwhile Smith’s expanded its original travel business. By the time it sold its 480 high-street branches last year (which are now branded TGJones, and are again up for sale), it had 1,280 outlets in railway stations, hospitals and airports around the world, and a 14% share of America’s travel-retail market.

Lately that expansion has appeared ill-judged. Over the past year Smith’s share price has plunged by 40%. On November 12th it posted pre-tax profits of £76m ($100m) before one-off costs, down by nearly a third year on year. Sales rose by 5%, but a write-down on its North American arm tipped it into a loss of £107m, compared with a £2m profit a year earlier. And it is forecasting profits for next year of a meagre £75m-85m.

The problems have piled up. In 2018 Smith’s barrelled into North America, the world’s biggest travel market. It acquired InMotion, a seller of (mostly) Apple accessories at airports, followed by Marshall Retail Group, a seller of tat at holiday resorts, a year later. Neither has grown as hoped. InMotion operates in a saturated market and depends on Apple’s innovation cycle, which has spun slowly of late. Marshall relies heavily on its Las Vegas outlets, which have never recovered from the covid-19 pandemic; in August sales at resorts were down by 16% year on year.

Worse, last year Smith’s uncovered £30m of accounting errors in North America, after supplier payments were booked incorrectly, which later grew to a £50m downgrade. “Local management probably felt under pressure to hit profit targets,” says Kate Calvert at Investec, a bank. The restatement cut reported profits by a third and wiped nearly £600m from the firm’s market value. The boss resigned. An investigation is under way.

Then America and Israel attacked Iran. The conflict sent jet-fuel prices soaring, prompting airlines to raise fares and cut capacity. In Britain, passenger growth stalled along with traffic to the Middle East. Domestic visits to America’s 50 biggest airports fell by 2.6% year on year in June, according to Placer.ai, an analytics firm. That has meant fewer sales of travel pillows and the like in airport terminals. Smith’s has blamed the war for a string of profit warnings this year.

But the Iran war wasn’t all. Smith’s runs shops in some of the most expensive spaces in airports. Higher airport rents caused its British profit margin to fall by 2.3 percentage points in the year to August. And some of its busiest Heathrow branches have been closed for refits this year, as Smith’s turns them into “one-stop shops” offering a wider range of products, to win customers from Boots, a rival.

There are signs that the investment will pay off—and other glimmers of hope, too. At Birmingham Airport sales per square foot rose by 30% after Smith’s rolled out its one-stop shops there in 2023, notes JPMorgan Chase, another bank. Footfall in American airports has finally ticked up, rising by 1.4% year on year in September.

Smith’s also has a new boss. Leo Quinn, who took over in April, has a record of successfully reviving struggling businesses. He has promised a “fundamental reset”, which will involve closing 100 InMotion and Marshall branches and opening 70 additional shops in North American airports. Despite its mishaps, Smith’s is still a market leader at selling snacks in airports. It expanded too quickly and in the wrong way. But the hardy travel retailer has survived worse. It remembers the days of the stagecoach and the steam train.

articles.title: Reform UK can’t stop talking about the burqa
articles.deck: Otherwise, Nigel Farage’s parliamentarians are surprisingly normal

paragraphs.text: NIGEL FARAGE is often dismissed as an English nationalist. Yet at elections in May, his Reform UK party made big gains in both Scotland and Wales. It is the second-largest party in the Senedd, the Welsh parliament, where it holds one in three seats. In Scotland it is third.

Reform has fallen back in the polls since then. But it is tied for second place nationwide, level with the Conservatives and behind Labour. If a general election were held now, Reform could expect to gain dozens or even hundreds of MPs. It might end up as the official opposition.

To some, Reform’s behaviour in Scotland and Wales is a warning. Its Welsh representatives want to ban the burqa, the full-face covering worn by some Muslim women. A minister from Plaid Cymru, the left-wing nationalist party governing Wales, compared this to anti-Jewish laws in Nazi Germany. On November 10th Joe Martin, a Reform MS, was banned indefinitely from speaking in the Senedd for requesting a debate on “the demographic replacement of white British people”. Reform has since boycotted debates there.

The party’s interest in the burqa borders on the obsessive. In Holyrood, home of the Scottish Parliament, Reform has demanded a ban four times since September; in Cardiff Bay, at the Senedd, it has raised the issue just as often. (In the House of Commons, where Reform has eight MPs, it mentioned the veil only once last year.) Reformers claim the burqa will provoke French-style street violence and that seeing veiled women on buses will retard young children’s mental development.

There are no reliable figures on how many women wear the burqa, but Muslims make up just 2% of the population in Scotland and Wales—one-third of the share in England. Jason O’Connell, a Reform MS who led a burqa debate in the Senedd, nonetheless insists it speaks to his party’s “core values”. Reformers may also be worried about Restore Britain, a far-right party that is nabbing voters. “It’s not a British thing,” says Malcolm Offord, Reform’s leader in Scotland. “We don’t cover our faces up, whether that’s with balaclavas or with burqas.” Many EU member states, he points out, have already banned the burqa.

Comparisons to Nazis look not merely over the top, but counterproductive. Mr Martin and his colleagues have milked the resulting limelight for all it is worth. The other Scottish parties, in contrast, have tried to ignore Reformers when they bang on about the burqa. Follow their lead and something surprising happens. Reform begins to resemble a normal political party.

Reform wants to “break up the consensus in Cardiff”, says Benjamin Hodge Mckenna, an MS; Angela Ross, an MSP, calls it a “dissenting voice” in Holyrood. Politics in both places could do with that. Scotland has become polarised by the question of independence, allowing the SNP to govern for 19 years despite mediocre results: the education system lags behind England’s and the rate of drug deaths is Europe’s worst. The Scottish Conservatives previously found success by being the most pro-union party. Lord Offord, who was a Tory minister before defecting to Reform, says the two parties are comfortable shouting at each other about independence, even if “in the meantime, the country goes to shit.” In Wales, a century of Labour domination ended only this year—and the Plaid government now has similar policies.

So far, the influx of Reform MSs and MSPs has not sparked much radicalism. Most are political novices and many have struggled to adjust to life in parliament. Plenty, however, think more about bread-and-butter topics than revolution. “We will spend a lot of time talking about the economy, a lot of time talking about health, a lot of time talking about education, a lot of time talking about the real issues,” says Lord Offord. At First Minister’s Questions he has been true to his word.

Motions tabled by Reform in Wales have urged the government to change its prostate-cancer strategy and to set up a register for lobbyists. A recent session in Holyrood saw Reform’s backbenchers ask about fire-safety regulations, rural crime, tax on small businesses and the future of a mothballed ferry port. They have signed up to various cross-party agreements reached by parliamentary committees. Working with others on these means “putting party politics to one side”, says Mark Simpson, a Reform MSP.

Reform’s success in Scotland and Wales has undermined a myth that voters in these places are inherently progressive. In the two parliaments, the party’s time is largely dedicated to the slow, rather boring job of legislative scrutiny and constituency casework. Unlike in Westminster, where the handful of Reform MPs are allocated little time to speak in Parliament, those in Cardiff Bay and Holyrood get plenty and are making the most of it. The party shows no sign yet of coming up with novel solutions to the countries’ ingrained problems. But it also displays no desire to burn the institutions to the ground (even if it is boycotting the Senedd).

Perhaps the greatest lesson from Reform’s first six months as a serious parliamentary force is one for its enemies. Comparing politicians to architects of the Holocaust, or seeking to silence them altogether, attracts publicity that helps them thrive. Better to work with them when possible—and use their wilder moments to remind voters that Mr Farage’s troops still struggle to focus on things that matter.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto: the real special relationship
articles.deck: America is Britain’s greatest cultural export

paragraphs.text: As video games go, “Grand Theft Auto” (“GTA”) could hardly be more American. Released on November 19th, the latest instalment, “GTA VI”, sets players loose on Vice City, a neon-pink caricature of Miami. Its streets spill over with obnoxious influencers, ’gator-wrestling rednecks and babes sporting Brazilian butt lifts. Speeding and shooting your way down them is like starring in your very own Hollywood fever dream: a cocaine-glazed mash-up of “Scarface” and “Fast & Furious”.

But “GTA” is not a Hollywood creation. It was born in Dundee, a Scottish city known for jam and the Beano comic. Rockstar North, which makes the game, is now owned by an American firm. Its mostly British development team, though, is based in Edinburgh—a city that is more Minas Tirith than Mar-a-Lago.

America has long been Britain’s greatest cultural export. From Victorian authors to 1960s musicians, British creatives have had a knack for repackaging American culture and making Americans wild for it. Forget about politicians, military types and spooks: this is the real special relationship. Better than selling ice to Inuits, Britain sells America to Americans.

Rockstar is just the latest to do so. Others include actual rockstars. Appropriating American rock, rhythm and blues made the Beatles and the Rolling Stones superstars. “Top Gun”, a 1980s film easily mistaken for American propaganda, was directed by Tony Scott—an advertising guru from Tyneside. “American Idol” and “America’s Got Talent”, reality-TV shows that embody the American showbiz dream, were dreamed up by British producers. Even all-American superheroes are often played by British actors. Think of Batman (Robert Pattinson), Spider-Man (Tom Holland) and Superman (Henry Cavill).

Whereas “Top Gun” celebrates American machismo, “GTA” is a satire: a franchise built on an extremist’s interpretation of liberal individualism. Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness? Why bother, when you can have money, excessive consumption and an inalienable right to sling grenades at pedestrians? Mouths water over 40,000-calorie “heartstopper” burgers. Pensioners fornicate on “senile isle”. “I’m living the dream, baby,” says the protagonist of “GTA V”, “and that dream is fucked.”

Americans seem not to mind. “GTA VI”, like “GTA V” and “GTA IV” before it, may well be the biggest entertainment release to date. Analysts reckon it earned back the roughly $1.5bn it cost from pre-orders alone. Within weeks it will probably eclipse the combined $3.7bn, in today’s money, garnered at box offices by Christopher Nolan’s “Batman” trilogy (yet more American stories told by a Briton). Most sales will be to Americans, enamoured of the caricature Britain has painted of them.

Britain is at once close enough to understand America and sufficiently distant to tease it, like a cheeky older relative with a faintly superior manner. Take a speech by King Charles III at the White House. Most world leaders try to flatter Donald Trump. Britain’s head of state likened the president’s new ballroom to Britain’s attempt to redevelop (read: burn down) the White House in 1814. Shortly after that Fanny Trollope, an English writer, toured the American frontier. Her 1832 travelogue, “Domestic Manners of the Americans”, passed harsh judgment: “I would infinitely prefer sharing the apartment of a party of well-conditioned pigs.” Americans were cross. They still bought her book.

Like other aspects of the special relationship, these cultural critiques mostly run one way. For American strategists, Britain is a useful airstrip—a tea break en route to the Gulf. For American creatives, targeting the British market is akin to reaching for pennies rather than pounds. Besides, most Americans simply do not think about Britain. Those who do imagine a land of live-action period drama, or a corner of Christendom fallen to sharia.

Britons, however, are America-mad. Americans dominate both the British charts and the box office. YouGov, a pollster, puts four Americans in its list of the ten celebrities Britons are most likely to recognise. There are only that number of Britons in America’s top 100. As outsiders who have long fixated on America—a condition with which The Economist sympathises—Britons are uniquely placed to celebrate its triumphs and satirise its excesses.

For Britain, the special relationship serves as an invaluable source of escapism. Why face the banality of your own decline when you can laugh at America’s absurdity instead? “GTA London”, a swinging-60s nostalgia trip, was a small expansion pack for the original 1997 game. There will not be an updated version. You cannot really have high-speed car chases in a country that builds motorways more slowly than Rockstar makes games. And a British version of the in-game radio, on which B-list celebrities press budding female popstars for invitations to their 16th-birthday parties, would be a tough listen these days.

Despite Britons’ sense of superiority over Americans, they cannot help but fantasise in American. “GTA” draws on this cognitive dissonance. Dan Houser, an English co-founder of Rockstar, once described “GTA” as a profile not of America but of “the America that was sold to the world”. Like Trollope’s book, the franchise is an outsider’s verdict on the country’s failure to live up to its glamorous image. Rockstar’s message is a confused one. America is both a botched experiment and a seductive, freewheeling fantasy. Vice City is a cesspit—and the best possible setting for a game based on freedom-loving fun. Mr Houser personifies the contradiction. Having spent a career making fun of America, he now holds American citizenship.
Why is Britain so good at selling America to Americans? Because, deep down, the American dream is also a British one.

articles.title: A new axis of malice threatens the global order
articles.deck: Russia, China, Iran and North Korea are co-operating like never before

paragraphs.text: When Russia began using jet-powered Geran-4 drones against Ukraine in May, the battlespace began to shift in the Kremlin’s favour. They were much faster than Russia’s earlier, propeller-driven models, putting huge strain on Ukraine’s defences. But the new weapons signified a shift with global dimensions too. They were the product of intensifying, often secret, collaboration by an axis of autocracies with overlapping goals: Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.

Once Ukrainian forces were able to inspect an intact Geran-4, they found it was based on Iran’s delta-winged Shahed suicide-drone, and upgraded with Russian-designed modules including a new warhead and optical navigation system (see diagram). The jet engine and anti-jamming antenna came from China, as did many other electronic parts. Internal markings showed that it was made at Russia’s Alabuga drone factory in Tatarstan, where as many as 25,000 North Koreans are thought to work in a complex packed with Chinese industrial machinery.

Collusion by this axis of malice goes far beyond the Geran-4. Its members are sharing military technology and expertise in ways that are altering the military balance of Europe, the Middle East and Asia. The network of manufacturers, traders, banks and ships that underpin collaboration is growing more sophisticated and resilient. And deepening economic ties are making the axis less susceptible to Western pressure. All that is making it harder to enforce UN and Western sanctions.

One consequence is that Western and Ukrainian officials believe North Korea has obtained from Russia much of the drone technology in—and expertise in using—the Geran-4 and other weapons. That has been part of a pay-off for North Korea providing arms and some 16,000 troops to help fight Ukraine. Similar drone components and tactics are being used by Iran in the Middle East, too. Iran continues to send drone engineers to Russia, long after sharing initial Shahed designs, according to Ukrainian officials. “They are still going back and forth, exchanging knowledge,” says Vladyslav Vlasiuk, a Ukrainian presidential aide on sanctions policy.

China, meanwhile, has been regularly sending military officers and technicians to Russian facilities that produce and operate military drones. China’s capacity to manufacture drones is unrivalled. But it lacks combat experience: its last war was against Vietnam in 1979. So it is hoovering up Russian knowledge to improve its own drone designs and tactics, hoping to gain an edge in a potential conflict over Taiwan. Russia, Iran and North Korea, in turn, are likely to rely increasingly on China’s AI stack for cyber-attacks, disinformation campaigns and autonomous weapons.

The axis is tilting the global nuclear balance as well. While China supplies Russia with machinery, drone parts and other “dual-use” items (with civilian and military applications), the Kremlin is helping it to build a missile-warning system and quieter nuclear-missile submarines, according to Western officials. Russia and China are also now enabling North Korea’s drive to become a fully fledged nuclear power. And covert support from Russia, China and North Korea has helped Iran to survive its conflict with America and Israel.

This global realignment was the backdrop for a showy trilateral meeting on November 19th between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping at a summit of Asia-Pacific powers in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Some pundits have compared the meeting to the Yalta conference of 1945. But officials involved did not expect any breakthroughs. The axis, meanwhile, grows stronger.

The nature of the axis coalition is debated by Western officials and scholars. Some see it as an emerging alliance of revisionist autocracies that threaten democracy worldwide. They liken it to the Eastern bloc in the cold war or the Axis alliance in the second world war. A book published this year by the Foundation for Defence of Democracies, a hawkish American think-tank, counted 600-plus instances of axis security co-operation in 2019-25, with a marked increase since 2022. Bradley Bowman, its lead author, argues that this co-operation in some ways surpasses that of the original Axis powers. It is “gaining momentum, making each adversary more formidable than they would be otherwise”.

Sceptics see the grouping more as a temporary “axis of convenience” without common long-term goals or ironclad mutual-defence commitments. They warn that exaggerating the threat could push the four countries closer together. Although China has had a mutual-defence treaty with North Korea since 1961, China’s commitment to that is questionable. Russia signed a new one with the North Koreans in 2024 and a more limited “strategic partnership” with Iran last year. This collection of bilateral links thus falls well short of a formal alliance like NATO, each member of which is formally committed to defend any other that comes under attack.

A closer parallel might be the Axis powers in the three years before the second world war began. They co-ordinated on foreign policy, intelligence and military affairs but largely on an ad hoc basis until Germany and Italy signed their “Pact of Steel” in 1939. A tripartite defence treaty including Japan followed in 1940. Another analogy is a syndicate of mafia bosses, who co-operate and compete simultaneously. What unites them is disregard for the law and reliance on underground networks of transport and finance.

Although quadrilateral axis meetings are not thought to occur, the four often vote in unison at the UN, helping to shield each other from sanctions or other actions. China, Russia and Iran also co-ordinate formally via international organisations such as the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation and the BRICs (which includes Brazil, Russia, India and China). But more often the four countries support each other in transactional, bilateral and covert ways. Spying on and stealing from each other is routine. And they often withhold their best military technology, sharing enough to prevent defeat, but not to secure victory.

Binding them together is a common desire to challenge American global leadership and to dominate their respective regions. “I don’t think they have in their minds an alternative order. They’re just trying to disrupt the US order, and then they’re trying to capitalise on that,” says Victor Cha, a former American national-security official now at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, a think-tank in Washington. But what began as transactional alignments has laid “the infrastructure for something that could last longer”, he says. That like-mindedness can show in their propaganda as well; state media in Russia and China in particular routinely share content with one another and, when it suits them, spread each other’s messages.

Axis members still have different and often conflicting goals. China, for instance, worries that Russia’s growing influence in North Korea is emboldening its leader, Kim Jong Un. In return for his help on Ukraine, the Kremlin has provided economic support and military tech that have helped him bolster his conventional and nuclear arsenals. That troubles China, which has long sought to avert another war on its north-eastern border. Were North Korea to obtain a fully fledged nuclear arsenal, China fears that it could provoke an American attack or prompt South Korea and Japan, both American allies, to develop nuclear weapons that would target China, as well as Mr Kim’s territory.

And yet, in the last year, China has revitalised its relations with Mr Kim, dropping public objections to his nuclear weapons programme, expanding cross-border transport links and lifting trade restrictions. As North Korea’s economy revives, it has more to spend on nuclear weapons. And its conventional forces are becoming more of a threat to South Korea as battle-hardened North Korean troops return home and adopt technology and tactics honed in Ukraine and the Middle East.

China and Russia have divergent aims and strategies in the Middle East too. China wants to stabilise the region, where it now has close relations with Gulf Arab states that Iran has bombed. Many of them supply China with oil or gas. Concerned that high energy prices are worsening its economic slowdown, China also hopes to open up the Strait of Hormuz. Russia, by contrast, seeks to destabilise the region, push up oil prices and gain leverage in negotiations with America over Ukraine.

But Messrs Xi and Putin share enough common interests in the Middle East for their actions to be complementary. Neither wants a fully nuclear-armed Iran. Yet they are anxious to ensure that its regime does not collapse (and possibly be replaced with a Western-leaning alternative). They also see the war there as a useful way to divert America’s military resources and undermine public support for its military intervention abroad.

The axis’s security interests appear to be compatible enough that their co-operation across a range of military technologies is deepening. When Russia started using North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles in 2023, they often missed targets or exploded mid-air. Russia has since made them more accurate and manoeuvrable by adding new components, including a Chinese-made receiver connecting it to Russian and Chinese satellite networks. The explosive charge has also changed to hexogen, which is more potent and made in Russia, according to Ukrainian experts. And the KN-23 can now carry cluster warheads, which inflict damage over a wider area. Those and other improvements appear to have flowed back to North Korea, which conducted a series of missile tests in recent weeks.

Iran’s missiles have been getting more accurate too. The ones that hit Qatar’s gas-liquefaction facilities at Ras Laffan precisely destroyed two “cold boxes”, the most vital and hard-to-repair parts of the plant. Iran was also able to strike American radars, aircraft and facilities across the Gulf. The British-American base of Diego Garcia, in the Indian Ocean, has been targeted too, as have American warships off Iran.

Although many of Iran’s missiles are based on old North Korean designs, it no longer needs outside expertise in building them and has developed its own generation of solid-fuel missiles that can be fired quickly. Even so, their recent accuracy may derive from Chinese and Russian intelligence helping to identify targets, according to Western officials. They believe Iran has access to a Chinese surveillance satellite. And perhaps more important, Iran (like Russia and North Korea) is now able to use China’s BeiDou satellite-navigation system to help guide its missiles.

Iran also still depends on specialist machinery, components and materials from abroad, especially China. The clearest support is through Chinese supplies of precursor chemicals for solid fuel, notably sodium perchlorate. A Chinese ship carrying the chemical exploded last year in an Iranian port. And Chinese ships continued to deliver it this year. There is also evidence of Chinese components being supplied to Iran’s proxy militias, including Hizbullah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen. Valuable details came from the contents of four containers seized in July in Aden, with Chinese cargo bound for a Houthi-controlled port. Analysis by Conflict Armament Research, a think-tank, shows it included parts for Iranian missiles. Those components appear to have been custom-made by a Chinese firm.

Whether China’s government is complicit in such exports is hard to determine. It denies supplying weapons to Iran, Russia or North Korea. But much of what it exports to all three are dual-use items, such as electronics and industrial machinery. Those exports sustain their military programmes and their broader economies, while Chinese consumer goods help to pacify their domestic populations. Russia, in particular, relies on imports from China, which are expected to reach $120bn-130bn this year, an 80-90% increase since 2021. While Western governments forbid the sale to Russia of dual-use items needed to make weapons, China is believed to supply as much as 90% of them.

Even if some of this trade is done without the Chinese government’s knowledge, many Western officials believe that (given its formidable surveillance capabilities) it either secretly approves or consciously turns a blind eye to exports that it knows will be used for military purposes. The Geran-4’s original engine, for instance, was made by a Chinese firm whose website specifies that it can be used in cruise missiles and drones. China tightened export controls on drone engines in October. But Ukrainian officials believe that Russia has already localised production at Alabuga.

Russian and Iranian weapons also often contain Western electronic components. But they are mostly imported via a complex network of trading firms and proxies, many of which are based in China or Hong Kong. China refuses to enforce Western sanctions imposed on dozens of such firms for supplying items for military use to Russia, Iran or North Korea. This year, China introduced rules that would penalise foreign companies and individuals for observing export controls or sanctions imposed on Chinese firms by other governments.

China’s big banks still generally comply with Western sanctions, fearing suspension from US dollar payments and clearing systems. But China has built a network of alternative financial institutions and mechanisms that is largely insulated from Western sanctions. It has also accelerated efforts to “de-dollarise” its trade with Russia, Iran and other targets of sanctions. More than 95% of Russia’s trade with China is now conducted in yuan or roubles, compared with about 25% five years ago.

That enables the oil trade that sustains the axis (see chart). China imports about 90% of Iran’s oil exports and roughly half of Russia’s. Since China mostly pays in yuan, Iran and Russia can use those revenues to finance purchases of Chinese dual-use tech. And the oil is mostly transported via a “shadow fleet” of ageing tankers, many of which are owned and managed through shell companies in Hong Kong and mainland China (as well as Dubai). Those tactics were pioneered by Iran but are increasingly used by Russia. As a result, the shadow fleet has expanded to more than 3,000 ships from about 200 in 2022. North Korea, meanwhile, imports almost all of its oil overland from China and Russia.

Transport links are thickening too. China and Russia are building a new cross-border gas pipeline that is due to open in 2027; they have opened new road and rail bridges and are planning new railway crossings. And they co-operate closely on expanding the Northern Sea Route through the Arctic. Since September, Russia and China have both opened new cross-border road bridges to North Korea. Russian and Chinese links to Iran, meanwhile, provide a window on the outside world. Iranian airlines still fly between Tehran, Moscow and Shanghai. Shipping between Russia and Iran via the Caspian Sea has surged this year. So has rail freight from China to Iran via Central Asia.

Closer axis collusion is not inevitable. If the wars in Iran and Ukraine end, demand for military technology may wane, along with the trade in oil under sanctions. With fewer incentives to co-operate, mutual suspicions could deepen. Axis members fear becoming dependent on each other and, given the opportunity, would like to expand commercial links with the West. Circumventing sanctions adds costs and Chinese companies, in particular, fear losing access to rich-world markets. With co-ordinated action, and strong leadership from the White House, that might give America and its allies some leverage. For now, though, the axis represents a challenge to which the West has no good response.

articles.title: The incredible shrinking legacy of Donald J. Trump
articles.deck: A three-way summit with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China diminished America

paragraphs.text: IT IS A curious sort of achievement. President Donald Trump has earned himself a giant place in history, while diminishing the office that he holds. That unhappy dynamic was on full display when Mr Trump met Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the margins of an APEC leaders’ summit in southern China on November 19th.

Mr Trump savoured his starring role, calling it a “big win for us” that Mr Xi met him at the airport, and gave him the seat of honour at an APEC dinner. He was less clear when explaining why the unprecedented three-way meeting might matter. On one hand, he called China and Russia “natural enemies” who, he told Fox News television, had been foolishly driven together by President Barack Obama. That might suggest that Mr Trump sees a chance to drive a wedge between Mr Putin and Mr Xi, in an echo of the manoeuvre pulled off by Richard Nixon and his envoy, Henry Kissinger, when they met China’s ageing despot, Mao Zedong, in 1972, and worked to split China from the Soviet Union.

On the other hand, Mr Trump seemed uninterested in wedge-driving. After declaring that vast, sparsely populated Russia naturally fears crowded, populous China, Mr Trump pivoted to bragging about how he is friends with Mr Putin and Mr Xi, presenting this as a good thing. Mr Trump sounded less like a statesman focused on the global balance of power than a needy high-school student crashing the cool kids’ party. “They both like Trump. Now, what happens after me, that I can’t tell you,” he told Fox News.

Stepping back from that Trumpian incoherence, the meeting left America worse off, while enhancing the standing of China and Russia. Harm was done even though the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting lacked real substance. At the time we went to press, it fell far short of being the “new Yalta” described in some breathless headlines: a nod to the conference during the second world war where Europe was divided into American- and Soviet-led blocs.

By all accounts, the original idea was Russia’s, as Mr Putin saw a chance to secure support from America and China for a Ukraine settlement on his terms. In essence, the Russian was asking Mr Trump and Mr Xi to help him carve out a European sphere of influence for himself, like a trio of bewhiskered 19th-century statesmen at a map-strewn mahogany table.

The nakedness of that Russian pitch appears to have embarrassed China. In late October Mr Xi irritably told the visiting German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, that he had no plans to co-host a Ukraine summit with America and Russia, and claimed he did not know where such rumours came from. Of course Europe should be included in any peace talks, Mr Xi added.

China is juggling competing interests when it comes to the Ukraine war. On the one hand, China does not want to see Mr Putin defeated by Ukraine and a united West. To that end, China supplies Russian armsmakers with everything from ball bearings to jet engines for attack drones, and keeps Russia’s economy afloat by buying its oil and gas. On the other hand, Chinese leaders resent how the war has gravely damaged their relations with Europe.

For Mr Putin, the meeting was the win. To sip tea with Mr Trump and Mr Xi, even while his missiles are murdering Ukrainian civilians in their homes and railway stations, exposes Western disunity and the failure of attempts to isolate him. Yes, he is China’s dependent junior partner. But he got to hobnob with Earth’s two most powerful men.

Mr Xi also gains. The world saw Mr Putin and Mr Trump, two leaders embroiled in disastrous wars in Ukraine and Iran, paying tribute to a China that is at peace. The site was carefully chosen. Shenzhen is a futuristic megacity, home to dancing robots, flying cars and other marvels. Mr Xi called the three powers “major victorious countries” of the second world war, who should now uphold world peace through mutual respect and avoiding one another’s “red lines”. On a darker note, if the meeting undercuts Western efforts to ostracise Russia, that suits China, too. Who knows when it might want to conquer Taiwan, the democratic island it claims for its own? How handy to inhabit a post-pariah world, in which big powers can invade the small with impunity.

In sad contrast, Mr Trump looked like a loser. Before the three-way meeting, he called it a chance to discuss “a lot of things”, including the Iran war. In Shenzhen, he downplayed the influence of China and Russia on that conflict, dismissing as “peanuts” the help that they give to Iran. In their meeting he called the three powers “uniquely” placed to tackle nuclear-arms control. Alas, as long as China has fewer warheads than America or Russia, it will decline to engage seriously on disarmament.

Trump aides defend their boss’s rogue-o-philia by citing his belief that a meeting is not a concession. Ignoring the long history of parleys between warring kings, Mr Trump told Mr Putin and Mr Xi that: “Too often past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements, and we feel the opposite.” That would be more convincing if Mr Trump consulted friends before meeting foes, and did a better job of hiding his excitement at meeting autocrats. By going it alone, Mr Trump undercuts the alliances that have long helped America project power. Weakening the American-led order is quite the concession to bad actors, even if Trump apologists refuse to see it.

Then there is Mr Trump’s vanity. He refuses to prepare for meetings, ignores facts that bore him and only half listens to what foreign leaders say. A former insider says: “He thinks it is just him, in the moment, that matters. Big guys talking and let others sweat the details.” The pursuit of fame drives Mr Trump, as shown by his willingness to meet Mr Putin and Mr Xi on their terms. It is why his presidency will be long remembered, just not as he wishes.

articles.title: Anthropic’s giant IPO puts the heat on OpenAI
articles.deck: Coding agents are big business. But what comes next?

paragraphs.text: You could forgive OpenAI’s bosses for feeling miffed. Their release of ChatGPT four years ago set the artificial-intelligence boom in motion. Before long countless chatbot imitators had emerged, but none has caught up in popularity. By last year OpenAI’s annual revenue had reached $13bn—then nearly triple that of its arch-rival, Anthropic (see chart).

And yet it is Anthropic, founded by OpenAI secessionists, that has raised the largest sum of all time through an initial public offering (IPO), with a total haul of $107bn. Before trading began on November 19th, after we went to press, the firm was worth $1.5trn, topping the $1.3trn at which the still unlisted OpenAI was valued in a recent private fundraising round.

OpenAI may have led the first phase of competition among model-makers, based around chatbots, but Anthropic trounced it in the second, where coding agents became the biggest source of business. Usage of Claude Code, Anthropic’s software-writing bot, has rocketed this year. As a result, Goldman Sachs, the lead investment bank on the AI company’s IPO, expects it to pull in $53bn of revenue in 2026, more than ten times the figure of a year before and comfortably ahead of OpenAI, which expects $35bn (though direct comparisons are tricky, as Anthropic registers all sales through cloud partners as revenue, whereas OpenAI strips out the share it pays to them).

Still, the past few years show how quickly leads can be lost in the fast-evolving AI market. Use of OpenAI’s own programming tool, Codex, has grown rapidly in recent months. More important, with both model-makers hunting for their next big source of revenue, a new phase in the competition looks set to begin. Anthropic and OpenAI are eagerly pushing to expand the use of agents into all corners of knowledge work. But OpenAI is also betting on a number of other means of monetising its technology. Which strategy will win?

Both firms are counting on blistering growth in the years ahead to justify their valuations. Goldman Sachs projects that Anthropic’s annual revenue will hit $636bn in 2030; William Blair, an investment bank not working on the IPO, forecasts $414bn. OpenAI, for its part, recently told investors it was shooting for $446bn in 2030.

Having lost ground to its main rival, OpenAI has lately been picking up the pace. Last week it told investors that revenue from its enterprise sales doubled in the third quarter compared with the preceding three months, helped by price discounts intended to undercut Anthropic.

For the pair, however, enterprise spending remains concentrated. Revenue from agents currently adheres to an “extreme power law”, says one Anthropic investor. The biggest customers contribute an unusually high share of sales, and the heaviest users within those companies—who are nearly always software engineers—are behind much of the spending.

That poses a risk if these users switch to cheaper models, as many have begun to do. But it also suggests that there is still plenty of scope to extend adoption. This year Anthropic and OpenAI have both rolled out general-purpose enterprise agents that non-coders can use to perform a wide variety of tasks. And in addition to working with the consulting giants, the model-makers have set up their own independent advisory businesses, with private-equity backing, to help customers deploy their technology. A person familiar with Anthropic’s Ode, which is supported by Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman, says that more than half of the clients it has helped to redesign their processes have boosted their profits by at least $10m. Last month Anthropic established a separate consulting venture with Hg, another private-equity firm, focused on Europe.

Aaron Levie, chief executive of Box, a cloud-storage company that works with both AI labs, says that having “the right kind of product experiences with the right sales efforts” could prove even more important than having the best models. Even so, the models will still matter—and here Anthropic holds a clear lead. Investors in both firms reckon performance on “long-horizon” tasks that take several hours or even days—such as building an app from scratch—will become increasingly important for the frontier labs as businesses make greater use of less capable models for simpler work to keep costs down. On MirrorCode, one long-horizon benchmark, OpenAI’s leading model, released last month, is still outperformed by the top offering from Anthropic as far back as July.

That may reflect Anthropic’s more specialised research programme. Whereas OpenAI has sought to remain at the frontier across a wide range of capabilities, including image and voice, Anthropic has focused on the ability of its models to write code and interact with other software.

That, in turn, highlights a difference in the strategies of the two. Although OpenAI has sought to regain ground in enterprise applications, the consumer segment remains a priority. ChatGPT has 1.2bn weekly users worldwide, almost 100m of whom pay upwards of $8 a month for a subscription. Even those who don’t pay provide OpenAI with revenue via the advertising business it launched in February, which by August had an annualised revenue of $1bn.

By contrast, Anthropic’s IPO prospectus barely mentions consumers. It has sworn off advertising, worrying it could muddy Claude’s ability to give helpful answers and incentivise the company to build addictive products.

That leaves OpenAI with a bigger addressable market. But its approach has drawbacks, too. In the consumer segment it must compete with Google, whose Gemini chatbot has gained ground over the past year, as well as personal agents such as Instinct and Meta’s Muse, which have beguiled users with their ability to take on tasks from arranging a dinner with friends to securing sold-out concert tickets.

OpenAI has deprioritised some efforts, shutting down its video-generation tool, Sora, in March. But it continues to pursue a strikingly broad set of opportunities. In the coming year it is expected to unveil a device—a small doughnut-shaped speaker—that consumers can use to interact with its AI systems. It is also developing a humanoid robot. The danger is that it spreads itself too thinly. Unlike Anthropic, which generated its first quarterly operating profit in the second three months of this year, OpenAI remains deep in the red. It will need to follow its rival into the public markets as soon as it can.

articles.title: Nvidia’s roaring results can’t hide its troubles
articles.deck: Jensen Huang’s departure will cause lasting damage

paragraphs.text: In certain respects it was like any Nvidia earnings call over the past few years. The chipmaker reported yet another quarter of blistering growth, notching up revenue of $116bn for the three months to October, more than double the figure from a year before. Operating profit soared at an even faster rate.

And yet the call on November 17th was unlike any in Nvidia’s history—for it was the first without Jensen Huang, who until a few days before had been the only person to run the company since it was founded three decades ago. Mr Huang’s resignation as chief executive late on November 11th, following revelations of affairs with a suspected Chinese agent and at least one subordinate, shook the company and its investors. Analysts dialling in were barred from inquiring about the circumstances surrounding his departure, and Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chair, said little about the process to choose a new boss (other than that the board had no intention of allowing Mr Huang to stage the comeback he is seeking). Instead, Colette Kress, Nvidia’s finance chief and interim boss, stuck largely to the numbers.

That will not be enough to dispel worries among investors that Nvidia’s outlook is less rosy without its superstar founder in charge. Although the firm’s share price perked up briefly after the call, it soon retreated, and is down by more than a tenth since Mr Huang’s departure. He played an outsize role in every facet of Nvidia—from its technical wizardry and carefully orchestrated supply chain to its charm offensive in Washington. How diminished will the company be without him?

Even before Mr Huang’s exit, the threats to Nvidia were mounting. Since the release of ChatGPT in late 2022 it has generated $300bn in free cashflow thanks to its AI chips, and seen its market value increase ten times over. But its share price has lagged behind the semiconductor industry since the start of this year (see chart 1). Rivals have been closing in. In simulations by Epoch AI, a research group, the newest chip designed by AMD outperforms Nvidia’s best when measured by the number of simultaneous requests they can handle (see chart 2). Google, a big Nvidia customer, has also developed high-performing AI processors, and is peddling these to others.

The dominance of Nvidia’s software layer, known as CUDA, has been eroding, too. It is widely used by model-makers and operates only on Nvidia’s silicon, which has helped keep customers locked in. Yet Anthropic and OpenAI have lately been making greater use of chips from AMD, Google and others, helped by the very models the labs are developing, which make it easier to rewrite chunks of code to run on other chips.

Mr Huang’s departure will accentuate Nvidia’s problems. For now, the company has plenty of momentum. Nvidia’s order backlog probably stretches into 2028, and on its earnings call the company raised its revenue forecast for the year ahead. It has secured hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of output from its suppliers, including for scarce high-bandwidth memory. And its engineers already have technical roadmaps in place for the next few versions of its chips.

Even so, Nvidia faces immediate challenges. One source of trouble could come from within the company itself. It is unclear how long it will take the board to appoint a successor. Whoever takes over is almost certain to restructure the top team; Mr Huang had some 60 executives reporting to him directly. As a result, the company risks an extended period of in-fighting and talent flight. A senior employee has already written to the board to warn of the loss of “irreplaceable talent” if Mr Huang is not reinstated.

Geopolitics will be another source of immediate trouble. America has long tried to limit the number of cutting-edge chips that end up in Chinese hands. In light of the spying scandal that has engulfed Mr Huang, export controls look set to tighten further. On November 16th the Commerce Department announced new rules requiring data-centre operators in a number of countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, to obtain a licence before buying advanced AI chips, in order to prevent remote access being sold to Chinese companies. America’s legislature is considering a handful of laws aimed at further controlling chip sales abroad. Timothy Arcuri of UBS, a bank, reckons that these kinds of rules could endanger a tenth of Nvidia’s revenue. And a merry-go-round of investigations into whether the company has ignored or even aided chip smuggling (which it denies) will add to the distraction.

Other threats to Nvidia from the departure of Mr Huang will take longer to bite. His personal relationships were vital in helping the company forge its supply chain. Nvidia is particularly dependent on TSMC, a chip manufacturer from Mr Huang’s native Taiwan. The ties he cultivated with it over decades have recently played a decisive role in ensuring Nvidia secures the supply it needs amid a shortage of production capacity for cutting-edge chips. The erstwhile boss also seems to have nabbed better deals than his rivals. SemiAnalysis, a research firm, estimates that Nvidia buys high-bandwidth memory from SK Hynix, a South Korean supplier, at a roughly 20% discount compared with rivals such as AMD. Such coups have boosted Nvidia’s margins, and may be hard for his replacement to replicate.

Many of Nvidia’s customers may also come to struggle as a result of his departure. With the cloud-computing giants increasingly turning to custom silicon, Mr Huang had been fostering an alternative ecosystem of “neoclouds” to diversify its customer base. Nvidia has invested in them directly, and offered other forms of financial backing, such as guaranteeing that it will buy their excess capacity if demand falls short. By one analyst’s estimate, neoclouds may make up as much as a quarter of Nvidia’s revenue. Many expect that Ms Kress will be more cautious in bankrolling them. The share prices of five listed neoclouds have fallen by an average of 20% since Mr Huang’s resignation. Developers of open-source AI, an approach enthusiastically backed by Nvidia’s former boss, will also be feeling nervous.

Nvidia’s leather-jacketed boss was undoubtedly a visionary. He was early to spot the potential for Nvidia’s chips to be used in AI, and for years he invested in CUDA despite mounting losses and grumblings from Wall Street. The company he built, and many others that rely on it, will feel his loss. Its rivals will be rubbing their hands with glee.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s fall is bad news for Silicon Valley’s accelerationists
articles.deck: Already their movement was on the back foot

paragraphs.text: For the “accelerationists” in Silicon Valley—who are eager to ensure artificial intelligence continues developing at breakneck speed—the fall of Jensen Huang is a heavy blow. Nvidia’s boss was the movement’s most credible spokesperson. In one of his final interviews before his resignation, Mr Huang decried the “alarmist” voices stoking anxiety over the technology’s pace of improvement, and argued against regulating AI.

Fellow accelerationists—among them Elon Musk, boss of SpaceX; Martin Casado, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz; and Garry Tan, head of Y Combinator—have been among the loudest voices calling for Mr Huang’s return. Already the group had taken a beating in the midterm elections, which will soon elevate dozens of AI-sceptics to power. The landmark listing of Anthropic, an AI lab that calls at every opportunity for regulation, lest its work end humanity, is yet another setback. All this has given jitters to the open-source AI community, which has benefited from the support of the accelerationists.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s monotone interim boss, is unlikely to imitate her predecessor’s fiery opposition to AI “doomers”. Mr Huang publicly bemoaned their talk of “science-fiction outcomes” and hinted at unspecified “ulterior reasons” for spreading fear; of Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s boss, he said they disagreed on “almost everything”. Mr Huang’s opinions found sympathetic ears in the White House. He grew close with Donald Trump over the past two years, with the president stating on November 16th that he “would not mind” Mr Huang being reinstated.

That looks unlikely, creating nervousness in the open-source AI community. It was already on edge over growing calls for American firms to be banned from using free Chinese models. In July Mr Huang came out against that effort, with Nvidia and more than 230 other organisations signing a letter urging the government to avoid “premature restrictions”. Whether Nvidia “will continue to aggressively promote the development of this ecosystem” in Mr Huang’s absence is an “open question”, says Anastasios Angelopoulos, boss of Arena, a platform for ranking AI models.

Mr Huang’s support for open-source AI went beyond policy statements. He was also one of its biggest funders, using Nvidia’s cash to invest in and acquire companies in the field. In September Nvidia said it would buy Hugging Face, a library of open-source models, for $12.9bn. It has also invested in Reflection and Thinking Machine Labs, two makers of open-source models, and developed a line of its own, called Nemotron.

Commercial logic may lead Nvidia to continue its support for the approach. On this week’s earnings call, Ms Kress said that the company remained “committed to fostering a vibrant open-model ecosystem”. Whether it will continue investing at the same pace is less clear. Ms Kress noted that the company was “rigorously evaluating” future investments.

Still, others in Silicon Valley would welcome a steadier pace. Daniel Yanisse, boss of Checkr, which offers AI-powered background checks, says he and many of his peers are ready for some deceleration, arguing that it would give more time for the technology to demonstrate real value without the pressure created by the accelerationists, who promise an imminent utopian future. People who are “actually busy running companies, not spending their day on X, don’t really believe in that”.

articles.title: Trump Inc is in free fall
articles.deck: Investors are souring on anything with ties to the president and his family

paragraphs.text: DEMOCRATS LOVE to point out the vast wealth the Trump clan has accumulated over the past two years. “While Donald Trump and his family enrich themselves, the American family is struggling,” said Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House of Representatives’ oversight committee, in a video after the recent midterm elections. Among Mr Garcia’s priorities is to uncover the many ways in which the first family has cashed in.

For the Trumps, however, the good times may already have ended. A basket compiled by The Economist of the stocks of 13 companies with ties to the family is down by more than half since the start of the year, having fallen precipitously in the past few months (see chart). Shares in Trump Media and Technology Group, the parent company of Truth Social, have shed 70%. Those of Dominari Holdings, an investment group that two of his sons, Donald junior and Eric, together own more than a tenth of, have lost 80%. GrabAGun, a firearms marketplace on whose board Donald junior sits, has also tanked, as has Mixed Martial Arts Group, a combat-sports operator he advises. As the family’s political fortune has turned, its ability to monetise the presidency has waned.

For a time investors lapped up almost anything with ties to the Trumps. Between the autumn of 2024 and the week before Inauguration Day in January 2025, the value of Trump Media more than tripled. Shares in Dominari Holdings jumped when the Trumplets signed on in 2025.

Juicy profits were also to be found outside the stock market. Over the past two years 1789 Capital, a venture-capital firm in which Donald junior is a partner, has acquired stakes in many of the world’s hottest startups, including Anduril, a drone-maker, Polymarket, a betting site, and SpaceX, a rocketry business that in June went public at an astronomical valuation. 1789 Capital reportedly went from managing a mere $150m in assets in 2024 to $3.5bn this year.

Add to that the family’s lucrative forays into crypto. As of January 2026 the Trumps had pocketed more than $2.2bn from $TRUMP, a meme coin, and other crypto activities, according to one estimate by congressional Democrats.

Yet sentiment has now shifted decisively against the president and his offspring. $TRUMP has lost 80% of its value since the start of the year. 1789 Capital appears to have stopped writing cheques in recent weeks. Kalshi, a competitor to Polymarket, dropped Donald junior as an adviser shortly after the midterms. Trump Media may soon face a financing crunch: from the end of this month investors will be entitled to demand repayment on a $1bn convertible bond it issued in 2025 to buy bitcoin.

Do not fret, for the Trumps will remain a wealthy lot. ProPublica, an investigative-news outlet, estimates that the president owns assets worth at least $2.5bn, including through his sprawling property empire as well as his stakes in big listed companies such as Alphabet, Apple and—less profitably of late—Nvidia. Nevertheless, for a president so keenly attuned to the stock market, the tumbling value of Trump Inc will surely sting.

articles.title: The global south’s smartphone king goes big on AI
articles.deck: Faced with stiffening competition and rising costs, Transsion plans its next act

paragraphs.text: On the streets of Nairobi, smartphones branded Tecno, Infinix or itel are a common sight. The sleek devices are all made by Transsion, a Chinese company that is the biggest phone-seller in the global south by volume. Last year it shifted 170m handsets, roughly two-thirds as many as Apple. In Africa more than half of phones purchased are Transsion devices.

The company has thrived by making phones at scale, tailored in price and design to its chosen markets. But with competition intensifying and the artificial-intelligence boom pushing up the cost of semiconductors, it must do more. So it is venturing into new products—and making its own bet on AI.

Transsion’s success has rested on three pillars. First, unlike many of its Chinese rivals, it went global early. Transsion’s founder first started doing business in Africa in the 2000s, and when he set up his current company in 2013 the continent was its focus. A few years later it expanded into India and South-East Asia. Today it sells handsets in over 100 countries through a vast web of 2,900 distributors, helped by ties with local telecoms providers.

Second is the tailoring. Transsion’s handsets typically cost less than a tenth as much as an iPhone, making them attractive to customers with little money to spend on a device. They are also designed to suit local needs. For Africa, where power outages are frequent, Transsion has focused on long battery life and speedy charging. It has also developed “sweat-resistant” USB ports that better cope with the hot climate. For gaming-mad South-East Asia, it has developed cooling cases, sold as a separate accessory. (The company’s built-in gaming app has 140m monthly users.)

Third is scale. Transsion makes about 40% of its smartphones in six factories of its own (four in China, one each in Bangladesh and Ethiopia) and outsources the rest to 17 contractors, mostly in China. Thanks in part to this hybrid set-up, the phone-maker has proved nimble, taking four to eight months to develop its smartphones.

The strategy had been working well. Revenue grew by 170% from 2019, the year it listed its shares in Shanghai, to 2024 (see chart). But since then it has stagnated. Since April 2024 the firm’s share price has fallen by roughly half.

In its newer markets, Transsion has encountered stiffer competition, including from global giants. In Brazil, Latin America’s biggest smartphone market, which Transsion entered in 2021, Samsung is pushing fancier devices with agentic AI. In the first half of 2026 the South Korean firm’s shipments to the country were 10% higher than a year earlier, while those of Infinix, Transsion’s main brand in Brazil, fell by 24%, according to Counterpoint Research, a firm of analysts.

Rising chip costs—a problem across the industry—are also biting. Memory chips accounted for nearly half the cost of making Transsion’s products in the first four months of the year, up from a fifth in 2023. The share has probably risen further since then. As a result, the company has jacked up handset prices, which has shielded its gross margin but caused a decline in the volume of smartphone sales in the first half of the year. Users are holding on to older devices for longer.

In response to these twin problems, Transsion is branching out. It is now selling customers not only smart watches, earbuds and kitchen appliances, but also energy-storage products, including portable battery modules, and even two- and three-wheeler electric vehicles. That may sound like a stretch, but in the global south consumers often stick to familiar brands, and it helps that Transsion’s operating systems are integrated across its products. Sales of products other than handsets made up 16% of revenue in the first half of 2026, double the share two years earlier.

But Transsion’s biggest long-term bet is on AI. Last month it raised $390m in a Hong Kong stock-market listing; it plans to use two-fifths of that to work on AI models and applications. Already some of its devices incorporate digital assistants and other AI features. The business is also collaborating with Chinese research institutions to work on things such as visual foundation models and voice recognition. A fifth of its employees are engaged in research and development. As Transsion transitions to AI, there will be plenty for them to do.

articles.title: The world’s carmakers are revving up in America
articles.deck: Donald Trump’s policies are only part of the explanation

paragraphs.text: America’s car market, like the pickups that are the profit engine of Detroit’s “Big Three”, is large, reliably solid and a bit old-fashioned. As global carmakers struggle in China against the onslaught by domestic electric-vehicle (EV) firms, and lose sales to them elsewhere, America’s market looks attractive. A growing list of carmakers are laying plans to boost manufacturing there. President Donald Trump may claim that his policies are the reason why. But other forces are also at work.

To be sure, the administration’s tariffs on imported vehicles have played a role. A desire to avoid them, and then hide behind a protectionist wall, partly explains the understated unveiling on November 9th by Honda of a $3bn investment in a factory in Ohio. Other plans have been revealed with more show. Gernot Döllner, boss of Audi, appeared at a campaign rally with Mr Trump shortly before this month’s midterm elections to trumpet a $4bn factory in Georgia. The stunt did little to help Republican candidates, who suffered at the polls. And it earned Mr Döllner an ear-bashing from politicians and unions back home in Germany. But the new plant should help Audi.

“Establishing a local manufacturing presence would bring us closer to American customers, strengthen our competitiveness and make our global business more resilient,“ Mr Döllner says. As part of the deal, Audi hopes as well to negotiate reduced levies on car imports, which cost it $1.4bn in 2025. American factories also give carmakers a hedge against uncertainty over the usmca, America’s free-trade deal with Canada and Mexico. Relying on lower-cost Mexican plants to supply the American market is far more risky while tariff-free access remains unsure.

Hyundai, Toyota and Mercedes-Benz have also announced big investments over the past year or so. In May Stellantis, which is struggling in Europe, promised that of the €36bn ($40bn) earmarked for its brands in its five-year investment plan, 60% would go to North America. (The carmaker’s biggest shareholder, Exor, part-owns The Economist’s parent company).

Mr Trump might also brag about turning Americans against evs by removing subsidies and rolling back emissions standards. As the rest of the world goes electric, the chance to sell more profitable gas-guzzlers for longer in America is a big draw for carmakers labouring to meet EV targets elsewhere. Where Bloombergnef, a research group, once reckoned EVs would make up 48% of American sales by 2030, it now puts the figure at 17%.

America, in other words, is going its own way. In September Antonio Filosa, Stellantis’s boss, said of car markets: “One is the United States…and then we have the rest of the world.” Yet the country would be alluring even without the actions of Mr Trump—and Audi’s and Honda’s factories are not due to start production until after he has left the White House. Carmakers decided on the scale, if not the location, of their investments several years ago. Since then the rout of foreign carmakers in China and fierce competition in a sluggish European market have made America the only choice, says Tu Le of Sino Auto Insights, a Detroit-based consultancy.

America is an enduringly big and lucrative place. Even if sales look unlikely to grow much in the coming years, competition from Chinese EVs is kept out by 100% tariffs (introduced by Joe Biden). And America has further attractions. As Mr Döllner notes, it is “one of the world’s most important premium car markets”. Profit margins for upmarket cars are typically fat. Soaring fuel costs (for which Mr Trump modestly refuses to take credit) have popularised hybrid vehicles, which are more profitable than petrol equivalents and where Japanese and South Korean carmakers such as Toyota and Hyundai are leaders. Sales of these should grow by 6% a year to 2033, far outpacing the market as a whole, says Bernstein, a broker.

Yet carmakers should beware. Retreating from global competition risks complacency, as America’s domestic firms discovered in the 1980s. In the end, they were punished for turning out shoddy, expensive vehicles by the competitors that trade restrictions couldn’t keep out for ever.

articles.title: Just how central should one person be to an organisation?

paragraphs.text: IT has not been a great few days for the idea of “founder mode”. The term was coined by Paul Graham, an essayist and venture capitalist, but the concept came from Brian Chesky, the founder of Airbnb. Mr Chesky gave a speech in 2024 laying out his belief that founders mistakenly delegate too much authority to managers below them as their firms grow bigger. He proposed a much more hands-on approach in which they dive relentlessly into the details, set the tempo of the company and make it clear where everyone should be focused. Instead of silos, a shared sense of purpose; instead of a leader insulated from the work, someone steeped in it.

Until a few days ago, this argument was strengthened by the example of Jensen Huang. The erstwhile boss of Nvidia had presided over an extraordinary success story, and had his tentacles everywhere. He flattened the organisation: around 60 people reported to him directly. He hoovered up information, by encouraging everyone in the chipmaker to send him emails about what was on their minds. He eschewed one-to-one meetings, arguing that it was better for lots of people to hear what he thought. He, and his wretched leather jacket, embodied the firm.

How could one person manage to be across so much, he was sometimes asked. I do nothing but work, he would say. Well, not exactly. Mr Huang’s energy levels were even more impressive than people imagined. His abrupt downfall after an affair with an alleged Chinese agent, and subsequent campaigning for reinstatement, raise questions about whether one person should ever be so essential to a big organisation.

Whether founder mode makes sense depends partly on how far the idea is taken. An all-in bet on the sustained genius of a single individual is always going to entail risks. But some of the precepts of founder mode are benign. In a new bonus episode of “Boss Class”, The Economist’s podcast on management, recorded before Mr Huang’s resignation, Mr Chesky describes his role at Airbnb as being akin to an editor’s. He reviews much of the work at Airbnb himself, using meetings with people several levels down the firm.

Whether a chief executive is a founder or a salaried manager, there is a lot to be said for this “skip-level” approach. Employees usually respond well to the chance to spend time with the boss. People waste ludicrous amounts of time second-guessing CEOs; it is often more efficient just to hear from them directly. And it’s good for bosses to see the quality of the people down the organisation. A ubiquitous chief executive does risk micromanagement and disempowerment, but layers of bureaucracy have drawbacks, too.

A study by Tristan Fitzgerald of Texas A&M University looked at what happens when founder CEOs either die or suffer serious illness, and have to be suddenly replaced by a professional manager. By comparing firms that go through this kind of abrupt transition with similar firms that continue to be led by founders, Mr Fitzgerald concludes that each type of manager brings distinctive skills. The switch to a professional chief executive means less internal innovation, more dealmaking, more leverage and more decentralised management structures. The financial performance between the two groups of firms in this particular study was a wash, but the way they made money was different.

Concentration of power brings more volatility with it, though this too can have upsides as well as downsides. In a paper published in 2001 Renée Adams of the University of Oxford and her co-authors found that the degree of centralisation in a firm (measured by, among other things, whether the chief executive was a founder and whether there was an independent chairman) was correlated with variability in corporate performance. The smaller the number of people exercising power inside a firm, in other words, the more likely it is that their decisions will have extreme consequences, for good and bad.

Perhaps the truest test of founder mode comes after the founder has gone. That’s not just when it becomes clear whether there is any sort of succession plan; it’s also when it is revealed whether a firm has been developing a culture or a cult. An omnipotent founder can make companies dependent on them, or they can instil values and standards designed to survive their own tenure. Businesses like Apple and Disney still bear the imprint of their long-gone creators. What will Nvidia stand for without Mr Huang in charge?
Step inside the world of work with our Bartleby newsletter. Each week our white-collar oracle muses on the agonies of office life.
