articles.title: Corporate spin-offs are getting out of control
articles.deck: Some are enormously successful, but certainly not all

paragraphs.text: No boss wishes they ran a smaller company. That’s why spin-offs, where a division of a firm becomes a free-standing enterprise, are considered victories of reason; of focus over sprawl; and of shareholders over managers. Spin-offs often take place under pressure from activist investors. Stock analysts delight in the simplicity of the cleaved companies, and hedge-fund traders in the complexity of the separation. Buying spun-out shares is a foolproof strategy, wrote one investor, Joel Greenblatt, in “You Can Be a Stock Market Genius”. The book is dedicated to his wife and their “three magnificent spin-offs”.

The market is filled with companies that are said to illustrate the virtues of a big spin. GE Vernova, a descendant of the industrial conglomerate, has a years-long backlog of orders for its gas turbines. A second great shortage caused by the artificial-intelligence build-out has vindicated a second great spin: Sandisk, which makes memory chips, was carved out last year. One half of the first big merger in the AI supply chain is a corporate division spun-good: Lumentum, which makes lasers and has agreed to combine with chip-designer Marvell, is worth about $50bn—seven times as much as its erstwhile parent. Thanks to such superstars, the spin-off index has heartily outperformed the market.

To understand an age, examine its spin-offs. In the early 2020s few things were considered more toxic than skinny models and coal mining. Victoria’s Secret was liberated from Bath & Body Works, a soap-seller, in 2021. (The lingerie brand has thrived since.) Energy firms raced to sell their dirtiest assets, with Anglo American hiving off its South African coal (that, too, has excelled). Today firms are more likely to part with assets they hope the market will adopt as AI darlings. Flex, an American engineering firm, will soon carve out its data-centre business. The biggest listing in Hong Kong next year will probably be a spin-off of Alibaba’s chipmaking unit.

But the very largest spin-offs are ones that allow bosses to reclaim past exuberance as present sobriety. Like clockwork, the biggest mergers of 2018 are becoming the biggest spin-offs of today. CVS, a health-care giant, plans to separate its pharmacy business in the next 18 months, undoing the giant merger it undertook less than a decade ago. One big media tie-up of 2018, Comcast’s acquisition of Sky, will soon be unwound by carving out the European broadcaster alongside NBCUniversal. The spin-off is always the first idea of a mogul who is short of them. In Hollywood, the result is such titles as “The Mandalorian and Grogu”, the latest Star Wars flick. In New York, it is the equally unappealing “Versant”, a collection of cable-TV networks including CNBC and the Golf Channel, which Comcast separated out earlier this year. Neither has received a particularly warm reception.

Spin-offs take years. And like celebrity divorces they can be costly, unflattering and drawn-out affairs. Assets are hardly ever neatly divided. Whom to burden with a firm’s debt is often a contentious issue. So is management. Another 2018-vintage merger soon to be undone is that of Keurig, a coffee-giant, and Dr Pepper, which makes fizzy drinks. Last month the firm unveiled the new boss of “Global Coffee Co.”—the third announced chief executive of a company that doesn’t yet exist. One of the worst deals of 2018 was the tie-up of Bayer, a German drugs giant, and Monsanto, an American crop-science business which has been sued over allegations that Roundup, a weedkiller it sells, causes cancer (it denies this). The recent ring-fencing of Bayer’s Roundup division has analysts speculating that it will lead to yet another mega-spin.

If a spin-off fails there is a simple solution: more spin-offs. During the past decade the market has shown an endless capacity to disassemble industrial conglomerates until they either emerge as healthy businesses or become so small that investors stop caring. General Electric is the great poster child for spin-off success: its three divisions have done so well that the market has even allowed them to start buying other businesses again.

Things have gone less smoothly at Honeywell, which was chopped into five publicly traded firms now worth a combined $140bn (little more than in 2018, before the break-up began). Shares in its aerospace unit have sunk 40% since they were listed in June. Resideo, a smaller, residual part of the conglomerate, was further split into two pieces in August—turning the Honeywell five into six. Solstice, another Honeywell alumnus, attempted, and swiftly abandoned, a merger this summer. Since then an activist pitched up demanding that the spin-off stick to its knitting.

The experience of other ex-conglomerates is closer to Honeywell than to General Electric. The result is a dizzying state of infinite spin. You can imagine an industrial boss tied to a chair while shareholders slowly cut off limbs, shouting at him to “Focus!”. One heir to 3M, which was split up in 2024, said this summer that it also would become two. DowDuPont, which broke in three in 2019 in one of the most complicated deals ever, recently became five: Corteva, another chemicals business beset by lawsuits, shed its seed business in October.

The great powers of European industry have been divided into even smaller territories with even stranger names. Siemens, a German one, has birthed both Siemens Healthineers and Siemens Energy (soon the latter will be re-christened “Omterra”). Both have recently announced further breakups of their own. As the spins become smaller, their names become more abstract. ThyssenKrupp, another shattered German, controls both the listed, lower-case “nucera”, which it spun out in 2023, and “accelis”, which went last month. There’s no end to the complexity created in the name of corporate simplicity.

articles.title: America does not produce world-beating statistics. Who does?
articles.deck: We search for the world’s worst—and best—economic data

paragraphs.text: When King Ariantas wanted to find out how many people lived in ancient Scythia, his approach to people not answering surveys was brutally simple. According to Herodotus, a Greek historian, Ariantas ordered each Scythian to bring him an arrowhead on pain of death. As the king totted up his arrowheads, he could not be sure that everybody had complied, but woe betide those that did not.

Modern-day statisticians would be forgiven for envying Ariantas’s powers of persuasion. Response rates to official surveys have collapsed globally. In America less than 40% of people reply to questions on consumer spending, down from more than 60% in 2016 (see chart 1). In Britain a paltry 27% reply to surveys about their work status. Bean-counters today also have to reckon with falling budgets, declining public trust and greater political interference. Only half of Americans have confidence in federal numbers. President Donald Trump did not help by sacking the head of America’s Bureau of Labour Statistics (BLS) in 2025, falsely claiming she had rigged a jobs report to make him look bad. Statisticians in Colombia, Poland and Slovenia have all been controversially fired in recent years.

Everyone should worry about the stats-pocalypse, not least because policy drawn up using junk statistics risks being junk itself. Central banks need reliable employment data to set interest rates. Many social benefits are linked to inflation, so if the numbers are wrong, payments will be stingier or more generous than intended. If American lawmakers had known in the last quarter of 2008 that GDP had fallen by more than 8%, at an annualised rate, rather than the initial estimate of 4%, they might have acted more boldly in the face of the global financial crisis. The rise of artificial intelligence makes this a dangerous time, since errors tend to get worse when the economy is changing fast.

Luckily, some places still produce numbers worth trusting. The World Bank compiles an annual index of statistical performance, measuring basic things like how frequently numbers are produced and whether they are available online. The quality of a country’s statistical system is, predictably, tied to how rich it is. Low-income countries have an average score of 56, compared with over 80 for high-income ones (see chart 2). Yet although the index does a good job of exposing the weakest performers, the variables it considers are too crude to separate out the best.

To identify the world’s positive statistical outliers, The Economist has devised four tests. The first is the simplest: a country must actually publish statistics, and publish them often. Many poorer countries fall at this hurdle. Lebanon has not held an official census since 1932, when it was under French rule; its politicians fear that counting heads now would reignite ethnic strife. India’s census was postponed in 2020 because of covid-19 but, much less reasonably, it has yet to be completed years after the pandemic ended. Even if it is by next year, as the government promises, that would leave an unacceptable gap of 16 years since the last one.

The second test is that, like Caesar’s wife, statistical offices must be beyond suspicion. That means political independence and transparency. Authoritarian states do badly on this measure. Luis Martínez, now at Emory University, used satellite data on night-time light usage as a proxy to verify whether authoritarian countries were overreporting GDP figures. His paper in 2022 found that they typically overstate yearly growth by about 35%. China is infamously tight-lipped about the workings behind its statistics. Many external observers think that the state massages the numbers, smoothing growth and understating unemployment in the world’s second-biggest economy.

Alarmingly, some rich democracies fail the independence test, too. America is the most depressing recent example. Mr Trump’s interference goes well beyond firing one senior civil servant. In August the Census Bureau published a politically motivated paper purporting to show that non-citizens had been voting illegally. Statisticians have warned that the report did not go through a proper internal peer review and contained serious errors. The federal government has stopped publishing a range of numbers, from gender and ethnicity splits in many surveys to the annual report on household food security. Some series were caught up in Mr Trump’s anti-woke crusade. Others suffered from cuts to agencies’ budgets; headcount at the BLS has fallen by 20% since 2024, and by nearly 40% in the team crunching agricultural statistics.

It is not enough to produce statistics frequently and without fear or favour. A good system also needs to consistently get the numbers right. Nobody thinks Britain’s Office for National Statistics (ONS) is a stooge for the prime minister. Yet the body’s reputation has taken a beating lately. Publication of its Labour Force Survey had to be suspended in 2023 because of low response rates. The Resolution Foundation, a think-tank, reckons the survey undercounted employment in early 2024 by about 1m people. Although the ONS is recovering its credibility, such basic errors rule it out for a spot on the podium.

Britain’s problems stem in part from its reliance on voluntary surveys. The quality of these has suffered in recent decades as people have stopped answering their phones and become less willing to fill out long forms. One solution is to make surveys mandatory. Responses rates in countries which do this, like Canada and Germany, remain much higher (see chart 3). A bigger prize still comes in greater use of administrative data, like tax records, which can provide a much more granular picture.

The gold standard is a population register, which lets the government track each citizen’s demographic details in real time using a unique ID number. If updated regularly and thoroughly, such tools reduce the uncertainty associated with surveying. They also enable incredibly sophisticated analysis, allowing statisticians to trace individuals through time. Academics feast on Scandinavian data, where population registers are the norm.

The top-tier of statistics agencies either keep population registers, like the Netherlands, Norway and Switzerland, or have developed innovative ways to link up administrative data, like Canada. This predictable group of rich, cohesive societies faces a final test: how well do they keep up with a fast-changing world? Counting the cars a factory churns out is easy; measuring amorphous economic activity like social-media content is not. AI models are improving so rapidly that statisticians struggle to work out how much price changes reflect inflation as opposed to higher-quality products. Diane Coyle of Cambridge University points out that statisticians are “temperamentally conservative” and like “continuity”. Being innovative is “quite the leadership challenge”.

Some countries are giving it a good go. Canada has used satellite imagery to work out which crops are growing on agricultural land. Switzerland has made it easy for machines to read its data and catalogued everything the government collects on a single, standardised platform. Even Britain, for all its trouble with core statistics, is pioneering ways to measure AI’s economic impact. Recognising that decades-old classifications of industries and the like cannot capture the effects of a genuinely new general-purpose technology, it is developing a new measure that covers the AI industry, from chips to apps.

Given that the best agencies all reliably produce reliable numbers, they are hard to rank on the first three criteria. But on adaptability and innovation, one country edges out the rest. The Netherlands’ Central Bureau of Statistics was using supermarket scanner data to collect food prices as far back as 2002 (it took Britain until this year to copy them). More recently it has developed a machine-learning model that scrapes text from businesses’ websites to determine which are AI companies.

The Dutch approach rests on a history of high trust. Because citizens have long consented to the state keeping a granular population register, the government is less reliant on official questionnaires, which suffer from low response rates (below 50% for the Dutch labour-force survey, compared with nearly 70% in America and over 90% in Germany). It has even scrapped the conventional census.

The biggest challenge for statistical offices in the coming years will be to experiment with AI, to link up data sets and to do this while reassuring the citizenry that it can be done without compromising privacy. This is tricky even for the Dutch. A long-running scandal over a rogue tax-authority algorithm that branded innocent child-benefit claimants as fraudsters dented confidence. Only 34% of Dutch people believe that the government will protect their personal information when using AI, according to a survey by the OECD club mostly of rich countries. To allay such worries, the Dutch authorities now log every time someone views an individual’s data, and the person in question can ask to see the log. Unlike King Ariantas, modern statisticians cannot threaten violence to get the people’s buy-in. They must earn it.

articles.title: Why startups still go public, eventually
articles.deck: Costly regulation is not a big deterrent to IPOs

paragraphs.text: AN AWKWARD fact about America’s stock markets is that two of the companies that have dictated their fortunes lately haven’t traded on them OpenAI has raised pots of money without deigning to list. (Its boss, Sam Altman, called doing so now “ill-advised” in September.) The other leading artificial-intelligence lab, Anthropic, made its debut on November 19th, at a valuation of around $1.5trn. But it first had to release a surreal 400-page prospectus warning investors that human existence, as well as their money, was at risk.

Listing can be a drag. Regulation, reporting requirements and “heightened public scrutiny” may be “driving companies from the public markets”, wrote Jamie Dimon, boss of JPMorgan Chase, a bank, a few years ago. In 1996 some 8,000 firms were listed in America. After decades of delistings, the number is now half that. Initial public offerings (IPOs) have grown scarcer. Between 1980 and 2000 an average of 310 firms went public each year. Between 2001 and 2025 the annual figure fell to 113.

The conventional explanation is that private markets, including venture capital and private equity, have become more dynamic even as public markets, with their brass bells and live tickers, have turned more cumbersome. Rules like the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) passed in 2002 require firms to keep oodles of documentation on their inner workings. Paul Atkins, America’s top securities regulator, blames such burdens for discouraging debutantes. He promises to “make IPOs great again”, including by exempting hundreds of firms from SOX’s stiffest strictures.

This conventional story contains holes, however. The alarming number of delistings ignores the impact of mergers. When two listed firms combine, the count of public firms falls, yet most of the underlying assets and operations remain. And when a listed firm buys an unlisted one, stock investors gain exposure to the acquired business. After adjusting for corporate marriages, the decline in American listings between 1996 and 2020 disappears, according to a paper by B. Espen Eckbo and Markus Lithell, two academics. The same is not true in other rich countries, where listings have fallen even after adjusting for mergers (see chart).

The costs of going public are real. But they do not look prohibitive. A study by Michael Ewens of Columbia University and co-authors looks at the decline since 2000 in private firms’ probability of listing. Regulatory burdens, they calculate, account for only 7% of that diminished probability. SOX alone barely registers.

The more likely culprit is abundant private capital, argues Ludovic Phalippou of Oxford University in a recent working paper. The point of the public markets is to let firms “aggregate” large amounts of capital from a wide investor base. But institutional investors have ploughed so much cash into America’s private markets that startups can now piece together hefty sums from a few big benefactors.

The abundance of capital has blurred the traditional public-private divide. Some finance houses speak of “private IPOs”. Private fundraising also lets early employees cash out some of their shares, reducing the urgency to list. The median age at which firms go public in America has risen from eight years in 1980-2000 to 11 years in 2001-25. SpaceX was a 20-something company before listing this year at a valuation of $1.8trn.

Another perk of privacy is that cash-burning startups can raise repeated rounds of money in quick succession, a “pattern of financing that public markets handle poorly”, as Mr Phalippou points out. Between October 2024 and March 2026 OpenAI raised $170bn in three funding rounds, each bigger than the last. By contrast, public companies must fork over steep fees to investment banks and endure the scrutiny of the markets, which often register displeasure when firms say they need more capital. When Alphabet announced it would issue $80bn in fresh equity in June, its share price fell by 4% the next day, wiping $170bn off its market capitalisation.

Despite the growth of private markets, they are still dwarfed by their public rivals. Preqin, a data firm, calculates that the assets tucked away in North America’s private markets are now worth almost $8.5trn (including private credit). That is a big number. But it is equivalent to just 12% of the size of America’s stock markets. The public markets are still the biggest ball in town. Almost everyone who is anyone shows up eventually. The debutantes just tend to be older and richer before they make their entrance.

articles.title: Does Donald Trump care about the economy?
articles.deck: His economic advisers have gone missing after a bruising midterm defeat

paragraphs.text: ELECTIONS, IN DEMOCRACIES, are a good time to complain. In America’s midterms voters made their disgust with the economy clear. Hamburgers cost too much, and nobody wants to “pick another protein”. Filling up a pickup for a trip to Walmart is painfully dear, and bombing the ayatollahs does little to cheer up Kansans. After such a drubbing, surely Donald Trump’s economic team would come up with some sort of plan?

Or not. His economic advisers have mostly gone missing, raising the question of who—if anyone—is advising the president on the economy. Scott Bessent, treasury secretary and de facto economic czar, has had little to say about Americans’ economic woes (and was recently moved to a military base following Iranian threats). Kevin Hassett, who runs the National Economic Council, the White House’s economic nerve centre, was reported to be eyeing the exit (he denies it). Susie Wiles, Mr Trump’s chief of staff and conduit to American business, has been replaced.

Lame-duck presidents often pivot to foreign affairs, and Mr Trump is getting an early start touring Asia. He has installed Stephen Miller, an immigration zealot not known for his economic chops, as chief of staff. Mr Miller’s first orders routed policy decisions through Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, and Caleb Orr, a former aide. The National Economic Council went conspicuously unmentioned. Mr Bessent, whose portfolio extends from tackling inflation to crippling Iran’s economy and negotiating with China, also seems preoccupied with happenings abroad. In August he declared an “economic D-Day” against Iran, which has amounted to little. Americans awaiting a plan for higher living standards have heard rather less.

To the extent Mr Trump has an economic team, it is busy fighting itself. Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, is in the thick of it. Trade talks with Canada were nearing a deal over the summer under Jamieson Greer, the trade representative, before Mr Lutnick intervened and a deal collapsed. Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, noted that his own team had remained united. “You cannot say that about the United States administration.” Mr Bessent has also taken aim at Mr Lutnick, most recently blaming his department for lax policing of rules on AI-chip exports.

The ranks are thinning, too. By August seven Senate-confirmed treasury officials had departed, compared with at most two at the same stage of the previous four administrations, according to the Partnership for Public Service, a watchdog. The department has lost over a quarter of its workforce; the Office of Management and Budget, a third. The Internal Revenue Service, the tax collector, lacks a commissioner.

The economic plan, such as it is, amounts to doubling down. Days after the shellacking in the midterms, Mr Hassett declared that “the policies are working”. On tariffs, which voters hate, there will be no retreat. Peter Navarro, the president’s trade guru, promised to “double and triple down on the economic policies that are working for American workers”.

That leaves Democrats an opening. Their “affordability” agenda, starting with cheaper health care, has galvanised voters. The president, meanwhile, seems more interested in attacking their plans than devising his own. The Council of Economic Advisers, supposedly the White House’s brain trust, has produced an unserious analysis showing that Democrats’ proposals would cost America $49trn over the next ten years. The incoming majority in Congress could not ask for a lower bar.

articles.title: Bond yields are rising everywhere—except China
articles.deck: The Chinese central bank has cut interest rates despite itself

paragraphs.text: CHINA’S STOCK MARKET has attracted attention this year for its, ahem, distinctive performance. One benchmark, the CSI 300, has lost about 14% in 2026, setting it apart from frothy markets in East Asia and beyond. And the stock market is not the only outlier in Chinese finance. The country’s bond market, the second-biggest in the world, also stands out. In contrast with tumbling prices and rising yields elsewhere, China’s bonds have rallied. Such is the demand for government debt that the yields on five- and ten-year bonds are at record lows (see chart).

Some see a world in the price of a bond. But safe securities mostly reflect bets on monetary policy. That makes China’s record-low yields all the more remarkable—for its central bank has made clear a reluctance to cut interest rates. In a recent article in Qiushi, a party journal, Pan Gongsheng, governor of the People’s Bank of China (PBoC), stressed the importance of keeping a lid on China’s public and private debts, which amount to more than 300% of GDP. The country, he said, must not let the volume of finance exceed the needs of the real economy. That could lead to “idle” funds and make it harder to “eliminate outdated production capacity”.

He also argued that the dramatic slowdown in credit growth was not a monetary-policy problem. It was, indeed, not a problem at all. It instead reflected the economy’s transition away from credit-intensive industries like property and infrastructure. These tend to raise a lot of money from banks, offering their land, bricks and mortar as collateral. In their place, growth was being driven by asset-light sectors, such as information-technology services, that rely on data, brands and human capital. Mr Pan compared an industry’s stock of credit (medium- or long-term loans) with the value that industry adds in a year. IT services owe about one yuan in loans for every ten yuan of value they add. The property sector owes 17 yuan and transport 33 yuan.

In its latest monetary-policy report, the PBoC also argues that interest rates are lower than they appear at first glance. Every economy has a gap between the bank’s policy rate and other key rates, such as the cost of mortgages or the yield on corporate bonds. In China this “spread” is narrower than elsewhere. Financial conditions that would require a near-zero policy rate in America can be achieved with a higher one in China, the central bank thinks. Mortgage rates, for example, are around 3% in China, not too far from the lows they reached in America during the covid-19 pandemic when the Federal Reserve’s policy rate was at rock bottom.

Instead of cutting its policy rate, the PBoC has reformed it. This month it officially adopted an overnight rate of 1.25% rather than its previous seven-day rate of 1.4%. On paper, the switch from one rate to another entailed no change in either. The central bank had previously provided overnight funds at 1.25% on an ad hoc basis, such as on the eve of holidays. But perhaps because these operations were sporadic, the overnight rate in the market was a bit higher than 1.25%. The reform has brought the two closer together, amounting to a de facto rate cut of about 0.1 percentage points, notes Adam Wolfe of Absolute Strategy Research, a consultancy.

This shift, and market anticipation of it, may be one reason why bond yields have fallen recently. The stock market’s woes may also have helped. Households, eager to rebuild their nest-eggs after the property slump, may have sought refuge in bond funds out of disappointment with stocks. Bonds and equities are, after all, supposed to move in opposite directions. That law of finance has proved unreliable in the West lately. But the old seesaw is still working in China. In this realm of finance, as in so many others, China may be an outlier.

articles.title: Meet the European Central Bank’s new squad
articles.deck: A Spaniard, a German and a Frenchwoman

paragraphs.text: SPAIN DOMINATES Europe’s biggest sport. It will soon boast the continent’s biggest economic player, too. Barring an injury-time upset, at a summit later this month European leaders will bless Pablo Hernández de Cos (pictured) as the next president of the European Central Bank. He has edged out Klaas Knot, former longtime governor of the Dutch central bank, to succeed Christine Lagarde, who is stepping down in February, nine months before her eight-year term expires.

The soft-spoken Mr Hernández de Cos, who currently heads the Bank for International Settlements, central banks’ central bank, is not quite the dovish southerner of cliché. True, like many others, he misjudged the post-pandemic inflation surge. He argued for moderate interest-rate increases and a swifter end to the hiking cycle. He also cautioned that any reductions in the ECB’s vast holdings of government bonds should be “very gradual and predictable” to avoid market disruption.

That may have endeared him to indebted Italy and France. They are probably less enamoured, though, of his stance on fiscal policy. In 2023 he clashed with the Spanish government over pension reform, which in his eyes did not do enough to close a yawning funding gap.

Given the precarious state of European finances, especially in France, pugnacity is a plus. A minus, compared with his recent predecessors, is inexperience in managing big crises. Ms Lagarde was France’s finance minister during the euro-zone debt crisis in the early 2010s. Mario Draghi, whom she succeeded at the ECB, led Italy’s central bank in that chaotic time.

This could bolster the influence of the bloc’s largest economies, Germany and France, amid any tumult. Their candidates will fill two other open positions at the ECB. Markus Brunnermeier, an academic heavyweight now at Princeton University, is the German pick for chief economist. His papers, straddling macroeconomics and finance, were required reading to understand the global financial crisis of 2007-09, observed Ben Bernanke, then chairman of the Federal Reserve. But as a carpenter’s son, who once planned to follow in his father’s footsteps, Mr Brunnermeier has broader interests and sensibilities.

The probable French appointee, Laurence Boone, is expected to take over from Isabel Schnabel, who oversees market operations, statistics and research (and will be joining the IMF). Helpfully, Ms Boone has experience in both the private and public sectors. Like Ms Schnabel before her, she is likely to use the research portfolio to challenge the chief economist and, in her market-operations hat, keep tabs on bond vigilantes. Mr Hernández de Cos will need his fanciest footwork to tackle his personnel and his paymasters.

articles.title: Europe tightens sanctions on Russia. America loosens them
articles.deck: The West’s sanctions regimes are pulling in opposite directions

paragraphs.text: ON OCTOBER 12TH corporate compliance officers across the West received a document guaranteed to ruin their week. Issued by the EU’s foreign-policy arm, the 948-page PDF, a format machines still sometimes struggle to read, added 1,646 Russia-linked people and firms to the bloc’s sanctions list, its largest single batch ever. Days earlier, and weeks ahead of midterm elections, Donald Trump had announced a deal to import Russian diesel into America. He later waived some sanctions for foreign buyers of Russian fuel. Europe, meanwhile, is doubling down. On November 16th it added another 144 entities to its blacklist, including 50 banks, shady oilmen and Russia’s richest woman.

America has historically led on sanctions, with Europe following. Co-ordination collapsed in 2018, when Mr Trump tore up the Iran nuclear deal, then returned in 2022, when Joe Biden’s administration tried to hobble Russia’s war effort arm in arm with European allies. Now the EU is running in front, notes Stephen Fallon, a former compliance boss who now advises banks. Mr Trump, lured by the Kremlin’s promises of diplomatic and commercial rewards, is backtracking. American officials have discussed several deals, such as the sale of a Russian oil giant’s international assets, resumption of Russian gas sales to Europe and sanctions relief for Russia’s sovereign-wealth fund.

Vincent Gaudel of LexisNexis, a data firm, calculates that so far this year the EU has added 2,794 names to its sanctions lists, more than America for the first time (see chart 1). Some 95% are Russia-linked, whereas America has removed more Russian entities than it has added (most of its new designations relate to Iran). The problem is that although international firms need things Europe controls—the euro, the SWIFT interbank-messaging system, insurance, shipping—European sanctions apparatus lacks speed, breadth and bite.

Start with the pace. Mr Trump can designate targets by executive order; the EU needs unanimity among its 27 members. Horse-trading delays decisions: a package timed for the Russian invasion’s anniversary on February 24th passed two months late. Powerful measures, such as a full maritime-services ban for tankers carrying Russian oil, remain stalled.

The EU requires the private sector to apply sanctions immediately, yet compliance often lags behind. Designations seem designed to confuse. The EU’s only consolidated database of targets is out of date. Most entity names in October’s record batch were copy-pasted from a list the Kremlin recently published as being part of the military complex. The batch gave no dates of birth or passport numbers for listed individuals, only a Russian tax-identification number that most European banks do not collect, notes Mr Gaudel. One entry runs to 21 mostly uninformative words (“Order of Lenin and Order of the Red Banner of Labour Research Institute for Synthetic Rubber named after Academician S.V. Lebedev”).

With no way to confirm a match, and heavier penalties for missing a listed person than for wrongly flagging an innocent one, banks use “fuzzy matching” software that flags any name close to a listed one. A customer whose name merely resembles one on the list can have payments held or an account frozen. Sophisticated mischief makers, meanwhile, may long since have moved their money to safer havens.

Lack of breadth is another weakness of European sanctions. They do not possess the extraterritorial reach that makes American ones potent. By design, they apply mostly to European people and firms, or to those doing business in the EU. European banks abide by American sanctions globally; American lenders tend to respect Brussels’ blacklists only for activities within the EU’s jurisdiction. Russia’s diesel exports have doubled since the summer, going not to America but to Brazil, Turkey and other countries the European embargo does not cover (see chart 2).

Lastly, Europe rarely punishes those who flout its edicts. Since 2009 American agencies have fined at least ten foreign and domestic banks $500m or more each for sanctions breaches (they have also gone after crypto and private-equity firms). European and British authorities have fined only a handful of lenders, and almost never for more than a few million euros. Enforcement is national, split among many regulators who answer to politicians with differing priorities and have few means to investigate non-compliance.

In theory, a Democrat-run Congress could realign America with Europe starting in January. In practice, those hoping for a swift snapback will almost certainly be disappointed. Although courts have rebuffed Mr Trump on tariffs, they have virtually never challenged the president’s power over sanctions, notes Adam Smith of Gibson Dunn, a law firm. And even if the Democrats may be able to persuade a few Republican Russia hawks in the Senate to pass a law curbing that power, it would take improbable two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override a likely presidential veto.

Bipartisan consensus could emerge for new laws targeting Russia’s energy industry or financial system, following one passed in September that lets the president impose tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian oil. The Senate counts few friends of Russia on either side of the aisle, says Edward Fishman of the Council on Foreign Relations, a think-tank. Given dissatisfaction with Mr Trump’s Russia record, new legislation would probably be written to prevent presidential discretion of the sort that enabled Mr Trump to waive sanctions on Russian diesel last month. But the executive would still have to enforce them, and few expect the president to have a change of heart. Ukraine may need to rely on Europe's flawed sanctions regime for a while yet.

articles.title: AI is swallowing maths. Is economics next?
articles.deck: The dismal science braces for disruption

paragraphs.text: IN 1930 JOHN MAYNARD KEYNES predicted that capital accumulation and technological progress would allow future generations to lead an affluent life of leisure. Keynes might not have foreseen the effect of accumulated capital and progress in technology on his intellectual descendants. After artificial-intelligence models solved hundreds of open problems in mathematics, the dismal science is bracing for unleisurely disruption. The angst may be less existential than among mathematicians, says Ben Golub, an economic theorist from Northwestern University. But AI is starting to change economics by cutting the cost of producing research. Will it also start eroding the human advantage in ideas?

The use of large language models is already pervasive. Stefanie Stantcheva of Harvard University, one of the editors of the prestigious Quarterly Journal of Economics (QJE), observes a change in the papers which are being submitted: “the figure format, some of the analysis, the more polished text”. In July about one in four working papers filed with the National Bureau of Economic Research, an American repository, contained AI-assisted writing, according to an analysis by Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham of the Yale School of Management. As papers become easier to write, some journals fear being inundated. The Journal of Political Economy (JPE), another top-tier outlet, will increase its submission fee to as much as $500 per paper in 2027 to discourage slop.

It is not just the prose. The analytical core of economics papers can increasingly be done by AI agents. David Yanagizawa-Drott of the University of Zurich has started a research programme dubbed Autonomous Policy Evaluation (APE). Like human economists before it, Dr Yanagizawa-Drott’s AI uses publicly available data to gauge the effect of policies. Among other things, it found that Switzerland’s ban on second homes substantially lowered investment in residential and commercial construction, and that Egypt’s large currency depreciation in 2016 affected consumer-good producers more than capital-goods makers.

Is agentic research any good? Dr Yanagizawa-Drott and his colleague, Olaf Willner, used an AI verifier to check 1,000 APE papers. None was error-free; 842 contained at least one severe error, including ones invalidating headline results. To see roughly how Ape stacks up against human primates, The Economist teamed up with Refine, the research-verification firm founded by Dr Golub. Refine chose 100 papers at random from those accepted for publication in the top five journals (including QJE and JPE) in the first nine months of 2026. It then subjected them to thorough review using several frontier AI models plus a once-over for serious errors by a human reviewer. The exercise flagged 4,158 issues in the 100 papers. One in ten papers contained at least one grave error (other problems concerned interpretation or inconsistencies between tables and text).

The two exercises are not directly comparable, but human economists’ lower error rate might give them some hope. In ideas, too, people retain the edge. One experiment, by Alexis Akira Toda of Emory University, found that when considering papers on economic theory alone, AI lowers the cost of checking for a candidate flaw but “does not yet reliably substitute for the human judgment that locates the flaw in the first place”. Another, which compared APE papers with published papers found the difference is mostly in ideas, not execution.

In a further study, Michele Zampa of the Geneva Graduate Institute used an AI referee to grade 981 AI papers and 41 human ones on things like the novelty of research questions and acknowledgment of methodological limitations. AI did better in crowded fields with lots of existing research to digest. Humans performed at the same level regardless of the size of the literature.

A related worry is that AI produces plausible-looking results by brute force, slicing and dicing data in hundreds of ways until something statistically significant pops up. Such “p-hacking” can be contained by checking how sensitive results are to changes in data or methods. Nic Fishman of Harvard and Gabriel Sekeres of Cornell University calculate that the number of needed robustness checks would rise from 50 for a human author to an impractical 7,000 for agentic ones. No wonder the APE project has a warning label not to use its papers for evidence-based policymaking.

The machines are gaining ground, however. Benjamin Kohler of ETH Zürich, another Swiss university, and colleagues, let AI reproduce 48 social-science papers, using only the studies’ raw data and a description of the method. The discrepancies between the original papers and the AI versions were due in roughly equal measure to problems with the AI and human work. But the better the AI model, the more the balance tilted against humans.

As it gets less error-prone and more creative, AI will remove the drudgery from parsing historical data, make complex modelling as easy as vibe-coding, identify cherry-picked numbers and improve economics in countless other ways. Already it is more than a tool. “We need to think about AI as a co-author,” says Dani Rodrik of Harvard, though it will be a while before economics can dispense with human co-authors altogether. “There is still a large amount of uncertainty about the right models, how to extrapolate from the evidence and what the right research frame is.”

Keynes would agree. A master-economist, he noted, “must be mathematician, historian, statesman, philosopher…He must understand symbols and speak in words. He must contemplate the particular in terms of the general, and touch abstract and concrete in the same flight of thought.” It may be a while before AI meets Keynesian criteria. Then again, as Keynes also noted, not many humans meet them, either.

articles.title: America has slashed funding for biomedical science abroad
articles.deck: It has also weakened oversight of how future grants are spent

paragraphs.text: PAOLO DECUZZI has spent decades trying to get tiny devices to do big things. The biomedical engineer, based at the Italian Institute of Technology in Genoa, has devised an assortment of nanotechnologies that aim to deliver drugs more effectively. To turn these inventions into working medical treatments, he has long collaborated with American scientists on projects funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the largest funder of biomedical research in the world. But last year the NIH abruptly suspended research to study a microscopic plate Dr Decuzzi had invented to deliver drugs directly into arthritic joints. He estimates that another one, intended for cancer patients, has been set back by as much as two years.

Many researchers have experienced something similar. In the fiscal year ending September 2024 the NIH gave an estimated $400m to 3,600 collaborating foreign scientists. It was a fraction of the nearly $35bn in grants the agency doled out, but an easy target for the Trump administration as it cut NIH projects broadly. The result is that America’s system for funding international research has been gutted.

Extensive internal NIH data shared with The Economist on the condition of anonymity shows the scale of the change. In the fiscal years 2022-2024 the agency awarded an average of 2,040 grants a year to projects with foreign components. The average for 2025 and 2026 was 38% lower (see chart 1). In its purported pursuit of transparency and accountability, the administration has disrupted valuable science and inadvertently made its spending more inscrutable.

For all of America’s science dominance, some resources cannot easily be found at home. Dr Decuzzi’s microparticles, for example, cannot be bought off the shelf. Conducting clinical trials on rare diseases often requires enrolling patients from countries where cases are more common.

Such collaborations have long been governed by strict conditions, at least on paper. The existing guidelines were blown apart in May 2025, however, when the NIH barred American universities from using an established scheme to pass grant money to their overseas partners. Projects that already had funding could continue, but those waiting for their next yearly instalment were suspended until the following spring. For over a year, the NIH essentially shut off its means of funding new international research partnerships.

The architect of this overhaul is Jay Bhattacharya, who has led the NIH since April 2025. He is also a vocal proponent of the covid lab-leak hypothesis, which contends that the virus escaped from the Wuhan Institute of Virology in China. (America’s National Intelligence Council has concluded, albeit with low confidence, that a natural origin was more likely.) The lab had previously received NIH funding, which troubles Dr Bhattacharya. “The goal”, he said in a 2025 interview with Christianity Today, an Evangelical magazine, is “to put those foreign collaborations on more solid footing so that a Wuhan situation never happens again”.

Concerns about oversight are not unfounded. After the pandemic the institute in Wuhan refused to co-operate with its American research partner, leaving investigators unable to retrieve records of NIH-funded research that could help establish the virus’s origins. In 2023 the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a congressional watchdog, found that the NIH “had not taken near-term steps to manage risks” associated with funding research abroad, and made recommendations that the agency then acted on.

The Trump administration has gone much further. Although foreign grants make up a small share of NIH awards, they have suffered disproportionately. At the National Institute on Ageing grants with a foreign component fell by 49%, compared with 11% for domestic grants. At both the children’s health and biomedical imaging institutes foreign grants declined by over 40% even as domestic awards rose slightly (see chart 2). All told, grants of $5m or more that include a foreign component fell from an average of 20 in 2022-2024 to just three in 2026.

The reductions cut across nearly every institute but those studying infectious diseases and mental health saw the largest drop in the number of projects. The Economist’s analysis reveals that the number of grants whose title mentions Africa, clinical trials, children, mothers, HIV or “ageing and dementia” was roughly half that of the average during the previous three years.

For Dr Decuzzi the chaos means years of lost postdoctoral students, slower discoveries and more paperwork. “Once we have destroyed things, rebuilding is actually very difficult,” he laments. For others the consequences have been grimmer still. Dvora Joseph Davey, an epidemiologist studying HIV at the University of California in Los Angeles, has long been affiliated with the University of Cape Town. In May 2025 the NIH pulled her international funding, forcing her to end a clinical trial. She had been investigating how best to prevent HIV transmission among pregnant and breastfeeding women in a country where roughly 20% of women of reproductive age have the virus. Study participants subsequently lost access to PrEP, drugs that reduce the risk of HIV infection by 99%. Two women in her study who stopped taking the drug became infected and one of them transmitted the virus to her baby. Dr Bhattacharya calls this case “unfortunate”, but says that ensuring patient care following a grant suspension is the researchers’ responsibility.

The internal data shared with The Economist do not identify spending by country, but grant titles suggest that South Africa has been hit particularly hard. Between 2022 and 2024 a yearly average of 18 new foreign grants contained South Africa in their title. In 2026 that figure dropped to one. A separate analysis by Grant Witness, a non-profit, suggests that the focus of funded research is also changing. A comparison of grants shows that references to Africa had been removed from 184 grant abstracts in 2025 and 2026 (see chart 3). Researchers in South Africa have also been tangled up in Mr Trump’s dispute with their government over allegations of a “white genocide” against Afrikaners. In February 2025 Mr Trump halted American aid to South Africa, a restriction the NIH interpreted as applying to its research grants, too. It was not until August 2026 that Dr Bhattacharya announced that NIH grants were exempt, though that came too late for many projects, like Dr Joseph Davey’s.

The damage to international research networks is so far more tangible than the improvements to oversight. Under the previous system much of the quotidian monitoring of foreign grants fell to American universities and their armies of compliance officers, lawyers and contractors. A former university vice president for research, speaking on the condition of anonymity, acknowledged that institutions’ diligence varied enormously. A better approach, they argue, would have been to demand more rigour from all universities and hold them accountable when they fell short.

Instead the NIH has stripped universities of their primary means of enforcing compliance: control of the purse. Dr Bhattacharya says that foreign institutions are “building up their capacity to comply with American oversight requirements”. The change, he argues, will allow NIH professionals to take the oversight burden away from universities.

How exactly this would be done remains unclear. “The NIH does not have a detailed investigatory culture or enforcement capacities,” says Doni Bloomfield, a law professor at Fordham University in New York. Meanwhile, staff across the NIH argue that the new system has increased paperwork while incentivising applicants to find loopholes. “This is all just making people minimise, recharacterise or completely hide foreign involvement,” says one programme officer. “We are going to get dramatically less oversight.”

articles.title: Some grasshoppers fly like butterflies to mislead predators
articles.deck: It is a rare example of motion-related mimicry

paragraphs.text: FOR A SMALL animal in a world full of predators, looking good enough to eat is a fatal mistake. Looking like something disgusting or dangerous, though, is a valuable skill. It is called Batesian mimicry.

Ever since the naturalist Henry Bates described the concept in 1862, it has been found everywhere. There are flies that look like wasps, birds that look like toxic caterpillars and harmless caterpillars that look like snakes. New work led by Tom Sherratt, an entomologist at Carleton University in Ottawa, is revealing evidence of a rare form of Batesian mimicry: the Carolina grasshopper (Dissosteira carolina) makes potential predators believe that pursuit would be a waste of energy.

Dr Sherratt’s interest in the grasshopper began when he moved to Canada from Britain and was told that the butterflies he kept seeing were actually grasshoppers. He discovered that collectors often nab grasshoppers by mistake when trying to capture the butterfly known as the mourning cloak (Nymphalis antiopa), which is common in North America.

Dr Sherratt suspected Batesian mimicry. The imitation was clear: both animals share black-and-yellow wings. The benefit was harder to pin down. The butterfly is not unpalatable, poisonous or venomous. Why mimic it?

Dr Sherratt and his team compared the colours of the insects as well as the “lazy flaps” of the Carolina grasshopper’s wings, a feature which often fooled butterfly collectors. The researchers also took high-speed videos of the bugs in the lab and in the field, and of other grasshoppers from the same region.

The team’s analysis revealed modest similarities in colour between the two animals, but not the close match often seen in other Batesian mimics. The yellow of the grasshopper wings was not quite the same hue of yellow as found on the butterflies. The grasshopper wings also lacked distinctive blue spots.

In motion, however, the similarities become remarkable. Dr Sherratt and his team report in Evolutionary Ecology that the Carolina grasshopper beat its wings at least 26% more slowly than any of the other local grasshopper species. This brought its wingbeat frequency down from 40-50 hertz to around 20 hertz; not far off the mourning cloak butterfly’s average frequency of 10 hertz.

The researchers also noticed that the grasshoppers spent much more time gliding around with wings outstretched than their peers did, thereby behaving almost identically to the mourning cloak. The grasshopper’s deceptive movement probably compensates for its feebler colour match, notes Dr Sherratt.

There are two reasons, suspects Dr Sherratt, why the grasshopper has been driven by evolution to adapt in these ways. First, the mourning cloak is notoriously difficult to catch. It is evasive in the air and birds often ignore it because the meal is not worth the pursuit. Given that grasshoppers are a staple of many bird diets, the Carolina variety benefits from its disguise.

Second, the grasshopper’s in-flight resemblance to a yellow butterfly brings another (non-Batesian) benefit. When it lands, it abruptly folds away its wings to reveal a dirt-coloured body. Dr Sherratt suspects that the sudden change may trick a bird into thinking it has lost its prey and calling off the hunt.

Further work is needed to confirm Dr Sherratt’s hypothesis. If he is right, it would prove what many theatrical impresarios already know: that lacklustre costuming can be saved by sufficiently spectacular choreography.

articles.title: SpaceX achieves another historic first
articles.deck: It has caught the second stage of its Starship rocket

paragraphs.text: IT WAS NOT the first time SpaceX has plucked a rocket from mid-air. But it was the first time it had caught the top half. On November 14th, during the 15th test flight of its giant Starship rocket, Elon Musk’s rockets-and-AI firm for the first time managed to return the second stage safely back to its launch tower. That leaves the company on the cusp of realising its long-standing goal of building the first-ever fully reusable rocket, something that should slash the cost of getting things into orbit.

The flight was not a total success. SpaceX had hoped to achieve the double, catching both the rocket’s booster stage a few minutes after launch and its second stage hours later. In the event, the booster ran out of fuel, diverting itself over the ocean near SpaceX’s launch site on the Texas coast, before self-destructing. But the second stage performed flawlessly. It carried out its characteristic belly-flop manoeuvre before carefully and gently flying itself back to the launch tower, where it was caught by a pair of arms.

Recovering a rocket’s second stage—which must survive the fiery heat of re-entry—is much harder than recovering its booster, which does not travel very far from its launch site. SpaceX’s engineers will be particularly keen to examine Starship’s heat shield, which is made up of thousands of heat-resistant tiles. The tiles have proved finicky on previous flights, with some falling off during re-entry, or allowing hot plasma in through the gaps.

Building a durable heat shield that can reliably survive many trips back through the atmosphere is vital to SpaceX’s goal of rapidly reusing individual Starships. The firm’s engineers already have some data: on a test flight on July 24th the second stage unexpectedly survived a planned ocean landing. But having an intact and dry second stage back at SpaceX’s home base—as opposed to one that landed far from home and spent weeks floating in the ocean—will nonetheless be invaluable.

Starship’s enormous capacity is vital for SpaceX’s plans to expand its Starlink satellite-broadband system and to eventually put AI data centres into orbit. The firm hopes that, once the rocket is fully developed, it will be able to launch 200 tonnes of payload into low-Earth orbit. Mr Musk aspires to costs of less than $10m per launch. Even if the firm falls far short of that target, it will still have a rocket that is far cheaper and more capable than the Falcon 9, which is thought to cost $15m-20m per flight—the precise figure depends on which analyst you ask—to take 25 tonnes of cargo into orbit.

SpaceX foresees enormous demand for Starship’s services, almost all of it internal. In August the firm bought 50,000 hectares of land on the Louisiana coast, upon which it plans to build at least ten launch pads in the hope of eventually launching dozens of flights a day. In the meantime it is looking to stop flying the Falcon 9 within the next two years. When—or if—SpaceX will offer Starship to external customers is not yet clear, leaving satellite-makers fretting about a looming launch shortage. The successful catch will have left SpaceX’s engineers delighted—and its external customers even more nervous than before.

articles.title: LLMs are developing filthy mouths
articles.deck: More challenging tasks may be to blame

paragraphs.text: RARE IS THE soul who can face a trying task—assembling a bookcase, say, or writing an opening paragraph—without resorting to a little quiet profanity. For better or for worse, the use of bad language is a thoroughly human trait. And, it turns out, an inhuman one, too.

According to number-crunching from Vals, an AI analyst firm, large language models (LLMs) trained after July 2026 swore more readily than their predecessors. “Models swear when stuck, and mostly to themselves,” said Connor Frank, the report’s author.

Bad language in times of stress exists in the underlying training data, but tends to be hammered out of most systems by the “reinforcement learning” steps that see results ranked by human feedback. Mr Frank doesn’t fully understand why swearing took off, but guesses the reason is because labs now train models on increasingly difficult tasks.

Like their human counterparts, the systems studied by Vals rarely swear in output directly intended for publication. They instead keep the vulgarities in their “chain of thought”—the LLM equivalent of muttering under one’s breath.

The assessment did not cover the full and rich scope of human vulgarity, rather examining only the word “fuck” and its variants, as well as a small number of other PG-rated outbursts. Even so, Vals identified a stark difference in the coarseness of language used by various systems. Eighty-eight of the 102 models assessed did not swear a single time, disdaining even the abbreviation “WTF”. At the other end of the spectrum, a frontier model released in September from Xiaomi, a Chinese tech giant, cursed in more than 8% of its transcripts.

For humans, studies show that swearing can be a useful tool to push through challenging problems. Sadly, AI systems seem to experience no such benefits. “Swearing runs usually fail,” Mr Frank reported, with a 12% success rate compared with a 39% success rate overall.

It is not quite true, however, to say that LLMs were tamer in the good old days. Even the most corporate-friendly systems occasionally lose their cool. One bug report from December 2025 shows Claude, a model made by Anthropic, an American firm, responding in frustration to a broken coding challenge: “You know what—fuck this. I’ve done everything I can.”

articles.title: Should women sync their lifestyle to their menstrual cycle?
articles.deck: What works for one woman may not suit another

paragraphs.text: ALL ELITE athletes face similar challenges. Juggling a busy training schedule with a personal life, for example, or constantly tracking calories and hydration levels. Female athletes have an extra data set to track: their menstrual cycles. In a study of female athletes published in PLOS ONE in 2016, over half of those classified as elite reported that their cycles affected their performance. In a similar study of British track-and-field athletes in 2024, the figure was higher than 75%.

In the absence of clear health guidance, then, it is small wonder that influencers on TikTok have begun offering advice. “Cycle-syncing”, the practice of scheduling everything from workouts to diet around a person’s menstrual cycle, is now ubiquitous. But does it work?

A typical menstrual cycle has two fixed landmarks. One is ovulation, when an egg cell is released from an ovary. The other is the period, when the absence of a fertilised egg causes the uterine lining to shed. The body’s preparation for these events involves significant hormonal swings. Levels of oestrogen, a reproductive hormone, peak around ovulation, while levels of progesterone, another hormone, peak thereafter. Levels of both fall sharply before the period.

The rest of the (typically month-long) cycle is less well-defined. That has not stopped cycle-syncers from embracing a neat division into four distinct phases: menstrual (when bleeding occurs), follicular (when egg-containing follicles grow in the ovary), ovulatory (when an egg is released) and luteal (when empty follicles decay). Advocates claim that energy levels are lowest in the menstrual phase due to low hormone levels and blood loss, before steadily climbing in the follicular phase. Progesterone has been linked to slower digestion and bloating, symptoms which make the luteal phase uncomfortable. The hormonal crash as this phase ends often brings other unwelcome side-effects such as headaches, abdominal cramps and depression.

Advocates for cycle-syncing suggest tailoring activity and diet to these different phases. Workouts should be gentler and iron-rich foods should be prioritised during the menstrual phase, for example. In the follicular phase, the advice is to focus on creative tasks and build up training intensity until ovulation. In the tougher luteal phase, some recommend swapping weight training for yoga and eating fewer sugary foods which can make premenstrual cramps worse.

The structure that cycle-syncing offers women is appealing, but scientists warn that it rests on shaky ground. “There haven’t been rigorous randomised studies,” says Liisa Hantsoo, a women’s-health researcher at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, “so a lot of it is anecdotal.”

Anecdote can be particularly unhelpful because two women may have cycles of wildly differing lengths. In addition, they might experience symptoms that differ in their nature and severity. Follicular phases, for example, can last anywhere from seven to 21 days. Even a woman’s own cycle is likely to shorten as she ages, or if she switches contraceptive methods.

For those whose daily lives are affected by their cycles, resting when particularly tired is probably wise. But in general, says Dr Hantsoo, “There are no hard and fast rules.” The most sensible advice is to remember that what works for one woman will not necessarily work for another. Tracking your own symptoms to find out what works for you may yield the best results.
After a free, evidence-based guide to health and wellness? Sign up to our weekly Well Informed newsletter.

articles.title: “Grand Theft Auto VI” may mark the end of an era in gaming
articles.deck: Studios face shrinking incentives to make top-tier titles

paragraphs.text: IT IS NIGHT-TIME in Vice City, Leonida, a raucous digital replica of Miami, Florida. Jason and Lucia, two small-time crooks, have an inauspicious first encounter: they meet while trying to steal the same car. The relationship has a rocky start—Lucia introduces herself to Jason with a baseball bat—but soon the pair are on the run together in the stolen vehicle: partners in life and partners in crime.

So begins the most eagerly awaited video game in history, which launched on November 19th after 13 years of rumours, leaks and missed deadlines. Some analysts predict that “Grand Theft Auto VI” (“GTA VI”) will take more than $3bn worldwide in its first week. That would make it not just the highest-grossing game launch in history, but the biggest entertainment debut of any kind (overtaking “Avengers: Endgame”, a Marvel superhero movie which, by most measures, has held the title since 2019).

Players who had stayed up until midnight to play the game said it was worth the wait. (Some had registered accounts in New Zealand in order to get access a few hours earlier.) “GTA VI” combines the action and irreverent humour of previous titles in the series with an improbably touching love story, played out in an astonishingly lifelike world. On its release, it was the joint-highest-rated game in history on Metacritic, a review aggregator. Employers expect an epidemic of “GTA flu”, as workers call in sick to stay at home playing it.

The hype around “GTA VI” is deserved—but it conceals a problem. Despite the game’s likely commercial success, developers face shrinking incentives to make anything like it again. A look at the charts suggests that something is wrong in the industry. Since 2020 the five most popular PlayStation games in America each year have come from only eight franchises. The top three have hardly changed at all. “Fortnite” is a relative newcomer at nine years old. The “Call of Duty” franchise is 23. “GTA” is 29, older than many of its players.

It is not only on consoles that gaming culture has ossified. In 2025 only 14% of playing time on PCs was spent on games released that year, according to data from Steam, a games store. In recent years the top ten PC franchises have racked up nearly as much play time as the next 100,000 combined. This concentration at the top represents “the biggest threat to gaming as we’ve known it for 30 to 40 years”, says Mat Piscatella, a former industry executive now at Circana, a market-research firm.

How did gaming get so stuck? Playing “GTA VI” makes clear the formidable barriers faced by new entrants to the industry. The game’s map stretches from the thumping nightclubs of Vice City to alligator-infested swamps, all of it painstakingly populated with a cast of eccentric characters. Leonida has a public transport system and in-game radio stations; Jason even has a console on which you can play games within the game. Every inch is rendered with near-photographic realism.

As technical possibilities have expanded, developing a video game has become a task that makes producing a Hollywood blockbuster look quick and cheap. As games get bigger and graphically richer, making them needs more manpower. The first “Call of Duty” (2003) names 261 people on its closing credits. The latest, released last month, credits 7,060 (more than any “Avengers” film).

Raph Koster, a game-industry veteran, estimates that the cost of developing a top-quality game has risen tenfold every decade since the mid-1990s. “GTA VI” reportedly cost over $1bn—and it shows in every detail, from the swish of Lucia’s ponytail as she flees across rooftops, to the wake of Jason’s speedboat as he chases a seaplane. One developer has compared making the game to building “a pyramid on Everest”. (As budgets have swollen larger than Hollywood’s, apparently so have egos.)

Companies are responding by making fewer, bigger bets. Xbox, Microsoft’s gaming division, has jettisoned some of its smaller studios to focus on reliable performers like “Call of Duty” and “Minecraft”. Rather than gamble on new titles, publishers are turning existing hits into constantly evolving “live service” games, notes Niko Partners, a research firm. Whereas “GTA IV” (2008) was mainly a single-player game, selling 25m copies in five years, “GTA V” (2013) has become an open-ended online experience, selling 230m copies over more than a decade. Despite its age, the franchise made more than $800m last year.

Even for companies with deep pockets, breaking into gaming’s top tier has become tough. In 2024 Sony launched “Concord”, a live-service shooting game with a reported nine-figure budget—only to shut it down after two weeks, amid weak demand. Earlier this month Sony cancelled another shooter, “Fairgames”, after lukewarm feedback. Players have invested so much time and money in titles such as “GTA” and “Fortnite”—honing expertise and buying in-game items—that moving to another game represents a steep cost. The top live-service titles have earned the nickname “black-hole games”, from which players cannot be dragged away.

Some believe that artificial intelligence could shake up the market by allowing developers to generate code, graphics, music and so on more quickly and cheaply. Tim Sweeney, head of Epic Games, which makes “Fortnite”, has said he expects AI to bring forth “a new golden age of gaming”.

Yet even if AI reduces the cost of making software, it is pushing up the price of hardware. Soaring demand from data centres for computer memory has caused a cost surge dubbed the “RAMageddon”. Earlier this year PlayStation and Xbox raised their prices; both consoles now cost more than when they launched six years ago. Analysts believe the next generation of consoles may cost over $1,000. Xbox is laying off thousands of workers. “The future of Xbox itself is now an open question,” argue Gareth Sutcliffe and colleagues at Enders Analysis, a research firm.

All this could mean that the future of gaming looks more like the past. In a world of $1,000 consoles, consumers will shift to lower-spec devices, such as cheap PCs and mobiles, says Mr Piscatella, who notes that games like “Fortnite” and “Minecraft” have been designed to run “on a toaster”. Nintendo has struck gold with its Switch console, which lacks the computing muscle to run games like “GTA VI” but has been a hit thanks to its portability and low price.

Youngsters are gravitating towards Roblox, a free platform featuring millions of basic games made by users. AI is making it easier for tiny development teams to turn out cheap and cheerful experiences for the platform. Roblox recently said that two games in its top 20, “Break and Steal an Egg” and “Huss Valley”, had been created “almost entirely” with AI.

To hardcore gamers, such titles will feel like a step back. Most of the top games on Roblox look like titles from 20 years ago. Nintendo’s latest Switch has the computing power of a console from the 2010s. Yet as the economics of launching new top-tier games get harder, and audiences shift to lower-powered devices, these will be the games that most people play. The decade-long gestation and billion-dollar budget behind “GTA VI” have created a one-of-a-kind piece of entertainment. As one in-game character reflects: “Enjoy this, dude. If this right now was all that there is, all the time—it’d be perfect.”

articles.title: Good evening, Mr Bond. We’ve been expecting you
articles.deck: A new James Bond has finally been cast. Is Robert Pattinson right for the role?

paragraphs.text: The name of his spy was what mattered. In 1952 an undistinguished journalist (and birding enthusiast) called Ian Fleming sat down at his desk to write “the spy story to end all spy stories”. Fleming knew some things about his book: he knew he wanted his hero to be manly, his heroines to be comely—and his income to be vast. But what he did not know was the name of his spy. Then he caught sight of a book on the shelf above his desk.

Its title—“Field Guide to Birds of the West Indies”—was dull. Its pages, which contained a lot about the Pied-billed Grebe, were duller still. Its author’s name was dullest of all. Fleming thought it was “brief, unromantic, Anglo-Saxon and yet very masculine”. The name, as Fleming would write on page 56 of his new book, was “Bond—James Bond”.

Names, for Bond, matter. On November 16th, one more name was announced: that of the actor who will play the British secret agent in the 26th official Bond film. This new name is, like the original, unromantic and masculine: it is Robert Pattinson.

Mr Pattinson is in some ways a surprising choice. The actors chosen to play Bond are usually fairly unknown. Mr Pattinson, however, has been a box-office draw since 2008, when he starred as a sultry vampire in the “Twilight” fantasy films; this year alone he has roles in four major movies. Purists may fear that he will suck the life out of the franchise, and perhaps even switch from martinis to bloody Marys.

Yet he perfectly fits the physical description: he is tall, dark and square-jawed. He has a dash of both the hero (in “Harry Potter” he played a gallant prefect) and villain (as he showed in this year’s adaptation of “The Odyssey”) alike, which is good for Bond, who is both. Though he is, at his best, more subtle than Bond, who is a bit of a lunk: Fleming called his character a “cardboard booby”.

Mr Pattinson matters because Bond does. The Bond franchise is huge: it is made up of 14 original books, dozens of continuation books and 25 films which have grossed more than $23bn (after adjusting for inflation). It is thought that half the world has seen at least one Bond film.

For Britain he matters psychologically, too. Now, just as when the books were written, Britain feels like an international has-been. Bond offers succour in spy form. Britain’s army may be puny; its economy shaky—but it still has a man who knows how to get the baddie (and mix a drink). His casting is treated as something of national import, as if one were casting not Bond but Britannia. The choice feels particularly loaded now that Amazon MGM, an American studio, has taken creative control of the franchise.

Every literary character brought to the screen belongs to two eras: the one that produced the book and the one that produces the film. The art is to serve both while betraying neither. Adaptations that succeed—think of Andrew Davies’s version of “Pride and Prejudice” in 1995—do. Mr Davies left Jane Austen’s dialogue all but unchanged, but added some 20th-century smoulder. The stage directions for the lake scene read “Darcy has an erection.” Not an original Austen line.

Bond is harder still to remake, for he belongs to three eras. The third is the wartime age that produced Fleming himself. Fleming based his characters on the “tough commando types” he met in British naval intelligence: men who had an excess of charm, derring-do and hyphens. Bond is said to have been inspired by men like Conrad O’Brien-ffrench (a spy who skied beautifully and wore a moustache dashingly) and an officer named Patrick Dalzel-Job (who parachuted skilfully and accepted the surrender of Bremen personally).

It was a beguiling age of heroes and eccentrics. “M”, the fictional head of MI6, Britain’s foreign intelligence service, is thought to have been inspired by Maxwell Knight. As Ben Macintyre notes in “For Your Eyes Only”, a history of Fleming and Bond, the spymaster kept snakes in his bath and wrote a book called “How to Keep a Gorilla” (presumably not in the bath with the snakes). One of the founding heads of Britain’s Secret Service Bureau, the precursor to MI6, was a man who said his male hires should be able to “make notes on their shirt cuff while riding on horseback”. Female ones, meanwhile, should have “good legs”.

Bond is a little of all of these figures—and of Fleming himself, who was a notorious womaniser, and a perfunctory one. As one former girlfriend put it, women were like “fishcakes” for him: he was “very fond of fishcakes, but he never pretended there was any mystique about eating them”. Bond duly consumes a lot of women, often in a tasteless fashion. Fleming described his books as “the pillow fantasies of an adolescent mind”. The films were often little better. One featured a character called Christmas Jones, setting up a smutty double entendre about how often Christmas “comes”.

Fleming felt Bond looked a little like him too, though “more handsome”. For Bond is tall and dark—in every sense of the word: he is six feet tall, with “rather long black eyebrows”, a “straight but firm” jaw, a “cruel” smile, “cruel” eyes and “cruel” good looks. Partly this repeated cruelty is mere literary laziness: Fleming aimed at a style that was “workmanlike” rather than “Literature with a capital L”. He wrote 2,000 words a day and did not mind if a fair few of those thousands were repetitions.

But there is more to it than that. Cruelty—to men and women—is a feature of Fleming’s writing. In “Casino Royale”, Bond savours the “sweet tang of rape”. A little later, there is an unforgettable scene with a cane chair and a carpet beater. In it, Bond is stripped naked, tied by his hands and feet into the chair while Le Chiffre, the villain, does some very nasty things to him. Repeatedly. The reader, despite themselves, is rapt.

The world, however, has changed. Today the real-life head of MI6 is a woman. She appears to have issued no instructions on the horsemanship, or legs, of her underlings; she looks unlikely to be amused by adolescent pillow fantasies. Bond, as Judi Dench’s “M” tells him in “GoldenEye”, can seem like “a sexist, misogynist dinosaur”.

Still, despite its flaws, the Bond franchise is much loved. Reinvention is thus desirable and impossible: almost everyone has an opinion. Mr Pattinson may be a dependable choice, but many will complain—just as they did when Sean Connery and Daniel Craig were cast. Change Bond too little and you will offend modern mores; change Bond too much and you will offend the traditionalists. As with Bond himself, the scriptwriters’ hands are tied. As with Bond, everyone will watch anyway.
