articles.title: Can the AI boom make enough money to sustain itself?

paragraphs.text: Both artificial intelligence and the tricky business of valuing stocks boil down to questions of timelines. Establishing what a company is worth is a hazy exercise at the best of times, full of courageous assumptions about which cashflows will arrive when. Consider, too, timelines for AI—the years, few or many, until the technology’s capabilities surpass humans’—and the exercise veers into incoherence.

Markets do not enjoy the luxury of coherence, though. Take the imminent listing of Anthropic, the first big pure-play AI developer to go public. Anthropic’s prospectus touts the many remarkable (and profitable) ways in which advanced AI could transform the economy, but also warns would-be buyers off. “Our decision-making may run counter to investors’ expectations,” it says, for instance with “forward investments…that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance”.

Still, somewhere between Utopia and Armageddon, investors need to find a way to pick a number. Anthropic is aiming to float at a valuation of around $1.5trn, which would make it one of the 15 biggest public companies in the world.

The listing comes at a precarious time for AI. Jitters about data-centre debt collided with midterm elections in America, where AI-sceptical candidates prevailed, and, bizarrely, with the revelation that Jensen Huang, the boss of the chipmaker Nvidia, was having an affair with an alleged Chinese agent.

Before all that, Anthropic looked set for a valuation of $2trn or more (see chart 1). OpenAI, its main rival, has punted its own listing into next year. Nvidia’s share price was about 30% below its recent peak as The Economist went to press. The “neoclouds”, which borrow, often prodigiously, to run data centres, have done worse. But a comeback may be on. Shares in CoreWeave, one of the largest, rose by 25% on November 11th, following strong earnings. The stock had previously been down two-thirds from its high point this year in May. And Anthropic’s IPO is, reportedly, heavily oversubscribed.

So the IPO will be a weighty moment. However many trillions Anthropic lists at, from then on it—and, increasingly, AI more widely—will be judged not with the gauzy optimism of venture capitalists but with the beady eyes of Wall Street. Investors will wonder whether the technology can possibly generate enough cash to justify these valuations or underwrite the colossal scale of data-centre construction planned over the next few years.

The numbers are vast. The Economist calculates that AI needs around $3trn in revenue by 2030 for the planned data-centre buildout to offer a conventional rate of return. Other analysts, including Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh of Columbia Business School and a duo at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, have reached similar figures. To put that number into perspective, all compensation for all workers—wages, plus perks like health insurance—adds up to around $16.5trn in America, or $35trn across the OECD, a club mostly of rich countries. So AI would need to lay claim to almost a tenth of today’s rich-world wages for the data-centre boom to pencil out. Of course, that could happen in a more benign fashion if the entire economy grows swiftly—and AI evangelists do also expect dramatic growth from here.

Safe to say, AI isn’t quite there yet. Anthropic has reported that its annualised run-rate revenue at the end of October was $81bn. OpenAI’s was $50bn as of the end of September. Toss in smaller developers, as well as Google’s, Meta’s and Microsoft’s revenues from their own models, and the AI model-makers might be generating around $200bn in total.

All that cash sits at the top of a funnel, cascading downward into the rest of the ecosystem—keeping other AI businesses afloat and persuading investors to hand them more money. The models that Anthropic, OpenAI and the others sell must be run on chips, most often designed by Nvidia and manufactured by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Those chips in turn rely on a bevy of components. A shortage of one, RAM, a type of memory, sent the stocks of the main South Korean memory-makers, Samsung and SK Hynix, soaring in the spring. Those chips must then be housed in a data centre, festooned with further complicated electronics. All that needs electricity to power it, too: a windfall for the makers of gas turbines, which generate much of the electricity behind the AI boom. Everything in AI-world, in other words, relies on revenue at the top of that funnel continuing to flow in, ideally at an ever-increasing rate.

Getting from $200bn to $3trn means a leap of an order of magnitude (or an OOM, in Silicon Valley-speak). Could that happen? Because so many of the largest players in AI have been privately held, tracing the exact path of their revenues is tricky. But the previous OOM did not take long. The combined revenues of Anthropic, OpenAI and a number of smaller developers (but not Google, Meta and so on) probably crossed $10bn around March of 2025. Today, that figure is $130bn.

The next leap will be tougher. One cause of AI’s recent wobble was a fear that revenue growth may be slowing. Alternative-data proxies like Ramp, which tracks AI spending on company credit cards, and TickerTrends, which collates data such as social-media posts and spending patterns from panels of businesses and consumers, point to slowing revenue growth among the AI developers. A model fitting those data sets to the revenue figures that Anthropic, OpenAI and others have released suggests three-month revenue growth slowed from 80-90% in the spring to 12% in October (see chart 2).

By usual standards, even the smallest of those numbers reflects extraordinarily rapid gains. And not every proxy is gloomy; figures from OpenRouter, a tool which helps developers switch AI providers, now show spending on Anthropic’s, OpenAI‘s and Google’s models surging out of an earlier funk. Still, the more that revenue growth tapers off, the further out of reach the next OOM may slip. Once Anthropic and, eventually, OpenAI list, the reporting requirements of public markets will make any such slowdown far easier to spot.

A trillion-dollar AI economy would change the world, in a way that today’s hundred-billion-dollar one has not. Right now, the technology’s economic impact is still limited outside the AI sector itself. Profit margins and revenue per employee have surged at the “Magnificent Seven” tech giants, but are close to flat for the “S&P 493”, the rest of America’s benchmark S&P 500 index of big companies. Software stocks have now largely rebounded from the clobbering they took at the start of the year, during the “SaaSpocalypse”, when investors worried that automated coding would make it easy to cheaply duplicate nearly any software product.

Macroeconomic figures also have not moved much. Productivity growth has been strong in America, but not much stronger of late than in the early 2020s. Meanwhile, it remains painfully slow elsewhere in the rich world, even in countries like Britain whose firms have adopted AI at a similar pace to America. Global bond markets also do not seem to be pricing in all that dramatic an uplift to growth.

So far the only profession truly upended by AI is software engineering. Many coders now hardly touch code themselves; instead, they supervise armies of AI agents. America’s “information” sector, which includes software publishing, has the highest and fastest-growing AI penetration rate in the economy, according to figures from the US Census Bureau (see chart 3). Mercor, an AI-data company, claims to spend more on AI agents than on employee salaries.

That is extreme, but not entirely unrepresentative. Tech companies’ AI spending looks nothing like the rest. The average VC-backed company spends around $100 per employee per month on AI, according to data from Ramp (see chart 4). Regular firms spend only $10 or so. Many, after a wave of “tokenmaxxing” AI enthusiasm, are becoming more cautious. In October Goldman Sachs, a bank, banned non-engineers from using AI coding tools, citing disappointing productivity gains and concerns about cyber-security risk. (Though JPMorgan, a rival, has since announced that it is doubling down on the technology.)

Where tremendous gains have been most visible is in the underlying capabilities of AI models. A report by METR, a non-profit outfit that embedded researchers at Anthropic, found the pace of improvement in Anthropic’s models may well have doubled in the past year. Recent months have brought a drumbeat of announcements of AI solutions to unsolved mathematics problems, or novel AI-enabled cyber-attacks.

But the surging investment in training AI models has also meant that each leap in model intelligence has been more expensive than the last. That raises the commercial imperative still further to deploy this intelligence profitably.

For now, selling access to AI has been an excellent business. Improvements have arrived fast enough, and the best models have been appealing enough, to let developers charge healthy margins. Anthropic’s gross margin in this year’s first half was 85%. At first glance, then, AI might remind investors of the previous generation of runaway software success stories.

But in their fundamental economics, AI and conventional software are quite different businesses. Software products, from software-as-a-service tools like Salesforce to Google to the social-networking giants, had several appealing characteristics from an investor’s perspective. Switching to a competitor was costly, so their moats were wide. Users would have to relearn how to use a complex tool from scratch. Network effects benefited the biggest players and stymied upstarts: why join a social-media site with no other users, or an ad network with few prospective customers? And, once the software was built, it was cheap to distribute. So, the bigger a company’s customer base, the more users it could spread its fixed costs across, and the tougher any rival would find it to compete on price.

Selling AI models has, so far, been something like the reverse. Switching is trivial. For developers, tools like OpenRouter make it as simple as changing a line of code. For consumers, one chatbot looks much like another. Many products, like Cursor, a coding agent, offer a drop-down menu to toggle between different model providers. Others like Instinct, a personal-assistant agent, make even that decision invisible by juggling among models on the back end, balancing performance and costs. And the cost of serving a new customer is not near-zero, as with regular software. Each new query must be run in an expensive data centre, on a scarce chip.

Still, Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s pricing power has held up thus far. Breakneck revenue growth relies on that position lasting. The firms can manage that either by continuing to make their current business model work, or by finding new ones. They are trying both. So far, though switching costs are low, users have been willing to pay a premium for the best models. But at the current pace of development, each gets only a narrow window, weeks or at most months, to recoup its training costs before a successor surpasses it.

Will cheaper models become a threat? Once a certain level of model intelligence is achieved, it tends to be commodified and plummet in price (see chart 5). That reflects competition between American AI players as well as the threat of Chinese fast-followers. Today’s best Chinese offering on the Epoch Capabilities Index, which aggregates a wide range of AI benchmarks, is Kimi K3.1 Pro, which scores around the same as GPT 5.5 Pro from OpenAI, which was the strongest publicly available American model just over six months ago, in April. Over the past few years, Chinese models have been consistently about that far behind.

Cheap models could be especially worrying if trained cleverly. Researchers at Bridgewater, a hedge fund, using tools from Thinking Machines, an AI startup, found that a small fine-tuned Chinese model beat the then-leading models from Anthropic and OpenAI at processing financial documents. Such fine-tuning requires investments in data and computing that only big firms will deem worthwhile, but if the finding holds more broadly, it will be a tempting way to lower the AI bill.

Still, some uses of AI will always demand the absolute best, especially those that are adversarial, like trading or cyber-security. There, success means staying ahead of rivals. And in other cases too it may be worth paying a premium. Large unsupervised swarms of AI agents, of the sort that OpenAI accidentally set loose to hack Hugging Face, an AI startup, earlier this year, still need top-flight intelligence.

The big developers’ lead on capabilities also could grow. The computational power needed to train the latest models is becoming a moat, keeping upstarts out. Chinese developers are constrained by a (thus far) smaller data-centre buildout and American restrictions on chip sales to China. And Anthropic says that it is getting better at impeding distillation, the process where less capable models are trained on the output of better ones, which has helped Chinese firms stay in the race on the cheap.

AI developers could find ways to shift their business to make spending stickier. In recent months Anthropic and OpenAI have announced a crop of specialist tools for law, science and finance. Anthropic has also set up a joint venture with Blackstone, a private-equity firm, Goldman Sachs and others to start selling bespoke AI services to businesses. Each is an effort to find revenue streams where the company can embed itself and dig a deeper moat.

But AI products can only ever be so sticky. By making computers easier to use, and more responsive to human-language requests, AI itself has simplified the process of moving from provider to provider. Anthropic cannily capitalised on this fact earlier this year, when its spat with the Pentagon drove a wave of sympathetic switchers from ChatGPT. Upon setting up Claude, users were given a prompt that they could paste into ChatGPT, asking the rival model to summarise what it knew about them. Claude would then digest the output, and be able to offer personalised responses from the get-go.

Another option for the model companies is proprietary trading. This could be of the literal sort. Nearly every rumour imaginable has been attached at some point to Safe Superintelligence, the secretive AI-research company run by Ilya Sutskever, a former chief scientist of OpenAI. A popular, if barmy, one is that it is using its models for high-frequency trading. A more likely version of that business model for Anthropic and its peers is prop trading of the metaphorical variety: monetising AI by using it directly, potentially in a joint venture, in domains like drug development or robotics, where breakthroughs could be highly profitable. For sufficiently smart models, restricting access to a few ultra-high-paying customers, which would also choke off the threat of distillation, could be a shrewder move than a wide release.

Politics could get in the way. America’s midterms were the first big elections where AI was on the ballot, and it fared poorly. Ahead of the results, The Economist found that Americans living near a data-centre site swung towards the Democrats by around five percentage points over the year, compared with voters with the same demographic characteristics elsewhere. Voters opted to restrict data centres in all but one of the 41 local referendums on the topic. Anti-data-centre candidates won stunning victories. Most consequential was the surprise election as governor of Texas of Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat who campaigned for a pause in data-centre construction. Texas is host to around a third of America’s data-centre buildout.

The potential moratoriums would hit projects not yet under way, most of them due in 2028 or beyond. In states that elected governors who support a data-centre pause, there are 25.6 gigawatts’ worth of not-yet-started data centres due in 2028, finds Maya Barkin of SemiAnalysis, a research firm. That is equal to just under half America’s current data-centre capacity.

Still, new data centres are comfortably profitable enough to fund tax cuts and payouts for the communities where they operate. Politicians and developers may well be able to negotiate win-win deals—though that may be easier in places with more Republican voters, who are a little less opposed to data centres. Ms Hinojosa has already toned down her rhetoric. After the election, she clarified that Texas is still pro-business. “It is not that I hate data centres,” she said, though she did accuse the industry of “taking advantage of Texas”.

A bigger risk is federal regulation. None of the proposals floating around Congress with any chance of passing so far would interfere much with the AI developers’ business models. But the new Democratic majority will be keener on regulating AI, and could pivot quickly if, say, a serious cyberattack makes AI risk a top-tier issue.

None of that will stop Anthropic from raising gobsmacking sums. Nor has the buildout of data centres yet shown much sign of slowing. But the business models and political environment that brought AI into the hundreds of billions in revenue won’t carry it into the trillions. For that, the industry will need to adapt and evolve. A looming question is whether Wall Street will have the patience to let it.

articles.title: Inside America’s first new submarine base abroad for 53 years
articles.deck: AUKUS is beginning to make waves on Australia’s west coast

paragraphs.text: Seahorse hotels had to be built first. The bony fish off Western Australia’s coasts are bad swimmers, spending most of their lives with their tails hooked around bits of rock, or human artefacts like piers and docks. So when the Royal Australian Navy began to upgrade HMAS Stirling naval base to host nuclear-powered submarines, divers were sent to relocate 263 of the creatures to grids of rebar nearby.

No detail is too small as Australia readies Stirling to host American nuclear-powered attack submarines from next year. That will make it the first American submarine base to be established abroad in half a century, turning it into a port that will project American power deep into Asia. Its site offers a big advantage over America’s existing bases: unlike its one at Guam, it is out of range of all but the most advanced conventional land-based Chinese missiles, but closer to Asian waters than other American submarine bases.

It is also the first big milestone for AUKUS, a deal that was announced five years ago by America, Australia and Britain to jointly design and build nuclear-powered submarines. The American presence at Stirling is part of the first phase, enabling Australian sailors to learn how to sail America’s Virginia-class attack submarines. They will deploy on the boats and maintain them at Stirling. One, USS Colorado, has just arrived at the base for a workover by the Australians, and will return for good at the end of 2027.

In a second phase, Australia is to buy from America and operate its own Virginias in the early 2030s, though there are doubts over whether these will be delivered on time or at all. Finally, Australia and Britain are to jointly design, build and operate a new class of nuclear-powered submarine. The first Australian boat would begin operation in the 2040s. Despite mischief from Chinese spokesmen, no nuclear weapons are involved, only nuclear power. That would let Australian subs range much farther than the country’s current diesel-powered boats without surfacing, giving Australia a punchier deterrent.

AUKUS remains controversial. Much of it was negotiated in secret because Australia was under contract at the time to buy French diesel-powered subs. When that contract was cancelled and AUKUS announced in 2021, it set off a big row. Only afterwards did it become clear to the plotters what a huge challenge it would be. Creaky shipyards in America and Britain would need a big jab of cash to meet the production targets. Some is coming from Australia, which has already handed over $2.6bn of a pledged $6.2bn. That, says Jennifer Parker of the Lowy Institute, a think-tank in Sydney, “is a drop in the bucket compared to what is needed”. But it is a real sign of Australia’s commitment.

This may help explain why a transactional Donald Trump has mostly left the deal alone, last year saying it was moving “full speed ahead”. But if the cash infusion does not jolt the Anglo-American submarine industrial base out of its torpor, Australia risks ending up with fewer boats than promised. Hence some Australians, particularly those sceptical of the alliance with America, still oppose AUKUS.

But Australia gets quite a bit else out of the deal. In order to share with a new partner the closely held technology used to build and operate nuclear reactors under the oceans, America and Britain have both had to revamp laws and regulations on sharing their most sensitive defence-tech secrets. These have brought Australia into the innermost sanctum of American alliances, in a circle previously occupied only by Britain. It has also unlocked related co-operation between the three on other cutting-edge technologies like AI, quantum computing and hypersonic missiles.

But the biggest development has been the decision to base four American submarines at Stirling, an hour’s drive south of Perth. That was not in the original AUKUS plan, and is a major change in plans for American forces in case of a conflict with China. The base will stay under Australian control; officially the foreign submarines will merely “rotate” through it. But that is a sleight of hand; each American sub will operate from Stirling for one to two years at a time. (A British sub may come to visit now and then, too.)

The American presence will be known as Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-W):“Surf West”. Already $1.5bn has been spent on readying the base for American subs, with another $4.1bn planned. At one pier, crews are driving concrete piles into the seabed (displacing those seahorses) to let it withstand pressure from the 7,000-tonne nuclear-powered sub in bad weather. Engineers are installing five different types of back-up power. Even a vessel with its own nuclear reactor needs auxiliary power, to prevent a meltdown while the reactor is undergoing maintenance.

An American commodore will command the American navy’s newly set-up Submarine Squadron 3 from Stirling. Secure communication equipment has been installed to let him talk to the Pentagon over classified channels. Nearby, housing is going up for some of the 1,200 American sailors under his command, along with a tax-free grocery shop stocking American snacks, open only to American sailors and their families. The island’s cricket oval has been taken over by building crews; a basketball court has taken its place nearby.

Enormous questions persist over AUKUS. The three countries’ plans foresee three to five Australian-flagged Virginias joining the American ones at Stirling in the early 2030s. But to meet the needs of both Australia and America, shipbuilders in Connecticut, Rhode Island and Virginia will have to raise their output from 1.2 boats a year to 2.3 by 2031. If they cannot, a future American president might not release any to Australia.

Even bigger questions loom about the capacity of Britain’s shipyards and nuclear industry, tasked with building 12 of the new AUKUS-class boats due to enter service in the late 2030s, instead of the seven that Britain first planned. If America and Britain cannot invigorate their shipyards, they could leave Australia with a nuclear-submarine base but no nuclear-powered submarines of its own.

articles.title: Indonesia’s vice-president resigns, escalating a destabilising feud
articles.deck: It could pit the country’s army and police against each other

paragraphs.text: ON PAPER, THE resignation of Indonesia’s vice-president on November 11th was a simple question of eligibility. Indonesia’s electoral law requires that the vice-president possess a secondary-school diploma or its equivalent. Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who was elected in 2024, can do one better: he has a university degree. But on October 30th Indonesia’s Supreme Court ruled that he had got into university without completing high school. In the days that followed, over 120 members of parliament called for his impeachment. Mr Gibran leapt before he was pushed.

In practice, however, there is little that is black and white about the latest trouble in a tumultuous year for Indonesian politics. The vice-president’s resignation comes amid the collapse of a political partnership between President Prabowo Subianto and Mr Gibran’s father, the former president Joko Widodo. The break between the two looks set to plunge Indonesian politics into further uncertainty.

Jokowi, as the former president is known, defeated Mr Prabowo in bitter presidential elections in 2014 and 2019, going on to lead the country for ten years. The two later reconciled, and a term-limited Jokowi offered up his son to serve as Mr Prabowo’s running-mate in the 2024 election. The unity ticket coasted to victory, cheered on by Indonesians happy at last to be offered political stability.

Little of that stability has been on display in recent months, however. As markets and voters turned against Mr Prabowo’s populist economic policies, the condominium between the president and his predecessor has come under strain. A break came on November 3rd, when police arrested Police General Listyo Sigit Prabowo (no relation to the president). Mr Listyo had just stepped down as the country’s top cop. Authorities now allege he had used the force’s wiretapping powers to snoop on Mr Prabowo’s communications.

That might seem a straightforward allegation of abuse of power, but for Mr Listyo’s long and close association with Jokowi. Mr Listyo owed his job to Jokowi. More than that, he was part of a close circle of officials with whom Jokowi worked before he became president, when Jokowi was mayor of the small city of Solo in Central Java and Mr Listyo was his police chief. After Jokowi was elected president, Mr Listyo rose rapidly. Authorities have not said that Mr Listyo bugged Mr Prabowo at Jokowi’s behest. But the links between the two men have raised suspicions among those close to the president. Under Mr Listyo, the police discouraged opposition to Jokowi’s administration, filing frivolous charges against critics and breaking up peaceful protests.

Jokowi leaned on the police in part because soldiers have long been more sympathetic to Mr Prabowo, a former army special-forces commander. The two forces have had a sometimes bloody rivalry ever since the police were carved out of the army in 1999. One risk, then, is that as relations between the two presidents fracture, each will use units loyal to them to seek advantage against the other. This could amp up tensions between two large groups of men with guns. Already there are signs of this. On the evening of Mr Listyo’s arrest, Mr Prabowo ordered 21,000 troops to urgently deploy to Jakarta, the capital.

That sets the stage for a tense environment as parliament prepares to fill the three years remaining in Mr Gibran’s term as vice-president. In the coming days the president will nominate two candidates, and the parliament will elect one of them as vice-president. Mr Prabowo enjoys a docile chamber, and will certainly get his pick of deputy. Undoubtedly a high-school diploma will be required this time. Unquestioning loyalty will be essential, too.

articles.title: The Japanese region where “eight-testicle women” outdo men

paragraphs.text: Susaki, a fishing town on Japan’s Shikoku island, boasts plenty of charms, including fresh seafood, nabeyaki ramen (served piping hot in a clay pot), and Shinjo-kun, an otter mascot wearing said noodles on its head. Locals also take pride in hachikin—spirited, outspoken, hard-working women with a reputation for outdoing men. The term, which comes from the local Tosa dialect, is used throughout Kochi prefecture. Its origins are murky, but according to a popular theory it combines hachi (eight) and kintama (testicles). A hachikin, in other words, has the cojones of four men.

Not everyone welcomes the label because of its vulgar origins, but plenty embrace it. Takenaka Kanako, a Susaki local who runs a soy-sauce factory, says being called a hachikin is a compliment; she greets your correspondent wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with the English words “Eight Balls”. Asked what makes Kochi’s women so formidable, Kusunose Kosaku, Susaki’s mayor, points to their ability to hold their drink. At local festivals, he recalls, some women knock back prodigious amounts of sake in one go.

Yet there is more to hachikin than drinking prowess. Kochi ranks first among Japan’s 47 prefectures for economic gender parity. Women have relatively high employment rates, and the gap in earnings between men and women is comparatively narrow. Miura Mari of Sophia University points to men’s earnings as a key factor. In wealthier, industrial areas, the male-breadwinner model remains strong. But in poorer places such as Kochi, men’s low wages make women’s labour indispensable to household finances and to the local community.

That does not make Kochi a feminist utopia. Women are severely underrepresented in politics, including on local councils. And the term hachikin can mask uncomfortable truths. Idolising women’s resilience can gloss over the burdens they bear, from earning a living while continuing to shoulder much of the housework and child care. “Men hardly pull their weight, and women end up doing all the work. It makes me furious,” says Ms Takenaka.

articles.title: Can anyone fix the China-Japan relationship?
articles.deck: The two countries need a go-between. Donald Trump is not an ideal option

paragraphs.text: WHEN FUKUDA YASUO, a 90-year-old former prime minister of Japan, died last month, China’s supreme leader, Xi Jinping, sent condolences. Mr Fukuda had devoted much of his career to stabilising Sino-Japanese ties. He worked behind the scenes to calm Chinese anger in the early 2000s over the then prime minister’s visits to Yasukuni, the shrine in Tokyo that honours Japan’s war dead, including 14 class-A war criminals. In 2014, when relations had frozen again over the disputed Senkaku Islands, he convinced Mr Xi to meet then-prime minister Abe Shinzo at the Asia-Pacific (APEC) summit in Beijing that year.

Another APEC summit, this one in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen next week, could be the setting for a similar ice-breaking meeting between Mr Xi and Takaichi Sanae, Japan’s current leader. Relations have been dire since Ms Takaichi suggested a year ago that Japan might respond with force to a Chinese attack on Taiwan. Chinese officials demanded that she should retract; she has not. Since then China has discouraged tourism, banned seafood imports, imposed tougher export controls on dual-use items, crucially including rare earths, and cut off most high-level government communication. Last December a Chinese jet is said to have locked its fire-control radar onto Japanese fighters; when Japan called its defence hotline with China, no one answered.

China’s animosity has become personal. Its state-controlled media slams Ms Takaichi as a “neo-militarist” because she is leading a big Japanese defence build-up in co-ordination with America (though it is in response to China’s many-times-greater expansion). Ms Takaichi has also long been outspoken about her belief that Japan is too apologetic about its past colonialism and wartime actions. She has not visited Yasukuni since becoming prime minister. But she still prayed to the shrine from a nearby car park in August, and sparked more Chinese rage when she sent a ritual offering in October.

Mr Fukuda was a “responsible statesman” with a “correct view of history,” Mr Xi said, adding that Japan’s leaders should “cherish the older generation’s hard work” and adhere to the four political documents signed between the two countries. That was a pointed admonition for Ms Takaichi, since these documents formally state that Japan “fully understands and respects” China’s position on Taiwan.

Ms Takaichi has insisted that her statements are consistent with Japan’s past policy on Taiwan. She has close ties to Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party, which advocates Taiwanese self-determination, and flaunts it on social media: she posted 37 photos on Instagram of her visit to Taiwan in April 2025, months before she became prime minister. She also posted a photo of herself with Taiwan’s representative to APEC on X last year.

China has shown no signs of openness to a meeting at this year’s summit, though it has accepted several non-government Japanese delegations in recent months. The most notable was a group led by a former foreign minister, Iwaya Takeshi, who met China’s foreign minister and one of its vice-premiers in Beijing in September. But officials in Tokyo see the trip more as a Chinese attempt to exploit divisions within Japan than an invitation to reconcile, given that Mr Iwaya is part of an opposing faction to Ms Takaichi’s within the ruling party. “She hates him,” says one official.

Some Japanese officials bridle at the question of how to fix the Sino-Japanese relationship. Japan, they note, has not retaliated against any of China’s actions and remains open to dialogue. China’s message, complains one Japanese official, is: “Bend the knee”. There is no point in begging a bully to speak with you, he adds.

China has inflicted only limited damage over the past year. The number of Chinese tourists visiting Japan dropped by 56% year-on-year from January to September. But overall spending has been increasing, with the largest share coming from Taiwanese visitors. The seafood industry was cushioned by having just emerged from another Chinese ban in 2023 that pushed it to find different customers. And Ms Takaichi’s refusal to retract her remarks has been popular domestically; more than 40% of Japanese favour her tough stance.

The part of China’s campaign that may start to hurt soon is the restriction on exporting rare earths. Japan is said to be only months away from running out of some of these, including yttrium oxide, used in making jet engines and semiconductors. Exports of yttrium oxide to Japan have fallen by 98% in the first nine months of this year compared with last year. China’s temporary truce with America over rare-earth controls has pointedly excluded Japan.

Japanese officials hope that America will raise the problem with China when Mr Trump meets Mr Xi at APEC, as he did in September, in part because Japan is part of America’s defence and semiconductor supply chain. But China is unlikely to soften its industrial punishment. It wants to make an example of Japan and “warn everyone against repeating Takaichi’s mistake” on Taiwan, says Ren Xiao of Fudan University in Shanghai.

If only Japan had a go-between like Mr Fukuda. Alas, they must make do with Mr Trump, who is unlikely to have Japan’s interests at the top of his mind at the APEC summit when he meets Mr Xi. Russia has also been raising pressure on Japan, perhaps in support of China’s campaign, by detaining a Japanese journalist and seizing Japanese tobacco businesses in recent weeks. Japan, it seems, may have to brace for a deeper freeze.

articles.title: Why Indians should have higher standards

paragraphs.text: HOW MANY cockroaches is an acceptable number of cockroaches in a commercial kitchen? Readers of this column, by definition a discerning lot, would no doubt set the limit at zero. The Bombay High Court, however, took the view that the “solitary finding” of two bugs was insufficient reason for the food-safety regulator to shut down a kitchen. “We are in India, we have to take a realistic stand,” the court’s acting chief justice cautioned officials in July.

Tukaram Mundhe disagrees. “These laws are Indian, not foreign,” says the man who, six months ago, was put in charge of enforcing them. The laws are meant for Indian conditions, he adds. They are drafted by Indian experts. And it is Indian people who implement them. The problem is “we have a very low estimate about ourselves,” he says. “Our thought process is ‘chalta hai’,” a Hindi phrase that means “it’ll do” or “good enough” and that is seen by many, including Narendra Modi, as an attitude that holds India back. That is what Mr Mundhe wants to change.

Until a few months ago not many people in Maharashtra, a prosperous western state with Mumbai as its capital, had heard of its Food and Drug Administration (FDA). That changed with the appointment of Mr Mundhe in May. Suddenly the FDA’s people were everywhere. They turned up stomach-churning violations ranging from vermin infestations and fungal growth on walls to expired food and poor handling in the kitchens of some of Mumbai’s best-known eateries and poshest private clubs. Even two canteens at the Bombay High Court were shut down for lacking licences. Tall, strapping and suitably mustachioed, Mr Mundhe quickly became a folk hero.

This is a familiar story. Every now and then a competent civil servant surfaces in a position that directly affects the public and actually does his job. The media duly elevate the official to something between a saint and an action hero. For a while citizens look on in stupefied wonder as they are reminded that the Indian state can work for their benefit. Then that official moves on to another posting and everything goes back to normal.

Mr Mundhe, whose incorruptibility ensures he does not keep any posting for long, hopes his impact will last longer. He has proposed an ambitious restructuring of the FDA to the state government. He wants to add hundreds of food-safety officers as well as many more laboratories and technicians to bolster the state’s ability to test food, drugs and cosmetics. He also wants to automate some of the FDA’s surveillance. One example is to use data streams the government already receives from several sources to track milk supplies from cow to glass. The goal is to create a robust institution rather than one that relies on an energetic individual.

Such ideas are not uncommon among India’s better bureaucrats, many of whom strive for excellence. Some even make progress at the margins. But they are the exceptions in a culture of chalta hai. As Niti Aayog, the government’s think-tank, put it in a report last year about the poor quality of official data, once a chalta hai mindset takes root it “shapes everything: how platforms are designed, how staff are trained, and how performance is judged. Slowly, quietly, quality becomes optional.” The Indian state has many weaknesses, but perfectionism is not among them.

Mr Mundhe’s answer is to involve the public. Among the first things he did upon taking over at the FDA was to build a modern website for citizens to lodge complaints. It is surprisingly slick, especially relative to most other official websites, which seem designed to induce seizures. The backend is more impressive still: an AI co-pilot helps his officers see which specific rules apply to which violations, points them to possible next steps and even drafts any notices that are to be served. It also automatically escalates complaints if junior officers ignore them. The FDA says it has been receiving more than six times as many complaints as it did last year.

“It doesn’t matter which government or party [is in power]. We, the people, have to take ownership,” says Mr Mundhe. The complaint portal, the high-profile inspections and the interviews are all aimed at reminding citizens that the state is not irredeemable. Indians, he says, should stop tolerating bad institutions. They should demand more. Most important, they should have higher standards. “When the public itself says chalta hai, of course the system will work as chalta hai.”

articles.title: China’s carbon-dioxide emissions have begun to fall
articles.deck: Its progress with electrification has been a big help

paragraphs.text: In the effort to slow the rise in global temperatures, no country matters more than China. It has been the biggest annual emitter of carbon dioxide for the past 20 years; its multitudes of factories, steel mills, cars and power plants released over 12bn tonnes of the gas last year, or nearly one-third of the world’s total. Still, that was a sliver less than the year before. In recent months, that fall has begun to speed up.

Data released last week by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a think-tank in Finland, show that China’s carbon-dioxide emissions dropped by 3.1% year-on-year in the third quarter of this year (see chart 1). The last time they fell so quickly was in 2022. That was during the covid-19 pandemic: lockdowns had stalled China’s economy. This time economic growth has picked up a little.

So Chinese officials have some cheering news to offer COP31, the annual UN climate summit which began in Turkey on November 9th and will end on the 20th. They might also boast that China’s exports of clean technologies are helping others to decarbonise. To be sure, the decline in emissions is still small. Yet China emits so much carbon that even little changes can alter the global trend (3.1% of China’s emissions equals 100% of Britain’s).

Some factors that have helped reduce emissions will not last for ever. A campaign to enforce safety standards in coal mines—after an accident in May that killed dozens of workers—pushed up prices of coal, so less of it was burned. The Iran war raised oil prices, to similar effect. Unusually mild weather reduced demand for power.

But a big reason for the fall is that China’s economy needs less fossil-fuel. A property bust has slashed demand for steel and cement, which are produced by burning coal. In the first half of this year the proportion of power supplied by coal plants dropped below 50% for the first time on record. That was enabled by breakneck investment in cleaner sources of energy. As well as plenty of hydro- and nuclear-power plants, China has installed 1,000 gigawatts (GW) of solar capacity since 2022—more than the rest of the world put together—along with over 300GW of wind (twice the total wind capacity in America).

China’s transport is electrifying fast. In September EVs and plug-in hybrids made up two-thirds of passenger car sales, up from a tiny fraction a few years ago (see chart 2). This has helped reduce demand for oil. Sinopec, a state-owned oil giant, expects the country’s oil consumption to fall in 2026 for a third consecutive year, by nearly 4%.

Electrification is tougher for lorries: China has the world’s largest fleet. They have to drive longer distances with heavier loads, so require more-powerful batteries. But Chinese-made lorry batteries have improved enough to meet this need. Half of the heavy-duty lorries sold domestically in September were electric (see chart 3). CATL, a Chinese firm that is the world’s biggest battery maker, has set up hundreds of stations where lorries can swap their batteries for new ones in a few minutes, avoiding delays caused by a lengthy charge mid-journey.

Can China continue to push emissions down? It has promised to become carbon neutral by 2060. That will require the latest quarterly drop not only to be sustained but to accelerate. One cause for concern is that its blistering roll-out of clean technologies has started to taper. Though EVs comprise an ever higher share of new cars, the number sold has been declining for ten months. Subsidies to buyers and EV firms have largely been withdrawn. Officials believe the industry is mature enough to withstand market forces and want uncompetitive firms to fold in order to reduce overcapacity. Cautious consumers are also buying less of everything as the economy continues to falter. All this will slow the rate at which petrol cars are taken off the roads.

During the first nine months of this year China installed less than half the solar power-capacity than it did in the same period of last year. Power firms are becoming more hesitant because they worry they will not make much money, says David Fishman of The Lantau Group, a consultancy based in Singapore. China used to guarantee generous prices for electricity from new solar farms. But since June last year they have had to sell power at market rates. Much of China’s electricity is traded via long-term legacy contracts which tended to favour coal. The grid also wastes much of the clean energy that is plugged into it because it cannot store or move enough of the excess power that is sometimes generated, such as on very sunny days.

China is trying to solve these problems. It is installing solar “power-towers” that can generate around the clock (a recently opened one in the western region of Xinjiang is pictured, previous page). It is building long-distance power lines and introducing electricity pricing that responds to fluctuations in the output of renewable energy. And it is imposing quotas on energy-intensive industries to make them use more green electricity. China’s rapidly proliferating data centres will guzzle an ever bigger share of power output, but the government is trying to steer them towards wind- and solar-rich areas in the west. All this should eventually revive the installation of clean tech. But officials are wary. Power cuts in 2022, blamed on overzealous environmental policies, still haunt many local governments. Even as coal-consumption declines, many of them are building more coal-fired power plants, just in case.

Although many analysts believe that China’s emissions have already peaked, the central government’s deadline for achieving this is not until 2030. There is little chance that it will revise the target: China prefers to underpromise and overdeliver on its climate commitments. The worst outcome would be if local officials and state-owned firms see the next few years as a chance to implement dirty projects while they still can, notes Lauri Myllyvirta of CREA. That would turn a climactic moment in China's green transition into a last hurrah for dirty energy.

articles.title: China’s exports of clean tech to South-East Asia are soaring
articles.deck: Unlike in the European Union, governments don’t fret about the influx

paragraphs.text: In recent years, China’s green-tech manufacturers have salivated over the market for their stuff in Europe. Demand there has surged as countries and consumers try to reduce their reliance on fossil fuels. European governments are becoming fretful about the impact on their industries and are trying to curb the influx, such as by imposing quotas on electric vehicles. But Chinese firms have options closer to home. Their exports to South-East Asia are soaring. Few in the region whinge.

The Iran war has supercharged South-East Asian demand. Many countries there depend on supplies of oil and gas from the Gulf. Fighting over the Strait of Hormuz has choked the flow, pushing up electricity prices and prompting a scramble for cheaper sources of power. In May the Philippines became the world’s second-biggest buyer of Chinese solar panels, overtaking Pakistan, according to Ember, a think-tank in London.

In recent months shops in the Philippines have barely coped with demand, says Ping Mendoza of the Philippine Solar and Storage Energy Alliance, a trade group. Waiting times for installing panels are now two or three months, instead of just a week. Unlike Pakistan’s relations with China, which are friendly, ties between the Philippines and China are bedevilled by territorial disputes in the South China Sea. But few in Manila worry about the tide of Chinese green tech. The Philippines does not have much industry that feels threatened. Westerners wonder whether some Chinese kit might pose security risks. There is little such angst in the Philippines.

Much of South-East Asia’s demand for clean gear from China does not relate to home markets. Countries in the region have been repackaging it for sale in the West, helping China evade American and European tariffs on Chinese goods. But the region is also rapidly emerging as an important end-market. In the first nine months of this year China’s exports of solar technology to South-East Asia leapt almost 60% by output capacity. To Europe, they fell by 11% (see chart).

Most governments in South-East Asia, eager for energy security, are pleased. In June Laos suspended the import of fossil-fuelled vehicles until the end of 2026. Malaysia is boosting tax incentives for firms to buy and use clean energy. Indonesia still subsidises coal, but its president, Prabowo Subianto, has vowed to increase the country’s solar-energy capacity from about 1.5 gigawatts (GW) to 100GW by 2029.

The prevailing desire in the Philippines is to “get as much [renewable capacity] built as possible”, says Colin Steley, an Australian who sells clean-energy kit there. Chinese firms are happy to help.

articles.title: Ted Plafker, a stalwart of our China coverage, has died
articles.deck: He was a giant among Western journalists in the country

paragraphs.text: China does not make reporting easy for foreign correspondents from the West. They are often harassed by local authorities when doing their jobs. They are routinely warned against reporting that offends the Communist Party. Resident visas can be hard to obtain. It is a difficult country for any Western journalist truly to call home.

Yet Ted Plafker, a native of New Jersey, did so. He arrived in China in 1989 after a bike trip through Europe and Asia. He planned to stay a few weeks and return to America to find work as a journalist. He ended up staying, witnessing that year’s upheaval in Tiananmen Square and meeting Roberta, who was to become his wife and mother to their three children. He wrote for several publications, including, from 1994, The Economist. He joined the newspaper’s bureau in Beijing shortly after it opened in 1997 and was its longest-serving member.

Ted became fluent in Mandarin (on top of Russian, which he had mastered already as a student at Wesleyan University in Connecticut) and a giant among Beijing-based journalists—for three years he headed the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of China (the government shuns it). He will be missed for his great wisdom on the country, as well as his unfailing kindness, helpfulness and good humour.

articles.title: Xi Jinping’s chief ideologue is worried
articles.deck: Wang Huning describes threats to the Communist Party and country

paragraphs.text: China’s ruler, Xi Jinping, is a student of history. Not history as one damn thing after another, but capital-H History: the grandiose kind that is picked over by philosophers and stoned undergraduates. Mr Xi has said that history progresses according to certain Marxist “laws”, advancing in “stages” on the road to communism. He often refers to “great changes unseen in a century”, suggesting that mankind has reached a new historical watershed.

The great-changes idea is probably not Mr Xi’s. The far more likely inventor is Wang Huning (pictured above), who is the Communist Party’s fourth-ranked leader and unofficially its chief ideologue (he is probably the author of “Xi Jinping Thought”, which all cadres must study). Once a professor of political science, Mr Wang stands out among the grey men atop the party. He is the only one who has been a senior adviser to three leaders. Although his public-facing role is merely as head of a toothless advisory body, he is omnipresent on committees that draft big decisions.

So officials would have taken note on November 3rd when People’s Daily, a party mouthpiece, published a bracing warning by Mr Wang: rather than steering history, the party risks becoming its victim. Mr Wang elaborated on a new phrase that was launched by Mr Xi at a meeting of the party’s Central Committee in late October. It is the “three even more formidables” (no doubt Mr Wang’s invention, too). It refers to growing challenges that the party leadership thinks it faces in safeguarding national security, sustaining reform and stability, and maintaining ideological purity.

Mr Wang worries that a changing world may catch China off balance: he cites “all kinds of storms” and “challenges coming one after another”, from the artificial-intelligence revolution and protectionism to the erratic behaviour of certain countries (meaning, obviously, America).

Changes in China are a growing threat, too. Mr Wang describes a country racked by inequality between people, regions and industries. He points to demographic headwinds as China ages and its population shrinks. “Intelligentisation” (presumably meaning AI) could cause social disruption, he writes. New ways of working, meaning the gig economy that employs 320m people, have eroded the party’s control over labour. These days in China “all kinds of ideas and values intertwine and clash”, frets Mr Wang. He calls “contradictions” in society “unprecedented”.

Many of these concerns have been aired before, including by Mr Xi (a book of worry-related extracts from his speeches was published in 2020). But Mr Wang’s attempt to summarise the party’s problems in one essay is unusually blunt. It relates how money-making opportunities and foreign ideas have corrupted some officials and caused others to lose faith in Mr Xi. The job of disciplining them, Mr Wang notes, is becoming harder as the party expands (it now has 100m members). At the Central Committee meeting, a resolution expressed concern about leaders born in the liberalising post-Mao years. They place “new demands on education”, it said.

Creating a numbered term to sum up these concerns gives them new political weight. The aim, clearly, is to ensure that they are studied assiduously at every level of the party. Lest anyone dare to think that economic or political reform might solve some of these problems, Mr Wang argues for more control. That echoes the views of the Central Committee, which called for further concentration of decision-making power in the hands of senior leaders. It said technology firms should be overseen by higher-ranking officials, and listen more to their party cells. It also urged officials to use the internet to unite “the masses” and said they should guide gig workers to “listen to and follow” the party.

But will this work? Karl Marx, who also liked to muse on history, wrote that “changes in the economic foundation lead sooner or later to the transformation of the whole immense superstructure.” Mr Wang appears not to believe that anything so dramatic is inevitable in China. He urged his comrades to “keep our resolve and press ahead bravely”. That should do it.

articles.title: Xi Jinping’s plan for a China-centric world order
articles.deck: A “community with a shared future” sounds soft, but is backed by muscle

paragraphs.text: When Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and nearly 20 other national leaders gather in Shenzhen next week, they will be treated by Xi Jinping to displays of China’s marvels. Drones will swarm and sparkle overhead, fleets of humanoids will usher delegates through conference halls and ultrafast-charging electric vehicles will shuttle them between venues. The message to the annual summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation forum—that China’s technology is cutting-edge—will be clear to all.

But there will also be a subtler message, signalling Mr Xi’s idea of how the world should look. The summit’s theme, “building an Asia-Pacific community to prosper together”, is a deliberate echo of his main foreign-policy doctrine: “building a community with a shared future for mankind”. Ma Zhaoxu, a vice-foreign minister, has made the link explicit, tracing the theme back to Mr Xi’s calls since 2013 for an “Asia-Pacific community with a shared future”.

To many observers, this language may seem obscure. It is certainly a mouthful. Even China hawks face a challenge in explaining to the public why a “shared future” is threatening (the literal translation, “common destiny”, has a more chilling, deterministic edge, which is presumably why a switch was made to softer wording in English). Yet this is not just a casual slogan. It has been written into China’s constitution and tied to every big diplomatic initiative that Mr Xi has launched for more than a decade. So it is worth asking what, exactly, he means by it.

A natural place to start is the Chinese government’s white paper, published in 2023, that tried to explain Mr Xi’s doctrine. Running to nearly 13,000 words, it might seem to cover a lot of ground. Alas, the content is overwhelmingly vague. Among its exhortations: countries ought to “work together in harmony and unity” and should “strengthen dialogue” while promoting “peace and development”. Hard as it is to disagree, it comes across more like a general wish list than a specific, operable plan. Chaguan found only four forward-looking commitments. China will not seek hegemony, China will cut carbon emissions, China will modernise its economy, China will work with other countries. All are restatements of existing policy and, again, not much to go on.

Chinese scholars have tried to put meat on the bones. Yang Jiemian of the Shanghai Institute for International Studies made a notable attempt this year when he declared that the doctrine deserves to be seen as a full scientific system. It offers specific goals (eg, lasting peace), has a road map defined by Mr Xi’s four global initiatives (on development, security, civilisation and governance), and is delivered concretely via Mr Xi’s Belt and Road Initiative for global infrastructure-building.

The trouble with such elaborations is that they peel back abstraction to reveal yet more abstraction. In the parlance of our times, it is turtles all the way down. What is Mr Xi’s “shared future”? Why, it is the embodiment of his global initiatives. And what are those? They are vehicles for principles like sovereignty, multilateralism and dialogue—which, in turn, bring us back to the definition of “shared future”. At least belt-and-road projects are tangible, such as railways in South-East Asia and roads in Africa. But they do not amount to grand strategy; they are overseas investments, some productive, some not. You must feel a twinge of sympathy for diplomats in Beijing when they are asked by their home governments for concise notes on Mr Xi’s “shared future”.

A recent book by Steve Tsang and Olivia Cheung of, respectively, the School of Oriental and African Studies and King’s College London, cuts through the ambiguity. They argue that the shared-future talk is a formal expression of Mr Xi’s true aspiration: the creation of a Sino-centric world order. But they also see an essential truth in Mr Xi’s repeated assertions that China is not seeking hegemony: he does not want to be burdened by global policing. He just wants recognition of China’s pre-eminence and other countries to defer to it, even when China’s behaviour impinges on their interests. His ideal world is one where sovereign leaders can do as they please within their borders—a world safe for autocrats and free of high-minded Western pontificators about rights and wrongs in other lands.

Students of Chinese history may feel they have seen this “shared future” before. It sounds a lot like the professed principle of mutual non-intervention that has been the much-touted lodestar of China’s foreign policy since the 1950s. The usual criticisms apply to both concepts. China has a history of meddling, such as backing African rebel movements in the Mao era or grabbing disputed territory—look at recent encroachments on waters close to the Philippines and across the unsettled border with India. Chinese officials do little when their closest partners mess with others. They have, in effect, enabled Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

What has changed since the 1950s is the context. China’s economic and military power is orders of magnitude greater. It can put real muscle behind its demand for non-interference in its own politics. That is worrying—especially if it ultimately gives China cover to do whatever it wants with Taiwan. But for now, governments and businesses around the world are more consumed by fallout from America’s war against Iran and from Mr Trump’s tariffs. The immediate uncertainty is not what Mr Xi might say in Shenzhen but how Mr Trump will behave as a gravely wounded president after the Democrats’ triumph in the midterms.

Set against that, talk of a shared future is less threatening precisely because it is not a bold new vision for the world. Rather, it is a rebranding of a long-standing strategy: deeply conservative, occasionally hypocritical and focused on China’s own betterment. Other countries may not love it. But they know it.

articles.title: Democrats’ strategy for ending the war in Iran
articles.deck: An unsuccessful attempt to impeach Pete Hegseth is a sign of more trouble ahead

paragraphs.text: THE LAWMAKERS who attended an event hosted by Elect Democratic Women, a pro-choice group, on November 10th are unlikely to have much sympathy for Pete Hegseth, Donald Trump’s secretary of war, who has sacked female generals and questioned the role of women in the armed forces. But Mr Hegseth might thank them for his narrow escape in an impeachment vote in the House of Representatives that afternoon. Eleven Democrats missed the vote—more than the seven-vote margin—with some delayed in traffic on their way back from the event.

That failure points to a bigger problem for Democrats. More than seven in ten voters who crushed Mr Trump’s party in the midterms on November 3rd said in exit polls that the war in Iran had been a crucial or major factor in their vote. Democrats are keen to respond to that fury, yet measures to remove Mr Hegseth, let alone end the war, will take time.

The articles of impeachment introduced by Thomas Massie, a maverick (and outgoing) Republican congressman, accused Mr Hegseth of starting the war illegally, ignoring congressional resolutions to withdraw and showing disregard for civilian harm, as well as transgressions relating to Venezuela, Yemen and strikes on drug-smuggling boats. Democrats and Republicans alike had expected that several Republicans would break with their party and vote against Mr Hegseth. In the end, Mr Massie was the only dissident. The department of war posted an AI-generated image of the congressman weeping.

An impeachment vote will almost certainly succeed in January, when Democrats have a majority and better-whipped members. Even then, Mr Hegseth would be tried in the Senate, where at least 11 Republicans would need to break ranks with their party and join Democrats seeking to remove him.

Many Republicans are privately advising the White House to replace Mr Hegseth now, while a Republican-controlled Senate could confirm a successor. Mr Trump seems untroubled. “He’s guilty of two things,” said the president on November 8th. “Basically winning two wars.”

As impeachment efforts rumble forward, Democrats will seek other ways to bring the war itself to a halt. In theory, the War Powers Resolution of 1973, passed amid broad discontent over the war in Vietnam, obliges presidents to obtain congressional authorisation to continue fighting after 60 days of conflict, with a 30-day extension allowed due to “unavoidable military necessity”. Presidents of both parties have ignored that injunction, however, dismissing it as unconstitutional. In June, in a sign of bipartisan frustration, Congress passed a resolution directing the president to remove armed forces from the conflict in Iran. It had the impact of a scolding letter. An attempt at another resolution failed in the Senate in September.

Chances of enforcing the War Powers Resolution in court will improve slightly in January, when Democrats can sue as the House. However, courts typically defer to presidents on matters of war. Congress could introduce new legislation but, like the impeachment of Mr Hegseth, any bill would need 67 Senate votes to overcome Mr Trump’s veto.

The more effective tool, in theory, would be to use Congress’s power of the purse. To avoid a government shutdown on December 11th, Congress must pass either a full funding bill or, more likely, a continuing resolution, a stopgap measure that extends current spending levels for a few months. A National Defence Authorisation Act, which spells out Pentagon policies and pay and which has passed each year since 1961, is also under negotiation. Charles Kieffer, a former staff director of the Senate appropriations committee, says that Rosa DeLauro and Patty Murray, the senior Democratic members of the House and Senate appropriations committees, respectively, might demand that Mr Trump end the war in exchange for passing a continuing resolution, though he suspects that neither would shut down the government in December over the issue.

Indeed, using defence spending as leverage is fraught with both material and political risks. The Iran war and other military operations has meant that the Pentagon has a gaping financial hole. Even if a continuing resolution were to be passed, it would leave the Pentagon with $400m less cash per day compared with last year, and $1.7bn per day short of the astonishing sums planned this year under Mr Trump’s proposed $1.5trn budget, notes Elaine McCusker, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a think-tank, who served as the Pentagon’s top budget official during Mr Trump’s first term. “People may not understand the kind of situation the military is in right now,” she says. “The people who get hurt by budget delays, shortfalls and uncertainty are not the people in a position of power to do anything about it.”

Democrats therefore acknowledge that they have little chance of choking off funds for the war until next year, when they control Congress. Even then, it will not be easy. Mr Kieffer recalls Democrats’ efforts to force George W. Bush to withdraw troops from Iraq in 2007, when the party controlled both chambers, by including that demand in a supplemental budget request, a top-up to the regular defence budget. Mr Bush vetoed that measure. Though it seemed ineffective in substance, “it gave the Democrats the political cover that they needed to go ahead and provide funding for the troops”, says Mr Kieffer.

Some Democrats hope that Republicans are so weary of the war that enough might support measures to hasten its end. Their near-lockstep vote to shield Mr Hegseth from impeachment is not encouraging. Meanwhile, the war drags on. America attacked Iran’s Qeshm island just before the elections. Iran continues to strike one oil tanker a day, on average.

articles.title: American workers face a surge in health costs
articles.deck: Employer-sponsored insurance, the backbone of American coverage, is becoming more frail

paragraphs.text: Health care ranks high on Democrats’ agenda in Congress, as they seek to restore subsidies to buy individual insurance and reverse cuts to Medicaid, the health programme for the poor. However, a different problem looms, too. In the coming weeks, the 157m Americans who receive insurance through employers will have to choose a plan for next year. The cost of their insurance is due to rise by an average of 8% in 2027, according to Marsh, a consultancy, the biggest price hike in more than 20 years.

Employer-sponsored health care has long been the backbone of American coverage. About half of Americans get their health insurance through their job, that of their spouse or their parents. But as health insurance gets ever more expensive, bosses are looking for ways to trim their spending, whether through making workers pay for more of their care in cash, cutting coverage or even scrapping health benefits entirely. Already, six in ten Americans worry about affording health care, according to KFF, a health-research outfit, a higher share than worry about petrol. As employers strip back coverage, that anxiety is sure to rise.

Because health premiums paid by employers are excluded from income and payroll taxes, the government incentivises bosses to compensate workers by offering them health insurance. However, employers are problematic middle men. An employer generally covers about 80% of an insurance plan’s cost, with staff paying the remaining 20% themselves, or an average of $7,500 for a family plan. Fast-growing insurance costs borne by employers limit workers’ salaries, usually in a way that is not transparent to staff.

Health costs spiked in 2021 as Americans resumed the surgeries and treatments that they had put off during the covid pandemic. But in recent years, premiums have risen faster than inflation and nominal wages (see chart).

There are many reasons for this. Years of consolidation have given hospitals greater pricing power. Workers are seeking more treatment for behavioural health and innovative cancer medicines are helping to drive up premiums, too. GLP-1s, popular anti-obesity medicines, have probably pushed up premium costs by about a percentage point, according to Marsh. A similar share comes from new artificial-intelligence tools that help hospitals to spot extra charges that a human might miss.

Some employers will shop around for different coverage, but all insurers face higher costs. So firms are changing their offer to staff. In 2026 roughly two in five large employers made workers pay a bigger share of their premiums, according to a survey by KFF. Next year, with costs rising even more quickly, monthly payment increases of around 10% are not out of the question, says Beth Umland of Marsh.

Another option for employers is to restrict who qualifies for insurance. Next year Disney, a big entertainment firm, will rescind coverage from employees’ spouses if they can get insurance through their own employer, a step that is hardly draconian. Other firms may impose more potent restrictions, for instance by limiting patients’ choice of doctors and services. Starbucks has stopped covering GLP-1s for weight loss, with more firms due to follow suit: 10% of the companies now offering GLP-1s to treat obesity don’t plan to do so next year, according to the Business Group on Health, an advocacy group.

Some employers may go further, eliminating health insurance completely. Small companies have been dropping coverage for decades, explains Paul Fronstin of the Employee Benefit Research Institute, a think-tank. In 2000 more than 80% of firms with 10-49 employees offered health insurance to their staff—now, just 59% do, a share that looks set to decline. The exchanges created by the Affordable Care Act, better known as Obamacare, offered individuals a new way to shop for insurance. However, premiums there are rising even more quickly.

With unemployment still low, companies have tried to avoid severe cuts, lest they drive away needed workers. Should the job market loosen, they might trim health benefits further. Democrats such as Abdul El-Sayed, a senator-elect from Michigan, have revived calls for universal health coverage. More cuts to employer-sponsored insurance give them new ammunition for their argument.

articles.title: How Florida withstood a blue wave
articles.deck: The quintessential swing state of 2000 is the bastion of Republicanism in 2026

paragraphs.text: “TO CALL IT a wave I don’t think would be fully accurate,” Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida, said the morning after Democrats won control of Congress. “It’s the political equivalent of a meteor strike that went all around the United States—blue states, red states, everything in between. And the one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of Florida.”

Indeed, even as Democrats popped champagne in states that had once been deep crimson, Republicans in Florida were elected to all open statewide offices. They held their congressional seats and retained control of both legislative chambers. They were not immune to Mr Trump’s unpopularity—they lost their supermajority in the legislature and, compared with 2024, Florida swung 10.2 percentage points to the left. But that was less than the national average of 15 points, and far below swings of 20 points or more in Texas, Georgia, South Carolina and Mississippi, where Democrats flipped crucial seats. Florida, long since evolved from being a swing state, is Republicans’ most defiant stronghold.

There are three main reasons Florida was spared the uprising against Republicans. The first is demographics, an advantage that Republicans elsewhere will struggle to mimic. For six years Florida politicians have advanced policies, from rejecting covid lockdowns to enacting universal school vouchers, to make the state a sanctuary for MAGA refugees. Although Democrats turned out a higher share of their voters this year, they could not overpower Republicans, who came into the election with 1.5m more registered voters. It helped Republicans that Hispanics, who propelled swings in other red states, were less keen on Democrats in Florida. Cubans make up half the state’s Hispanic voters and, unlike Mexicans or Puerto Ricans, have been fused to the Republican Party since the days of Ronald Reagan. Exit polls show they moved left but didn’t flip.

The second reason for Republicans’ success is that—unlike in Texas, Kansas or Iowa— Democrats in Florida ran mediocre candidates who struggled to raise money. In the race to succeed Mr DeSantis, who was term-limited, Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee, outraised David Jolly, his Democratic opponent, $173m to $27m; Mr Jolly managed his own campaign, refused to debate and, insiders say, was allergic to asking for cash. In Florida’s Senate race, Angie Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, surprised Democrats by winning the nomination in August, and continued to surpass naysayers’ expectations. But whereas James Talarico in Texas and Annie Andrews in South Carolina campaigned on messages of unity, Ms Nixon was known for yelling at her Republican colleagues in the legislature with a pink bullhorn. In the general election she succeeded in driving turnout, including of voters who opposed her.

National Democrats refused to cough up much cash themselves, both because they doubted some candidates and because running ads in Florida is so expensive—supporting a statewide candidate means placing ads across ten media markets and appealing to an electorate so diverse it can feel like Manhattan and rural Alabama stitched together. Where the party did spend, in four Democratic congressional districts gerrymandered to favour Republicans, candidates held on. “Going forward Democrats can either invest or continue dying in Florida,” says Fernand Amandi, a Democratic strategist in Miami.

The third reason that Florida Republicans thrived is that their message reflected the politics of 2026, not 2024. David Johnson, a Republican operative in Tallahassee, had warned candidates against fighting culture wars, largely because Republicans in Florida had already won them—the state had banned firms with state contracts from promoting diversity, and transgender women from competing in women’s sports in public schools. On the campaign trail Mr Donalds duly emphasised affordability, promising to cut insurance and health-care costs to preserve the “Florida dream”. Mr DeSantis contends that Republicans elsewhere had lost the plot.

Which Republican politician might offer a model of how to do better? Mr DeSantis, of course, at least according to him. “The most dangerous place in Florida last week was between Ron and a Fox News camera,” says a Republican strategist. A massive property-tax cut that Republicans put on the ballot, Mr DeSantis says, gave their base a reason to turn out. Even as Washington failed to deliver what Mr DeSantis calls “bold conservative change”, the governor managed to halve the state’s debt and shrink its government to make the economy boom. “Florida shows how you can build a coalition not only to convert on all your promises in good times but also to withstand the bad times,” he declared on Fox News on November 4th.

That same day, Mr DeSantis’s odds of becoming the Republican presidential nominee in 2028 jumped from 5% to 18% on Kalshi, a betting website. The last time Mr DeSantis ran for president, in 2024, his campaign flopped, his robotic delivery no match for Mr Trump’s enduring appeal. Now Mr DeSantis’s narrative is sufficiently compelling that Republican voters will give him another chance, argues Steve Vancore, a Florida pollster.

The trouble with narratives is that they can change. Mr DeSantis has much to boast about now, but some of his policies may not age well. The measure to slash the state’s property taxes on primary residences may look less like a victory by 2028, when towns in Florida are slashing budgets for police and fire departments. Mr DeSantis admits that the state, which has no income tax, may need a trust fund to help local governments. In 2026, Florida has become America’s most important red state. If these midterms have taught America anything, though, it is that no politics are permanent.
