articles.title: An emerging consensus on trans politics
articles.deck: Voters want neither trans kids playing girls’ sports, nor politicians obsessed with it

paragraphs.text: The most effective Republican ad of 2024, many strategists agreed, was one that declared that “Kamala is for they/them” and Donald Trump was “for you”. This year, conservative groups tried to repeat the trick, devoting at least $183m to attack ads on transgender issues, according to AdImpact, a research firm. The strategy failed to protect Republican seats. Yet where trans-related issues were put to voters directly, the response was different.

Four states considered ballot measures to restrict girls’ and women’s sports to biological females. All passed, including in solidly Democratic states. That points to a new phase in the fight over trans rights. A growing share of voters don’t want trans kids playing girls’ sports. Nor do they want politicians to focus on the issue.

Two-thirds of Americans favour laws requiring athletes to play on teams that match their sex at birth, up from 58% in 2022, according to the Pew Research Centre. Around 30 states already have rules on trans athletes. In June the Supreme Court upheld such policies. Some 59% of adults approved of that ruling, almost twice the share who disapproved.

Though all the ballot measures this year concerned gender and sports, the specifics of the initiatives in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington varied. Arizona’s includes requirements that trans people use bathrooms at schools and sports facilities that match their sex at birth. Washington’s measure, passed by a 12-point margin, requires medical documentation to verify sex for each child seeking to play girls’ sports.

Even as a majority opinion emerges on trans sports, it is a deciding issue for vanishingly few Americans. In Washington state, the trans measure passed despite Democratic congressional candidates winning nearly two-thirds of the statewide vote. A poll by AP-NORC in October found that just 11% of voters considered trans issues a top priority.

“After 2024 voters really thought that Democrats were overly preoccupied with these ‘social issues’,” says Tré Easton of Searchlight Institute, a Democrat-aligned think-tank. In this election, with voters concerned about affordability, it was Republicans who were caught in their own culture-war traps.

In a sign of shifting politics, James Talarico, the incoming Democratic senator from Texas, once called God “non-binary” but said during his campaign that he opposes “trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness.” Sherrod Brown, Ohio’s Senator-elect, took out his own ads in response to Republicans’ trans attacks during the campaign. “With everything going on,” his ads asked, “that’s what they are talking about?”

articles.title: The fight over Republicans’ future has begun
articles.deck: After a staggering loss, the party is battling over whom to blame and how to move forward

paragraphs.text: AS THE DIRE results came in on November 3rd, young Republicans at Butterworth’s, a MAGA haunt a stone’s throw from the Capitol in Washington, sipped glumly on cocktails such as the “Senate Majority Martini” and “The Red Wave”. “This is historic”, noted one, “in the same way the Hindenburg was historic.”

Donald Trump has commandeered the Republican party for over a decade. It is now adrift, with developments since the election only adding to the confusion. On Capitol Hill, Republicans are moving in different directions. On November 10th House Republicans elected as their leader Jim Jordan of Ohio, a co-founder of the hard-right Freedom Caucus who sought to overturn Joe Biden’s election in 2020. In contrast, John Thune of South Dakota, a veteran senator who has clashed with President Trump, was easily re-elected as the party’s leader in the upper chamber, despite efforts by more right-wing lawmakers to delay that election.

The Nvidia scandal adds further uncertainty; the party is only beginning to grapple with questions of how the administration handled intelligence that Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s boss, was having an affair with an alleged spy. The president’s support of artificial intelligence had become a divisive issue among Republicans, even before this scandal erupted over the industry’s most important executive. Mr Trump’s dominance of the party has for years papered over its fissures. They are now being laid bare.

The president himself remains defiant. On November 6th Mr Trump told CBS that his deportation drive had been “too tough” and that he was open to a deal on immigration with Democrats. An hour later, as if to declare himself the most MAGA of all, he appointed Stephen Miller, a nationalist and immigration hardliner who spearheaded that drive, as his new chief of staff. Within MAGA, loyalists to the president remain. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the governor of Arkansas, was among those to parrot Mr Trump’s line that he was not on the ballot: “I don’t think that this can be a line drawn against him.” A few MAGA media figures, namely Mark Levin and Laura Loomer, continue to support the Iran war and America’s relationship with Israel.

Yet all this compounds problems for the president, who is already vulnerable to critics blaming the midterm loss on his policies and hubris. Since the election a noisy group of MAGA purists have contended that Mr Trump let the movement down. On November 4th J.D. Vance, Mr Trump’s vice-president, did not blame Mr Trump by name, but took the stunning step of blaming his boss’s policies, including the war, a failure to lower costs and the relationship with Israel.

MAGA-purist vodcasters such as Tucker Carlson and Steve Bannon had already broken with Mr Trump over the war before the election; they were scathing after it. On November 5th Natalie Winters, the co-host of Mr Bannon’s “War Room” show, alleged that White House officials such as Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, had made “shady deals” and that “the actual grifters in the administration” were tarnishing “the entire MAGA movement”. She stopped short of implicating the president.

Mr Carlson called the results a “disaster”, on his show on November 4th. “You could mark it on your calendar,” he added: “Trumpism gone.” He blames war, corruption (Mr Trump was “vain and venal”) and the president’s decision to endorse flawed candidates. The administration had been too focused on fighting anti-Semitism, he argued, a stance he dubbed “Jewish lives matter”. Mr Levin, for his part, skewered Mr Carlson as a “loathsome creature” who had worked to “sabotage the president, the GOP and the midterm elections”.

As brawls continue within MAGA, Republicans’ old guard, severely diminished but still defiant, is hoping for a resurrection. “The American people have rejected our party’s shift toward economic populism,” asserted Mike Pence, Mr Trump’s vice-president in his first term, in an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal, glossing over the populism espoused by many Democratic candidates. Mitt Romney, the last pre-Trump Republican to have run for president, in 2012, offered a more sweeping critique on X, pointing to the war and corruption, as well as Mr Trump’s “weaponised justice, ICE brutality, mountainous deficits, hiding Epstein, abandoning allies and coddling enemies”.

Between the MAGA purists and the old guard is a more fluid category of Republican, who could be charitably called pragmatists. Ron DeSantis, the term-limited governor of Florida, failed to win the Republican presidential nomination in 2024. He now hopes the MAGA movement might give him a second look.

Consider Ted Cruz, who after Tuesday’s sweep is poised to be the last remaining Republican statewide office-holder standing in Texas. In his own election autopsy on his podcast, he paid lip service to the need to rebuild as a “true blue-collar party”, but pointed to a pre-Trump solution: Republicans had to be “real free-market conservatives”. Mr Cruz, a long-standing proponent of muscular foreign policy who once cheered on Mr Trump’s war, felt compelled to change tack after the election, saying that the war should have been “brief, decisive and over”.

More fights will break out. Even as Mr Vance appeals to the MAGA purists, many within the MAGAverse despise him, not least for his ties to Silicon Valley, where he worked before running for Senate. MAGA purists are vehemently opposed to the conflict in Iran, championed by Pete Hegseth, the secretary of war, who narrowly avoided impeachment on November 10th. Yet Mr Hegseth’s purge of supposedly woke generals from the Pentagon has earned him ardent fans within the right-wing “manosphere”.

The most explosive argument may be over Nvidia. Republican hawks had opposed Mr Trump’s decision, after being lobbied by Mr Huang, to ease export restrictions of Nvidia chips to China. On November 9th Mr Bannon repeated his allegation that Mr Huang is himself a spy.

More battles will emerge over why the White House did not respond to a classified report from Marco Rubio, Mr Trump’s secretary of state, warning that Mr Huang’s mistress might be a Chinese spy, alongside concerns over why Mr Lutnick failed to keep America’s advanced chips from China. The election is over. The Republican brawl is just beginning.

articles.title: Donald Trump has an unusual chance to make progress
articles.deck: He also has an unusual gift for blowing such chances

paragraphs.text: Not long ago, after a whopping defeat in midterm elections, the president made some conciliatory noises and some belligerent ones. He issued a warning to the opposition party that was taking control of the House. “You can’t legislate and investigate simultaneously—it just doesn’t work that way,” he said. “You can’t go down two tracks at the same time.” Yet when they did go down both tracks, he did, too, battling congressional investigations while collaborating with his congressional adversaries to achieve legislation on trade and the environment. When crisis struck he worked with the House to deliver an historic economic rescue package—even though by then, in a party-line vote, the opposition had impeached him.

That president was, of course, Donald Trump, in his first term. This time around, after an even bigger midterm rebuke, he is sending more intensely mixed signals. He has floated the idea of working with Democrats to solve one of America’s most vexing problems, its broken immigration system. Yet he has appointed as his chief of staff Stephen Miller, the enforcer of his brutal deportation agenda, whom Democrats despise and even some Republican legislators consider too hardline. Given the priorities of the Democrats, particularly those elected from what were Republican states and districts, Mr Trump has a bigger opportunity than in his first term to make progress, including for the working-class voters he has always claimed to represent. One can hope. But the historical pattern, and this president’s particular pattern, suggest he won’t.

Freed from facing voters again, intent on a legacy and looking to history for vindication, second-term presidents tend not to retreat from signature positions after midterm reversals, notes Frances Lee, a professor at Princeton. “They tend to take a hard line and persist,” she says. President George W. Bush sent more troops to Iraq despite Americans’ despair over that war; President Barack Obama outraged Republicans by using executive orders to protect some immigrants in the country illegally. Mr Trump has taken to brandishing a red hat emblazoned with the word “veto”, a familiar threat in his circumstances. In the first five and a half years of his presidency, Mr Bush issued not a single veto, a record surpassed only by Thomas Jefferson. After the crushing Democratic victory in 2006, he vetoed 11 bills, edging out Mr Obama, who, after his midterm drubbing in 2014, vetoed ten.

Presidents Bush and Obama achieved some legislative compromises. Yet unlike those two predecessors—and unlike any president in memory—Mr Trump has made conflict core to his political appeal. Having been dismissed after the midterms as seeming “more like a bitchy old woman than an alpha male” by Tucker Carlson, a vodcaster, Mr Trump may see restoring his image as a fighter as his best path to consolidating Republican support. He knows there is nothing like an impeachment to accomplish this. “There are those that say that worked out to my advantage,” he volunteered after the midterms, referring to his two impeachments in an interview on “60 Minutes” on CBS.

The desire to be seen by his base as a fighter may explain his refusal to eject his cartoonish secretary of war, Pete Hegseth, as, after the midterms of 2006, Mr Bush forced Donald Rumsfeld out. Mr Trump also faces an obstacle Mr Bush did not. The shambolic Trump administrations have so damaged the reputations of most who have joined that this president is unlikely to attract any appointee with the standing of Bob Gates, a former CIA chief who was confirmed with bipartisan support to replace Mr Rumsfeld.

Base politics and incompetence would probably also doom a foray into immigration reform. Mr Trump has never summoned the discipline to deliver on complex initiatives he promised, from rebuilding America’s infrastructure to fixing its health-care system to streamlining its bureaucracy. He has also always prioritised the loyalty of his most hard-core followers, relying on their support, particularly during primaries, to intimidate other Republican officials. His suggestion he might work with Democrats on immigration brought immediate howls of protest from MAGA stalwarts, furious at the prospect of “amnesty”.

There is one further possibility for progress, which sets Mr Trump apart from his presidential predecessors: on issues that appeal to his base, but not to traditional members of his own party, his idiosyncratic politics gives him a chance to work with the opposition. He has, in the past, signalled openness to such Democratic proposals as raising the minimum wage or capping interest rates on credit cards. However, the nature of this opportunity brings its own obstacles. Such ideas divide leaders of his party, some of whom have clung to Republican economic orthodoxy throughout the populist Trump era. With some Republican politicians already questioning tenets of Trumpism after the midterms, the president may not want to put his control of the party at greater risk. “I think he would like to be a kingmaker,” Ms Lee says. “And if he alienates the party sufficiently, he won’t be.”

That may be Mr Trump’s fate regardless, given the policy to which he has shown the greatest ideological commitment. Although he has succeeded in persuading even Democrats to embrace some tariffs, such as on electric cars from China, his enthusiasm for a global trade war is unpopular. Yet he seems certain to battle any attempt by Congress to restrain his use of tariffs. Here he may find a precedent in the only other president to serve non-consecutive terms, Grover Cleveland, a Democrat whose doctrinaire commitment to the gold standard split his party when it nominated his successor, William Jennings Bryan, in 1896. Bryan was defeated, and the Democrats did not find their way back to the White House for 16 years.

articles.title: Colombia’s El Tigre is taking no prisoners
articles.deck: Drug lords and social-justice warriors are in the president’s sights

paragraphs.text: Pistol on belt and walkie-talkie in hand, President Abelardo de la Espriella strides along with security forces on night-time raids. Alleged criminals, paraded in handcuffs, are struck dumb. Colombia’s new sheriff taunts them, then packs them off to jail with one of his signature lines: Bienvenido a la Patria Milagro—“Welcome to the Miracle Nation.”

The videos posted to the president’s social-media channels provide a gratifying show for Colombians tired of crime. Mr de la Espriella, a flamboyant right-wing populist who calls himself El Tigre, promised an iron fist and rip-roaring growth. Approaching 100 days in power, the Tiger has got started on both.

But it will take more than TikTok videos to break the influence that armed groups which run drug-trafficking and illegal mining operations hold over swathes of the country—and certainly more to tackle Colombia’s fiscal crisis. Meanwhile Mr de la Espriella’s illiberal instincts have set him on a collision course with Congress and the courts. And the left-wing coalition that lost to him by less than one percentage point in the presidential run-off is encouraging his critics onto the streets.

Mr de la Espriella’s government entered office at a time of calamity. Three days after his inauguration an earthquake struck Colombia, killing more than 300 people and causing over $13bn of damage. Mr de la Espriella and his ministers responded in a telegenic manner. They visited the affected areas and promised a “Miracle Fund” for reconstruction (which in fact has been slow to materialise).

Since then, security has been Mr de la Espriella’s main concern. Under Gustavo Petro, his leftist predecessor, armed groups expanded, security deteriorated and cocaine production hit new highs. Mr de la Espriella has scrapped peace talks attempted under Mr Petro, which had failed to make progress. He has stepped up bombardments of armed groups, killed several high-ranking gangsters and signed off on extraditing some individuals to face prosecution in America. All of this is recounted in a daily stream of self-aggrandising online content, some of it grotesque. Mr de la Espriella crows over the body bags of those killed in operations.

Many Colombians welcome the change in narrative. But the increase in operations has been “modest”, says Javier Flórez of the Ideas for Peace Foundation, a think-tank. “It’s essentially the same: captures, kills, seizures.” A different strategy will be needed to break the power of criminals who reign over parts of Colombia. After security forces killed one ringleader in September, the late kingpin’s gang declared a lockdown of Santa Marta, a coastal city, as a show of force; it told businesses to close and residents to stay at home. Mr de la Espriella flew in with the armed forces and had fighter jets rip through the skies. Locals stayed inside, nonetheless.

The government wants new tools to swat enemies. A “submission law” rules out peace talks but offers reduced sentences to criminals who confess, hand over assets and turn informant. A proposed anti-terrorism statute would let the executive designate terrorist groups and freeze the assets of anyone collaborating with them. Elizabeth Dickinson of International Crisis Group, an NGO, sees these policies as “carrot and stick”. Human-rights groups worry that Colombian leaders might also use the stick to intimidate civil society.

Mr de la Espriella has a limited budget for security and other operations. Public debt is about 60% of GDP. Without action, the government projects a fiscal deficit of 9.4% of GDP in 2027. Debt service will swallow almost a quarter of the budget. So difficult is the situation that his government is talking to the IMF about a loan programme, which could perhaps be worth $20bn (4% of GDP). At the end of October the government unveiled a tough tax-and-spending reform. It would cut the number of goods eligible for special lower rates of VAT, broaden the income-tax base, cut the state payroll by one-fifth and also give the president powers to trim spending by decree. Corporate-tax rates would fall from 35% to 31%; big new investors would get a rate of 20% for 16 years. Fiscal conservatives were pleasantly surprised. “It’s not what you expect from a populist,” says Mauricio Cárdenas, a former finance minister.

But getting it passed will not be easy. Mr de la Espriella’s party has only a handful of seats in Congress. There is a nominal pro-government majority, but Mr de la Espriella claims not to want to do the usual trading of jobs and resources for political support. Rafael Nieto, a senator from the right-wing Democratic Centre, says the government wants to impose bills, not debate them. His party, the largest, is wary of tax rises. José Manuel Restrepo, the vice-president, has said Colombia could default if the bill is not passed. “Now we’ll really see the capacity of the president, beyond the spectacle,” says Mr Cárdenas.

So far Mr de la Espriella has shown little desire to compromise. In October he appointed as interior minister (responsible for managing Congress) Alejandro Ordóñez, an ultra-Catholic former attorney-general who burned books in his youth. The choice fits the president’s call—alongside his tubthumping on security—for a “cultural counter-revolution” to restore traditional values. Mr de la Espriella has arranged for dozens of works related to feminism, sexual diversity and Colombia’s peace processes to be removed from the National Museum. He signs off messages with “Long live Christ the King!”, despite court warnings about the state’s religious neutrality. The hope seems to be that a culture war will galvanise Mr de la Espriella’s base before regional elections in October next year. “It creates soldiers for the cause,” says Luis Ernesto Gómez, a former deputy minister of interior.

In this and much else, Mr de la Espriella is following Donald Trump. Colombia has joined the “Shield of the Americas”, the United States-led military coalition waging war on the region’s drug-traffickers. America has sent drones to help hunt them down. Colombia has also signed on to Mr Trump’s anti-globalist agenda. It withdrew a candidate for the International Criminal Court, and may leave the court altogether.

Mr de la Espriella shares Mr Trump’s thin skin. He fired the head of the statistics agency, apparently for saying he found no evidence that Mr Petro’s government had fiddled labour-market figures. Critical journalists have lost their jobs. “There’s clearly a far-right authoritarian populist tendency,” says Mr Nieto, the senator. “But there’s still time to correct.”

The streets are already heating up. The Historic Pact, the left-wing opposition, will join unions and students for a national strike against spending cuts on November 19th. About 60,000 demonstrators took part in anti-government protests last month. Mr de la Espriella dismissed them as a “small minority that wants to stop Colombia”. As the numbers grow, that line will be harder to hold.

articles.title: How Paraguay’s digital bank became a massive bomb
articles.deck: The country prospered under President Peña. Then his buddy’s business went bust

paragraphs.text: Drones piloted by TV crews whirr over Santiago Peña’s mansion in the hills. Below, investigators debate how to open the former president of Paraguay’s walk-in safe, hidden inside a secret passage. A policeman is asked if reports that they might blow the vault open are true. “No,” he laughs. “People live nearby.” Besides, an explosion could bring an infinity pool that sits above it pouring down.

Paraguay has been in tumult since November 3rd, when regulators seized an upstart bank called Ueno. Three million customers were frozen out of their accounts (Paraguay has about 7m people). Many couldn’t pay for food, fuel or medicine. Some $850m of government money remains stranded. Within days, Mr Peña was impeached and arrested. Investigators say he abused his position to benefit the digital lender. They say Ueno sucked in state funds and disbursed extravagant loans to cronies. Mr Peña denies wrongdoing.

When preparing to take office in 2023, Mr Peña tapped Ueno’s chairman, Carlos Carvallo, to lead Paraguay’s Central Bank (BCP). Mr Peña was friendly with Miguel Vázquez, Ueno’s CEO, who sought to make the bank Paraguay’s first billion-dollar startup. Mr Peña’s asset declarations show Ueno lent him around $315,000; prosecutors say the borrowings were higher than that, and that they were used to build his summer residence (where the vault was found). He held shares in the bank’s holding company until last year. The central bank, under Mr Carvallo’s care, approved Ueno’s speedy expansion.

In July a BCP regulator warned his superiors that Ueno’s finances were dire. They ignored, threatened and removed him. But his memo reached Horacio Cartes, a powerful former president and a businessman whose companies manufacture cement and cigarettes. Mr Cartes is the leader of the ruling, conservative Colorado Party; he was once a mentor to Mr Peña, though the two recently became enemies. Mr Cartes hinted in October that he had dynamite. “Word to the wise,” he smouldered to a camera, before triggering a detonation at his quarry. “Stand clear.”

Both Ueno and Mr Peña’s political career are in smoking ruins. Those arrested alongside Mr Peña include Mr Vázquez, other Ueno executives and Mr Carvallo, who as recently as October was named Central Bank Governor of the Year by LatinFinance, a financial news service. (Most of those arrested deny any wrongdoing or knowledge of Ueno’s activities.) Pedro Alliana, Mr Peña’s anodyne vice-president, was sworn in as Paraguay’s new leader on November 6th. His cabinet is stacked with people loyal to Mr Cartes.

Thanks to a deposit-insurance scheme, over 1.8m people have begun getting their money back (up to a cap of $38,000). That covers the majority of Ueno depositors and has helped calm demonstrations. But the impact on the economy will take time to become clear. Paraguay’s GDP has more than doubled in real terms since the start of the century. But job losses linked to Ueno’s collapse could dent things. And worried people have stopped spending.

Larger depositors are not guaranteed repayment. Ueno held some $520m in state pension funds. Some people aren’t receiving pensions; many fear they won’t get them in the future. “We feel disappointed, disillusioned, offended,” said Karina Fernández, a doctor, at a demonstration outside Congress. “It’s extremely painful.” The collapse will also affect remittances, the country’s third-largest source of foreign exchange (a record $1.35bn in 2025) after beef and soya. Ueno’s banking app made it far easier for the million Paraguayans who work in Argentina, Brazil and Spain to send money home, says Belarmino Balbuena, a rural organiser who travelled 300km to Asunción, the capital, to protest. “This issue affects the whole population.”

Past political scandals in Paraguay have not dulled growth for long. But the harm done to perceptions of the central bank’s independence could weigh on foreign investment, says Fernando Masi of CADEP, a local think-tank. Brazilians have been founding factories and Argentines throwing up towers, driving record foreign direct investment of $1.2bn last year.

In recent years vaccine refuseniks, blockchain enthusiasts and assorted tax-phobics have also flocked to Paraguay. An unprecedented 50,000 people applied for residency in the nine months to September. Political upheaval and blocked bank accounts could cause some liberty-lovers to consider alternative places, such as Bolivia. “Paraguay is seen as a safe haven,” said Travis Miller, an American entrepreneur, on X (where he goes by Bitcoin Capitalist). “It’s like a nuclear bomb going off.”

The scandal is an opportunity for Paraguay’s opposition parties ahead of elections that are due in 2028. Founded in 1887, the Colorado Party has lost only one democratic election, 18 years ago. But having now burned through Mr Peña and Mr Alliana—the heir and the spare—Mr Cartes’s outfit is left with nonentities (Paraguay’s presidents are limited to a single five-year term). Miguel Prieto, a 37-year-old former mayor from a centrist party, is the most popular challenger.

Mr Peña and his ilk are responsible for “eroding everything we built”, says Dionisio Borda, a former finance minister. “It makes me a little sad, and also angry.” He is advising Mr Prieto on how, if elected, he might soothe fizzing discontent with corruption, injustice and poor public services. Before all that goes boom, too.

articles.title: Machu Picchu’s “mafias” are costing Peru real cash
articles.deck: The astonishing Inca site deserves more wrathful management

paragraphs.text: Machu Picchu has a reputation for being tough to visit. Head to the Taj Mahal or famous spots on the Great Wall of China, and you can secure tickets a few days ahead. But until recently the ticketing platform for Peru’s famed Inca ruins often showed the site fully booked for nearly six months. Although tourists can queue up for a shot at some of the 1,000 tickets sold daily at the foot of the mountain, many have simply gone elsewhere, says Juan Stoessel of Casa Andina, a hotel chain. “We constantly got calls from guests cancelling their reservations because they realised they couldn’t secure tickets.”

The monument’s fame is not the sole cause of this logjam, according to an audit by the Peruvian comptroller’s office. It concluded that between August 2024 and December 2025 tourism agencies exploited weaknesses in the official ticketing website to make more than 200,000 reservations. Most were for tickets that they never ultimately bought.

The government report did not speculate about the agencies’ motives, but many Peruvians see the workings of a “mafia”. Tourists who are blocked from buying tickets are more likely to fork out for access secured by third parties who are working in cahoots with corrupt officials, says Maycol Ugarte, who represents the national government in the district where the site lies. “They’re tarnishing the image of Machu Picchu.” Some tourists, he says, end up paying $300 for entry, more than five times what it should cost.

This is frustratingly familiar. In 2023 some 70,000 people were believed to have got into Machu Picchu in irregular ways. Back then, the government vowed to outsource the job of ticketing to a company that it thought would do better. But that sparked angry protests from people claiming to be outraged by the “systematic privatisation of Machu Picchu”. Demonstrators blocked train services that haul tourists to the ruins. Eventually the government took back control.

Authorities have unveiled a new website that they insist is harder to hack. But there appears to be little appetite to bring the wider problem of corruption at Machu Picchu to heel. The only person known to have been charged recently with selling access to the monument is a security guard handed a five-year jail term for taking a bribe of 100 soles ($29) to sneak someone in. Mr Ugarte wants a criminal probe that would see ringleaders properly prosecuted. In the meantime, he thinks bureaucrats who oversee Machu Picchu’s ticket sales should be rotated to different jobs every few months.

Machu Picchu has long been the crown jewel of Peruvian tourism. Once a getaway for Inca royalty, the site today attracts some 1.5m visitors a year. This pumps millions of dollars into an under-developed region that is home to a lot of indigenous Peruvians. But annual visits remain just short of their pre-pandemic peak. Some think the ticketing troubles are partly to blame. Protesters with various grievances who are more often choosing to block the site as a way of gaining attention have also taken a toll. “It’s shameful,” says Mr Stoessel. “The big loser is Peru.”

articles.title: Gadi Eisenkot has a chance to form a new government in Israel
articles.deck: Both his foes and his supposed allies may yet prevent him

paragraphs.text: GADI EISENKOT cleared the first hurdle on his path to power on November 8th when Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, gave him the mandate to form a new government. But he will have to overcome more formidable trials, including the breaking of election promises, if he is to replace Binyamin Netanyahu, the prime minister who lost his coalition’s majority in the election on October 27th.

In a short ceremony at the president’s residence, Mr Eisenkot conceded that “no one can stand for all the commitments they made. We will all have to make compromises.” He hopes to swear in a minority “emergency” government, formed of four Jewish opposition parties. Neither Arab nor Jewish ultra-Orthodox parties would formally be part of his coalition—at least to start with—but they would offer support when needed.

Mr Eisenkot’s rationale is that removing Mr Netanyahu is the most urgent priority. In recent weeks the prime minister has tried to drag Israel into another war with Iran and urged the head of the country’s secret service to investigate the Arab votes and disqualify the election results. To form a coalition with a majority would mean lengthy negotiations and he has only six weeks before the president asks someone else to try forming a government.

Persuading enough parties to secure a majority would mean a lot of promise-breaking. During the election campaign the four Jewish opposition parties committed themselves to universal national service. The ultra-Orthodox parties are demanding, as a condition for joining a coalition, exemption from military service for students of religious seminaries. Three of the four Jewish parties oppose including the Arab parties in a coalition. Mr Eisenkot himself has set a series of conditions, including condemning Hamas, the Islamist militant movement responsible for the massacres of October 7th three years ago, as a terror organisation. Those are difficult for the Arab parties to accept.

But the four main Jewish opposition parties only hold 48 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. A minority government would be a way of avoiding the tricky compromises while leaving open the possibility that Arab or ultra-Orthodox parties could formally join the coalition at a later date.

Mr Eisenkot, a former chief of the Israel Defence Forces, is a relative newcomer to politics. He entered the Knesset in 2022 and has been a party leader for only a year. This was an advantage in the election. His party’s fresh appeal helped it far outperform other parties in the opposition. But Mr Eisenkot has his work cut out to get an unruly camp in line. “We have various permutations for a coalition,” says an adviser to one of the party leaders. “But the four parties have to agree on one first.” His rival opposition leaders are already trying to outmanoeuvre him.

Chief among them is Avigdor Lieberman, of the nationalist Yisrael Beiteinu party. Mr Lieberman began his political career nearly four decades ago as an assistant to Mr Netanyahu but he has now sworn to end his rule. Yisrael Beiteinu won only seven seats in the election, but Mr Lieberman still fancies himself as both a coalition builder and future prime minister. He has begun his own freelance operation, negotiating with the ultra-Orthodox parties. He has ruled out being part of a minority government, especially if that would mean relying on support from Arab parties.

Meanwhile, Mr Netanyahu has not bowed out. Lawyers for his Likud party are trying to challenge the election result, claiming foreign interference and irregularities among the Arab voters. The Shin Bet security agency, headed by one of Mr Netanyahu’s loyalists, is investigating these claims but the resolutely independent attorney-general has ruled that there is insufficient evidence to question the vote-count or haul Arab politicians in for questioning. The election results have been ratified.

The prime minister’s fallback is to try to stymie the opposition’s coalition-building. On November 7th Mr Netanyahu called for a unity government, which presumably he would lead, instead of “a government relying on Islamists that will dismantle Israel from within”. He warned that “with a government such as this Israel simply will not survive.” Mr Eisenkot’s response was to describe the prime minister as “hysterical”. He will need his wits about him if he is yet to fulfill his election promise and replace Mr Netanyahu.

articles.title: Republicans blame Israel for their defeat
articles.deck: The Democrats’ victory could accelerate the decline of the Israeli-American alliance

paragraphs.text: The blame started before voting in America’s midterm elections ended and the extent of the Republicans’ drubbing was revealed. In an interview on election day Donald Trump said that America would cut off military aid to Israel “at the end of the year”. Israel no longer needs it, he explained; the country is “thriving”. But there was another reason, the president added: “It’s a bad talking point.” J.D. Vance, the vice-president, was more direct. On the day after the election, he blamed the war in Iran, and also America’s relationship with Israel, for the Republicans’ defeat.

Israel has been falling steadily out of favour in America. Its brutal campaigns in Gaza and Lebanon had already angered voters and politicians on both ends of the political spectrum. The unpopular war with Iran has drawn further attention to the $3.8bn Israel receives annually from America, nearly all of it as subsidies for the purchase of American-made arms and other military supplies.

America’s alliance with Israel featured in a number of high-profile contests, including that of Abdul El-Sayed, the senator-elect from Michigan who fiercely criticised military aid. Other candidates took pride in not accepting donations from AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobby. AIPAC itself said two weeks before the election that it would stop endorsing candidates, a tacit admission of the toxicity of its brand.

Messrs Trump and Vance’s words were not lost on Israelis. “The fact Trump said this on the day of the midterms was a political message that Israel is currently unpopular with both parties,” says Avner Golov, a former senior director on Israel’s national-security council.

Barack Obama signed the current ten-year $3.8bn package, which is set to run out in 2028. The Israeli government was aware that negotiating a new package would be tricky. Growing numbers of Democrats are particularly hostile to Israel, and the Trump administration—and Republicans more widely—are loth to give money to foreigners. In light of this, Binyamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, told The Economist in January that he favoured gradually phasing out American aid over the next ten years. Talks had started in recent months about the future of aid, but Mr Trump’s election-day announcement took Israeli officials by surprise.

“It’s been clear for years that the terms of the alliance with America were going to have to change,” says Alon Pinkas, a former diplomat who served as Israel’s consul-general in New York. “Now it looks like Netanyahu has agreed with Trump to end the current aid agreement, without anything ready to replace it.”

The future of the relationship is unclear. Mr Trump has suggested that Israel will be able to continue buying American arms, on its own dime. But Israeli officials worry that a Democratic-controlled Congress will limit the kinds of weapons Israel can buy and restrict how it can use them, especially in the occupied Palestinian territories. For over half a century successive American administrations have been committed to maintaining Israel’s “qualitative military edge” in the Middle East, supplying it with advanced weapons systems, years before America’s Arab allies. That may be up for debate as well.

An end to American aid would blow a $7bn hole in Israel’s finances in the next two years. After three years fighting multiple wars, it has been on a spending spree to refresh the IDF’s arsenal, ordering planes, helicopters and more. Israel will owe another $10bn after 2028 for kit it has already ordered, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Israel’s economy could withstand that, though it would mean cuts to the national budget in the coming years. “In financial terms it’s regrettable, but not an earthquake,” says Yigal Newman, a professor of finance at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem. “American aid is barely half a percent of Israel’s GDP.”

But, he points out, it would also be a blow to Israel’s standing as America’s key ally. Israel’s relationship with America not only boosts its military and economic power, it gives Israel diplomatic cover as well. America frequently deploys its veto in the United Nations Security Council to block anti-Israel resolutions. It puts pressure on other countries, such as Britain, which has announced sanctions on Israel over the violent settler attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. If the new Congress is considering similar sanctions, Israel will be more exposed internationally.

All is not lost for the alliance, which goes far beyond arms sales. America maintains radar and intelligence-gathering installations in Israel and recently expanded an airbase used by American aircraft in the Negev. The two countries co-operate intensively on missile defence and intelligence sharing. Israel has access to America’s surveillance satellites. America’s arms companies make use of the Israel Defence Forces to test their weapons on the battlefield.

And Israel still has supporters in Congress. Chuck Schumer, the probable majority leader in the senate, and Hakeem Jeffries, his counterpart in the House of Representatives, are on the more Israel-friendly wing of the Democrats. “The size of the Democratic victory suggests that the influence of the far-left on bills will be limited,” says Dov Waxman, a political scientist at University of California, Los Angeles.

But the relationship has fundamentally changed. Mr Netanyahu, who lost his majority in the Knesset on October 27th, has long presented himself to Israelis as the ultimate expert on America. Yet he has overseen the most drastic deterioration in his country’s standing in America in Israel’s history. Israeli diplomats privately accept that their prime minister, his hardline policies and hard-right coalition are “toxic in America”. A change in government in Jerusalem would help. But the alliance is becoming more brittle.

articles.title: Jordan is worried about a resurgence in jihadism
articles.deck: The war in Iran is helping to fuel it

paragraphs.text: Jordan has largely escaped the violence that has ravaged the Middle East in recent years. But on October 23rd, that seemed under threat. After Friday prayers three men opened fire on a funeral procession emerging from a church in Hammoud, a village in the southern province of Karak. They pursued mourners inside, smashed windows and sprayed bullets at pews. They killed nine people and wounded dozens. The gunmen then drove home.

King Abdullah donned fatigues, visited the wounded and vowed revenge. His warplanes struck what officials said was an Islamic State hideout in southern Syria, allegedly linked to the gunmen. It was a botched attempt to deflect attention from Jordan’s failures, say Western diplomats. Meanwhile at home, Muslims were banned from congregating after prayers.

The attack on the church, coupled with the killing nearly two weeks later of a Muslim policeman guarding the Sri Lankan embassy, has raised fears of a resurgence of violent fundamentalism. Its apparent retreat across much of the region had been a rare encouraging development of late.

Officials and experts are struggling to explain the shift. Its slide into authoritarianism kept Jordan calm for years. The most recent fatal terrorist attack before October was eight years ago. Since then authorities have in effect banned protests, dissolved the largest trade union and outlawed the Muslim Brothers, Islamists who are Jordan’s biggest political movement. The once-lively press and cultural scene have withered. This summer the king revived the use of mass executions. Repression is easier than politics.

Nobody in Jordan publicly celebrated the attack on the church. Yet the gunmen appear to have counted on local sympathy. They returned to their own village, apparently in search of protection; it took the authorities three days to detain them.

Jihadism and takfir, declaring other Muslims apostates, have a local history. Anyone who supports a tyrant is deemed an infidel and thus a valid target, including the policeman at the embassy. In 2016 militants took refuge in a Crusader castle near Karak and battled security forces. At least 18 people were killed. Islamic State flags once flew farther south.

Neighbouring Syria—where a former al-Qaeda commander is president and has been feted by the White House—may provide inspiration for fundamentalism’s revival. Despite reforms, eight-year-olds are still taught about martyrdom; 16-year-olds learn about jihad, albeit led by the king. The radio on a bus to the airport was playing a sermon denouncing Jews as apes.

The war with Iran may also be playing a part. Officials emphasise its economic benefits. American military aid has increased. Disruption at ports on the Red Sea and in the Gulf has routed trade Jordan’s way. Saudi Arabia and Iraq are now more reliant on Aqaba, the kingdom’s only port. Trans-shipment traffic is up by 150% so far this year. The region’s other economies are stuttering; Jordan’s gdp is growing by nearly 3%. Muhannad Shehadeh, the deputy prime minister for economic affairs, envisages a kingdom criss-crossed by railways, digital hubs and tourism projects, reconnecting a region riven by conflict.

Many Jordanians, however, are angry about the conflict. Fuel prices have risen. Projectiles that officials dismiss as “flying objects” are landing more often. Since a ceasefire in June, Jordan has intercepted scores of Iranian salvoes.

Many Jordanians resent America’s military presence and their country’s role, as they see it, as the forward defence for Israel. Anger could soar if Iran carries out threats to hit infrastructure as well as military bases. “The war with Iran isn’t our war. We shouldn’t be part of it,” says a veteran of the Muslim Brothers.

Repression can work for a time. But forcing radicalisation underground makes it harder to detect and contain. Being the underdog, says one Islamist, makes his sort more popular. The Brothers once led vast protests against America’s regional wars. Without such outlets, argues a lawyer who represents terrorist suspects, expect public anger to take less civic forms.

articles.title: Welcome to Africa’s treason belt
articles.deck: Why African autocrats favour lawfare to stymie opponents

paragraphs.text: From the moment Tundu Lissu was seized, after a public meeting in April 2025, it was clear that his would be no ordinary trial. The Tanzanian opposition leader had been cycling through jail cells with almost farcical regularity since his first arrest, on Christmas Eve in 2002. Between 2016 and 2017 he was arrested eight times and charged on six occasions, as well as shot with 16 bullets in 2017. Even so, this time felt different. Mr Lissu knew Samia Suluhu Hassan, Tanzania’s brittle and autocratic president, feared him. In the months following his detention, says a source close to Mr Lissu, police subjected him to psychological tricks meant to force a confession. Cameras tracked his every move, even to the toilet. He was put in a cell with death-row inmates.

So the judges’ verdict, announced to a courtroom surrounded by armed police on November 6th, came as little surprise. The chairman of Chadema, Tanzania’s biggest opposition party, was found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in prison. (He is appealing the verdict.) Since Mr Lissu had been on trial for treason, an offence carrying the death penalty, his family and supporters can breathe a sigh of relief. Still, it is a curious outcome for a case where the only physical evidence of wrongdoing prosecutors could muster was a video deemed inadmissible in court.

If Mr Lissu’s case is egregious, it is hardly exceptional in the region. Scores of Chadema members face treason or terrorism charges in Tanzania. Over the border in Uganda, Kizza Besigye is on trial for treason; in Rwanda, Victoire Ingabire is in the dock charged with inciting unrest. Venâncio Mondlane goes on trial in Mozambique on November 17th, accused of instigating terrorism, among other things. Brian Mundubile, in Zambia, has been held on treason charges since an election in August. The clustering of such cases can be read as the stress response of political systems that are beginning to come apart under pressure of public dissatisfaction.

This corner of Africa has evolved its own authoritarian style, distinct from the coups of the Sahel or the wars of the Horn. Most of its countries are, like Tanzania, peaceful. Several have been ruled for decades by the same parties, which see themselves as guarantors of that stability and have become hard to distinguish from the state. Politics borrows a liberal lexicon of rights, elections and constitutionalism. Underneath, it is a dirty game where one player holds almost all the cards.

In several countries this kind of hybrid rule is now being pulled apart from opposite directions. On the one hand, the erosion of democratic norms has reduced the incentive for would-be autocrats to keep up their liberal façades. The latest Mo Ibrahim index, a biennial report on African governance, finds that measures of democracy, including participation in formal politics, have worsened in most of Africa over the past decade. On the other hand, urbanisation and social media are making it harder for ruling parties to engineer consent, as leaders in Kenya, Madagascar, Mozambique and other places that have recently faced Gen-Z protests know well.

Opposition leaders are increasingly disinclined to play along with elections they know they will not be allowed to win. “No reforms, no election” was Mr Lissu’s allegedly incendiary slogan, refusing to participate unless the process was made fair. Mr Mundubile and Mr Mondlane went so far as to declare themselves winners of tainted ballots (without giving evidence to support their claims).

Instead they are seeking alternative tactics, particularly street protests. After four presidential campaigns Mr Besigye in Uganda said he would stop fighting elections and instead pursue “Plan B”. His allies say he meant a non-violent uprising; the state alleges he was organising armed rebellion. Mr Mondlane brought Mozambique to a standstill by co-ordinating demonstrations from his Facebook page. Prosecutors will try to show that his calls for “Turbo V8” protests incited the ensuing violence, which included attacks on government offices and police stations.

The line between violence and non-violence is blurry. Protests turn riotous in response to, or anticipation of, police aggression (and sometimes egged on by agent provocateurs). Opposition leaders are courageous and often principled, but like those in government, they too know how to fight dirty. Some may have been planning to go beyond civil disobedience.

It is hard to know for certain, because courts are not really trying to uncover the truth. Entrenched regimes remember the Arab spring, and see even the mildest protest as potential insurrection. In Uganda, the army chief (and president’s son) has threatened to hang Mr Besigye and had one of his lawyers abducted. Mr Besigye has not been in court to defend himself since collapsing in the dock in July. Prosecutors claim he was caught plotting assassination. But even their main witness, a former soldier in the British Army who was secretly recording his meetings with Mr Besigye for Uganda’s government, testified that he thought the guns supposedly found on the defendant were planted there. “We are all in this pretend game, like there’s a trial going on, but it’s really not,” says Olive Kobusingye, Mr Besigye’s sister.

Since these trials are political processes more than legal ones, they are often surrounded by talk of negotiations or pardons. In Uganda, the president’s brother says he is negotiating for the release of Mr Besigye (whose allies deny talks have begun). In Tanzania, the authorities offered Mr Lissu in private to pardon him if he agreed to leave the country. The final verdict is likely to have turned less on the merits of the case than on the internal politics of Tanzania’s divided ruling party. Since the bloody crackdown that followed last year’s sham election, some within it have urged reconciliation with the opposition. Hardliners around Mrs Samia are said to prefer making a scapegoat of Mr Lissu.

Treason cases in Africa rarely lead to convictions. But since such offences are often non-bailable, they remove pesky politicians from public life for months or even years. “It is a great way of getting rid of opposition leaders,” says Nic Cheeseman of the University of Birmingham. Mr Lissu’s sentence should keep him out of politics for most of the next election cycle.

Because these methods are useful, governments are likely to keep using them. Though diplomatic pressure may have deterred Mrs Samia’s government from forcing the death penalty on Mr Lissu, the world is more tolerant of its repression than it once was. Whether lawfare can save regimes on the ropes is another matter. “They are storing up trouble,” says a Western diplomat in Tanzania. Across the region lurks the spectre of unrest, even of coups. Treason trials are the mark of paranoid regimes, increasingly on edge.

articles.title: Africa’s solar revolution is vast and speedy
articles.deck: Zimbabwe shows that official statistics probably underestimate its scale

paragraphs.text: If at first you cannot find the new power project in an industrial area of Harare, Zimbabwe’s capital, try looking up. The Limpopo Way Power solar farm has no conventional site, just rows of panels across the rooftops of two tobacco warehouses, and an agreement to supply a factory. In Zimbabwe, as in much of Africa and Asia, the signs of an energy revolution are everywhere.

Assessing its true scale is still tricky, however. Few African governments publish timely data on solar installations. Those that do are probably underestimating their expansion. The best guess comes from two think-tanks, Ember and Africa Tech Futures Lab, using data on exports of Chinese solar panels to the continent. Assuming that three-quarters of those panels have been installed, and including imports from other countries, they reckon that Zimbabwe has added 948MW of solar power since the start of 2023, equivalent to a third of its previous grid capacity.

Africa will install a record 17GW of solar capacity in 2026, the researchers think, or about 100,000 panels a day (see chart). In 19 countries, installations have more than doubled since last year; in the Democratic Republic of Congo, they have risen six-fold. A megawatt of solar produces less power than a megawatt of hydro or coal (even in sunny countries, it gets dark). Still, the amount of extra electricity generated would roughly match the entire annual growth in demand. Imports of Chinese batteries are growing even faster.

Where do all the panels end up? At Centragrid, a 25MW solar farm outside Harare, an engineer warns visitors not to be alarmed as panels clank backwards to track the sun. Such utility-scale plants are more efficient than a panel on a house, but they account for only a quarter of the capacity that Africa is adding this year. The rest appears to be what is known as distributed solar, panels installed by households or, especially, by businesses exasperated with the rickety grid. In South Africa and Namibia about 80% of such installations are found in firms, not homes.

Zimbabwe is a prime example of this revolution. Mines, farms and tourist lodges are harvesting photons. In villages, sunlight powers water pumps. The UN is backing mini-grids. Most of the country’s power still comes from coal, which is also expanding, or from the Kariba dam, which cradles the world’s largest artificial lake. But even there, plans are afoot to float 500MW of panels on its waters.

Isaiah Nyakusendwa, who leads an association of renewable-energy firms, talks of a solar “explosion” that nobody planned from above. A decade ago, solar panels cost about a dollar a watt; now, retailers are quoting 20 cents or less. At the lower end of the market firms’ business practices are not always as clean as their energy. Some customers have had their fingers burnt as their systems have caught fire.

Finance is still hard to come by. In 2024 the UN and Old Mutual, a financial-services group, set up a renewable-energy fund, which has deployed just over $6m so far. A few retailers offer rent-to-buy schemes. But systems often draw on customers’ savings. Salesmen describe a surge in interest at the end of the tobacco harvest or when the diaspora comes home for Christmas, and a drop when school fees are due.

The solar industry has been “built off the back of power cuts”, says Joshua Smyth of Solar Energy Projects, which installed the rooftop farm at Limpopo Way. Last year a faulty generator forced the president, Emmerson Mnangagwa, to finish his state of the nation address in the dark. This year the utility has done better at keeping the lights on. But the tariff rises that are paying for a stronger grid give consumers another reason to abandon it.

The danger for utilities is that they get sucked into a “death spiral”: as big customers opt out of the grid, the costs get passed on to others, who follow them out of the door. In Pakistan, the most dramatic case, grid sales have dropped by 11% in three years. In South Africa, after years of blackouts, the utility is now grappling with a surplus. Zimbabwe’s state electricity company is trying to encourage private firms to sell solar power into the grid, and hopes demand will grow fast. Its officials strategise from a brick tower, redolent of a 20th-century citadel; solar shops cluster nearby, like rebels at the gates.

For now, though, Africa’s electricity systems are a bricolage, as is evident from a visit to an informal settlement on the outskirts of Harare. One resident, Mavis Masakara, sells meat from a fridge outside her modest bungalow. Three sets of cables snake through her living room, curling round the family portraits: one that connects to a petrol generator, another to the grid, and a third to a panel on the roof.

articles.title: Europe has been living beyond its means. Now the bills are due
articles.deck: It accounts for half the world’s social spending, but its fractured politics make cuts difficult

paragraphs.text: Europe’s COBBLED squares have echoed this autumn to the sound of police sirens and shattered glass. The continent is undergoing one of those periodic spasms, when parliamentary politics struggle to handle social discontent. In France and Germany, protests began against underinvestment in education. In Spain and Italy, it was a housing crisis. Across the continent there is anger at rising prices. The shared underlying problem is this: many Europeans want levels of public spending they can no longer afford, while fragmented parliaments and populist politics make it almost impossible to fix the problems.

For decades Europe has offered its citizens an unusually comfortable level of benefits and protections. European Union countries spend 10% of GDP on public pensions, on average, nearly twice the share in America. EU countries devote nearly 30% of GDP to public social spending, compared with less than 20% in America. Angela Merkel, a German former chancellor, once noted with disapproval that Europe accounts for 7% of the world’s population, 25% of global GDP and 50% of global social spending. Europe, she concluded, “will have to work very hard to maintain its prosperity and way of life.”

Some countries, notably hers and the Nordics, did the hard work and made the protective state more affordable, although even Germany is now facing a crunch over social spending. Less responsible countries have kept on borrowing and ducking hard choices. Five have public debt levels at or above 100% of GDP, including France, Italy and Spain. Ten, including Belgium, France and Italy, are now subject to the EU’s “excessive-deficit procedure”. This is a sort of naughty step, designed to put those who break the union’s rules (which cap debt at 60% of GDP and budget deficits at 3% of GDP) under scrutiny and correct their wayward behaviour.

Governments in such countries are under fresh strain from higher interest rates on their debt. France, for example, will spend €91bn ($102bn) on interest on its borrowing in 2027, up from €79bn in 2026. Meanwhile, rising prices and higher energy costs make it politically difficult to cut pension and welfare payments.

The clamour from populists is drowning out those who try to talk sense about the budgetary arithmetic. Allianz, a European insurer, has devised a global “social resilience index”, to measure the vulnerability of different countries to unrest. It calculates that between 2020 and 2025 70% of strikes, riots and civil unrest took place in “advanced economies…where prosperity coexists with political polarisation and weak reform capacity”. Ludovic Subran, chief investment officer at the insurer, notes that this mix is particularly combustible because cost-of-living pressures are hurting so many people.

Take Belgium, which will have a budget deficit in 2026 of 5% of GDP, and debt of 112% of GDP. On November 6th its prime minister, Bart De Wever, offered to resign over his government’s failure to agree on a budget for 2027. The populist-nationalist leader has failed to wrangle a five-party coalition into agreeing on deficit cuts, for example by modestly raising VAT. Or consider the Netherlands, whose young centrist prime minister, Rob Jetten, is running the country’s first minority government since the second world war, and has struggled to secure support for his budget.

Even in fiscally responsible Germany Friedrich Merz, the chancellor, has said that the welfare state is “no longer affordable”. Last year social spending rose by 6%; it now accounts for around 30% of GDP (see chart), two percentage points above pre-covid levels. Social-security charges, levied for pensions, health care and the like, are equivalent to around 42% of gross wages; without reform these are projected to reach nearly 50% by 2040 (employers cover half these costs). A sluggish economy and Germany’s deficit-limiting debt brake mean the federal government is in a tight fiscal spot, with more than €100bn of (cumulative) consolidation needed by 2030. Some two-thirds of Germans agree that the welfare state is no longer affordable; yet a majority oppose most specific proposals for cuts.

By far the most worrying is France. It has battled each year to pass a budget ever since President Emmanuel Macron rashly called snap parliamentary elections in 2024, which shrank his centrist governing minority. The lower house of parliament, once dominated by big parties of the left and the right, is now split into three hostile blocs. The noisiest components are the populist-left of Jean-Luc Mélenchon and the populist-right of Marine Le Pen. This pair are also pollsters’ favourites to face each other in the run-off in the presidential election next spring. The climate in parliament, says Michel Barnier, a centre-right former prime minister and now a member of the lower house, is “pre-insurrectional”.

Against this backdrop Sébastien Lecornu, the fourth prime minister in three years, is trying to get a budget through parliament by the end of the year. His plan, which would curb the budget deficit from 5.4% of GDP in 2026 to a still-hefty 5% in 2027, involves €43bn of savings. Most controversially, these include the freezing in nominal terms of most pensions (the single-biggest budget item) and civil-service pay. The opposition has cried foul. Teachers and other public-sector workers have joined the marches. Protests have broadened into anger that pensioners are the casualties of a debt problem. “My placard is crappy, so is my pension” read one home-made sign at a recent demo in Paris.

As ever, voters want public finances fixed, but not at their expense. A poll suggests that 85% of the French think it is urgent to curb public debt, but 56% also think the pension age should be lower. Mr Mélenchon and Ms Le Pen each vow not merely to protect pensions but also to bring down the retirement age. Both their parties are against the proposed pension freeze. Roland Lescure, the finance minister, insists that the government will pass a budget, even if it has to use special constitutional measures to force it through parliament. “When I say we should freeze pensions, it’s not to annoy pensioners,” he says. “Rather it’s to say: if we want to spend more on young people, others will have to pay.”

A decent welfare state, with dignity in ill health, poverty and old age, is as central to the idea of what Europe is all about as are walkable cities and long holidays. The ageing continent cannot sidestep tough choices about what sort of support it can continue to afford. Yet Europe is losing its capacity to have a measured debate about how to do this. If governments cannot find a way to forge majorities for difficult decisions, those choices will end up being imposed by the bond markets in a crisis.

articles.title: A judo champion enters the presidential race in France

paragraphs.text: “I know what it’s like to fight,” declared Teddy Riner, which by itself came as no surprise: France’s multiple Olympic gold-medallist in judo knows exactly how to throw an opponent to the ground. But when Mr Riner spoke on November 9th he was referring to high-level sport of a different sort. Seated before a sober bookshelf and French tricolore flag, he stunned France by saying that he was running for president. Within 48 hours Mr Riner’s declaration on X had been viewed 14m times—more than three times the viewership for Marine Le Pen’s presidential-style address after the recent riots.

France has since then been talking about little other than the bear of a man they affectionately call le grand Teddy. Some asked if the declaration was an AI-generated hoax (it is not). A Socialist politician called it a “farce”. Emmanuel Macron said that Mr Riner’s candidacy “can only benefit the country”, prompting some to suspect the president’s hand, if only to stir the race up ahead of next year’s presidential election.

Teddymania partly reflects the flatness at the political centre. The race has been dominated by the extremes: Ms Le Pen on the populist right, who is poll favourite to win, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the populist-left. Mr Riner pitched himself, in Macronesque terms, as “neither right nor left”. “France doesn’t need a professional politician who recites talking points and spends all day squabbling,” he said, “It needs common sense, firmness, justice and a government that sets things right.”

Polling analysts do not take Mr Riner’s bid too seriously. He has a small team, no party, little time, and needs 500 elected officials to endorse him. But the judoka is wildly popular among varied demographic groups. He could in particular damage Mr Mélenchon, who relies on the youth vote. A poll suggests that 22% of the French would consider voting for him. If so, he could possibly qualify for the run-off. Footballers (in Liberia) and cricketers (in Pakistan) have been elected leaders elsewhere. Mr Riner is a national treasure. And the rebellious French dislike a pre-written electoral script. If nothing else, his candidacy has injected some hope and energy into the race. France, said Mr Riner, had given him the “opportunity to dream big”.

articles.title: Spain’s rail crashes are a grim backdrop to the election
articles.deck: Once a source of national pride, high-speed rail now causes anguish

paragraphs.text: WHEN SPAIN’S first high-speed train from Madrid to Seville was inaugurated in 1992, it was much more than just a railway line. It was a symbol of the country’s emergence as a modern democracy. In the years since, high-speed lines have covered much of the country, becoming a source of national pride.

Yet now, ahead of a general election on November 29th, the rail network has become a source of anguish. Two crashes on the same line to Seville, first in January and then in October, killed a total of 115 people (see map). “Psychologically, for a lot of people it’s a symbol of what’s gone wrong in Spain” in recent years, says Luis Garicano, a Spanish economist at the London School of Economics. That includes relentless political polarisation under Pedro Sánchez (pictured), the Socialist prime minister, the taint of corruption surrounding his party and an ever-worsening housing crisis.

The timing of the second accident could not have been worse for Mr Sánchez, whose Socialist Party is trailing in the polls behind the centre-right People’s Party. It and the populist-right Vox party are projected to win about 200 seats between them in the 350-seat parliament, against around 105 for the Socialists. In what looked like an effort to help Mr Sánchez, the main labour unions led a general strike on November 11th, the first since 2012, to protest about evictions, rising rents and the high cost of living.

The centre-right opposition wants to build more houses, control immigration and cut taxes. But it also accuses Mr Sánchez of incompetence, not least in his running of the railways, whose recent crash exposed a string of failures. These start with the computerised train-control system, which dates from 1992. It failed during the October crash, for the 170th time this year. A new system is due to start on the Seville line in 2027, a year later than planned. European Union prosecutors are investigating the possible misuse of European funds that paid for this and other improvements. One problem is that successive governments prioritised expanding the system rather than maintenance spending, which is only around half the European average per kilometre.

The government’s critics point to political interference in Adif, the state outfit that runs the railways. It has had seven presidents since 2012. José Luis Ábalos, who was Mr Sánchez’s transport minister from 2018 to 2021 while also running the Socialist Party, is serving a jail sentence for corruption. The Adif director in charge of rail safety was a former Socialist spin doctor.
On November 10th King Felipe and some political leaders attended a sombre state funeral for the victims in Toledo cathedral. The rail disaster will continue to cast a long shadow over the vote.

articles.title: Donald Trump is in a hurry for peace in Ukraine. Vladimir Putin is not
articles.deck: The American-brokered talks leave many questions unanswered

paragraphs.text: IT WAS NOT the first time—or even the third—that Donald Trump had trailed a “big beautiful” peace for Ukraine. But his latest promise, made days before the first trilateral peace talks since February, set alarm bells ringing in Kyiv and European capitals. In the event, negotiations in Abu Dhabi over November 10th and 11th raised more questions than they answered.

The talks, which lasted just six hours, had set out to discuss the small matter of post-war European security. About the only firm outcome was a large prisoner swap, by now a ritual conclusion. The real test was due to come on November 12th when American negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner took a set of ideas to Moscow for Vladimir Putin. These were understood to include “Article 5-style” security guarantees for Ukraine—from America, Britain, France and Germany, as well as NATO itself. For now, though, there is no expectation that Mr Putin will sign any sort of deal that strengthens Ukrainian’s security.

The Americans have dangled several sweeteners to coax Mr Putin into a deal. One is to plug Russia back into European energy markets (in breach of a new EU law). “Not a chance of us agreeing to that while the war is still raging,” added a senior Ukrainian official. Another is to discuss Russia’s dubious claims that Europe threatens its own security, something Mr Putin has been demanding since before his full-scale invasion in February 2022. “Discussing Europe’s security architecture with Putin is like asking a rat to approve the design of a rat trap,” wrote Andrei Kozyrev, a former Russian foreign minister, on X.

Russia’s wish-list is long enough to spin talks out indefinitely. The Economist understands Russian negotiators want guarantees that NATO will “stop expanding east” and a pledge that the alliance will cut forces and weapons near its borders. They also want Ukraine to declare neutrality and shrink its army. (Ukraine wants the reverse: Western support for a defensive army at least 800,000-strong.)

Ahead of the talks, American officials insisted any new arrangement would have NATO “remaining central to European collective defence” and would respect Ukraine’s sovereignty. A source close to the White House claimed the proposals had the backing of European partners and NATO. “Nobody has been able to solve this conflict while everyone is telling us how [to do so],” the official said.

Insiders say President Trump’s midterm defeat injected new urgency into the talks. The arrival of Democratic majorities in Congress in January offers a deadline to his main negotiators, who could face investigations over alleged conflicts of interest. For Russia, it may be the last chance to do a deal while Mr Trump controls Congress. Ukraine’s negotiators are privately sceptical of a breakthrough this year, but have been instructed to keep an open mind, if only to avoid annoying Mr Trump.

Ukrainians still assume things will get worse before getting better. The country enters winter with its energy infrastructure in its worst shape since the war began. Reserves and spare parts are running low. It has all but run out of Patriot interceptors, needed to destroy ballistic missiles. Russia, meanwhile, still has a stockpile of 700 such missiles, is producing another 110 a month, and is midway through a campaign to make Ukrainian cities, chiefly Kyiv, uninhabitable. It is destroying bridges, water systems and power grids. It would be odd for Mr Putin to stop now.
“Our American friends want a breakthrough,” the senior Ukrainian official says. “Seeing what the Russians are doing with our infrastructure, it’s hard to believe one is coming.”
