articles.title: How navigating red tape became the European way of life

paragraphs.text: Europe has spent centuries searching for ways to unite its quarrelsome peoples. Christianity had a go, as did various emperors, to little avail. Esperanto never quite caught on. Football and the Eurovision Song Contest bring the place together for a few nights each year. Perhaps Europe’s common culture is found not in stadiums or concert halls, but oozing from its government offices: battling red tape is the thread that binds the continent together. While Europeans disagree on politics, cuisine and religion, all are united in living under the administrator’s ink-stained thumb. From Dublin to Athens there is a reassuring familiarity to being informed that the correct form is unavailable, that another office must be consulted (preferably by fax), then that the deadline expired yesterday. The European Union in Brussels, the spiritual home of the paperwork-industrial complex, is a fitting culmination of attempts to forge ever-closer union. Where mere emperors failed, the rubber-stamping Eurocrat has triumphed.

All polities spawn paperwork. (Your columnist, a former correspondent in India, can attest to the subcontinent’s own procedural prowess.) Yet Europeans have elevated petty officialdom from a necessity to a fine art. The creation of rules, then their punctilious enforcement, is the je ne sais quoi that helps give Europe its particular charm. Multiple tiers of government invent rules often grumpily enacted by another level. If there is such a thing as a European way of life, it involves filling out forms in triplicate.

Every European has a horror story to recount. Charlemagne is no exception. Tax authorities in Belgium wrote recently to inform him that he was not, in fact, the father of his three children. (Come and pick them up at your convenience, was the response.) Some years ago it was French tinpot functionaries who refused to believe that the Stanley Victor Gregory Pignal identified on your columnist’s passport was the same person as the Stanley Victor Grégory (note the accent) Pignal named on his children’s birth certificates. After months of haggling it turned out to be easier to redo an entire set of identity documents—expunging the stray accent—than to try to reason with the apostles of clerical pedantry.

Even when the bureaucracy runs smoothly, try running a business in this place. The EU’s 27 countries between them regulate entry into more than 5,700 professions—over 200 per country—from the commonplace to the obscure. Woe betide an aspiring tiler, mushroom expert or well-sinker who would like to set up shop in Hungary without negotiating an obstacle course of certificates. (Nearly a quarter of EU workers toil under a regime that requires a recognised qualification.) Because the regulations vary from one country to the next, a Polish electrical engineer is unlikely to be allowed to fix a fault in neighbouring Lithuania, say—so much for the EU’s vaunted single market. Each country has its own labour code. Luxembourg’s alone runs to 2,160 pages.

Some places, like Estonia, have tried to tame the paper beast, making digital filings the norm. Still, Europe increasingly feels like a land in which something is forbidden unless it is expressly authorised. Want to offer shoppers across-the-board discounts? That is verboten in a slew of EU countries unless the promotion falls in a few specific weeks of the year. A German school that wants to order textbooks for its pupils may have to put out the contract to public tender under EU rules. Fair enough. But because the price of books is fixed under German diktats, all bids from suppliers come back at precisely the same price—and the contract is then allotted by drawing lots. (Perhaps unsurprisingly, German businesses spend 7% of their turnover on satisfying bureaucrats’ lust for box-ticking.) Value-added tax, a European innovation that has since gone global, kicks up a rich harvest of administrative lunacy. In the Netherlands, rabbit food until last year got taxed at 9% while hamster owners needed to spring 21% (official reason: the hamster is definitely a pet, while the rabbit might one day become a meal). Different yoga classes still attract different VAT rates, too, depending on how much sweating is involved.

All the red tape has compounded the economic malaise that has befallen Europe. American venture capitalists guffaw at the continent’s quaintly medieval ways. In Germany startups hoping to raise money can be required to get a notary to read all the investment documents aloud word for word. Since the small print can run to dozens of pages, this can take hours, if not days (the recital is interrupted for bathroom breaks). Every planning application from Poland to Portugal is a bureaucratic odyssey that must take into account the mating habits of each local newt and snail, no matter the pressing need for new homes. A bid to increase the capacity of Dublin airport in 2023 ran to 7,000 pages. The whole thing had to be printed out for submission to the authorities—before being scanned again by the very same authorities.

The EU machinery in Brussels, the final boss of the continent’s norm-setting apparatus, was once painted as a prodigious purveyor of rules: tabloid tales of how it regulated the curvature of bananas still haunt the place. Recently it has tried to paint itself as a force for deregulation. In theory every cost imposed by a new edict must be matched by one that is being repealed. Confusingly, the very same measure is sometimes enacted and repealed at the same time, a novel case of Schrödinger’s regulation. This summer a green packaging law took effect, which requires any firm selling goods across borders—even tiny ones—to appoint up to 27 local representatives to oversee their packaging waste. EU-wallahs, having belatedly realised the madness of the scheme, have since tried to junk it. But the law has taken effect before its scrapping has been agreed; officials hope nobody enforces it instead. Even when Europe decides to cut red tape, it finds itself tied up in knots.

articles.title: Andy Burnham has ignited the Rejoin debate
articles.deck: But Britain’s prime minister has yet to say what he really wants

paragraphs.text: At Labour’s conference in September Andy Burnham suggested Britain might “go all the way” and rejoin the European Union. The prime minister’s counterparts in Brussels may have thought this an unserious basis on which to negotiate. The cabinet is split, as is Parliament. Mr Burnham sounds nonchalant. As he breezily remarked to The Economist: “Who knows how it plays out in the endgame here?”

Yet Britain’s prime minister has won a hearing in Brussels. Few there think rejoining is imminent, and it is not at the top of anyone’s in-tray. But Mr Burnham’s is getting credit for breaking an omertà in Westminster that has held since 2020, when the Brexit divorce was finalised. His musings appear to Eurocrats as if he is probing the limits of British public opinion. It is quite a contrast with Sir Keir Starmer, his predecessor, who spent most of his time in Brussels stubbornly ruling things out. “It’s not just an internal Labour matter, no,” says a European diplomat. “It is something big, the start of a debate about rejoining.”

At a summit on November 20th, Britain and the EU are expected to finalise a package facilitating youth mobility and trade in food and emissions. In a speech around then, Mr Burnham plans to sketch out options for a long-term relationship. He insists he is open-minded about the possible model. But recently he has defended the free movement of people, once a taboo, and pointed out the deficiencies of rule-taker status. Join the dots and they point towards Britain rejoining the EU.

The electoral gambit is obvious: a promise to get closer to Europe may help patch up Labour’s splintered coalition. But British manifesto pledges (if that is what Mr Burnham’s musing becomes) have a habit of landing on Brussels’s doorstep. The 2016 Brexit referendum, after all, began life as an attempt by David Cameron, then prime minister, to unite the Conservatives. “[Mr Burnham] is pursuing a political manoeuvre,” says a diplomat. “But if he wins, it will become more serious.”

Some observers are puzzled. Even as Mr Burnham talks airily of rejoining, British negotiators haggle over far smaller matters, such as how many students would get visas under the November deal. The generous explanation is that they are driving a hard bargain to help sell the deal at home. Even Lord Cameron, once a firm Remainer, has warned Mr Burnham against starting “a decade-long debate” over rejoining.

British ministers insist Mr Burnham is serious. Why else talk about free movement, among the most divisive questions in British politics? Mr Burnham “believes passionately” in getting a “fundamental shift” in the relationship, Stewart Wood, a foreign-office minister, recently told a gathering in Brussels. He urged his audience to understand “quite how much of a political risk the prime minister is taking”.

Some in Brussels reckon the rejoin debate was inevitable. British public opinion has shifted decisively (see chart); economic growth has taken a hit. Mr Burnham is “the product of a decade of Britain after Brexit”, Lord Wood said. The Brexit gamble was premised on a world which has disappeared, with Britain no longer able to ride a wave of free trade governed by multilateral institutions. Instead, the country is being squeezed by the rivalry between America, the EU and China.

That makes the current relationship an unstable equilibrium. As the EU tries to shield its market from aggressive competition—over cars, plastics, steel and more—Britain will be on the sharp end, compelled to lobby for exemptions every few months in an ill-tempered game of whack-a-mole.

Both sides see China as an early test of the rapprochement. Britain wants to be part of the “Made in Europe” scheme, which will use subsidies and procurement to protect European industry from Chinese rivals. Draft conclusions for the summit would, in effect, oblige Britain to raise its tariffs to match the EU’s for supply chains including electric cars if it wants to enjoy a “trusted partnership” on industrial policy. The EU worries that Britain’s relative openness to China has eroded the British market for European carmakers. But for some it has become a test of allegiance as much as economics. Does Britain want to be under the European umbrella, or not?

In Labour, the debate is becoming binary—rejoin or the status quo. Halfway-house models like Norway’s are falling out of favour. Mr Burnham has killed a proposal by Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, to seek further sector-by-sector participation in the single market through dynamic alignment with EU law, which was a non-starter for the bloc. Some expect Mr Burnham’s food deal, which will require the adoption of EU law without a say, to make the case for a seat at the table self-evident.

Ironically, all this is happening just as Europe may soon look less attractive to progressive Labour voters. Marine Le Pen might become France’s president next year; the Alternative for Germany party is thriving, too. Both favour nationalist agendas that could paralyse European policymaking. Some in the British government think that strengthens, rather than weakens, the case for leaning in and buttressing Europe against Russia. Still, it would test Mr Burnham’s salesmanship.

Negotiations could nevertheless be surprisingly quick. Britain’s return would be a big win for the EU. The country’s laws are mostly still aligned with the bloc’s, and its negotiators are seasoned. But a return of Britain’s budget rebate is out of the question. European governments disagree over whether it would have to join the euro and the Schengen area. Some see British queasiness on these scores as a sign that, deep down, it does not want to be in the club.

What is more, Britain’s opposition parties do not want to be in the EU. The nightmare scenario is a narrow victory for rejoin in a referendum, won on a misleading prospectus with insufficiently broad support in Westminster. Such a mandate might crumple in the negotiating room. If Britain sincerely chooses to rejoin, though, with all the obligations that entails, then it can. The country’s hardest step is the first: working out what it truly wants.

articles.title: Britain’s Tories want even more Brexit
articles.deck: By saying they will pull out of the European Convention on Human Rights, they threaten big trouble

paragraphs.text: IT IS ALWAYS harder to deal with the European Union when political consensus is lacking at home. Looked at from Brussels, why bother with the effort to agree on a closer relationship with Andy Burnham’s Britain? After all, opposition parties say they will tear it up.

Neither the Conservatives nor Reform UK talk much about Brexit these days, because of its unpopularity. But both still promise to reverse Mr Burnham’s planned “reset” with the EU. That would irk businesses wishing to scrap trade barriers, especially in food and agriculture, through closer alignment with the bloc. If the reset boosts exports and lowers food costs, many firms will want to keep it. A shadow-cabinet source admits privately that the Tories might therefore seek a fudge that retains the deal but gives Parliament a theoretical emergency brake on future EU laws.

What worries the EU more is the opposition’s pledge to pull out of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, now requires all her parliamentary candidates to support this. EU diplomats suggest she may not have thought through the consequences. It is not just the embarrassment of Britain, a creator of the ECHR, joining Belarus and Russia as the only European countries outside it. More seriously, ECHR membership is assumed in both the post-Brexit trade and co-operation agreement (TCA) and the Windsor framework that softens the customs border between Great Britain and Northern Ireland. It is also in the Good Friday Agreement.

Some Tories argue that other EU countries dislike the ECHR, and especially the court that enforces it. But disapproval and withdrawal are different matters. A forthcoming paper by the Centre for a Better Britain, a think-tank linked to Reform, outlines various options for scrapping all post-Brexit EU treaties, identifying which can be expected to trigger retaliation. One such is pulling out of the ECHR. These treaties are built like a Jenga tower: pull out one key brick and the whole edifice can fall. The most likely response to British ECHR withdrawal would be scrapping the Windsor framework and the TCA as a whole—in effect implementing a version of Brexit so hard that even Boris Johnson avoided it in 2020.

At the next general election voters may therefore face a perverse choice. No party favours the status quo. Labour and the Liberal Democrats will probably campaign for a closer relationship with the EU. At the same time the Tories and Reform will promise to pull out of the ECHR. Anand Menon of UK in a Changing Europe, a think-tank, says this points to just two alternatives: moving to rejoin or reverting to a no-deal Brexit. The mushy compromise that has so far prevailed may no longer be on offer.

articles.title: Can e-sports boost Sunderland—and Britain’s armed forces?
articles.deck: High hopes for the new British Arena

paragraphs.text: “This was just a wasteland.” Graeme Miller, who ran Sunderland City Council for six years until 2024, gestures out of the window of the newish and still sparkling City Hall building. The site lay vacant for nearly two decades after the Vaux brewery closed in 1999. Now City Hall stands at the centre of a fresh clutch of office buildings facing the River Wear.

Sunderland, once the world’s biggest shipbuilding hub, has been in decline for decades. Its last shipyard closed in 1988. Tucked on England’s north-east coast, the city of 290,000 sits third-bottom for earnings in a ranking of Britain’s 63 largest urban areas. It is dead last for businesses per person. Voters showed their discontent at local elections in May, handing the populist-right Reform UK 58 of the council’s 75 seats. Labour went from 54 councillors to five. “People still are not happy, even with all of this,” laments Mr Miller.

Might e-sports help give Sunderland a brighter future? Enter British Esports, founded in 2016 by Chester King, who also runs a health-care business, and chaired by Andy Payne, a veteran of the video-games industry. Their venture has set up shop in what was a vacant Audi dealership next to Sunderland Football Club’s Stadium of Light. It has also turned a row of town houses and connected office space into its National Esports Performance Campus, where touring gaming pros can stay.

The former car dealership has been transformed into a 15,000-square-foot (1,400 square metres) e-sports venue, dubbed the British Arena. (“We couldn’t believe no one had used the name before,” says Mr King.) On a clear Thursday evening in October the arena hosted its second event, relaying a Sunderland away match on its giant screen. The 250-seat venue is barely 100 metres from the 49,000-seat stadium, which provides a handy source of footfall on match days—and also highlights the gulf between e-sports and traditional ones.

Mr King wants the British Arena to be more than just an entertainment venue. He hopes it will help elite gamers learn to perform to a crowd, while supporting careers in hospitality, broadcasting and coaching, too. E-sports can teach skills in business and marketing to those who may not be drawn to formal education, says Gregg Hill, a lecturer in e-sports event management at the University of Sunderland. Being the home of British Esports will build Sunderland’s reputation as a forward-looking digital city, enthuses Liz St Louis, the local authority’s aspirationally titled director of smart cities and enabling services.

Sunderland Council is not the only part of the British state putting faith in e-sports. So are the armed forces, aware that Ukraine’s battlefields have swarmed with drones piloted by youths with PlayStation controllers. The British Arena’s first official event was the International Defence Esports Games, at which Canadian personnel beat France in Counter-Strike 2 and Britain took the Rocket League title.

Where once the armed forces recruited from the playing fields of Eton, they now see value in gamers. The Ministry of Defence formally recognises e-sports and last year installed a room of gaming PCs on the Royal Navy’s flagship aircraft-carrier.

Back at City Hall Mr Miller insists that Sunderland’s economy is on the up. Ocado, an online grocer, and Apexon, a technology-services firm, have taken space in the new offices. A takeaway app, Just Eat, is testing robot deliveries in the city.

So far, e-sports and Sunderland seem a good fit. The city gets an optimistic owner for underused buildings; British Esports gets low prices and a welcoming local authority. Not to mention revenue from all those football fans’ pre-match pints.

articles.title: Britain’s super position in quantum technology
articles.deck: Some of the industry’s bets are already paying off

paragraphs.text: Quantum computing is a bit like the strange laws of physics it relies on: scary enough to give national-security wonks nightmares, yet still sufficiently puny for sceptics to dismiss. Perhaps no country wants it to work more than Britain. Three of the world’s top five quantum clusters are on its soil, reckons the European Centre for International Political Economy, a think-tank. On November 6th at a showcase in London, Sir Peter Knight, a pioneer in quantum technology, reiterated a goal to make a quantum computer that can outperform supercomputers in Britain by 2035. Yet even now other quantum technologies are proving their worth.

Mostly this is down to quantum sensing, which exploits the sensitivity of quantum systems to faint changes around them. Use cases in medicine have abounded for decades (MRI scanners, for instance); now they are multiplying. A spinout from the University of Nottingham, Cerca Magnetics, makes brain-scanning helmets fitted with quantum sensors that can detect subtle magnetic fields. It has made an operating profit in each of the past five years. Others are experimenting with diagnostic tools for breast cancer, and finger-prick tests for diseases such as hiv.

Another application for sensing is positioning, navigation and timing (PNT). Knowing where you are, where you are going and what time it is has always been useful for soldiers. The war in Ukraine, meanwhile, has shown how easy it is to jam satellite systems such as gpS. So the Royal Navy has been trialling quantum navigation with compact atomic clocks, which do not depend on signals from space.

Similar uses stretch beyond the battlefield. Britain’s latest national risk register identifies the loss of pnt, whether from technical failure or a cyber-attack, as a “significant” risk. It recommends that private firms keep “resilient backup systems”—such as atomic clocks. Days before the register was published, in July, a nationwide network outage in Australia demonstrated the potential for disruption. Faulty software from Telstra, the country’s biggest telecoms company, halted trains and payments and blocked some emergency calls. The British government’s budget in October included £138m ($185m) for quantum-sensing kit to be used for defence, health care and transport.

Useful as brain scanners and atomic clocks may be, they are merely heralds in the march of quantum tech. The highest hopes are pinned on quantum computers’ mathematical powers. Large-scale machines would be able to do some sums vastly faster than today’s supercomputers, transforming computational chemistry and materials science. Subodh Kulkarni, the boss of Rigetti, an American firm that operates in Britain, thinks that running quantum processors alongside the artificial-intelligence chips used today will make it quicker and cheaper to train large language models.

For now, quantum computers’ error rate is too high for them to be reliable. British startups are working to fix this: Riverlane is building error-correction systems, while Phasecraft is developing algorithms that can do useful work even on error-prone machines. Through ProQure, a £1bn procurement competition, the government is supporting promising firms and helping validate their prototypes.

The most advanced machines will in all likelihood be built in the “golden triangle” spanned by Cambridge, London and Oxford, home to hardware firms such as Quantum Motion and orca. Yet pleasingly for jam-spreading politicians, the industry extends far more widely around the country than that for AI. Glasgow is one of the world’s top quantum clusters. The quantum supply chain runs through Sheffield in the north of England all the way to Newport in south Wales.

Turning all this into a lasting lead will take more scale-up capital and infrastructure, says Sir Peter: “Every now and then, I wake up in the night thinking, ‘What happens if it doesn’t work?’” But over time he thinks the odds of that have fallen. “It’s going better than I’d hoped.”

articles.title: What is killing Britain’s prisoners?
articles.deck: Less violence and drugs than heart disease and cancer

paragraphs.text: “Feculent and noxious”, said John Howard of England’s prisons in 1777. Convicts, the reformer wrote, were “pining under diseases” and “expiring on the floors”. Conditions have improved since. And yet in 2017 Annabella, a 45-year-old diabetic, died after having spent 21 hours lying unresponsive on her cell floor.

There has scarcely been a worse time to be a British prisoner since detailed records began in the early 2000s. Rates of violence, self-harm and drug use are at or near record highs. With prisons running at 98% capacity, it is not unusual for prisoners to spend over 22 hours a day locked in a cell no bigger than a garden shed.

More than ever, they are dying there. Between 1992 and 2012 prisons in England and Wales recorded an average of 2.2 deaths a year for every 1,000 inmates. Last year there were 4.5 per 1,000—more than in any other outside the covid-19 pandemic.

Why? Headlines about violence, or synthetic opioids smuggled in on drones, suggest an epidemic of dramatic deaths. But our analysis of over 5,000 fatal-incident reports, from the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman, suggests a more prosaic reality. Britain’s prisoners are getting older and frailer. Though drug deaths have crept up, most of the rise in prisoners’ mortality rate comes from “natural deaths”, meaning those caused by routine ailments like heart disease and cancer (see chart 1).

Sad, quiet deaths in jail are not new. Compared with other people, prisoners are sicker and more likely to come from deprived areas, meaning they are more likely to die a natural death at a younger age. But last year there were 2.6 such deaths for every 1,000 prisoners, more than double the average rate between 2000 and 2010.

The simplest explanation for the rise in natural deaths is that the prison population has aged rapidly. Since 2014 Britain’s median age has held steady at 40 years. The median age in the prisons of England and Wales, in contrast, has risen from 32 to 37 over the past decade. Since the early 2000s the number of prisoners aged 50 or older has more than doubled. For the first time they now outnumber prisoners under the age of 25 (see chart 2 ).

That is partly because prison sentences have lengthened. Last year a government review found the number of prisoners serving life sentences had more than doubled since 1993. The average non-life custodial sentence had risen from 16 months to 22.

Old sex offenders, meanwhile, have increasingly been handed long sentences. British police take such crimes far more seriously than they used to, and have launched investigations into historical cases. Among men in prison over 50, 43% are there for sex offences committed decades ago. For those over 80, it is almost 100%.

Ageing populations have more medical problems. James Hard, a clinical director in the NHS, says “the level and complexity of need” among prisoners is higher than at any time in his 20-year career. Their being in prison does not help. Poor diets, limited time outside cells and a lack of fresh air in them mean that health problems appear roughly ten years earlier in prisoners than among the general public. And the older ones are less able to withstand such dismal conditions than the youngsters who used to outnumber them.

For those who fall ill, prison is a difficult place to get good medical treatment. Adrian Usher, the Prisons and Probations Ombudsman, says that the prison service is “really good at dealing with trauma”, but that “chronic conditions are much more challenging.” There is a tension between the need for security and that for compassionate care. Prisoners making vague health complaints are often met by prison staff with reason to be suspicious.

Those that are believed may be able to visit an on-site doctor, but diagnosis and management of chronic conditions need specialist appointments. That means trips to hospital, which require spare prison officers to act as escorts. A report from the government’s chief medical officer last year found that, with staff in short supply, prisons are forced to ration such escorts. As rates of violence and medical emergencies increase, Dr Hard says routine appointments often have to be rescheduled so staff can tackle crises. Overcrowded prisons therefore have more sick inmates than ever, and less capacity to treat them.

Mr Usher says it is hard to gauge whether someone died “while they were in prison or because they were in prison”. But prisoners receive 24% fewer hospital appointments than the general population (after adjusting for age and sex). They also miss more than 40% of them—almost double the rate outside prison. A study earlier this year found that prisoners in England experience between 41 and 67 times as much avoidable medical harm as other people. Jessica Pandian of INQUEST, a charity that investigates deaths in custody, says that “natural deaths” is a misnomer. “People are dying from wholly preventable conditions.”

Mark Juniper, who led a recent review of health care in prisons, says they could be used as “an opportunity to help a population that is difficult to access outside prison”. Officially, the government strives to achieve “equivalence of care” for those in prison and outside. But prisoners need more resources per person to achieve the same outcomes. In a country where 50% of people tell pollsters they would support capital punishment, and with the NHS looking threadbare, throwing cash at criminals is not likely to win votes.

It is normal for society to withhold rights from prisoners, but in theory Britain’s inmates keep their right to health care. In practice, they often do not. “I was pretty shocked by the reality of what happens inside,” says Dr Juniper. “We put people in prison as punishment. We don’t sentence them to death.”

articles.title: Britain’s nicest prison

paragraphs.text: Much is made of Britain’s Dickensian jails. HMP Dartmoor was opened in 1809, the year Charles Darwin was born. Just now it is temporarily closed, after high levels of radon gas were found within its walls. But with 122 prisons across England and Wales, not all are so decrepit. HMP Millsike, opened last year, is replete with solar panels and air-source heat pumps. So which is the best prison to be a prisoner in?

Judging from the Ministry of Justice’s annual performance ratings, it is Haverigg in Cumbria. Housing about 490 men, mostly sex offenders, it scored 97.5 out of 100 on its report card. Last year it recorded just four assaults on prisoners and none on staff, while 97% of inmates were signed up to activity programmes. What is more, no one escaped.

Haverigg is an “open prison”, a category that tends to outperform the rest in part because of who is sent there. Open prisons are generally reserved for low-risk offenders who are often close to the end of their sentences. As a result, they can afford prisoners a much greater degree of freedom than others. Inmates can move around the prison, and can apply for temporary licences to leave and attend medical appointments, visit family or work.

Selection bias, however, is not the whole story. Prisoners who can get to hospital under their own steam find it a great deal easier to stay on top of chronic health conditions. Those with a licence to work have a much better chance of getting a job after they are freed, which in turn makes them less likely to reoffend. Six weeks after release from an open prison, 43% of ex-inmates are employed—over double the national average. For those released from Haverigg, that rises to 58%.

Open prisons also excel at getting inmates into behavioural and education programmes (probably in part because their prisoners are already relatively well behaved). Declining access to such activity is one reason for the sense of crisis in other British prisons. Self-harm and drug use are more likely among those who feel bored and hopeless from spending 22 hours a day in a cell. Yet programmes that give them a sense of purpose are among the first things to be cut when staff are short. Their survival in open prisons suggests they could help reduce the chaos in others. In Haverigg, prisoners train to be equine therapists at an onsite racehorse rescue.
Not all prisons can be open. But those that are do pretty well at turning inmates into functioning members of society. The rest should learn from them.

articles.title: Is Britain ready for net-zero migration?
articles.deck: Getting what you want isn’t all it’s cracked up to be

paragraphs.text: When Nigel Farage returned to politics, during the 2024 general election, he made a wild suggestion. “Net migration should be zero,” said the leader of the populist-right Reform UK. Given that it had reached an all-time high of 944,000 the year before, it felt a preposterous goal.

Barely two years on, this wild suggestion may become reality. Migration has plummeted. When, later this month, the Office for National Statistics publishes net-immigration figures for the 12 months to June, they may reach a three-decade low (excluding the lockdown years). The number for the calendar year of 2026 could be negative, says James Bowes of Warwick University, forecasting that 54,000 more people will leave than arrive. Britain would become a country of net emigration for the first time since 1993.

Mr Farage was not alone in his broad goal. Every government since 2010 was elected on a pledge to cut immigration. David Cameron, as prime minister, wanted to reduce the net figure to “tens of thousands”. So did his successor, Theresa May. Boris Johnson, the prime minister behind Britain’s immigration spike, said numbers “will come down”. Rishi Sunak promised a cut. Even Sir Keir Starmer, a former Labour leader, said: “Read my lips: I will bring immigration…down.” People are used to being failed by their political class. What happens if they get what they want?

In some ways it is heartening. Britain’s political class is racked with learned helplessness. Cabinet ministers complain that the “levers of power” are not connected to anything. Migration figures say otherwise. The government pulled one lever and made it easier for people to move to Britain. Millions did. The government decided this was too much, pulled another lever and numbers fell steeply. True, they bodged it both ways: Mr Johnson did not expect millions to come; Mr Sunak’s changes were not meant to cut net migration to near-zero. Governing is hard. But it is possible.

Any politician expecting a thank-you is in for disappointment. Some parts of the debate will stay the same. When headline numbers shrink, others seem bigger. Small-boat crossings may be falling, yet they will account for a heftier chunk of net arrivals. Progressives once huffed that they were only a “tiny proportion” of overall migration. That particular argument has run its course. A world of “net-zero migration” is one in which the face of immigration is, more than ever, a man in a dinghy.

Other aspects of the immigration debate have already shifted, with concern about the flow turning to concern about the stock. Britain has undergone a sweeping demographic change. In 2004, when it opened its doors to migrants from eastern Europe, about one in ten people in Britain were foreign-born. Now, the number is one in five. Between 2021 and 2024 alone the number of foreign nationals rose by about 2m people, points out the Migration Observatory. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary (and also the first to say “Boriswave” at the dispatch box), has made it difficult for recent arrivals to make their stay permanent.

And so a migration debate about stopping people coming turns into one about kicking people out. Reform has promised mass deportations; Mr Farage erected a mock airport-departure board for one press conference. Others go further: “Millions. Must. Go” is the slogan of Restore Britain, a far-right party. A lesson learned by Lord Cameron and Baroness May is now being learned by Mr Farage. Someone, somewhere is always harder.

Enormous numbers shifted the debate, with concern about immigration shooting up after the ons confirmed quite how big the recent influx had been. Will tiny ones—or negative ones—have the opposite effect? While opinion barely budged among Leave voters for whom immigration is an existential topic, liberal opinion moved sharply when arrivals exceeded one million. A majority of Remainers, Labour voters and even Liberal Democrats now think immigration has been too high for the past decade.

Maybe the bill coming due will change their minds. The government’s short-term fiscal projections see the economy as a simple machine: immigrants are poured in at one end and gdp comes out the other. Some economists worry the recent glut of often low-earning immigrants will be bad for the public finances over the long term. But for now immigration still determines how much the chancellor can spend. Voters are not really prepared to make sacrifices for lower migration, says Christabel Cooper of ThinkLabour, a Labour-friendly think-tank. They may have to.

With a long-frozen immigration debate going into flux, Britain’s progressives will shape it as much as conservatives. Once-verboten ideas are already being aired. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, is teasing the prospect of a return to freedom of movement between Britain and the EU, which some still see as political poison. At the same time, Ms Mahmood is trying to stem a tide that is already turning. “We look at the present through a rear-view mirror. We march backwards into the future,” said Marshall McLuhan, a media theorist. The lesson applies as much to migration policy as to the new tech he was talking about.

Perhaps even older neuroses can emerge anew. A country being flooded is one thing; a country being drained is another. For much of the 20th century, emigration was the public-policy ill of its age. “Stay here and fight it out,” declared Winston Churchill in a bbc address shortly after the second world war, imploring people to stay in Britain rather than escaping to Australia or Canada. Britons may re-learn the lesson that a country people want to come to is better than one people want to leave. In short, there is always something else to worry about. After nearly two decades of trying, the British state has delivered what voters have long said they wanted. No one will be happy about it.

articles.title: Despite recent misses, political polling is more accurate than ever
articles.deck: But elections in America and Brazil illustrate how hard the task is becoming

paragraphs.text: “We should always be afraid of many things,” muses Andrei Roman. “There’s not much we can do about them, though.” His gloom is not for humanity in general, but for one of its less celebrated endeavours: election polling.

Mr Roman’s polling firm, AtlasIntel, was spot on in its soundings of American voters before the recent midterm elections. But most pollsters underestimated the Democrats’ support. And AtlasIntel did get it wrong twice in Brazil’s recent presidential election, first suggesting that Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the left-wing incumbent, would win the first round of voting and then that Flávio Bolsonaro, his opponent, was ahead in the run-off. Many other pollsters made the same mistake.

Are polls getting worse? Our analysis suggests not. Building on a dataset created by Will Jennings and Christopher Wlezien, two professors of political science, The Economist analysed polls of 469 elections in 49 countries between 1946 and 2026. Over the past 80 years, we found, polls have become slightly more accurate. An average of polls conducted within ten days of an election predicts a given party or candidate’s share of the vote with a mean error of just two percentage points (see chart 1).

That result is all the more remarkable given the methodological challenges besetting pollsters. There are many reasons why polling should not work, but it does. In fact, it works better than the alternatives.

The principle behind public-opinion surveys is simple. If you ask a large enough sample of random individuals in a population for their view on a given topic, you can say with a reasonable degree of accuracy that the whole population shares their beliefs. Early polling pioneer George Gallup likened it to tasting a soup. Providing the soup is well-mixed, you need only one spoonful to know how it tastes.

In practice, it can be very difficult to ensure that a sample is truly random. Famously the Literary Digest, an American magazine, inferred in 1936 from 2.4m postcards sent in by readers—a sample size unheard of today—that Republican Alf Landon would be elected president. Instead, Franklin Roosevelt was re-elected in a landslide. The sample may have been huge, but it was not random.

What followed was the first of many reinventions for the polling industry as it embraced “scientific” methods. In the 1950s and 1960s most pollsters relied on face-to-face interviews at random addresses. In the 1970s and 1980s many shifted to telephone interviews, calling numbers at random. But the willingness of ordinary voters to speak to pollsters has waned. “When I started doing this, the idea was you could do a phone survey and get a 50% response rate,” recalls Doug Rivers of YouGov, a polling firm that partners with The Economist. Now he reckons the response rate is 1-2%.

As a result, a majority of pollsters have given up on using strictly random samples. Instead, the most common form of polling now involves self-selected panels of online survey-takers, who are paid for each survey they complete. Rather than randomness, pollsters rely on quotas of different types of respondents and post facto “weights”, which adjust a sample to make it representative of the whole population. In a recent poll of Americans by Léger, a Canadian firm, 60% of respondents were 55 or older, for example. After weights were applied, they made up only 41% of the survey—a far cry from the ideal of random sampling.

Contrary to some conspiracy theories, pollsters have a strong interest in getting election surveys right. Rather than money-makers, election polls are in effect advertisements intended to persuade customers to commission research on other topics. If pollsters fumble an election, it hurts their reputation. “We always used to say political polling is 90% of the publicity and less than 1% of the revenue,” says Ben Page, a former boss of Ipsos, another polling firm.

Pollsters’ judgment remains critical, however. In 2016, for example, the New York Times gave four pollsters the same raw data from Floridian voters in that year’s presidential election. After weighting, the groups came back with four different conclusions about how the election would go. One showed Mr Trump leading by a percentage point; another, trailing by four.

Polling firms must play methodological whack-a-mole, correcting errors from the previous election and anticipating future mistakes. In recent years discussion has been dominated by the issue of “non-response bias”: the idea that those who do not want to be polled lean in a particular direction politically. As politics in many Western countries has become less about economics and more about cultural issues, educated voters—who are more likely to respond to polls—have moved towards centre-left parties. A team of political scientists including Messrs Jennings and Wlezien found that polls have tended to overestimate left-wing parties by an average of 1.4 percentage points globally.

In America, this effect has been compounded by Republican scepticism of the institutions, such as universities and the media, that often commission or produce polls. In the past three American presidential elections, polls substantially underestimated support for Donald Trump. In its poll in October of the Senate race in Kansas, the Washington Post reported that 32% of Democrats responded to its survey, compared with only 12% of Republicans. The large gap suggests not only that Republicans were underrepresented, but also that the few who did respond may not have been representative.

Along with non-response bias, online pollsters have to contend with “low-quality” respondents, who are more interested in bagging the reward for completing the survey than in giving their opinions. Mr Page compares the struggle to weed out such participants to drone warfare between Russia and Ukraine, with each side innovating just as fast as the other.

“Polling is increasingly about statistical modelling as much as sampling,” says Mr Jennings. One of the most successful polling initiatives of the midterm elections was a collaboration between the New York Times and Siena College. This year the team adopted an incredibly complicated system of survey weights which involved estimating the left-right position of every registered voter in the country, to ensure polls were ideologically representative. On top of that, rather than weighting for each demographic characteristic separately, the pollsters created a system that assesses respondents by how unusual their unique combinations of characteristics were, compared with the population (“energy balancing”). The previous method would have overestimated the winning margins of Democrats who won Senate races by three points, on average. The new system showed almost no bias.

So what were pollsters doing wrong in America and Brazil? “Mobilisation was a huge component of the result for both the first round and the run-off, like never before,” says Mr Roman of Brazil’s election. “Voters didn’t show up for Lula in the first round, and they really showed up on a mass scale in the run-off.” After Mr Bolsonaro’s victory in the first round, centre-left voters realised that he might really become president. Lula’s supporters were energised, particularly on social media. Overall turnout rose from 119m to 124m, with larger increases in municipalities won by Lula, especially in big cities. In the end he won with 52% of the vote—four points higher than his share in pre-election polls.

Surveys also seem to have misjudged turnout in America’s midterms. The Economist analysed seven polls released in October that included a detailed breakdown of the composition of their sample. Respondents who said they had voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 outweighed those who had plumped for Donald Trump by two percentage points. That number already indicates some turnout adjustment on the part of pollsters: in reality she lost the election by 1.5 points. However, exit polls suggest that the actual electorate this November was even bluer, having preferred Ms Harris by five points. If you retrospectively adjust the polls to account for this, they go from showing Democrats with a 9.5-point lead to 11.5, explaining around half of the polling error (Democrats won by 14 points).

For Democrats, this enthusiasm advantage was partly driven by black voters, especially in the South, who helped elect Democratic senators in deep-red South Carolina and Mississippi. The New York Times estimates that they made up 24% and 33% of voters in those two states respectively, up by three percentage points compared with 2024. Elsewhere, Hispanic voters showed up to vote in greater numbers than in previous midterm elections. Meanwhile, many Republicans stayed at home. In counties and districts won by Ms Harris with more than 80% of the vote in 2024, turnout in the midterms was around 81% of that in the presidential election. In those where Mr Trump won with more than 80% of the vote, the figure was 12 percentage points lower.

The elections expose a particular weakness of opinion polls. “My general view is that surveys are totally crappy these days about getting non-voters,” says Mr Rivers. By their nature, those who respond to polls are more likely to be highly engaged, and more likely to vote, than those who do not. At the same time, respondents are optimistic (or dishonest) when answering questions about their likelihood to vote. Unlike demographic questions, which are fairly consistent over time and which respondents tend to answer accurately, turnout is fluid. “The typical approach would be to ask people on a scale of one to ten how likely you are to vote,” says Mr Page. “But if you get a big increase in the number of people who say they are eight, nine or ten, do you believe them or not?”

Despite this weakness, the polling misses also show that pollsters are striving to improve their estimates. In Brazil polling firms re-weighting their surveys after the first round to reflect the electorate that voted for Mr Bolsonaro. This was methodologically sound, even though it led them to overstate his support in the second round. Meanwhile, American pollsters were trying to correct their errors in the election of 2024, when they underestimated Republicans (see chart 2).

The Economist’s forecast of this year’s congressional elections aimed to anticipate polling errors, based on historical data. Our model incorrectly judged that pollsters were overestimating the Democrats, since projected landslides tend to underwhelm. It also judged that the low share of undecided voters in this year’s polls was a good sign for Republicans, because undecided voters tend to vote against the president’s party in midterms. These factors meant that the central forecast of our model compounded the pollsters’ errors, rather than remedying them.

The similarities in the polling misses in America and Brazil might lead some observers to predict the same skew in polling of other elections. Optimistic centrists might, for example, conclude that polarising right-wing candidates will always galvanise centre-left voters to defy the polls. Indeed, that is the hope of French centrists, who are looking warily towards next year’s presidential election. Marine Le Pen, the leader of the populist-right National Rally, leads opinion polls of the first round with around 35% of the vote, on average. She also leads most hypothetical polls of the second round. In the past two presidential elections, Emmanuel Macron, France’s centrist president, defeated Ms Le Pen soundly, with a slightly higher vote share than polls had predicted.

However, the historical evidence for repeated polling errors is thin, let alone across different countries, or in presidential elections with different candidates. Indeed, the second-placed candidate in most polls is a left-wing firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, with around 17% support. He is one of the most polarising and unpopular figures in France, whereas voters have warmed to Ms Le Pen since 2022. A contest between the two is unlikely, therefore, to inspire a surge of voters determined to foil Ms Le Pen. What is more, French pollsters may have learned from their previous mistakes, or even overcorrected. Though a polling error is certainly possible, relying on one is never a good idea. (The Economist’s forecast model of the French election will be published next year.)

Likewise, social democrats hope that Pedro Sánchez—a left-wing escape-artist who is prime minister of Spain—can repeat his poll-defying feat in 2023 and cling to power. That year, polls underestimated his Socialist Party (PSOE) by around three percentage points. It was just enough to cobble together a coalition of leftist and regionalist parties to stay in power. The Economist’s poll tracker for the election on November 29th shows 27% support for PSOE, just behind the centre-right People’s Party on 31%. However, since 2023 Mr Sánchez’s coalition partners have taken a tumble and the populist-right Vox has gained ground. The combined right-wing parties are polling at 50%, so should secure a majority under Spain’s electoral system. The left trails on 35%, with regional parties on 9%. There is still time for public opinion to shift, but if the polls hold, only an unusually large error would save Mr Sánchez.

Next year anxious poll-watchers will no doubt hope for a polling miss that favours their preferred candidates in Poland and Italy, too. However, there is no sign that polling errors are growing, nor that their slight past skew to the left has become a bias to the right. An average absolute polling error of two points does not preclude the possibility of a big miss but, given the ever deeper potential pitfalls, is remarkably accurate. From early in the midterm campaign, the polls clearly indicated a big win for Democrats and a swing from Latinos in particular. That the polling averages foresaw the biggest blue wave in a generation, rather than two, seems forgivable.

Most important, polls look better than the alternatives. In many of the most infamous polling misses, such as Britain’s vote to leave the European Union or Mr Trump’s election in 2016, the polls came closer to the final result than most pundits did. A survey of 33 British journalists before the Brexit referendum found that 32 of them expected the country to vote to remain in the EU, for example. Some vaunted alternatives, such as social-media monitoring, have never taken off. Others, such as prediction markets or AI-generated surveys, themselves depend on polling. The famous prediction-market “whale”, who made $80m betting on Mr Trump’s re-election in 2024, reportedly commissioned private polling from YouGov, for example.

As good as the polls’ record is, their creators should be clear about their imperfections. For pollsters that chiefly means being transparent. Methodological notes by the Washington Post and the New York Times about the surveys they had commissioned helped contextualise their polling in this election, for example. More information about sampling and weighting can improve scrutiny, making it easier to weed out fake polls and cowboy pollsters. Publishing survey results even when they are surprising can help avoid “herding”, whereby polling is skewed by pollsters’ reluctance to go out on a limb.

Consumers of polls, meanwhile, must understand their limitations. They should treat any individual poll with a dose of scepticism. Where possible, they should refer to averages of multiple surveys, such as those produced by The Economist. In all elections, they should be ready for the polls to be off by a few percentage points in either direction for every party or candidate. The polls are better than ever, but they are not infallible.

articles.title: Global bullies have turned uncertainty into a weapon
articles.deck: America and China see profit in keeping the whole world on edge

paragraphs.text: IS THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ open or closed? Nobody can answer that question with confidence. The maritime choke point is not a barn door that is either open or shut. It is a place of unknown dangers for shippers, sea captains and governments. For Iran, a bankrupt, isolated mid-size rogue, engendering that uncertainty creates leverage over stronger, richer foes.

Is Russia behind recent bomb hoaxes that have alarmed European politicians and business bosses? Nobody knows, and that is also the point. Russia’s aim is not to convince adversaries to believe its twisted version of the truth. Since Soviet times, it has specialised in deniable attacks that leave others doubting whether anything is true.

So far, so roguish. Such agents of chaos as Russia and Iran have long relished their ability to keep stability-loving rivals off-balance. Today, the unwelcome shock involves America and China playing the same game. Not long ago those two giants saw an interest in upholding a stable and predictable global trading order (while bending its rules as needed). Now the two countries seem to like ambiguous rules and hard-to-enforce agreements that leave trade partners dependent on their goodwill.

To be sure, statesmen have been masters of ambiguity since they wore robes and swords, and carved treaties on stone tablets. In the modern era, what is more, America had always been careful to avoid offering hard-and-fast security guarantees to allies, lest they started foolish conflicts, believing that Uncle Sam would come to their aid.

President Donald Trump is different. He breaks new ground by treating inconstancy as his superpower. This is true in foreign policy, as he threatens to bomb countries before offering them friendship in the next breath. It is the case in trade policy, as he adjusts tariff rates and export controls on a whim. When Trump aides are asked how foreign governments or investors are supposed to agree to big, long-term deals if the terms may later change, they serenely reply that “there is a value to uncertainty.” In their telling, doubt usefully reminds foreigners that access to America’s market is a privilege, not a right. They note the advice of the president himself: if outsiders wish to avoid tariffs, all they need to do is make things in America.

In Trumpworld, American dominance is enhanced when foreigners do not know where they stand. In the context of the Ukraine war, that might involve Europeans pleading for continued access to American-made weapons or the Starlink satellite-internet system owned by Elon Musk. In future, it might involve access to the best AI models. Foreign pleading is the pay-off.

China is also breaking new ground. It spent decades tut-tutting at America’s high-handed and changeable ways. Officials in Beijing would accuse America of nagging trade partners to open their markets, only to turn round and enact export controls and other curbs before a foreign rival became too formidable a competitor. America changes the rules when it fears losing a game, they would grumble. Worse, America claims to enjoy a “long-arm jurisdiction” to enforce its laws worldwide, as Chinese legal experts complained.

The grumbling lasted until China became dominant in the production of vital industrial inputs and world-class technologies, from rare-earth elements to batteries. Just in time for Mr Trump’s uninhibited second turn at the presidency, China found itself in a position to retaliate in relative safety. In the past couple of years China has enacted its own export controls and long-arm laws to punish foreign companies if they obey American laws and sanctions that hurt China.

If a multinational firm is now paralysed with doubt, not knowing how to balance laws in America, where it is listed, with those in China, where it sources important components, that is no accident. In an echo of Mr Trump’s line—to avoid tariffs, make things in America—China has its own form of blackmail to propose. If companies wish to avoid the vaguely written, politicised rules that govern export licences for rare earths and the like, they can make products in China and export them as finished batteries or electric cars. The offer is not subtle: China-based factories have no trouble sourcing rare earths; dependence is a small price to pay.

If carrots do not work, China has sticks to use on foreigners trying to de-risk and diversify away from dependence on its supply chains. Specific rules aim to stop foreigners building up stockpiles of critical minerals, and even govern the export of machines to process and recycle them. Some Chinese controls are currently suspended as trade talks continue with America and Europe, yet hang like a sword over negotiators.

At least China is still bashful about weaponising uncertainty. Even as it keeps countries on edge, its officials insist that their government is a rule-abiding champion of globalisation and openness, though nobody actually believes this. In contrast, Trump administration officials do not pretend that their president’s word is his bond. Unblushingly, they portray his unreliability as a sign of strength and cleverness. In this, Trump-era America resembles Russia and Iran more than it does a traditional great power.

For the mark of a true rogue is to inspire fear, but not care about getting caught. On November 9th France blamed Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps for cyber-attacks that remotely turned freezers into ovens in hundreds of French supermarkets. The attacks were not subtle: traces of Persian were found in the hackers’ computer code. What logic guides Iran to spoil food in a French supermarket, without hiding its traces? Logic has nothing to do with it. In brutal times, sowing doubt is the win.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s recklessness leaves Nvidia with no good options
articles.deck: His affair will bring lasting damage to the company

paragraphs.text: Editor’s note: Jensen Huang resigned on November 12th.

Few companies have looked as unassailable as Nvidia in recent years. Its whizzy chips, together with its software and networking gear, made it indispensable to the artificial-intelligence boom, affording it an outsize share of the profits from the technology. Now Jensen Huang, who co-founded the company and has led it for over three decades, has weakened Nvidia to a degree that no rival could have hoped to achieve. On November 12th, as The Economist went to press, its board was reportedly preparing to oust him.

Mr Huang’s unravelling has been swift. In a short memo on November 8th he confessed to an extramarital affair, apologising to his family and his company. At the same time Nvidia’s board announced it had launched an investigation into whether he had “been the target of a foreign-intelligence effort”. The admission followed reports that he had been romantically involved with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean data-centre company that buys Nvidia’s chips. American officials suspect Megaspeed of smuggling banned chips into China—and believe Ms Huang to be a Chinese agent (a claim rejected by the Chinese government).

Then on November 11th The New York Times reported that Mr Huang also had an affair with an executive who reported directly to him. Nvidia’s share price, which had been down by 7% since Mr Huang’s memo, plunged by a further 9% in after-hours trading after reports his job was in jeopardy. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s finance chief, is widely tipped to step in as interim boss if he goes.

Two questions now loom large. Can Nvidia, until recently the world’s most valuable company, thrive without Mr Huang? And can the AI build-out, which the company has done so much to bankroll, survive the shock?

It may be the affair with a subordinate that seals Mr Huang’s fate, but it was his entanglement with the Megaspeed executive that raises the most troubling questions. Since October 2022 America has barred the sales of its leading-edge chips to China. Yet Chinese firms have found ways round the ban. Some do so by renting computing power in data centres abroad. Others rely on intermediaries in South-East Asia that smuggle chips into China.

Megaspeed, a “neocloud” that rents out access to AI processors, is suspected by American officials of operating across both routes. It took its current name in 2023, the year Ms Huang was listed as its managing director, and soon became one of the biggest buyers of Nvidia’s chips in South-East Asia. Culper Research, a short-seller, estimates that Speedmatrix, Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary, imported $4.6bn-worth of goods between December 2024 and January 2026, most of them servers packed with Nvidia chips. As far back as September 2024 American officials began investigating Megaspeed. (The firm denies the allegations.)

None of this seemed to give Nvidia’s boss pause. He and Ms Huang were repeatedly photographed together, and his company continued to vouch for its customer. Late last year Nvidia said its own checks had found no evidence of diversion. Last month Mr Huang called his dealings with Ms Huang “completely normal and not unusual”, and insisted that Nvidia had “counted every one” of Megaspeed’s chips. In recent days Bloomberg and the New York Times have independently reported that Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, intervened last year in the Commerce Department’s investigation of Megaspeed. An Nvidia spokesperson says that the company regularly consults export-control officials to share knowledge.

President Donald Trump’s administration seemed no more troubled. Mr Huang has been one of Mr Trump’s favourite businessmen, and a frequent presence at his side. Yet the president appears to have been warned about the relationship at least twice. Reportedly he was briefed on the intelligence about Ms Huang roughly a year ago. In May, as he flew to China with a group of executives, Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, reminded him of it shortly before Nvidia’s boss joined the trip during a refuelling stop in Alaska.

The administration will now have to answer for why it took no action on the warnings, and why it continued to allow Mr Huang to wield so much influence on a matter of national security. Three Republican committee chairmen have summoned Mr Huang to a closed-door congressional briefing on November 18th. Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, will also face scrutiny, particularly once Democrats take control of Congress in January. Chris Coons, who is set to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has promised to investigate “the insane relationship between the Trump administration, Chinese spies and AI billionaires”.

The scandal could also revive a handful of stalled bills to tighten China’s access to AI chips. One would turn into law the administration’s policy of blocking the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China. Another would require exporters to show that their chips have not been diverted, for instance by verifying where they are.

If Mr Huang goes, it will be a sorry end to a brilliant career. He co-founded Nvidia in 1993 to make graphics chips for video games. But in the mid-2010s Mr Huang became convinced that AI would transform computing, and that Nvidia’s form of chip would provide its essential building blocks. The bet proved prescient. Between the start of 2023 and the beginning of this year Nvidia’s share price rose 13-fold. In October 2025 it became the first company to be worth more than $5trn.

Finding a permanent successor would be hard. Jay Goldberg of Seaport Research Partners, a firm of analysts, reckons that “nobody can fill Jensen’s leather jacket”. Although Nvidia has grown into a giant, with some 40,000 employees, it is run as an extension of its charismatic leader. Mr Huang is a micromanager, with some 60 people reporting directly to him. His ties with suppliers such as TSMC, a Taiwanese chip manufacturer, and SK Hynix, a South Korean memory-maker, have helped secure scarce capacity. Some outsiders have been floated, including Lisa Su, boss of AMD (and a distant relative of Mr Huang). Yet any newcomer would inherit a firm full of the old boss’s loyalists.

Nvidia’s performance may hold up for now. Mr Goldberg notes that many of its chips are sold out into next year, and demand for AI gear remains strong. But the saga looks set to be a lasting distraction, even if Mr Huang is replaced. On November 9th shareholders filed a class-action accusing the company and Mr Huang of misleading investors when they responded to reports about the relationship between him and Ms Huang.

Mr Goldberg also thinks that Mr Huang’s exit would “take a lot of the spirit out of” the investment boom. Nvidia’s boss is one of AI’s loudest cheerleaders; his leather jacket, stadium keynotes and sermons on the technology have made him a rock star among the tech faithful. Lately he has also become the industry’s banker, using Nvidia’s cash to bankroll AI startups and its balance-sheet to guarantee the debts of myriad data-centre projects. With Mr Huang gone, the web of deals he has spun may start to unravel.

articles.title: A franchise revolution is stirring in China
articles.deck: It is bringing buzzy retail brands to every corner of the country—and beyond

paragraphs.text: Yang Guofu spent much of the 1990s running from the chengguan, a dreaded troop of goons with the authority to rough up street vendors in the name of tidier cities. At the time he was grilling squid from a cart in a north-eastern town. Since then Mr Yang has turned his business into a global restaurant franchise with more than 7,000 outlets. His company, Yangguofu, dishes up a spicy Chinese soup known as malatang. Most of its shops are in China, but it has expanded to more than 20 other countries, opening in London and Rome last year, and in Luxembourg last month, far from the reach of the chengguan.

Mr Yang is part of an oddly timed retail revolution. Consumer spending in China is by most accounts miserable; retail sales grew by a lousy 1.1% in September, year on year. Once-popular Western brands are struggling. And yet walk down the street in a typical mid-size city in China and you are likely to see dozens of new retail shops wherever you look. There are myriad milk-tea outlets. On the streets of Nanchang, a south-eastern city, every corner seems to have a GoodMe selling teas and treats. Snack shops, such as Busy Ming, which peddles a wide variety of sweets, crisps and dried meats, are almost as numerous. The snow-man mascot of Mixue, a popular cold-drinks franchise, is now ubiquitous.

The growth of these businesses has been striking. Between 2023 and 2025 China’s 300 largest food- and drinks-franchises may have opened more than half a million outlets. That is roughly five-times the number opened in America during its franchising heyday between 1964 and 1969, when McDonald’s and Holiday Inn first took off. Today Chinese brands such as Mixue, Busy Ming and JI Hotel control some of the world’s largest franchise networks in their industries. The explosive growth required at least 100bn yuan ($15bn) in fresh capital in 2025, The Economist reckons, much of which came from household savings.

Until recently consolidation of China’s retail sector has been tedious. It is made up of millions of small-time entrepreneurs, many of whom run single-shop enterprises in small cities. In 2018 just 13% of restaurants were part of a corporate chain. But by 2025 that rate had shot to 25%, a sign these entrepreneurs have been signing up to franchises in droves. Hotels, an industry once dominated by dingy independent businesses built into housing units, have consolidated even faster.

A handful of factors have come together to make this possible. Chief among them is the honing of China’s distinctive franchising model. American fast-food giants make most of their revenues from royalties and rents paid by franchisees. McDonald’s, for example, owns many of the properties from which its burger joints operate; last year rents provided nearly 40% of its revenue. China franchisors, by contrast, act more like suppliers. They source raw materials and use sophisticated logistics networks to provide them at low prices to franchisees. They also sell equipment. These are the source of nearly all Mixue’s revenue, for example. Only in the past few years have such supply chains become sufficiently mature in China.

Ferocious competition in China has been another factor. Tepid consumer demand in recent years means that margins are razor thin for most retail businesses. That makes scale essential, and one way to achieve it is to open as many shops as possible with the help of franchisees. The brands, in turn, must keep license fees and royalties low in order to recruit new shop owners.

This model, which helps to lower prices, suits China’s reluctant spenders. Cotti, a coffee chain that has opened 18,000 shops since 2022, charges nothing upfront to its franchisees. Yangguofu asks for just 8,888 yuan to open one of its shops, and then an annual management charge of 5,000. The cost of renting the outlet, refurbishing it and stocking it with the brand’s equipment is covered by the franchisee. The main financial arrangement between Yangguofu and its restaurant operators is for the soup base that goes into its malatang, sales of which account for about 90% of the company’s revenue.

The final ingredient is capital. Funding retail enterprises in China is notoriously difficult. For years the central government has frowned on retail brands raising public capital. It would rather funds be channeled into favoured industries, such as chipmaking and artificial intelligence. Since 2022 retail businesses have managed to grab less than 2% of the total equity-capital raised on mainland Chinese bourses.

China’s ascendant retail brands have instead been built on household savings. Not long ago Chinese workers poured their savings into the property market. At its peak in 2021 up to 80% of household wealth was tied up in the value of flats. But a popping of the property bubble that occurred around that time has meant fewer funds flowing to the sector. Much wealth has ended up in bank deposits, but more than ever it is going into franchise outlets, says Chen Luo of Bank of America.

Many of these franchises are going global. As of the end of last year the top 50 Chinese food- and beverage-retailers were thought to have opened at least 6,800 overseas shops cumulatively. These outlets are important because margins are often juicier outside China. Extending supply chains to other countries can be difficult, but some are trying. One Chinese hotel chain has just started shipping room modules to Europe in a bid to make its hotels there cheaper to construct and more uniform.

Back home, the unbridled growth of franchises has not been without its challenges. Shops have been closing rapidly even as many more open up. More than 2,500 Mixue outlets appear to have been shut last year. Brands are grappling with inconsistencies in operational standards and divergent business philosophies among their franchisees, says Zhu Danpeng, an industry analyst. Rapid growth has made quality control difficult. Tianlala, one rapidly expanding tea-shop chain, acknowledged such shortcomings this year after numerous complaints surfaced online. It has forcibly shut many stores. Growing a franchise is one thing. Sustaining it may prove another.

articles.title: Everything is going wrong for SoftBank
articles.deck: Masayoshi Son’s all-in bet on AI is looking shaky

paragraphs.text: At the start of the summer, the outlook was sunny for SoftBank and its swashbuckling boss, Masayoshi Son. The giant investment firm briefly toppled Toyota as Japan’s most valuable company. At the end of June the net value of its assets reached ¥72.3trn ($445bn), an increase of 80% in just three months thanks to gains in its artificial-intelligence holdings. Mr Son crowed that investors had once again underestimated SoftBank (and himself), likening his creation to a goose laying golden eggs: “What matters is not the eggs. It is the goose itself.”

The period since has not been a fertile one. By early August the net value of SoftBank’s assets had dropped to ¥58.3trn, as the share prices of many of its big investments tumbled. From its peak in June, SoftBank’s market capitalisation has fallen by more than half (see chart); it now ranks only ninth in the Japanese league. Analysts had expected the firm to report a modest profit in the most recent quarter, but on November 10th the company disclosed a $7bn loss, much of it the result of write-downs linked to its American data-centre investments. Mr Son’s eggs look less golden than cracked.

To understand what has gone wrong, consider the four elements of SoftBank’s bet on AI: semiconductors, models, robotics and infrastructure. One of SoftBank’s biggest holdings is its stake of about 90% in Arm, a British company that made its name creating blueprints for chips in smartphones and other gadgets. Now Arm is pushing into selling its own silicon for use in AI data centres. Investors are worried that royalties from its original business will slow faster than new profits can replace them. Such concerns have sent Arm’s stock down by more than 50% since mid-June. In the same period shares in Intel, an American chipmaker and another of SoftBank’s investments, have also fallen by more than half.

Turn next to Mr Son’s $65bn bet on OpenAI. The model-maker has delayed its plans for a public share offering, allowing its arch-rival Anthropic, which set its price range on November 10th, to beat it to the stock market. That will slow any payout for SoftBank, which borrowed vast sums to invest in OpenAI. Analysts estimate that the ratio of SoftBank’s debts to the value of its assets has risen from 16% at the end of September to somewhere between 20% and 25%, SoftBank’s self-imposed notional maximum. Some expect it to hit 28% by March. That has made lenders twitchy. This month spreads on SoftBank’s five-year credit-default swaps hit a four-year high, implying a 31% probability of it being unable to service its borrowings.

Another of Mr Son’s debt-fuelled bids, to buy the robotics arm of ABB, a European machinery-maker, is also in peril. This month regulators in China, the division’s biggest market, blocked the sale of the local business to SoftBank. They are said to be uncomfortable with the prospect of Mr Son harvesting data from ABB’s machines to help OpenAI and others train models. SoftBank and ABB are exploring whether a carve-out of the Chinese business would salvage the deal, though doing so would make the purchase less worthwhile.

Last, and the latest to run into trouble, is SoftBank’s investment in AI infrastructure. This includes what will, if built, be one of the world’s largest data centres, a ten-gigawatt project in Ohio for which OpenAI is the primary tenant. Yet having rushed to nail down contracts for its data centres, SoftBank has cancelled reservations for power-generation equipment, taking a $3.7bn writedown.

The company has given few details about the written-down kit, other than to deny that it was related to the project in Ohio. But the situation suggests that SoftBank may be rethinking its broader ambitions. Part of what lies behind the recent market turmoil surrounding AI is a change in the political wind. Several victorious Democratic candidates in America’s elections this month, including the next governor of Ohio, campaigned aggressively against data-centre development.

Mr Son is not alone in having staked his firm and his reputation on AI. He may yet be vindicated, if Arm’s data-centre business takes off or OpenAI’s listing is a roaring success. He and his firm have suffered setbacks—and staged comebacks—before. As a new chapter in the AI fable unfolds, will the goose produce once again?
