articles.title: YouTube’s dominance has Hollywood running scared
articles.deck: Studios and streamers alike are struggling to respond to its success

paragraphs.text: IN THE MOVIE industry, there are two competing storylines. The darker one —call it old Hollywood—prevailed on November 9th when Skydance, the newly formed combination of Paramount and Warner Bros, laid out plans to reduce its $87bn debt. Like other media giants, such as Netflix, its near future is one of attrition and job cuts, glossed over by promises of big hits to come. The other storyline—call it new Hollywood—is less well known and more upbeat. It is made on YouTube.

To glimpse it, your correspondent travelled to an unmarked building in the Hollywood hinterland of Burbank, home to the new 32,000 square-feet studio of Smosh, a YouTube comedy channel as old as the video platform itself. The precise whereabouts are kept secret to deter over-zealous fans. Suffice to say, it is not glitzy. Similarly, Smosh’s comedy has less polish than prestige TV. Yet it is a YouTube sensation. Smosh has more than 45m followers across its channels, revenue that has grown fivefold in the past three years and a headcount that has tripled to 100, says Alessandra Catanese, its boss. “I’ve been making this joke lately, but I’m totally serious. Paramount, Disney and Netflix: their layoffs are our draft,” she says.

Burbank is home to much of this YouTube demi-monde. Its scruffy creators are not big enough to offset the malaise of old Hollywood. But they have started to rattle the incumbents, which have been forced to battle YouTube for screen time in part by imitating its ways. Whether what some call “YouTube panic” is working is debatable. Yet it may be unavoidable. In the words of Mark Fischbach (aka Markiplier), who earlier this year mobilised his 40m-odd YouTube followers to turn his self-financed horror film “Iron Lung” into a box-office hit, “YouTube is the thousand-pound monster lurking over everyone’s shoulder.”

YouTube’s effect on the media zeitgeist has been palpable this year. After “Iron Lung”, two young directors who honed their craft on YouTube released “Backrooms” and “Obsession”, which became blockbuster films. The platform’s disruptive force has become increasingly evident on TV. Nielsen, a data gatherer, measured YouTube’s share of America’s TV watching at 15.8% in August, almost as much as Netflix and the streaming services of Disney, Paramount and Warner Bros combined (see chart). That is double its level in early 2023, when YouTube overtook Netflix as the biggest streamer. When it comes to attention, “YouTube is by far the biggest winner,” says Ernesto Pagano of BCG, a consultancy.

The platform’s economic heft is becoming more apparent, too. For the first time this year it disclosed annual revenue, reporting $60bn from ads and subscriptions in 2025. That was more than Netflix’s $45bn and far more than other streaming platforms. KPMG, an accounting firm, estimates that it easily outspent its peers on content last year, shelling out $28bn, compared with, say, $18bn at Netflix. The more content YouTube streams, the more data it has to improve its algorithm, further boosting viewer engagement—and revenue.

YouTube’s megabucks enable it to throw its weight around in ways that challenge Hollywood’s incumbents. It is investing in more traditional fare such as sports. Next year it will offer the ad-supported tier of Peacock, the streaming service of NBCUniversal, at no charge for its Premium subscribers. Its creators, as they earn more money, are pouring it back into making longer, more professional shows.

YouTube benefits from a business model that has less risk than that of its rivals. Whereas studios and streamers pay upfront to commission content, and own or license the resulting work, YouTube usually pays nothing in advance. Instead it takes a 45-55% cut of ad revenue and channel subscriptions. This pay-for-performance approach makes YouTube less of a hostage to fortune than its peers, who can waste huge sums on films that bomb.

The platform’s ownership by Google, a pioneer in artificial intelligence, has also helped it to develop new technology to support creators. AI tools offered by YouTube are used to simplify editing, autodub content into other languages and automatically tag products that appear in clips. Many in Hollywood fret about leaning too heavily on AI, because surveys suggest it turns audiences off. But while other streamers such as Netflix use the technology to trim production costs, YouTube leads the way in using it to boost revenue—for its creators and itself.

YouTube’s growing clout has stirred a belated fightback. Several streaming services, including Netflix and Disney Plus, have introduced swipeable short-form vertical videos similar to YouTube Shorts. Last year Ted Sarandos, Netflix’s co-chief, dismissed the creator community as a place for “killing time”. Now he is eating his words. Netflix has pledged $1bn over three years for deals with creators, according to LightShed Partners, a media-research firm. In some cases it is paying lavish sums upfront for new shows. Next year, for instance, it plans to stream a kids’ competition by Mark Rober, a YouTube science geek, that an insider at the company describes as “Pop Idol for scientists”. With Netflix’s support, the budget is said to be equal to what Mr Rober normally spends on content in a year.

The poaching extends beyond creators to YouTube executives. In October Sony Pictures, one of Hollywood’s biggest studios, named Fede Goldenberg, who at YouTube helped bring “Iron Lung” and other hits to the big screen, as head of one of its film divisions. The hope is that he will turn more creators into film-makers.

Evidence for the success of Hollywood’s response is so far mixed. Netflix’s share price is down by almost a third this year as revenue growth has slowed. Disney has had a better year; its shares have risen by around 5%. But the company has become heavily reliant on theme parks to generate profit. Skydance aims to bundle HBO Max and Paramount Plus together in early 2027, which may yield a stronger competitive position in streaming. But the merged studios also need to shave $6bn off their overheads.

YouTube is not impregnable. Neal Mohan, its chief executive, dismisses attempts to poach its creators as “flattering”. But there are signs of genuine concern. YouTube has reportedly offered millions to ensure some creators release shows exclusively on its site. And it faces upstarts of its own. TikTok, a short-video platform, is working with Tubi, a free streaming service owned by Fox Corp, to develop ten original long-form series. Meta has rolled out a version of its Instagram app for smart TVs, on which users can now watch Reels, its short-form videos. Last month it offered creators the opportunity to test horizontal videos of up to 90 minutes.

Yet YouTube is far ahead for now—and Hollywood as a whole is stronger for it. Not long ago, Netflix was a force for creative destruction, breaking the stranglehold of broadcasters and cable companies to usher in the streaming revolution. In a recent podcast interview, its retired co-founder, Reed Hastings, drew an analogy with the 1950s and 1960s, when the rise of television drove the movie industry into a funk until a new breed of talented film-makers broke through in the 1970s. Today, he said, YouTube is analogous to TV back then, and Netflix to the movies. “We have to take up the creative bar and push ourselves to be ever more gripping,” he argued. “It’s hard to out-YouTube YouTube.”

articles.title: The company behind Barbie wants to be an entertainment giant
articles.deck: But Mattel remains a struggling toymaker

paragraphs.text: Games are afoot at Mattel. In recent weeks the business behind Barbie dolls and Hot Wheels cars, which has seen its market value plunge by 20% this year, has replaced its chief executive and much of its leadership team. Big shareholders are calling for a sale. Interested buyers are said to include Zuru, a maker of water pistols, and Authentic Brands, custodian of trademarks from Care Bears to Juicy Couture. Mattel’s new boss is instead counting on remaking it from a traditional toymaker into a buzzy entertainment firm.

It is a bad time for producers of playthings. The Iran war has sent commodity prices soaring. Toys of the sort Mattel makes require plastic, and plastic requires crude oil. Parents, feeling the pinch from inflation, are turning stingy. In a recent survey by Mintel, a research firm, 65% of toy buyers said price is now their top consideration. Many are turning to retailers’ cheaper own-brand alternatives.

The challenges go deeper still. Anthony Bonadio of Wells Fargo, a bank, reckons the industry is in structural decline. Birth rates are falling and children are abandoning toys at ever-younger ages. On average, American children aged between eight and 18 spend 7.5 hours per day on screens, leaving little time for physical toys.

Global sales have grown at a meagre compound annual rate of 3% over the past decade, mostly through higher prices, according to UBS, another bank. Even that overstates things. Circana, a data provider, points out that much of the growth has been in categories where nostalgic adults are propping up sales. That includes trading-card games (think Hasbro’s “Magic: The Gathering”) and building sets (Lego).

The pattern is reflected at Mattel. On November 5th it reported that sales of Hot Wheels (another favourite of kidults) were up by 6% in the third quarter, year on year. But those for Barbie were down by 10%, and Fisher-Price, a brand for infants, plunged by 15%. The company slashed its annual forecast for sales and profits.

It will fall to Mattel’s new leadership to bring back the joy. Roger Lynch, who took over as its boss last month, previously ran Condé Nast, publisher of Vogue. Before that, he was in charge of Pandora, a music-streaming service. On his first earnings call he said that what drew him to Mattel was what had drawn him to Condé Nast: its intellectual property (IP). UBS reckons Mattel’s stable of names is worth $8.7bn, nearly double its current market value. They could form the basis of lucrative films, video games and live experiences.

To date, Mattel has struggled to make use of this treasure trove. “Barbie”, the top-grossing film of 2023, boosted operating profit by around $100m (or 15%) that year. But the uplift in doll sales was short-lived. “It was more about ladies dressing up in pink and showing up at the movies,” says Jaime Katz of Morningstar, a research firm. Mattel’s latest films, “Masters of the Universe” and “Matchbox: The Movie”, have been flops.

Video games have also been a disappointment. In 2018 Mattel set up a mobile-gaming studio in collaboration with NetEase, a Chinese gaming giant; this year it acquired its partner’s 50% stake in the venture. But releases such as UNO! Mobile, based on the card game, have been better at attracting eyeballs than generating money. Because mobile games are cheap to make—more so now with the rise of artificial intelligence—competition is fierce.

Even so, rivals have had better luck than Mattel cashing in on their IP. Hasbro worked with a video-game studio to produce Monopoly Go!, an adaptation of its infamous board game; the app, released in 2023, generated $41m in royalties for the toymaker in its most recent quarter alone. Mr Lynch will be hoping for similar feats from Mattel’s IP. Barbie may soon be put to work once again.

articles.title: Quebec’s strategic maple-syrup reserve is running dry
articles.deck: The province’s cartel is losing its grip

paragraphs.text: QUEBEC’S STRATEGIC maple-syrup reserve is probably sweeter in the imagination than in reality, with its whitewashed barrels stacked from floor to ceiling in industrial halls. Yet the reserve, established in 2000 to stabilise prices and supply, is in a sticky situation: this winter it will run dry.

The last such calamity was in 2008, the result of several bad seasons. Barely had the reserve recovered when a few years later over $18m-worth of syrup was skimmed in a heist. More recently a series of poor harvests in the early 2020s and a sustained upswing in demand has left its barrels depleted. The reserve will be empty by February.

In a recent interview Luc Goulet of Quebec Maple Syrup Producers (PPAQ), an industry group, laid part of the blame on the uncertainty over American tariffs, which has led some buyers to bring forward purchases of Canadian syrup. But rising demand also reflects consumers’ shift away from refined sugars in favour of more natural options. Canada’s producers, which dominate the global supply of maple syrup, now make twice as much as a decade ago. Yet even that has not been enough to keep pace.

The industry has long centred on Quebec. In the early 2000s PPAQ, which controls the province’s wholesale market for bulk syrup, alongside managing the reserve, introduced strict marketing restrictions and output quotas. A paper published last year by Qingbin Wang and co-authors at the University of Vermont found that although these measures had helped to stabilise prices through good and bad harvests, they had stymied the ability of Quebec’s producers to expand their output as demand rose.

Between 1999 and 2005 Quebec accounted for 80% of North American production. By 2023, the latest year available, its share was down to 65%. Production in neighbouring New Brunswick has spurted. Buyers, who blend and package the syrup, are also sourcing more from America, particularly Vermont. Some of the biggest, such as Lantic and Turkey Hill Sugarbush, have built their own reserves. Quebec’s sweet deal may be ending.

articles.title: The panic over personalised pricing is overdone
articles.deck: Lawmakers are getting ahead of themselves

paragraphs.text: One of the great promises of artificial intelligence is personalisation. The ability to crunch vast amounts of data and generate tailored content at scale raises all sorts of possibilities: individualised lesson plans for pupils in a classroom, treatments geared to the needs of specific patients, financial advice for a person rather than a persona. But in one area in particular, personalisation looks poisonous.

Legislators in America and beyond are queuing up against personalised pricing, the idea of charging people different prices for the same product based on what firms know about them personally. The states of Maryland, Connecticut and New Jersey have all passed laws this year restricting the practice. New York already requires the use of personalised pricing to be disclosed; a more draconian law is awaiting the signature of Kathy Hochul, the state’s governor. On October 28th the Federal Trade Commission ordered some of the country’s best-known firms, including Delta, Uber and Walmart, to hand over information as part of an investigation into personalised pricing. Regulators across the Atlantic are also swarming around the topic.

This is both unsurprising and misguided. It is unsurprising because the public hates the idea. Dynamic pricing, the practice of varying the price of things like airline seats or ride-hailing fares over time in response to demand, is controversial enough. Personalised pricing, which means you might pay more than someone else who is buying an identical product at the same time, sounds even more galling. When people are asked how they feel about this possibility, they give it a big thumbs-down. Given the march of AI and widespread concerns over “affordability”, it’s no great shock that policymakers are rushing to curtail the practice.

That doesn’t make them right to do so. In the proper circumstances, personalised pricing is perfectly acceptable to people. If you make bids on an auction site like eBay or negotiate a deal on behalf of your company, you are reaching a price based on your own willingness to pay. If you take part in a loyalty programme, you actively want your previous behaviour to affect prices. Entire industries depend on risk-based pricing that reflects information about individuals: the laws in Connecticut and New York, for example, have exemptions for insurers and lenders.

Personalised pricing would make products cheaper for some. In a paper published in 2022, Jean-Pierre Dubé and Sanjog Misra of the University of Chicago conducted an experiment with ZipRecruiter, a jobs marketplace, to see how differential pricing plays out. They found that adjusting prices based on employers’ willingness to pay yielded both higher profits overall for ZipRecruiter and lower prices for a majority of its subscribers. In June Colorado’s governor, Jared Polis, vetoed a state law on personalised pricing for fear that it would make life less affordable for most consumers.

Competition increases the likelihood that consumers would be better off in a world of individualised pricing. In an earlier paper, Mr Dubé and his colleagues looked at what happened when two Chinese cinemas started to offer discounts to consumers based on their smartphone location data. Each chain had an incentive to offer deeper discounts when people were closer to a rival chain, encouraging the other to respond with defensive price cuts of their own.

There are good reasons to worry about personalised pricing. Without robust privacy rules, firms will be tempted to use consumers’ personal data without their consent. There is a real benefit to having reference prices; if every price were tailored to individuals, customers might never be sure whether they were getting a good deal. But these concerns, combined with consumers’ instinctive aversion to the idea, is also reason to think that lots of firms will tread carefully.

Amazon suffered a public backlash way back in 2000, when some DVD buyers were aggrieved to find that they were being charged a different price for the same title. The firm pledged then not to use customer demographics to set prices. In September John Furner, the boss of Walmart, made the same promise in an open letter. “We price the product, not the person,” he wrote. The crackdown on personalised pricing is understandable. But it risks hurting lower-income shoppers and piling on compliance costs in order to prevent something that may not materialise. That’s a bad deal.

articles.title: There has never been a scandal like the Jensen Huang affair
articles.deck: A journey through the annals of corporate crises

paragraphs.text: Editor’s note (November 12th 2026): This article has been updated to take account of Jensen Huang’s resignation.

In the gossip columns it is the story of a steamy affair between an American billionaire who wears a leather jacket and a younger woman who allegedly works for Chinese intelligence. On Wall Street it illustrates a three-fold concentration risk: the danger of a stock market which depends on one technology, which depends on one firm, which depends on one man. In Washington they talk of a rotten Commerce Department, the closeness of President Donald Trump to tech bosses, and divisions in the Republican Party over China. “Two clichés make us laugh. A hundred clichés move us,” wrote Umberto Eco of the film “Casablanca”. And so it is with the Jensen Huang affair: not one scandal, but many.

The annals of corporate crisis contain nothing like it. Chief executives frequently face trouble in the boardroom over something that has happened in the bedroom. Every few years some more serious crisis fundamentally changes how the world views an important firm. These things do not happen simultaneously. John Browne was the oil industry’s “sun king”. In 2007 the BP boss resigned after telling a “white lie” in court about a relationship: a mark on the man, but not so much his firm. Conversely, there was not one individual to blame for, and nothing titillating about, BP’s oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico three years later. Rupert Murdoch’s media empire has been shaped by his five marriages and four divorces. But Wendi Deng, his wife at the time, never hacked phones for the News of the World.

After the crisis comes the crisis response. This means a press release which attempts to maximise contrition and minimise legal risk. Mr Huang sent an all-staff email which mixed the panicked clichés of the disloyal husband (“cannot undo what I have done”) with those of the disgraced leader (“privilege of my life”). In all communications, the word “independent” must be used as frequently and liberally as possible: Nvidia’s “independent directors” tasked “independent counsel” to do an “independent investigation”. Sides are quickly chosen. Mr Trump jumped to Mr Huang’s defence. “He’s got to stay in that seat, at all costs” said one presenter of “All-In”, a bro-ish tech podcast, going all-in to defend Mr Huang and protect the stock market.

Bad news often begets more bad news. Reports then emerged that Mr Huang may also have slept with a subordinate and on November 12th Nvidia announced that Mr Huang had resigned from the firm. He went quicker than most. Volkswagen’s boss resigned within a week after its emissions-rigging scandal in 2015. The boss of Wells Fargo lasted a month after the bank was fined for opening thousands of fake accounts in 2016. Boeing’s boss stuck around for a year after a 737 MAX crashed in 2018.

The worst crises linger. Boeing’s next boss was felled by the same issue. The very worst become lengthy trials. In the early 2000s Roland Dumas, a French government minister, was tried (and eventually acquitted) over his girlfriend’s lobbying for a state-owned oil firm. Some end up immortalised in salacious books. The same girlfriend recounted the affair in a tell-all entitled “The Whore of the Republic”.

Mr Huang’s Chinese affair could go down as the most expensive shag in history. Nvidia is worth perhaps $500bn less than it was at the end of last week, which ranks this among the most costly corporate crises of all time. (The sum is greater still when you consider that the rest of the market is up.) The ultimate financial cost depends on two hard questions. How much was the influence wielded by Mr Huang in the White House actually worth? And can Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who Nvidia’s board said will run the company until a permanent successor is found, maintain the carefully balanced financial deals that Mr Huang assembled? Both matter not only for the chipmaker’s shareholders, but all of Silicon Valley. Mr Huang was the industry’s most vocal lobbyist and its keenest financial backer.

The worst scandals are obvious in hindsight. Researchers drew attention to Volkswagen’s dodgy emissions figures a year before it was sued by the American government over “dieselgate”. A report by a short-seller on Mr Huang’s dealings with his mistress, Alice Huang, was published in May. That she might be a Chinese agent would have been obvious to Mr Huang had he inquired about her background: before going into business, Ms Huang worked at a Chinese state-run broadcaster known by its unimprovable acronym, “CCTV”. Mr Huang’s lack of inquisitiveness is bested only by that of Neil Bush, son of one American president and brother of another. When travelling in Asia during the 1990s, women would show up uninvited to his hotel room and have sex with him. “It was very unusual,” Mr Bush said later during his divorce proceedings.

A great scandal is like a sponge, soaking up everything around it. The Huang affair is likely to become the focus of corruption inquiries by Democrats in Washington. How might it have been prevented? Investment restrictions have been adopted in recent years to prevent the Chinese from acquiring secrets by buying companies. But there are no good rules to stop them sleeping with executives. Never has the stock market depended on so few people so unaccustomed to being playboys.

The best precedent for the Huang affair has nothing to do with Silicon Valley, and it exploded all the way back in 1963, the year Mr Huang was born. John Profumo, an up-for-it British government minister with a national-security brief, had an affair with a young showgirl who was also said to be involved with Yevgeny Ivanov, a Soviet naval attaché. It mattered little that an official (indeed an “independent”) inquiry determined that no state secrets had been compromised by their relationship. Harold Macmillan, the prime minister, resigned soon after. Profumo withdrew from public life and spent the remainder of his days helping the poor of London’s East End. How will Mr Huang spend his?

articles.title: For boomers, economic boom times are over
articles.deck: Across the rich world, the geriatric share of income and wealth is ebbing

paragraphs.text: The riots in France gave another airing to a familiar grievance: that baby-boomers have cornered the market. After cushy careers, the gripe goes, people born between the mid-1940s and mid-1960s own all the best houses and most of the stock market, while receiving generous pensions to boot. Politicians, knowing that these oldies vote in large numbers, fall over themselves to hand them goodies. Younger adults are stuck with expensive housing, insecure work and a crumbling education system. In June Samuel Moyn of Yale University published a tome on the scourge, titled “Gerontocracy in America”.

Mr Moyn’s book and the sentiment it reflects may, however, be out of date. A range of data analysed by The Economist suggests that the world has passed peak boomer. Elderly incomes are falling relative to those of working-age people, the young are accumulating more wealth and governments are introducing more policies that benefit the stripling. The unwinding of boomer communism, as the phenomenon is less charitably described, is a ray of hope for indebted governments, which cannot afford to continue to lavish perks on an ageing population. It also suggests that Western political systems are less ossified than commonly assumed.

Boomer communism was the result of the postwar settlement. The welfare system of the 1950s and 1960s treated working men well but did far less for everyone else. Many older people, women in particular, made do with meagre occupational pensions and quickly outlived their savings. Old age was a synonym for destitution. In America in the mid-1960s close to 30% of people over the age of 65 had incomes below a threshold required to meet basic needs, compared with just 10% of working-age folk. In Canada in 1976 (the earliest available data) 47% of elderly households were poor (under a looser definition), versus 15% of 18- to 64-year-olds. Even when pensioners were not poor, they were rarely rich. In Britain in 1961 the income, after benefits, taxes and housing costs, of the median pensioner was 30% lower than that of the median person of working age.

By the 1980s poverty among the elderly became politically unsustainable. British newspapers were full of stories of pensioners “freezing to death”, for which they blamed stingy pensions. Scandals in nursing homes gripped America and France. Politicians who could safely ignore old people when there were few of them started paying attention as their ranks swelled. Strong economic growth at the time gave governments plenty of fiscal space for handouts to the old. They made pensions more generous and indexed them to wages or prices, expanded health care and added targeted help (for housing, heating, public transport and other amenities).

Britain, which has the best historical data, shows how things changed. In the 1990s and 2000s the incomes of pensioners soared. By the mid-2010s the retired had nearly as much coming in as working-age Britons (see chart 1). The trends were similar elsewhere. We estimate that the income of the median elderly household in America, after taxes and benefits, rose from 57% of that in other households in 1979 to 90% in 2012. From 2003 to 2019 the median disposable household incomes of elderly Italians, relative to those of working age, rose from 79% to 92%. By 2015 Greek pensioners had come close to out-earning younger compatriots. In many rich countries, the earnings of working people stagnated or fell, especially after the global financial crisis of 2007-09.

Governments’ big mistake was to help oldies who did not really need it. Plenty of boomers were already reaping the windfall of long bull markets in property and equities. This wealth was supplemented by income from generous defined-benefit pension schemes, which mostly tied payouts to final salaries. In addition, almost every country offers goodies to its elders that by any rational accounting it should not.

Most oldies get discounted or free admission to museums and art galleries. All Londoners aged 60 or over, from the poorest to the poshest, can ride many buses and the Tube free of charge. Spain subsidises pensioners’ holidays. Donald Trump’s big tax bill of 2025 gave taxpayers over 65 an additional $6,000 annual deduction.

Despite the aches and pains, in other words, being old can be pleasant. But maybe not for much longer. We found data on working-age and pensioner incomes for 32 rich countries. In 26 of them the elderly are declining relative to the young. Working-age Greeks now earn nearly 20% more than pensioners receive. Had British oldies’ progress of the early 1990s to the mid-2010s continued, their incomes would be 10% above the working-age median. In fact they are 10% below it. The median incomes of America’s elderly have not gained on the non-elderly for over a decade. Child poverty has fallen sharply in recent years, and now is only a bit higher than elderly poverty (see chart 2). Even in Brazil, where the median older household once got 20% more than working households, things are coming back into balance.

Younger people are not just earning more. Many have also found better-quality work. Economists have long argued that European job markets are subject to “insider-outsider” dynamics, in which old people sit in well-paid and protected roles while younger ones suffer on insecure, temporary contracts.

One way to quantify insider-outsider dynamics is to compare how common temporary work is among different cohorts. In much of the 2000s and 2010s younger workers in OECD economies were becoming relatively likelier to fill temporary roles, suggesting that insider-outsider dynamics were intensifying in the club of mostly rich countries (see chart 3). More recently, though, the gap has narrowed.

Americans over 70, who make up 13% of the population, do hold a huge share of their country’s overall private wealth—about a third, according to the Federal Reserve. But since the late 2010s their share of wealth has grown more slowly than their share of the population. Young people, many of whom have bought into the stock market, are doing surprisingly well. American millennials (born between the early 1980s and the mid-1990s) may mope about their lot but they are richer than any earlier generation at their age. Early signs provide some indication that Gen-Zers are accumulating wealth even faster (see chart 4).

The elderly’s dominance of the housing market is also not what it used to be. In the decade to 2019 the median age of American homeowners rose from 54 to 58. But since then it has not budged—even as the population has aged. In England, which has less precise data, the share of homeowners aged 65 and over has been flat at about 36% since 2017-18. This implies that younger people are finding it easier to get on the “housing ladder”.

Economic gerontocracy has peaked for a few reasons. One relates to the economy. Excluding the short downturn of 2020, amid the covid-19 pandemic, the rich world has not experienced a synchronised recession for two decades. Strong demand for labour has boosted workers’ wages, which in turn has made it easier for them to accumulate wealth. Post-covid inflation, meanwhile, probably hit old people harder than youngsters. Wages have kept up reasonably well with rising prices, whereas many defined-benefit pensions pay a fixed nominal amount. Inflation has also eaten up the savings on which many oldies live. A paper published by the European Commission found that the recent “cost-of-living crisis” hit pension-age households nearly three times as hard as those of working age.

These relative gains in favour of the young would have occurred even if politicians kept their pro-oldie bias. In fact, policy is also turning less boomer-friendly. Over the past decade many European governments have liberalised labour markets. This benefits younger workers (since firms are more willing to take a chance on a fresh hire if they can sack people more readily) at the expense of the old (who are now easier to get rid of). Quantitative indicators produced by the OECD suggest that in recent years employment-protection rules in Greece and Italy have become less strict. France has made firings more predictable for employers, including by capping compensation for unfair dismissal.

The clearest shift away from gerontocracy may be in public spending. Wonks at the University of Pennsylvania allocate federal spending in America to different age groups. Using their methodology, we estimate that until the 2010s Americans over 65 received ten times as much federal money per person as other age groups did. Outlays on Social Security and Medicare, the health-care programme for the elderly, vastly outweighed spending on child benefits (lots of education spending is within the purview of states and cities rather than the federal government).

Pots of money continue to flow to the elderly. But because so many people are ageing so fast, individual oldsters are losing out. By 2024 the American old were getting six times as much government largesse as younger cohorts rather than ten times. In the majority of the other 29 rich countries we examine, we find similar trends. In Italy old-age spending has gone from almost 15 times as much as spending on families and children before the pandemic to less than ten times as much.

Some of the narrowing of the largesse gap has to do with how much governments are splurging on the old. Many have put a lid on health-care spending, which disproportionately flows to the elderly. After soaring during the 2000s, American health spending has been roughly flat as a share of the economy. Many other countries in the OECD have also bent the health-care curve, thanks to expanded use of cheap generics, stingier payments to health-care providers and other cost control.

Public pensions are changing, too. Reforms in the 1990s had, bizarrely given ageing populations, reduced the average age at which people in the OECD retired, from about 65 to 61 (see chart 5). Pension systems thus had to support old folk for longer. Now governments are encouraging people to stay in work. In the past decade the average age at which an Italian man retires has increased by four years. Even in France, which has one of the world’s most generous pension systems, the age at which people hang up their boots is rising.

A new database of pension reforms, maintained by the IMF, suggests that after years of giveaways, policies are becoming somewhat more hardnosed. Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, recently said that his government would reform the “triple lock” on the state pension that raises it by inflation, earnings growth or 2.5%, whichever is highest. In 2025 China, where most men retired at 60 and women in blue-collar jobs could do so as young as 50, began implementing its first increase in the retirement age in over 70 years (to 63 for men and 55-58 for women by 2040).

Even as they have tried to contain spending on the old, governments have become less stingy with the young. Many have increased handouts to families, often in an attempt to boost fertility rates. Since 2024 Germany, Ireland, Japan, Poland and South Korea have introduced or expanded child allowances. Parental leave has grown more generous, too. Uncle Sam is chipping in $1,000 to seed investment accounts for children born in 2025-28. Whether or not such policies meaningfully boost birth rates (and economists are sceptical), they certainly increase the incomes of young parents and their existing offspring.

Perhaps some regression towards youth was inevitable after decades when everything seemed to go oldies’ way. Daniel Stockemer and Kamila Kolodziejczyk of the University of Ottawa and Aksel Sundström of the University of Gothenburg manage a data set which tracks the ages of political cabinets across the world. Our analysis of their data suggests that in the 2000s and 2010s, old people were increasingly overrepresented. More recently, however, this trend appears to be turning.

In America’s House of Representatives the average age at the start of the current Congress in 2025 was 57.9 years, down from 58.4 in early 2021. It may be younger still next January, given the results of the midterm elections on November 3rd. The Senate will certainly get less geriatric: newly minted senators are nearly 15 years younger than the incumbents they replace. In Britain the average age of MPs elected in 2024 was 49, down from 51 five years earlier. In recent years the share of French ministers who are 40 or under has jumped from about one in ten to one in four. President Emmanuel Macron is 48, and first took office at the age of 39.

Policy almost everywhere remains biased towards pensioners. The old hold a formidable stock of property and financial assets, and the coming pressure on health and long-term care will be severe. But for the first time in decades, governments are beginning to recognise that they do not exist to serve the needs of a single constituency. Slow growth and high public debt make it impossible to increase pensions indefinitely. Low fertility makes the cost of excluding parents from work more obvious. And to the extent that politicians look out for their own kind, these shifts may continue. The golden age of the golden oldie may be nearing its end.

articles.title: Italy’s proposed exit tax causes ructions
articles.deck: Taxing rich emigrants’ capital gains may be good in theory. Practice is harder

paragraphs.text: Only a few days after Giorgia Meloni, Italy’s prime minister, said her draft budget bill for next year would contain an “exit tax” on wealthy emigrants’ capital gains, she was back-pedalling. On November 5th her deputy economy minister, Maurizio Leo, said the government was “open to changes”. From tax lawyers to politicians, critics have been vocal. They include Matteo Renzi, who as prime minister proposed a flat tax of €100,000 ($111,000) on rich immigrants’ income from abroad. Introduced in 2017, it has been credited with making Italy attractive to foreign professionals. A populist measure, he says, will waste a decade of work.

In principle an exit tax has something to be said for it. It removes the incentive to move abroad to dodge capital-gains tax on, say, shares or bonds that have risen in value. Several countries have adopted such taxes (see map). Under Italy’s draft law, which is subject to a vote next month, residents with more than €800,000 of financial holdings worldwide who leave the country will pay a 26% capital-gains tax, regardless of whether they sell their stash. It covers gross financial assets (ie, before liabilities or debts), including derivatives and crypto assets as well as equities and bonds—a broader base than in other countries. Anyone resident for six out of the ten tax years before leaving Italy will be liable.

But the tax has its flaws. Gains are to be calculated from the purchase price of assets, even if they were bought before someone arrived in Italy. Emigrants might also grumble about getting a bill for unrealised gains, although if they move to another European Union country and hold on to their nest-eggs they will be reimbursed after five years. Tracking those liable and calculating what is due may also be fiddly. And the Italian government will reap little: it expects merely €3.4m next year, €6.7m in each of the following four and €3.4m a year from then on.

Government insiders say that besides courting voters before next year’s parliamentary election, Ms Meloni has acted in the belief that Britain would introduce an exit tax, leaving Italy as the only G7 country without one. That fear seems misplaced. Last year Rachel Reeves, then Britain’s chancellor, pondered a 20% charge on unrealised capital gains on emigrants’ business assets. But she ditched the idea after warnings that it would prompt rich folk to move to places with no such levy—such as Italy.

In 2022 Germany switched to a system that, like Ms Meloni’s proposal, taxes gains on the paper value of emigrants’ assets. Hitherto tax had been due only if assets were sold within ten years. Ulrich Stoll, who heads the Stiftung Familienunternehmen, a lobby group for family companies, argues that the new set-up inhibits entrepreneurs’ mobility. Mr Stoll, who also owns one-sixth of Festo, a 101-year-old engineering firm, says that under the new regime it would have been prohibitively costly to work in America for six years, a spell that proved useful for his career.

A well-designed tax might allay such concerns. Christian Kempges, a lawyer at Baker Tilly, a consulting firm, says he can think of no country that has got exit taxes right. He suggests they should kick in only if an asset is sold, but with no time limit—and that the OECD should devise a rule to apply to all its members. Ms Meloni may be pushed into changing her plan. But her worry is losing votes, not losing the rich.

articles.title: Where to find the anti-AI trade
articles.deck: The worse chipmakers do, the better Indian equities perform

paragraphs.text: MOST OF THE world’s traders were still enjoying a weekend break on Sunday November 8th after a rough few days in the markets—except those in Mumbai, India’s financial capital. Its two big bourses opened for a 70-minute special session to mark Diwali, the festival of lights, and to welcome Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth. Trades made during this so-called Muhurat session are meant to be particularly auspicious. Investors are supposed to make long-term purchases: buying gold and silver is common as are conviction bets for the sake of the grandchildren.

Investors in India had plenty of reason to be optimistic. The Nifty 50, a benchmark, has risen by more than a tenth over the past month, becoming the best-performing stock-market index in Asia. In the week running up to Diwali, it stood out in a sea of red as investors elsewhere feared that an AI bubble had finally burst. The index rose by 2.4% on November 5th as the NASDAQ fell by 5.5%. The rally even extended to the rupee, which on November 6th reached its highest level since April.

Indian equities have largely sat out the AI boom. Investors saw the country as a victim of disruption rather than a disruptor itself. In February 2026 the market plunged after the launch of Claude Code, an AI tool. A viral note from Citrini Research, a firm of analysts, added to the gloom, concocting a scenario in which India seeks an IMF bail-out in 2028 as its coding industry falters. India earns about 10% of its GDP from services exports. (Predictions of doom are still far from being borne out: employment in IT has grown and total Indian services exports are up by 8.7% so far this fiscal year.)

Now that investors are re-evaluating AI’s prospects, India has gained. Since May India’s tech stocks have traded in the opposite direction to AI hardware stocks (see chart). As investors have become concerned about overexposure to AI hardware (memory chips and the like), they have rotated to AI wetware, the coders who use the tools. The Nifty IT index, which includes consultancies such as Infosys and Wipro, has risen by 28% since July, having previously fallen by 36%. The seesawing is mostly about sentiment, points out Anmol Garg, of DAM Capital, an investment bank. Excessive pessimism about Indian IT companies was the counterpart of excessive optimism about chipmakers. Both excesses are now subsiding.

Foreign investors have rushed back to India after a long absence. On November 5th Indian equities received $1.6bn of foreign inflows in a single day, the most since February 2021. It was also a reversal of the year-long trend: $30bn has left India in the first ten months of 2026. It is not only AI that is tempting investors back. Valuations look more attractive, says Shibani Kurian of Kotak Mutual Fund: earnings have been growing at a “robust clip”. By the end of October the Nifty 50 was trading at close to its cheapest ratio of price to earnings for a decade.

There are other auspicious developments. Indian assets have benefited from lower oil prices. The country imports about 90% of its oil, historically from the Gulf. As investors bet that a humbled Donald Trump would seek a deal with Iran to stabilise the oil market, the rupee rallied and the yield on government bonds fell. There has also been encouraging chatter that the government may remove long-term capital-gains taxes from foreigners.

Sadly the 70 minutes of Sunday trading ended in anti-climax: the market finished slightly down, for the first time in nine years. AI stocks rallied the next day and Indian stocks largely missed out on the exuberance. Those holding on to shares for their grandchildren should not mind too much. There is plenty of time for Lakshmi to do her thing.

articles.title: The future of Trumponomics: compromise or failure
articles.deck: How the art of the deal may yet prevail over the art of denial

paragraphs.text: DONALD TRUMP has a knack for fitting his politics into four letters. His supporters relish wearing red baseball caps emblazoned with MAGA. After his party got thumped in the midterm elections, he posted a picture on social media of the familiar cap bearing a new slogan: VETO.

A sign of things to come? Perhaps. With Democrats set to control both chambers of Congress starting in January, gridlock may seem inevitable. Yet Mr Trump would not be himself if he did not also expect to make deals. “After a couple of months of vetoes, they’ll call,” he predicted of Democrats. “And we’ll work together.”

Such bipartisan bargaining would certainly be a departure from the first two years of the president’s second term. With Republicans controlling the House of Representatives and the Senate, Mr Trump passed a sweeping tax-and-spending law that disproportionately benefited the rich and swelled projected deficits. Much else, from his massive tariffs to mass deportations, was enacted through presidential powers that he continues to hold. What, then, will Trumponomics look like in its remaining years?

On fiscal policy, two looming deadlines may provide opportunities for negotiation. The first concerns government funding. It expires on December 11th, a month before members of Congress are sworn in, but a temporary extension could leave the next budget deal to the new Democrat-controlled legislature. The second deadline, to raise the debt ceiling, could provide even greater leverage for Democrats later next year, when failure to reach an agreement would risk a default. Mr Trump struck deals with Democrats on both issues in his first term, at times siding with them against Republican congressional leaders.

Any fiscal bargain could prove expensive. Mr Trump wants much more money for the armed forces. His budget for 2027 proposed a rise of roughly 40% in defence spending, although the full request is highly unlikely to be met. Democrats, meanwhile, want to restore tax breaks for health care that expired at the end of 2025 and otherwise ease financial burdens on households. Hakeem Jeffries, their leader in the House, has prioritised expanding the child tax credit and earned-income tax credit, a top-up for low earners.

In the old guns-versus-butter debate, America’s usual answer is to “spend more on both”, observes Rohit Kumar, who served Mitch McConnell, a Republican former Senate majority leader, as deputy chief of staff and is now at PwC, a consultancy. For every additional dollar the Pentagon receives, he reckons, Democrats could demand a matching increase for domestic programmes.

All of this would add to the deficit. Allianz Research, an arm of an insurance company, expects a fiscal loosening of about 0.2% of GDP in 2027. Additional demands could include delays to planned cuts in Medicaid (health care for the poor) and food stamps. How much red ink this adds will depend partly on offsetting budget tweaks elsewhere. Democrats could try to restrict tax breaks for data-centre investment or impose a new levy on the AI industry, suggests Mr Kumar.

Compromise may also shape Mr Trump’s ambitions for America’s artificial-intelligence boom. In the past two years Mr Trump has championed data centres, taking a “let it rip” approach to regulation. But Democrats prevailed in races for the governorship in Georgia, Ohio, Texas and elsewhere promising pauses or other limits on new construction. Incoming governors who back such measures won in states that account for 41% of planned data-centre capacity, according to Cleanview, a research firm. It would be wrong, though, to conclude that these governors want permanent bans on data centres. Most merely want their operators to pay more for electricity, notes Gabe Horwitz of Third Way, a centre-left think-tank.

That could open the door to another bargain for Mr Trump, in a perennially promising area of reform: permitting. A bipartisan bill backed by the president would speed up construction of power plants and transmission lines, while requiring large data centres to shoulder more of the costs they impose on the grid. Its chances of passing before January have dimmed, with some Democrats now hoping to extract further concessions after their electoral victories. But it is still possible to imagine a deal that makes it easier to build while shielding households from higher electricity prices.

Even where Mr Trump can act without Congress, he may face new constraints. After a big setback at the Supreme Court, what remains of his chaotic tariff campaign faces more legal challenges. Democrats are preparing congressional investigations and legislation to curb his trade powers further. These efforts may achieve little without enough Republican support to override a presidential veto. Yet a bigger constraint could be public opinion: nearly two-thirds of midterm voters said his tariffs had hurt the economy. That might encourage Mr Trump to ease some duties, says Ryan Majerus, a former American trade official now at King & Spalding, a law firm. He could find an off-ramp in a pending court ruling on “Section 301” tariffs, which are supposed to punish countries for unfair trade.

Mr Trump’s room for manoeuvre may narrow in other ways, too. In the past he has repeatedly pressed the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates. Now a Democratic Senate could block his attempts to install another loyalist on its board, strengthening the central bank’s independence. Public pressure may also encourage Mr Trump to soften his immigration crackdown. In a post-election interview with CBS, a television network, the president acknowledged that his deportation policy “might be too tough” and said that he would “love to do something on immigration” with Democrats, particularly for long-term undocumented workers.

Mr Trump’s willingness to compromise is, of course, far from certain. Only hours after his CBS interview he appointed Stephen Miller, an architect of the “tough” deportation campaign, as White House chief of staff. The appointment of a hardliner may have been meant to put paid to the popular notion that “Trump always chickens out” in the end.

Still, with Democrats controlling Congress, bargaining may offer the best route to advancing Mr Trump’s remaining economic agenda. When it comes to confrontation with triumphant Democrats, TACO may prevail over VETO.

articles.title: Lessons from a miserable month for hedge funds
articles.deck: The struggle to invest in anything other than AI

paragraphs.text: NOVEMBER, WITH its post-election market swings and the Jensen Huang affair, has so far been bruising for hedge funds. But October was brutal: many funds had their worst month since the covid-19 pandemic began, according to JPMorgan Chase, America’s biggest bank. A wobble in markets’ enthusiasm for artificial intelligence forced a sell-off of technology stocks. The surprise re-election of Brazil’s left-wing president, worries over France’s sovereign debt and tumult in credit markets added to the pain. A Bloomberg index of the industry’s returns fell by 1.7% in the month. The biggest fund at Millennium, a giant manager, lost 2.3%. The main fund of Arini Capital Management, a fast-growing credit shop, was down by 19.7%.

By the time tech stocks plunged again on November 5th, managers were already so light they had little left to sell. According to data compiled by UBS, another big bank, there were six days in the previous month on which funds had unloaded more. Hedge funds sometimes get the blame for market falls. This time they were innocent, though they have been given food for thought. The industry has been coasting on the AI boom: the Bloomberg returns index still ended October 4.1% higher then it began the year. But October exposed the dangers of being caught on the way down.

One category, multi-strategy funds, has more to ponder than most. Whereas a typical hedge fund implements the vision of a single portfolio manager or a few working together, multi-strategy funds recruit several, all of whom are free to pursue their own trades. The central fund constrains them only by controlling capital allocation among its various “pods” of traders and imposing a strict risk policy to limit losses. In theory the managers’ independence makes their trades unrelated, raising the whole fund’s risk-adjusted performance compared with that of one manager. In booming markets returns are also less volatile than in single-manager funds.

Multi-strategy funds were pioneered by such luminaries as Ken Griffin of Citadel and Izzy Englander of Millennium. Others have enjoyed remarkable success, too. PivotalPath, a research firm, estimates that just ten large ones control gross assets worth $2.2trn. . But in recent years their rise has levelled off—and in recent weeks the tight risk policies have begun to pinch. Many force managers to start unwinding positions when losses exceed only 5%. Lose more than 7.5%, and a pod may be shut down. With leverage, even small movements are enough to derail trades.

October’s movements were more than enough to force liquidations. By November 9th, when investors had cooled on the financial instruments enabling the buildout of data centres by giant technology companies from Nvidia to Meta, 32% of hedge funds’ books were exposed to AI, down from 47% in June.

Managers became timid. Funds, which borrow from markets as well as using their investors’ cash, reduced their net leverage by eight percentage points in the week to November 6th, reports Morgan Stanley, another bank. This may reflect more than caution: it has been a bumper year for attracting new investment, the best since 2007. But mindful of scaring investors away, fund managers are also eager to limit damage to their returns with too much deleveraging.

The episode raises questions for the multi-strategy model. Its supposed advantage is the managers’ independence. With several supposedly making insightful independent decisions, the fund should be protected should some calls not pay off. Gains from a trade on steel, say, could cushion losses from a bet on neocloud firms. But it is increasingly difficult to avoid AI. In July a plunge in chipmakers’ share prices forced funds to sell stocks and bonds whose value depended on the technology’s success. Burned, many managers promised not to load up again. Just a few months later, they must have déjà vu.

There are two reasons for this. The first is the sheer amount of the financial system now within the reach of multi-managers. Finding a broad enough range of instruments with which to deploy $2trn-worth of firepower is hard even in normal times. The second is that now almost no corner of the world economy is untouched by AI. A portfolio manager buying copper futures is of little use to balance the risks taken by a colleague backing neoclouds if the price of copper depends on AI’s future development. The growing pervasiveness of one technology may ensure the multi-strategy hedge fund’s best days are behind it.

Correction: In an earlier version of this article we said that the ten largest multi-strategy funds controlled assets worth $2.2trn. The figure refers to ten large funds, not necessarily the biggest. Sorry

articles.title: The return of the snatch-and-grab state
articles.deck: A new history of confiscation sheds light on modern economic warfare

paragraphs.text: AS A QUAKER, A. Mitchell Palmer did not relish conflict. In 1913 the American congressman turned down an offer to serve as secretary of war. But conflict in Europe challenged his pacifism. Six months after America joined the fight against Germany and Austria-Hungary in 1917, Palmer was appointed Alien Property Custodian. The job put him at the forefront of the economic battle against the two aggressors. Tasked with seizing enemy-owned assets across the American economy, his office hoovered up factories, stocks, buildings, patents and more. Soon it began auctioning these to raise money for the war effort. By 1918 Palmer was helping to finance the fighting with the enemies’ own wealth. Germany began the war as the world’s third-biggest foreign investor, after Britain and France. By the time the guns fell silent, more than half of its foreign assets had been confiscated.

The story of Germany’s expropriation is an important episode in “The Age of Confiscation”, an insightful new book by Nicholas Mulder of Cornell University. Armies have often financed themselves by looting their enemies. But because so many German-owned assets were located in Allied jurisdictions, many of them could be taken with little more than a pen stroke. As Mr Mulder writes, Germany was the first country in the 20th century to have its assets expropriated on every continent.

Today the West’s enemy is Russia. After its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Western governments moved quickly. By 2023 they had blocked some $60bn in Russian oligarchs’ assets, from villas in Saint-Tropez to yachts in the Caribbean, and frozen some $300bn-worth of Russian central-bank reserves held in the West (mostly at Euroclear, a Belgian depository).

Yet Western leaders have remained divided over what to do with these assets. Some of the bling and boats were auctioned and in 2024 Ukraine’s allies agreed to use the interest earnings on Russia’s reserves to extend a $50bn loan to Ukraine. But Belgium complained that confiscation of the Euroclear reserves could leave it liable for damages equal to a third of its GDP. Others worried about the risk to Europe’s reputation as a bastion of strong property rights, which could make the continent less attractive as an investment destination. Christine Lagarde, the head of the European Central Bank, warned that seizing Russia’s assets would “start breaking the international legal order”.

As Mr Mulder explains, such debates have a long history. For centuries governments’ confiscatory capabilities developed hand-in-hand with property rights. Once states grew strong enough to protect claims to property, they also took powers to abrogate them. When Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch jurist, argued that all societies were formed to protect property rights, he was careful to create an exception. Sovereign rulers, he wrote, maintain the right of “eminent domain”, allowing them to seize private property for the public good. The idea caught on. Grotius’s theory was adopted by the Founding Fathers in America and by Napoleon in post-revolutionary France.

Because property rights tend to support economic growth, observers have often understated the role of confiscation in the history of rich, prosperous states. In 1989 Douglass North and Barry Weingast, two economic historians, argued that Britain’s Glorious Revolution of 1688 brought on “the elimination of confiscatory government”. That was an oversimplification. The power of confiscation moved from the monarchy to Parliament, but the state wielded it to redistribute land, raise money for wars and the like. Some 83% of constitutions adopted between 1850 and 2008 enshrine the right to expropriate property for the public good.

Things get especially messy in times of war. In America Palmer seized not just factories and businesses from rich Germans in New York, but also the possessions of poor immigrants. Thousands of American women who had married German and Austro-Hungarian men also lost their property. Britain pursued a similar campaign against enemy-owned businesses across the empire. But it also forced British investors to sell the British state American securities, which it needed as collateral for loans from America. It bought them supposedly at market prices but paid the investors in sovereign bonds rather than cash.

Confiscation is also contagious. Europe’s embrace of it during both world wars was carefully studied by the leaders of the continent’s former colonies. During the 1950s a wave of nationalisations spread across the Middle East and Asia. In 1956 Gamal Abdel Nasser, Egypt’s president, snatched the Suez Canal from the British and French. Law 285, which initiated that seminal expropriation, was modelled on the Trading with the Enemy Acts that Britain and America had used during the first world war.

The contagion is spreading again. The Kremlin responded to the seizure of Russian assets by taking over Western firms’ concerns in Russia and distributing them among Vladimir Putin’s cronies. Four years into the war the country has more billionaires than it did in 2022 (even if it is harder for them to flaunt their wealth in Mayfair or on Avenue Montaigne). Autocracies, including post-colonial ones, are also catching the bug: in recent years juntas in the Sahel have seized Western-owned gold and uranium mines. America is not immune, either. This year Donald Trump, who called eminent domain “an absolute necessity” during his first presidential run in 2016, has ordered the capture of Venezuelan oil tankers and threatened to seize the Panama Canal and Greenland.

The brief spell of globalisation and peace around the turn of the millennium, when foreign assets ballooned and seizures all but stopped, was a historical anomaly, Mr Mulder thinks. It also left the world replete with property there for the taking.

articles.title: Scientists are at last starting to understand endometriosis
articles.deck: That should lead to quicker diagnosis and better treatment

paragraphs.text: The endometrium is a layer of tissue in the uterus which typically thickens during the menstrual cycle. If a fertilised egg doesn’t implant, this lining typically thins and sheds. But in women with endometriosis, tissue similar to the endometrium starts growing outside the uterus. The condition can warp and bind together pelvic organs, including the ureter, bladder and bowel, and even spread into the abdominal wall. Over time it leads to nausea, vomiting and intolerable pain. It is estimated that 190m women have the disease.

Modern medicine cannot cure endometriosis, and treatments are inadequate. Its causes are still largely unknown. Obtaining a diagnosis can take almost nine years, requiring such invasive surgical procedures as laparoscopies (in which small cameras are inserted through a slit in the abdomen) and biopsies (in which tissue samples are removed for testing). Even then, results do not always correlate with the symptoms, making it hard to assess the severity of the condition.

Fortunately, there have been a number of promising scientific developments in recent years. “There’s been a surge in awareness of the condition,” says Krina Zondervan of Oxford University. More patient data have helped, too. Australia, Denmark, France and Spain have launched action plans to improve clinical care or boosted funding for the condition. After decades in the dark, researchers are rapidly moving towards a clearer understanding of the forms endometriosis takes, less invasive ways of diagnosing the condition and a variety of possible treatments.

Dr Zondervan’s work helped trigger this transformation. In 2023 she and her colleagues published the results of what was then the largest-ever study of endometriosis. It compared the genetic data of 60,000 women who had the condition with those of more than 700,000 without it. Among the genetic markers common in patients were a number linked to other painful and inflammatory conditions. This suggests potential avenues for treatment.

The following year Dr Zondervan and her team published a detailed map of the types of cells in the uterine lining, including those embedded deep in tissue layers. This allowed them to describe how cells communicate throughout the menstrual cycle, and to pinpoint the cell types most likely to be affected by the genetic markers associated with endometriosis.

More progress was made in April when a team led by Dora Koller, a researcher at the Sant Pau Research Institute in Spain, published the results of an even larger genetic study. It covered 1.4m women, including more than 105,000 with endometriosis. Their results linked specific genes to immune-system responses and hormonal processes characteristic of endometriosis, as well as identifying a genetic connection with chronic fatigue, a symptom that doctors frequently dismiss. Such work will help scientists identify genetic risk factors for endometriosis.

Dr Koller, who has endometriosis herself, says her team’s results support the idea that the disease affects the whole body, rather than being confined to a woman’s pelvis. She says their study could guide new drug development and give researchers clues about whether existing treatments that work for other painful diseases could be used for endometriosis, too.

Research efforts on quicker and less invasive means of diagnosing the disease have also ramped up. Katherine Burns of the University of Cincinnati, who has also experienced endometriosis, has spent time studying white blood cells in the menstrual fluid of women with the disease. She has found they are distinctive in two ways: the cell nuclei are smaller, and they have more lobes than their healthy equivalents. Dr Burns is now using that information to develop ways to diagnose endometriosis without the need for surgery.

Another diagnostic approach is to rely on molecular biomarkers such as proteins and microRNAs (short molecules that regulate gene expression) that feature in the body’s inflammatory and immune response to endometriosis. In March scientists from various organisations, including HerAnova Lifesciences, a Boston-based firm, reported that detecting several of these biomarkers could be used to diagnose endometriosis. In 61.5% of these cases, vaginal ultrasounds and imaging had missed signs of the disease.

An even less invasive way to diagnose and monitor endometriosis was described in the Lancet Obstetrics and Gynaecology in April. Researchers at Oxford found a new imaging agent (a dye or contrast that is injected into the body to see microscopic biological processes) that was well tolerated by patients with superficial peritoneal endometriosis, the most prevalent early-stage form of the disease. 99mTc-maraciclatide, as the agent is known, attaches to cell receptors that signal inflammatory conditions, causing it to accumulate in areas where there is inflammation. The hot spots can then be seen with imaging tools. Maraciclatide, which is being developed by Serac Healthcare, a pharmaceutical company based in London, hopes to go through phase-3 trials (when compounds are tested at scale in humans) and validation in the near future.

More avenues for treating endometriosis are also opening up. In March, Gesynta Pharma, a Swedish pharma company, announced that it had begun its phase-2 clinical trial of Vipoglanstat. Instead of interacting with hormones, as existing treatments do, the drug blocks an enzyme that is needed to make a pain-related chemical in the body. In doing so it reduces pain and inflammation, making life more bearable. A non-hormonal treatment developed by EndoCyclic Therapeutics, a biopharmaceuticals firm, was cleared by America’s drug regulator for phase-1 human trials in March. Called ENDO-205, it aims to go one better: clearing lesions and reducing the rate at which they recur.

More funding may well lead to more progress. Much of the work so far has been done “on a shoestring”, says Dr Zondervan. America’s National Institutes of Health allocates less than 0.1% of its budget to endometriosis—far less than that for much rarer conditions (Crohn’s disease, for example, receives about 15 times more money per patient). A programme launched in 2024 under President Joe Biden to fund women’s health research, including endometriosis, was cut this year.

With more cash researchers could conduct trials on women from across the world, to understand how varied the effects of endometriosis are. They could also generate richer data to help distinguish between the disease’s many forms and investigate the different types of lesions involved. Such advances could, then, drive the development of targeted therapies that might bring relief to millions.

articles.title: The blood-brain barrier may contribute to cognitive function
articles.deck: Studies in mice suggest it is more sophisticated than once thought

paragraphs.text: AS THE COMMAND centre of the human body, the brain requires the best protection biology can supply. The hard, bony casing of the skull helps to shield the organ from threats outside the body. But dangers lie within, too. Blood can contain toxins and pathogens which would wreak havoc in the brain’s delicate environment. Keeping such vandals out is the job of the blood-brain barrier, a tightly packed network of cells coating the interior surfaces of blood vessels leading to the brain.

In a new study, published in Cell on November 11th, a team led by Andrew Yang, a neuroscientist at the Gladstone Institute of Neurological Disease in San Francisco, has shown that the blood-brain barrier is surprisingly sophisticated. By cataloguing the proteins that were allowed through the barrier in mice, the researchers found that it plays a far more active role in brain health than previously thought. The barrier both protects the organ and keeps it supplied with beneficial proteins. The team believe their results may suggest a new approach to treating Alzheimer’s disease.

The blood-brain barrier is more like a bouncer than a brick wall. Its cells keep the harmful stuff out while letting in a select few essential molecules found in blood, such as oxygen and glucose, which fuel neural processes. It also ensures that conditions inside the brain are optimal by expelling any unwanted molecular by-products back into the bloodstream. By controlling what gets in and out, the barrier keeps the brain’s chemical environment stable and its neurons firing properly. But which molecules are on the brain’s guest list, and why, have so far remained unclear.

To answer this question, Dr Yang and his team tagged the proteins in mouse blood with small chemicals that would be invisible to mouse biology. By subsequently extracting brain tissue and identifying any tags within it, the researchers could see which proteins had ended up where.

“What we started seeing is that there was an unexpected breadth and diversity of proteins in the blood that made their way into the brain,” says Dr Yang. Of the 861 tagged proteins, 92 reached the brain’s tissue. Further contrary to their expectations, such physical features as size or electric charge did not affect which proteins made it through. Most had also been produced in organs far from the brain.

The surprises did not stop there. “We thought [the proteins] would cross and then just get dumped into the brain,” says Dr Yang. Instead, his team found that the proteins appeared to target specific cells. One protein, known as apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1), began accumulating in cells called astrocytes which perform a variety of supporting jobs around the brain.

In cells kept alive outside the mice’s bodies, the researchers found that APOA1 helped the astrocytes deliver molecules of cholesterol to the neurons, which use the stuff to build and maintain connections between one another. APOA1, which is produced primarily in the liver, thus appeared to support a crucial neural process.

APOA1 also engaged with a gene whose reduced function has been linked to the risk of Alzheimer’s disease. When the team applied their protein-tagging technique to mice with an early-stage Alzheimer’s-like condition, they found that less APOA1 got through the blood-brain barrier. Conversely, when the researchers engineered the mice’s livers to produce extra APOA1, they saw a corresponding rise in the protein’s levels in the brain. The number of neuronal connections in treated mice increased, and their performance on movement and memory tests improved. “If validated in humans, this work could open an entirely new therapeutic field,” says Egle Solito, an immunobiologist at Queen Mary University of London.

The blood-brain barrier’s connection to Alzheimer’s is not new. It has long been known that a weakened barrier, accompanied by a leak of harmful proteins into the brain, is an early sign of the disease. But Dr Yang’s findings suggest that it is not only the barrier’s erosion that may be harmful but also its failure, while still intact, to supply protective proteins to the brain. He reckons many more surprises await.

articles.title: AI has proved that a theory underpinning fundamental physics is trustworthy
articles.deck: The key insights appear to have come from human physicists

paragraphs.text: ON OCTOBER 26TH OpenAI, an artificial-intelligence lab, announced that one of its unreleased models had taken a significant step towards solving one of the open Millennium Prize problems, some of the biggest challenges in maths. Known as the Yang-Mills existence and mass gap problem, it is closely related to models of the subatomic world routinely used by quantum physicists. Those eager to see the proof have had to wait while a committee of five external physicists assessed its validity. On November 10th they declared themselves satisfied.

The problem concerns a set of equations, known as Yang-Mills theory, which physicists have long used to describe the working of three of the four known fundamental forces: electromagnetism and the strong and weak nuclear forces. The fourth force, gravity, requires a separate description known as general relativity.

Physicists have good reason to trust Yang-Mills theory. They use it to make predictions about particle behaviour which are borne out to a staggering degree of accuracy. Mathematicians, however, being of a more rigorous bent, would like to confirm it stands on firm mathematical footing.

The first part of the Yang-Mills problem aims to do just that. That involves proving the theory breaks no rules and has no exceptions, all without making any simplifying approximations. The committee which OpenAI convened has confirmed that, in their judgment, the model has successfully cleared that hurdle. To do so, the physicists checked that the AI’s formalisation of its solution in Lean, computer code confirming the proof’s internal logic, corresponded to the problem at hand. Although the committee has published the formalisation, which runs to around 1m lines of computer code, the AI’s 1,147-page “natural language” proof—which, the committee members said, “we do not claim to fully understand”—has not yet been shared. No reason for this secrecy has yet been given.

What is known for now is that the proof builds on techniques developed in the 1980s by Tadeusz Balaban, a researcher at Rutgers University. “There were no obvious showstoppers in his programme, but [it] was very complicated,” says Edward Witten, a mathematician and physicist at the Institute for Advanced Study in New Jersey, who helped formulate the official Yang-Mills problem statement. “I actually believe if there had been ten Balabans, this would have been done by the 1990s.”

Dr Witten calls OpenAI’s proof a “very important milestone”, but reckons it is unlikely to change how physicists work. A solution to the second part of the Yang-Mills problem, which involves showing that the theory predicts no massless particles (and on which OpenAI’s latest results shed no light), would be a different story, however. Such a proof may shed light on why subatomic particles called quarks bind together to form the protons and neutrons found in atomic nuclei. Though the AI had Dr Balaban’s work to draw upon when proving Yang-Mills’s solidity, Dr Witten believes no such handholds exist for the mass gap. “At the risk of possibly sounding foolish,” he says, “my guess is that it’s pretty far off.”
