articles.title: How the Democrats will wield their power
articles.deck: The party has control of Congress, at last. Now it must govern

paragraphs.text: In Democrats’ quest to restrain Donald Trump over the past two years, no tool was more frequently deployed than the sternly worded letter. Democrats sent these missives regularly; the president and his associates ignored most of them. Such is the plight of the minority party in Congress, which lacks power to call hearings or issue subpoenas, much less pass laws.

That will change when Democrats grab the gavel on January 3rd, having won a thumping majority in both the House and Senate. They will probably have around 260 seats in the lower chamber. The task now is to live up to the twin promises of the campaign: boosting the fortunes of ordinary Americans and checking the president. Their hope is that substantive victories will pave a path back to the White House in 2028. The risk is that they fall short, or overreach, and create an opening for a Republican recovery.

The main problem is that the Democrats’ win, though triumphant, still leaves them far short of the 290 seats in the House and 67 in the Senate that would have given them a veto-proof majority. They are unlikely to advance major legislation. They may, however, manage to make modest deals with the president that appeal to his populist instincts, such as capping drug prices.

Indeed, the first order of business for Hakeem Jeffries, the presumptive speaker of the House, will be to try to reinstate the funding that Republicans cut for Medicaid, the health programme for the poor, and the subsidies for individual insurance on the Obamacare exchanges. Democrats will also move to end the Iran war and scrap Mr Trump’s tariffs, which they argue (correctly) have driven up costs. One bill, the “End Trump’s Tariff Tax Act”, would repeal levies on Canada and various laws that Mr Trump has used to support his trade war. Most of these initiatives stand little chance of becoming law; the point is to force confrontation with Mr Trump and telegraph their priorities to voters.

Yet Congress does have an important tool at its disposal: the budget. Government funding expires on December 11th. Letting it lapse at that point seems unlikely; Democrats will not want to welcome their new majority with a shutdown. Instead, Congress will probably agree to stopgap funding through February or March, then hash out a proper budget for the rest of the fiscal year—which is when Democrats might extract concessions on health care, tariffs and other priorities, if they are savvy and Mr Trump is pliable.

Achieving other big policy changes will be difficult. Democrats have long grumbled about spending money on a costly, ferocious deportation campaign rather than basic support programmes. However, Republicans have already moved to protect funding for immigration enforcement through the remainder of Mr Trump’s term. The president continues to try elaborate legal methods to sustain his tariffs, none of which require congressional approval.

As for the Iran war, Democrats could try to bar funding to prosecute it, though that would require bringing some Republicans on-side to overcome the Senate filibuster—and even among Democrats, cutting off all funding is controversial. It is more likely that Democrats could make money contingent on more thorough disclosure about the war, from casualties to weapons stockpiles, says Damian Murphy, a former Democratic congressional staffer now at the Centre for American Progress, a think-tank. The Pentagon has largely kept lawmakers in the dark over the past year. Democrats imposed similar reporting requirements during the Iraq war after flipping Congress in 2006.

If progress on economic issues may prove incremental, Democrats could be more aggressive in their efforts to check the president. In the Senate, Democrats can block Mr Trump’s judicial appointments and cabinet nominees. That would matter most if one of the conservatives on the Supreme Court were to leave the bench before the 2028 election—two are in their late 70s. Then Senate Democrats, led by Chuck Schumer, would probably copy the tactic of Republicans who refused to consider Merrick Garland, Barack Obama’s nominee, in 2016. Meanwhile, lower-court confirmations will definitely stop. Republicans will ram through as many as possible in November and December, before the Democrats take over.

Oversight will dominate the agenda. Democrats will move to issue subpoenas to officials and force testimony. Exposing the administration’s perceived self-dealing will be the biggest focus. Mr Trump has supplied them with ample material and voters have taken note. Two-thirds of Americans say Mr Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself; in exit polls, nine in ten said government corruption was a major factor in their vote. Democrats may, for instance, explore how a manufacturing firm whose investors include Donald Trump junior, the president’s eldest son, secured a loan from the Pentagon, and whether Gulf states have sought leverage over Jared Kushner, Mr Trump’s son-in-law and foreign envoy, by investing billions in his private-equity fund. Democratic leaders also talk up plans for hearings on tariffs, Iran, the draconian immigration agenda and much else.

Democrats know full well that the administration will stonewall by asserting the right to keep certain communications confidential. So instead they will seek information from firms and people who have dealt with the White House. Mr Trump will try to shield those communications, too. In August the Office of Legal Counsel issued an advisory opinion outlining an expansive scope for “executive privilege”. Yet firms are not waiting to get right with the incoming majority. “We couldn’t even get an email returned from these guys for two years,” says a Democratic aide in the Senate. “Now they all want to let us know how they’re not MAGA.”

Democrats will seek to show that they are the party of clean government. Cue a raft of reform proposals. A ban on stock-trading by lawmakers may well pass. The rest are meant as messaging. Jamie Raskin, the incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee, wants to require pardon brokers to register under federal law, much like lobbyists representing foreign governments. He also wants to force Mr Trump to disgorge the luxury jet he received from Qatar. Robert Garcia, who will chair the House Oversight Committee, wants to stop bosses of federal contractors from donating to political campaigns or parties. He calls this closing the “Musk loophole”.

The risk for Democrats is that they get bogged down in futile attempts to boot Mr Trump from the White House. They have already impeached him twice. The party’s base and lawmakers in safe seats will demand a third attempt. Democrats in the House have introduced seven such resolutions in his second term. A recent one failed in a procedural vote, but not before gathering support from 70% of the Democratic caucus. People need to “understand the constitutional math”, says Mr Raskin, that is, the two-thirds majority required in the Senate to convict and remove a president. Mr Raskin was the lead House impeachment manager after Mr Trump tried to steal the 2020 election; he says the tool is no “panacea”. If any conduct were to get a president barred from office, that would have been it—and still the Senate let Mr Trump off the hook.

Mr Jeffries’s goal will be to maintain the majority in 2028, which means he will have to protect competitive seats held by moderates; targeting the president will not be a winning message in their districts. Democratic leadership will probably try to satisfy the base by impeaching cabinet officials instead. Pete Hegseth, the secretary of war, will probably be the first target, for waging war without congressional authorisation and ordering extrajudicial killings of alleged drug traffickers, among other things. Robert F. Kennedy junior, the health secretary, may be next, having presided over the worst measles outbreak in 35 years.

Election landslides often engender hubris, and Democrats are not immune. After a historic victory, the same voters who elected Democrats so resoundingly may soon accuse them either of timidity or overreach. Messrs Schumer and Jeffries have their work cut out.

Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief, our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance, a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters.

articles.title: The Democrats have won the biggest congressional landslide in 50 years
articles.deck: Black, Hispanic and young voters helped power the party’s victory

paragraphs.text: GEORGE W. BUSH described his party’s midterm loss in 2006 as a “thumping”; Barack Obama called his setback four years later a “shellacking”. There may not be a sufficient superlative in the English language for the magnitude of the midterm defeat that Republicans suffered on November 3rd, but Donald Trump might call it “yuge”.

When The Economist went to press on November 5th, Democrats were expected to win the national popular vote for the House of Representatives by 13 percentage points, the largest congressional margin of victory for either party since 1976, in the wake of the Watergate scandal. They are on track to win around 260 of the 435 seats in the lower chamber, more than they obtained amid the financial crisis of 2008. The party has secured at least a 54-46 majority in the Senate, including victories in five states that Mr Trump won by double digits in 2024. Betting markets are nearly certain that it will win the two remaining uncalled races in Alaska and, shockingly, Mississippi, which backed Mr Trump by 23 points two years ago.

In state contests, Democrats comfortably unseated Republican governors in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, and are expected to claim another in Alaska. By winning state legislatures, too, they gained unified control of government in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, and are likely to do so in Arizona as well.

A wave this big washes up everywhere. In 343 of the 346 contested House districts with at least 80% of votes counted, Democrats won a higher share of the vote than they had in the 2024 presidential election. But the trend was most pronounced in the South, a repudiation of the notion that the region is particularly unresponsive to national trends, due to its high concentration of loyal Democratic black voters and loyal Republican white Evangelicals. Compared with 2024, Democrats gained two more points of margin in the region, on average, than the party did outside it. It was only the jaw-dropping Senate upsets in South Carolina and probably Mississippi that rendered the otherwise stunning wins elsewhere in the South look more ordinary: Democrats won North Carolina’s Senate race by 20 points and Georgia’s by 18, and came within two points of winning Louisiana’s. The party is likely to flip five or six House seats in North Carolina that had not been considered competitive.

The region’s Republican state legislators may well bear some responsibility for their party’s woes. After the Supreme Court earlier this year weakened an important provision of the Voting Rights Act, in Louisiana v Callais, lawmakers in Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee redrew their House maps to eliminate majority-black districts. That seems to have sparked a backlash. Turnout in a midterms election is always lower than in a presidential one. In Deep South states, however, the decline in turnout was smallest in counties where most voters are black, and largest in those with the fewest black residents. Outside this region, where the Supreme Court’s ruling did not prompt further redistricting, there was no such disparity.

Across the country, pre-election polls detected a “last in, first out” pattern to Republican support: the Hispanic, Asian and younger voters who had moved right from 2020 to 2024 said that they planned to abandon Republicans in 2026 in even greater numbers. District-level results and exit polls both show they kept their word. Democratic gains were largest in areas with big shares of residents who were foreign-born or of Mexican descent, and comparatively small in those with lots of older voters. Although Hispanic and Asian voters were much more likely to list prices or the economy as their most important issue, rather than immigration, it is little surprise that the party waging a sweeping deportation campaign suffered an unusually harsh electoral rebuke in the places where most immigrants live.

The scale of Democrats’ victory in the popular vote, along with the concentration of their gains in Republican-voting areas, also disproves the conventional wisdom that entrenched partisan polarisation gives modern parties a relatively high floor of support. Neither Barack Obama nor Bill Clinton, two popular Democratic presidents, ever won the White House or had their party win the House by such a big margin. According to the NORC Civic Health & Elections Project (CHEP), a large pre-election survey, Democrats managed to peel off a healthy slice of erstwhile Republican backers: 6.5% of respondents who said they voted for Mr Trump in 2024 supported a Democrat for the House this year, compared with just 2.8% of those who said they plumped for Kamala Harris in 2024 and opted for a Republican House candidate this time.

Democrats also enjoyed a strong advantage in turnout. In chep’s data just 7.6% of former Harris voters stayed home or supported third parties, compared with 12.2% of Mr Trump’s. And despite the overall decline in voter numbers from a presidential election to a midterm, fully 14% of this year’s electorate did not vote in 2024. CHEP estimates that Democrats won these new entrants by 22 points.

With victory of an almost unimaginable scale in hand, Democrats are already licking their chops in anticipation of the 2028 election cycle. If they secure the expected 56 seats in the Senate, where terms last for six years, they will be clear favourites to hold the upper chamber regardless of which party wins the presidency. If Democrats can manage a second consecutive wave election two years from now, as they did in 2006 and 2008, they could plausibly hope for a 60-vote supermajority that would enable them to pass legislation without Republican support.

articles.title: A political revolution in Texas
articles.deck: What will Democrats do with control of America’s most iconic red state?

paragraphs.text: “EVERYTHING IS BIGGER in Texas, including the shock of this win,” Gina Hinojosa said in her victory speech on November 3rd. Though she had spent months telling voters that a Democrat could win the governorship, she clearly hadn’t believed it. At an election-night watch party for James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate, staffers refreshed early-voting results pages, wondering if stellar numbers were a glitch—pundits had reckoned he could win only narrowly. By midnight, bleary-eyed Texans in “Talafreako” shirts flooded downtown Austin cheering in disbelief: Democrats had swept Texas, claiming the Senate seat by a 12-point margin, replacing every Republican statewide official on the ballot, picking up one congressional seat and flipping the Texas House. Republicans had outspent them more than two to one. It was a stunning upset in what has been America’s biggest red state.

Democrats won back some Texans who had voted Republican in 2024. This year average margins of victory in four South Texas districts topped 20 points, as dismay over economic issues and immigration-enforcement tactics sent voters rushing back to Democrats. The party also, at last, convinced more longtime Republicans to try something new. Collin, Denton and Tarrant counties, Republican-leaning suburbs north of Dallas, all flipped. Democrats won four of the five congressional seats that Texas Republicans gerrymandered last year, ostensibly in their favour.

What will Texas Democrats do with their new power? Kendall Scudder, the state Democratic Party chairman, insists Texas Democrats are different from their national counterparts. “A lot of us really believe that the government should provide you with positive services, be fair to everybody and get the hell out of your lives,” he told The Economist the morning after the election. The task now, he added, is to “start dispelling these myths that they perpetuate through Fox News that we’re a bunch of tax-and-spend liberals, but instead be responsible stewards.” Asked whether the party would prioritise rolling back social policies, such as Texas’s strict abortion ban, he didn’t respond directly. Instead, he said he hopes Democrats in Washington can reverse the cuts of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, particularly to health care. Texas has the country’s highest rate of uninsured citizens; less money for rural health care is due to force hospital closures across the state.

Ms Hinojosa’s defeat of Greg Abbott, a three-term governor, was even more of a surprise than Democrats’ victories in Congress. Constraints on her power within the state remain. Her Trumpian campaign promise to send every Texas household a $1,500 cheque, dubbed the “corruption tax refund”, could cost the state $17bn and is unlikely to gain the support of the Republican-controlled state Senate. State agencies, university boards and policy commissions are staffed by some 2,500 bureaucrats, many of whom serve six-year terms and none of whom the governor can sack. Nor can Ms Hinojosa reshape the courts. Seven of the state’s nine Supreme Court justices were appointed by Mr Abbott.

Nevertheless, she plans to start dismantling many of Mr Abbott’s policies. She campaigned against data centres, which Mr Abbott initially welcomed, and wants to end “corporate welfare”, which businesses fear will mean ending tax breaks. Ms Hinojosa and Mr Talarico also fought bitterly against the state’s $1bn school-voucher scheme, which launched this autumn. Expect Ms Hinojosa to fire the Republican education commissioner and for Sarah Eckhardt, the new Democratic comptroller, to start scrutinising public funding for private schools.

The party’s other priorities include anti-corruption legislation and cutting property taxes; those levies rose by 86% during Mr Abbott’s tenure. Nathan Johnson, the incoming attorney-general, may join other blue states—still a surreal phrase—in suing the Trump administration. “After getting punched in the face for 30 years, it’s now time to get to work,” says Jason Sabo, a Democratic lobbyist in Austin. The immediate task for Democrats is staffing up. “We don’t have the muscle,” says Mr Scudder, who joked that he has suddenly realised he must plan an inauguration.

Democrats’ thrill at winning in Texas is tempered by the knowledge that this year was unusual. Dissatisfaction in Texas, as elsewhere, was extreme. Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee, was an abysmal candidate and Mr Abbott’s long tenure provided Democrats with an easy target at which to direct voters’ angst. Republican candidates and deep-pocketed donors are likely to attempt a broad, well-funded comeback. In the Lone Star State political realignment doesn’t happen overnight, says Cal Jillson of Southern Methodist University. “Even if Democrats don’t disappoint,” Mr Jillson explains, “Texas is not a blue state now.” The party will work hard to make it so.

articles.title: The prairie fire behind the Democrats’ big win
articles.deck: Wins in Iowa and Kansas revived the left’s rural populism

paragraphs.text: WHILE RUNNING for governor of Iowa, Rob Sand, a Democrat and the state’s auditor, reprised a campaign slogan used by Iowa Democrats of an earlier era: “It’s time to rotate the crops.” Voters agreed. Iowans elected Mr Sand to be their first Democratic governor in 15 years. Democrats won a Senate seat and flipped three congressional districts in the Hawkeye State, too. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, the pastor of America’s largest United Methodist church, was the first Democratic senator elected by the state since 1932.

Mr Hamilton’s victory is the most stunning and idiosyncratic of these results. He had the challenge of competing in a state that Donald Trump had won by 16 points in 2024. He had the benefit, however, of possessing ample charisma in a race against an opponent lacking it. The Republican incumbent, Roger Marshall, a doctor, is a dismal campaigner. It didn’t help that he was plagued by reports that he sued his patients to collect medical debts.

Across Democrats’ victories on the Plains, a few common themes emerge. Mr Hamilton was buoyed by the unpopularity of Donald Trump’s war with Iran, as were Democrats everywhere and those in farm states in particular. The war has increased the price of petrol, diesel and fertiliser—all crucial inputs for farms. Sarah Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister who flipped a red district that contains liberal Des Moines and rural southern Iowa, yoked her Republican opponent to the president. One of her ads featured Mr Trump describing himself as “the best president for Iowa” and asking Iowans to re-elect the incumbent, Zach Nunn. That Mr Trump’s endorsement was used as an indictment of Mr Nunn reveals the extent of Iowans’ dissatisfaction with the man they have thrice backed in presidential campaigns.

Democrats in the Plains were also able to harness surging national populism and give it a distinctly local character. Agrarian populism spread through the Plains during the Gilded Age, and reared again during tough times for farmers in the 1930s and 1980s. Josh Turek, Iowa’s Democratic senator-elect, calls himself a “prairie populist”. Mr Sand, incensed that Iowa’s Republican legislature curtailed his powers as auditor, campaigned for more transparency and less corruption. Sam Forstag, a millennial firefighting paratrooper, looks likely to win a House seat in western Montana. He preached economic populism and the need to get money out of politics—ideas that could hold appeal in a red state once home to New Deal Democrats and a strong labour movement.

When pressed on policy, these candidates resemble Democrats in other states. Mr Turek denounces billionaires, wants to raise the minimum wage and reverse federal cuts to welfare. Yet they avoided alienating Republican voters by using distinctly post-partisan rhetoric and expressing discontent with the record of both major political parties. Mr Sand started his town halls by singing “America the Beautiful” and encouraging voters to clap for Republicans in attendance. Democrats in Middle America sometimes complain that their coastal strategists fall in love with rural candidates who seem straight out of “central casting”, without considering how authentic those candidates appear to actual rural Americans. In this cycle, Kansans and Iowans seemed to see themselves in the Democratic challengers.

That was not true for Dan Osborn, a populist independent who lost a Senate race in Nebraska. Unlike Messrs Turek and Hamilton, he seemed to have contempt for Trump voters. Leaked audio revealed him saying: “Billy Bob in fucking Red Cloud, Nebraska, who lives next door to the fucking Trump store as you pull into town, and is waving the Trump flag, all he knows is he’s on the winning team.”

This year’s victories on the Plains will bolster Democrats’ hopes that the region offers more opportunities. Democrats have long bemoaned their loss of support in Iowa since the state helped launch Barack Obama to the presidency in 2008, then padded his win four years later. As the party prepares for a presidential contest two decades after Mr Obama’s first election, they hope that Iowa will offer promising terrain, as will its neighbours.

articles.title: Hero or liability? The debate over Abdul El-Sayed
articles.deck: Michigan’s pugnacious populist wants to shake up the Democratic Party

paragraphs.text: “I tell my friends he’s like our generation’s JFK,” says Imran Aijazuddin, referring to his friend, Abdul El-Sayed. The mood at Dr El-Sayed’s election-night party is similarly exuberant. The pugnacious populist won the hard-fought Senate race in Michigan by seven points, exactly as he had predicted in May. He will be the first Muslim to serve in the upper chamber. And his victory gives the left wing of the Democratic Party a powerful new voice in Washington. Moderates, though, have a different take on the result.

Nearly everyone agrees that it was an exceptionally ugly and chaotic race. Donald Trump referred to Dr El-Sayed as a “jihadist”. Mike Rogers, his Republican opponent, falsely accused Dr El-Sayed of believing that America deserved the September 11th attacks. Then, in the final days of the race, Haley Stevens, his defeated rival in the Democratic primary, endorsed Mr Rogers. She had become increasingly angry about Dr El-Sayed’s confrontational style and fierce criticism of Israel.

Had Dr El-Sayed lost, moderate Democrats might have taken comfort in a setback for the insurgent left. The unwaveringly self-assured Dr El-Sayed has made little secret of his disdain for the party’s establishment. He has talked of backing primary challenges to Democrats with whom he disagrees, such as John Fetterman, a senator from Pennsylvania. “Ideally, you put one ogre on a pike and then everyone else gets the message,” he told donors.

Such combativeness appeals to progressives. Bernie Sanders, the democratic-socialist senator from Vermont, called Dr El-Sayed’s primary win “the most extraordinary victory…in modern American politics”, praising his defeat of the “Democratic establishment”. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a progressive congresswoman, lauded his “agenda that speaks directly to working people”. Dr El-Sayed backs Medicare for all and universal free child care. In his victory speech, he declared that winning a Senate seat was never the goal. His ambition, rather, is to “transform our politics”.

Yet Dr El-Sayed’s victory was less impressive than his supporters suggest. His seven-point margin was modest compared with the scale of the Democrats’ national gains. His race was close enough that the hated Democratic establishment had to put plenty of money to work in Michigan to support him. Other Democrats won in deep-red territory, such as Kansas and South Carolina, while Dr El-Sayed merely retained a seat already held by his party.

Candidates in the mould of Dr El-Sayed underperformed elsewhere, too. Based on endorsements by leftist groups and opposition to Democratic Party leadership, we identified 32 such Congressional nominees before the election. Most ran in deep-blue districts. But among the eight who stood in places that Kamala Harris won by fewer than ten points in 2024, their average vote shares were 1.5 percentage points lower than you would expect based on past voting and demography.
That is unlikely to dim Dr El-Sayed’s zeal. The party’s comfortable Senate majority gives him plenty of room to snipe at its establishment—and to cement his status as a hero of the progressive left.

articles.title: Republicans are in for a brutal presidential contest
articles.deck: And Democrats suddenly have a unifying agenda

paragraphs.text: If future HISTORIANS want to pinpoint the start of the campaign for the presidency in 2028, they might consider the moment late on election night of 2026 when Chris Christie, the once and probably future Republican presidential candidate, brought the hammer down on the vice-president, J.D. Vance.

As stunning results came in from Ohio, Mr Christie, serving as an analyst on ABC, zeroed in on the most vile act of the midterms: the choice by that state’s Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, to broadcast an advertisement in which the mother of his opponent, Amy Acton, called her a liar. Dr Acton had not seen her mother, Donna Arthur, in nearly 50 years, not since Ms Arthur fled with her husband after he was charged with raping his stepdaughter, Dr Acton, then 12. When the ad drew criticism from some Republicans, Mr Vance said he was disgusted by their “whining” and praised Mr Ramaswamy’s “audacity”.

Mr Vance will be remembered for that embrace “more than anything else” from this campaign, Mr Christie predicted, as he helped make that so by recalling it on ABC. “He stood behind that ad!” Mr Christie expostulated. “A man who wrote a book on Catholicism stood behind that ad. It’s a disgrace.” Mr Christie later added that the Trump era was over and that, for voters, “character matters”. That was perhaps a rosy inference, one of many being made—including that gerrymandering can backfire and the richest man in the world cannot buy an election outcome—yet, like the others, one borne out by facts. Dr Acton thumped her opponent. She is the first woman elected to serve as governor of Ohio, and the first Democrat in 16 years.

This was, in all, a bad election outcome for Mr Vance. Despite repeated trips to his home state of Ohio, he also saw his old Senate seat there go to a Democrat, Sherrod Brown. Moreover, as the vice-president’s dabbling with profanity and innuendo on the campaign trail had already shown, the cruel, vulgar style of MAGA politics never really worked for anyone but Donald Trump, and even for him the act has worn thin. Worse, still, Americans have also repudiated the substance of Trumpism.

Mr Vance has laboured to position himself as Mr Trump’s heir. But he can expect brutal competition if he does, in the end, choose to run. He wants to ascribe Republicans’ defeat solely to the war on Iran, from which he has gingerly distanced himself. But, protean though he is, Republican challengers will not let him duck responsibility for the full Trump agenda. Some of those historians may instead date the start of the presidential campaign to November 2nd, when Ron DeSantis, Florida’s Republican governor, accused unnamed members of his party of “gaslighting” Americans by pretending the war had not raised costs, as well as “corporatism” and failures on artificial intelligence and big tech.

Republicans are paying the bill for their strong leader and his idiosyncratic agenda. In the campaign to come, they must battle over what their party stands for, if not trade wars on friend and foe, shooting wars in the Middle East, state capitalism, public debt, self-enrichment in office and unchecked executive power. By contrast, Democrats, who for two years have lacked a national leader or a coherent politics besides opposing Mr Trump, emerge from the midterms with a blueprint for unifying the party and winning nationally. In his eccentric, Republican-defeating way, Mr Trump even did the Democrats a favour on election day by appearing to take an issue that bitterly divides them off the table. He said he would stop $4bn in aid to Israel by the end of the year.

Success in the South and Midwest brings the Democrats a ballasting geographical diversity. To hold their gains, let alone build on them, they will have to appeal to the socially moderate voters—Latino, black and white—who made the victories possible. Candidates such as James Talarico and Josh Turek, senators-elect from Texas and Iowa, tapped into anger against both parties, talking up decency, bipartisanship and even, at times, Mr Trump.

They also embraced an economic populism that is the through-line for successful Democratic candidates from North Carolina to Michigan to Texas. One of the canniest and most ambitious Democrats, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, released a five-page memo on election day describing her campaigning for candidates from the centre to its left. The memo did not mention climate change or any social issues but touted her focus on “economic populism, confronting concentrated wealth and power, and revitalising American democracy”. Words such as “justice” and “equity” made no appearance.

That Democratic leaders are aware of the danger of tying up Congress in futile impeachment proceedings may not prevent them from being dragged down that path. But this was also a bad midterm outcome for the party’s radical legislators, since its big House majority will deprive them of leverage. The priorities of the party’s precious new office-holders are to begin lowering prices by ending the war in Iran and to restore congressional authority over tariffs. Beyond that are such equally popular measures as banning stock-trading by members of Congress and reversing tax cuts for millionaires, a move Mr Trump has, in the past, suggested he could support. A veto would mean, for Democrats, a compelling campaign issue.

In fact, opportunities beckon for Mr Trump, too. He may yet have the chance to memorialise himself not just by “regrassing” the White House lawn, an achievement he celebrated the day before the election, but by, say, accomplishing landmark legislation to reform immigration. That would deprive Mr Vance and the Republican Party of a cherished campaign issue, illegal immigration. But Mr Trump would not care about that.

articles.title: El Salvador’s president thinks he can eliminate Haiti’s gangs
articles.deck: Nayib Bukele has dispatched 2,000 troops to the island

paragraphs.text: President Nayib Bukele has gained fame around the world for making El Salvador safer—albeit in a deeply vexing way. Leaders from Latin America trek to see the mega-prison in which he has locked up thousands of men accused of being in gangs, often without due process. Even domestic critics acknowledge that his round-ups have improved everyday life for most people. But now Mr Bukele wants to go further. Since October 22nd he has deployed over 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers to gang-ridden Haiti. He has warned its gangs (in Haitian Creole) that he can “finish with you too”.

Haiti has slumped into appalling chaos since its last elected president, Jovenel Moïse, was assassinated in his bedroom in 2021. Gangs control most of the capital, Port-au-Prince, as well as some areas outside it. At least 16,000 Haitians have been killed during the anarchy; 1.5m have been displaced (see chart). Two years ago Mr Bukele boasted that he could sort the mess out.

A pretext emerged on October 18th when four Salvadoran aviation technicians serving in Haiti as part of a UN-backed “Gang Suppression Force” (GSF) were ambushed and disappeared. Although they are probably dead—bodies purported to be those of the Salvadorans were handed over for testing on October 24th—Mr Bukele says he is mounting a rescue mission. Few believe that finding lost comrades is his sole aim, given what he has said about Haiti before, and the number of men he has sent. The Salvadoran force in Haiti now outnumbers all the soldiers serving with the GSF, who are drawn from six countries including Chad and Guatemala.

Mr Bukele’s operation marks the largest deployment of foreign troops to a country in the Americas, outside the remit of a UN mission, in many years. Much about it is murky, not just the scale of his ambitions. In 2024, speculating on the possibility of intervening, Mr Bukele said he would need a resolution from the UN, along with Haiti’s consent, and for costs to be covered.

Only one of these preconditions is clearly in place. On October 28th, six days after Salvadoran troops started to arrive, Haiti’s government said it had authorised the deployment (the terms of the agreement are not public). The United States also appears to have given a nod. Donald Trump is reported to have told Mr Bukele, during a phone call, “You have to do what you have to do.” Some Salvadoran troops flew in on an American military plane. Countries including Colombia and Haiti’s neighbour, the Dominican Republic, have also pledged logistical support—citing their joint membership of the “Shield of the Americas”, a group of countries that have promised to work with Mr Trump to combat gangs in the region.

Mr Bukele says El Salvador is paying at least 90% of the operation’s expenses. But some doubt this can be true; they wonder if money from the United States is involved. Deploying 2,000 soldiers to a country with no infrastructure, where even the water will make you sick, is extremely expensive, says Adam Isacson of the Washington Office on Latin America, a think-tank in the United States.

The UN confirms the Salvadorans are not working within the remit of the GSF. (Mr Bukele reportedly promoted the general in charge of his contingent to three stars before dispatching him, perhaps so he outranked the two-star Mongolian general leading the UN team.) The deployment risks creating “confusion and challenges for co-ordinating operations and for determining accountability for any possible violations of international law”, says William O’Neill, the UN’s expert on human rights in Haiti. It could be the beginning of the end for the GSF, says Jake Johnston of the Centre for Economic and Policy Research, another Washington think-tank.

What might Mr Bukele achieve? “He may get some tweets out of this; videos of stuff that goes boom,” says Mr Isacson. A brief deployment may impress Salvadorans. But at least some people believe Mr Bukele could make Haiti safer in the long term. Luis Contreras, a Salvadoran security analyst, thinks the gangs are no match for soldiers. “Any army could do it,” though it might take a while, he says.

Haiti’s situation is so desperate (half the population of 12m suffer acute hunger) that many in the region welcome Mr Bukele having a go. Haitians have to be “pragmatic”, says Jean Walnard Dorneval, a former Haitian defence minister. “We cannot simply sit idly by for fear of collateral damage while gangs have been traumatising the population.” There is a chance that Mr Bukele’s iron-fist reputation may scare gang leaders into negotiating.

Yet the risks of getting bogged down are huge. Mr Bukele may underestimate Haiti’s problems: on October 29th he insisted that El Salvador “lived through a nightmare that was even more horrific than what the Haitian people are enduring right now”. Pacifying El Salvador required both tough law enforcement and negotiations with gangs. A large army, police force and a functioning administration were able to round up tens of thousands of men. In Haiti the gangs govern territory, levy taxes and hold military-grade weapons. Mr Bukele “does not know the terrain and tactical environment”, says Frank Mora, a former Pentagon official.

The worry, if Mr Bukele’s ambitions in Haiti turn out to be large, is of a scorched-earth strategy that kills a lot of civilians. Human-rights groups are already reporting increased casualties in the area where the Salvadorans went missing. The UN force in Haiti operates cautiously; its troops rarely leave their base. Many observers, including in the Trump administration, mock its weakness: they think Haiti’s agonies are being drawn out by a “bunch of ninnies and losers not willing to use enough force to show who is boss”, says Mr Johnston. Their certainty may soon be put to the test.

articles.title: André “Mad Dog” Janones is a hero of the Brazilian left
articles.deck: Can politicians elsewhere in the world replicate his online campaigns?

paragraphs.text: The night he was re-elected as Brazil’s president, snatching victory from what seemed like sure defeat, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spoke to supporters in the streets of São Paulo. Lula, as the left-wing leader is known, gestured to a guest by his side. “I want to thank this comrade here, our general, who played a pivotal role in this campaign,” he told the crowds.

The man feted on October 25th was André Janones, a 42-year-old congressman for a small environmentalist party who some think was the architect of Lula’s surprise victory. He is the brains behind “Lula’s Army”—a channel on WhatsApp that acquired more than 10m followers in the three weeks before the run-off vote. Its success has made Mr Janones a cult hero on the Brazilian left. It has also caught the eye of leftist leaders around the world—including Pedro Sánchez, Spain’s prime minister, and Claudia Sheinbaum, Mexico’s president—who wonder if they can emulate his strategy in their own countries. “It’s replicable and I think it’s necessary,” Mr Janones tells The Economist. “In all honesty, I think this could be what sweeps the far right off the map.”

After Lula performed poorly in the first round of voting on October 4th, Mr Janones—a former lawyer whom colleagues dubbed “Mad Dog” for his scalding of right-wing candidates in advance of the elections in 2022—promised despairing left-wingers that if they followed his orders they could turn things around. At his request, Brazilians banged pots and pans when Lula’s rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, was interviewed on television. They flooded Instagram with images of themselves wearing Brazil’s national colours and making an “L” shape (a pro-Lula symbol) with their fingers. Mr Janones held late night livestreams on which he refused to speak until at least a million viewers had tuned in. “EVERYONE, URGENT! GET TAPPING, AND MAKE THIS VIDEO EXPLODE!” was a typical command.

Behind all this, says Mr Janones, lay a studied plan to game the algorithms that drive social networks. He ordered his followers to comment on and “like” pro-Lula posts before sharing them, to boost their engagement. He told his “army” not to respond to misinformation about their candidate, on the basis that any engagement could widen a post’s reach. Actions of the army were carefully co-ordinated. “When four million people posted the exact same photo at the exact same time, the algorithm interpreted it like a plane crash or a terrorist attack like 9/11 and blocked the reach of any other posts. That’s how we glitched the algorithm,” he says.

Lula’s Army was far from the only thing that helped swing the election. Having for weeks run an old-fashioned campaign, Lula himself began posting selfie-style videos online. In the weeks before the run-off, his government pushed through an amendment guaranteeing workers two days off a week, and forgave sole traders their federal tax debts. But Mr Janones’s channel “was a turnout machine”, says David Nemer at the University of Virginia, bringing out pro-Lula voters who had abstained in the first round. “It gave a campaign that had just proved it couldn’t talk to the internet a voice that could.”

WhatsApp groups inspired by Mr Janones’s effort are popping up around the world. Guides detailing his techniques are circulating online in French and Japanese. He has been invited to advise politicians in Colombia, Venezuela and the EU, among other places. The week after Brazil’s election he turned up in Argentina, where he met members of the Peronist opposition. And Mr Janones says he plans to continue mobilising Lula’s Army at home in order to press a conservative-dominated Congress to pass Lula’s bills.

The lawmaker has some reservations about his digital playbook. He says he felt uncomfortable encouraging people to ignore pro-Bolsonaro posts, rather than push back against them. But like many in the Brazilian left, he believes social media have long handed their opponents an advantage—and that the ends justify the means. “My strategy is a strategy of war.”

articles.title: Can the pope’s tour of Latin America win back disenchanted youth?
articles.deck: Feminism and mysticism are providing reasons to question the faith

paragraphs.text: Pope Leo’s tour of South America, beginning on November 6th, is a marathon. Over 12 days he is traveling some 31,000km, visiting Uruguay, Argentina and Peru and giving around 40 speeches. In some ways it is a homecoming: the pontiff spent two decades as a missionary in Peru. The roadshow, coming three weeks after the pope underwent surgery for lung cancer, will draw big crowds. A bigger question is whether it can help win back Latin America’s waning faithful. The region’s educated young, in particular, are gradually going off organised religion.

In the decade to 2020 the share of people around the world who say they do not identify with any organised religion—call them the “nones”—grew by a percentage point, to 24%. This shift may appear small, but behind it lies much change. Every religion other than Islam stagnated or shrank over that period, when taking population growth into account. The share of people who say they have no religious affiliation declined slightly in Asia and barely budged in Africa or the Middle East. But it soared in Europe and the Americas. And of the three countries where the share of “nones” grew the most, two (Chile and Uruguay) are in Latin America.

To see what this looks like on the ground, trek to Uruguay—the country in which Pope Leo is beginning his grand tour. Its constitution has long enforced an exceptionally strict division between church and state. Easter week, known as “Holy Week” in the rest of Latin America, is called “Tourism Week”. Christmas is dubbed “Family Day.” Not by chance, Uruguay legalised marijuana, gay marriage and abortion much earlier than its peers.

The share of Uruguayans who identify as Catholic has fallen by almost half since 1995, to 33%. Only 9% of Uruguayans say they practise the faith regularly. Many young people are unenthused by the pope’s visit, the first since 1988. “I just think: what a waste of money,” says Lucía Castillos, a 31-year-old caterer in Montevideo, the capital. “How much are we spending on this visit that we could be giving to people who have nothing to eat?”

Ms Castillos says her scepticism towards the church grew during a recent upswell of feminism all across Latin America. What began as mass rallies in Argentina in 2015 protesting against killings of women later swept into Chile and Mexico, where demonstrators also demanded access to abortion. “Catholicism springs from the premise that women are inherently flawed,” she believes. “That vision just doesn’t square with feminism.”

Some of Latin America’s new “nones” are unapologetic atheists. “To me, it all seems crazy,” says Virginia, a 29-year-old primary school teacher in Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina: “A dove impregnating a virgin, evangelical Christians speaking in tongues, Orthodox Jews dressed in wigs.” But the evidence suggests that many of these people are in fact swapping organised religion for a much looser kind of spiritualism.

Many of them tell pollsters they believe in esoteric things, such as “energies”. Syncretism and folksy superstition is common. Some Brazilian “nones” dabble in Candomblé and Umbanda, two traditions that combine Roman Catholicism with west African religious practices. Mexicans of all stripes celebrate the Day of the Dead, a Mesoamerican spin on All Souls’ Day. Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, embodies this growing spiritual mish-mash. The libertarian has a strong interest in Judaism but has not denied rumours that he has also sought a medium’s help to speak to his dead dog.

Organised religion remains a powerful influence on the region’s politics, even if its grip on hearts is loosening. Recent years have seen increasingly vocal interventions in many countries by evangelical Protestant groups, and politicians are putting in much more effort to court them. Evangelicals were firm supporters of Jair Bolsonaro, Brazil’s president from 2019-23, and of his son Flávio who recently failed in his bid to win the same job.

The godless in Latin America remain more likely than those elsewhere to say that organised religion helps society, rather than harms it. The Catholic church is still the most trusted institution in Latin America, according to Latinobarómetro, a polling organisation, well ahead of outfits such as armies and the media. That reflects a history of (mostly) do-gooding, as well as the dim view many Latin Americans take of their secular institutions, such as legislatures and the courts. The result is that the pope’s words and actions on the road will be scoured for political subtext.

Some in Argentina hope that Leo’s four-day stop there could squeeze a touch more humility from Mr Milei—who is broadly succeeding in stabilising an economy in crisis but can be aggressively unsympathetic towards people affected by his policies. Before becoming president in 2023 Mr Milei had lambasted Leo’s predecessor, Francis. He called the late pontiff, who was Argentine, an “imbecile” and “the representative of the devil on earth,” though he later apologised. Pope Leo plans to visit a centre for disabled children. Argentine bishops have repeatedly expressed concern about the impact of Mr Milei’s cuts on the poor and sick.

The pope’s last stop, in Peru, ought to be much more straightforward. It remains one of the most devout countries in the region. And many Peruvians have warm memories of his years working in the country. Even in a rapidly secularising region, good deeds are infallibly popular.

articles.title: Paraguay’s swaggering digital bank has fallen

paragraphs.text: Editor’s note (November 5th): Shortly after this story was published Paraguay’s president, Santiago Peña, resigned.

Ueno Bank is ubiquitous in Paraguay. The bank sponsors stadiums, music festivals, the national football squad, a bar, and the country’s top racing driver. Its credit cards garner big cashbacks at supermarkets. Though it only received a full banking licence in 2023, the fintech startup now caters to 2.9m Paraguayans: almost two-thirds of the adult population. At craft fairs co-organised by the country’s first lady, glamorous Ueno promoters in tight jeans issue indigenous artisans with card readers.

For many Paraguayans, accustomed to keeping their cash under the mattress, Ueno helped them open their first bank account. Its branches offered touchscreens, frothy coffees and comfy sofas: a far cry from the awkward hours, staid decor, hefty deposit requirements and scowling security guards of competitors. Often likened to Monzo or Revolut, Ueno hoped to achieve a $1bn valuation and thus become Paraguay’s first unicorn.

That was until 3:23am on November 3rd, when the Banco Central del Paraguay (BCP, the central bank and banking regulator) seized control of Ueno and began to formally dissolve it. Police collared Ueno’s CEO, Miguel Vázquez, and took him to a high-security jail. Other executives from the bank were hooded and cuffed. They face charges including breach of trust, irregular book-keeping, and attempted fraud. Tearful depositors, frozen out of their savings, had to be held back from branches by the police. The BCP’s president Carlos Carvallo, himself Ueno’s boss until three years ago, resigned at the request of Paraguay’s president, Santiago Peña.

Protesters marched towards the presidential palace. The opposition said it was preparing to impeach Mr Peña, who until last year held shares in Ueno Holding, a related company. His vice-president, Pedro Alliana, also faces impeachment. In a video message, Mr Peña said that 98% of Ueno’s clients would get their money back through deposit insurance and that those responsible for the crisis would be punished: “The financial system is strong.”

Behind Ueno’s collapse lie a series of events that tarnished its youthful image. The bank’s share of government business has ballooned on Mr Peña’s watch. Around $850m of public money is now deposited with Ueno, including a tenth of the country’s public pensions funds. Itti, a sister company of the bank, handles reams of sensitive citizen data after winning more than a dozen state contracts. The president has “a direct responsibility” for the crisis, says Rafael Filizzola, a centre-left opposition senator. “This is a criminal conspiracy to use public funds in private businesses linked to Peña.” (Mr Peña has denied any wrongdoing.)

Also under scrutiny is fast-and-loose lending by Ueno itself. Last month it emerged that the bank had disbursed roughly $150m to small companies linked to its shareholders and employees, seemingly breaching regulatory rules and putting its own balance sheet at risk. Senators loyal to former president Horacio Cartes—whose family owns a different bank, and who has recently fallen out with Mr Peña—began to pile on pressure.

As the negative headlines multiplied and investors took fright, Ueno’s $350m bonds due in 2031, issued in March, lost around 12% of their value. Last week, the company announced a $100m recapitalisation. It was too little, too late. BCP officials said on Tuesday that Ueno’s solvency ratio has fallen below half the required minimum, and that its investigators had uncovered more irregularities.

“Uncertainty reigns,” says Esteban Caballero, a political analyst. The ruling Colorado Party controls both houses of Congress, but is split between supporters of the president and Mr Cartes, his former patron. A banking reserve fund has been authorised to reimburse Ueno’s clients up to the value of $38,000 within 15 days; lawmakers have voted to speed this up. Beyond that amount, the BCP will only offer “the greatest protection possible”. As for Ueno, another financial institution was recently rumoured to be negotiating over its acquisition. Some worry that biometric information Ueno gathered from its clients could be sold to the highest bidder. “This is sensitive data,” says Maricarmen Sequera of TEDIC, a digital-rights NGO.

Others fear the scandal could take the shine off South America’s star non-oil economy, which expanded by 6.6% in 2025. Unlike a crisis in 1995 that wiped out half of Paraguay’s banks, the broader financial system is safe, says Fernando Arriola, a former Wall Street banker and the director of Paraguay’s fintech chamber. But medium-sized companies that stored their cash with Ueno will suffer. “This will affect the market,” Mr Arriola adds, blaming regulators for being asleep at the wheel, Ueno for lending too generously to associates, and the president for failing to avoid perceptions of favouritism.
Mr Peña often calls Paraguay an “awakening giant”. If the sorry tale of Ueno is anything to go by, that colossus has feet of clay.

articles.title: The latest Ebola outbreak could be the worst ever
articles.deck: New cases in Kenya and Nigeria show that the outbreak is unchecked

paragraphs.text: “SANITISE,” says the security guard outside a school in Nairobi, gesturing towards a dispenser. Since Kenya reported its first-ever case of the Ebola virus last month many venues in its capital have made visitors disinfect their hands and get their temperatures checked. Officials tell people to avoid large gatherings. “I want to appeal to Kenyans going forward that we can also avoid handshakes or hugging,” said Patrick Amoth, the director-general at the health ministry. “We can just wave.”

The precautions reflect growing concern about the spread of an Ebola outbreak that emerged in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo this year. The Kenyan case involved a businessman who had been living in eastern Congo but returned home to Kenya via Uganda on October 3rd. He died two days later. Kenya has since reported eight more cases (and another death), all of them contacts of the first. On October 20th another of Africa’s largest economies, Nigeria, reported its first case of Ebola in a decade. A woman who had travelled to Uganda tested positive in Abuja, Nigeria’s capital.

Since the outbreak was officially declared in May there have been more than 10,500 confirmed cases of the gruesome and terrifying virus. Almost half (5,130) have so far resulted in death, with all but four of the fatalities in eastern Congo. Fewer than a quarter of new cases there occur in patients who are known contacts of previous cases, says Jean Kaseya, the director of Africa Cdc, a public-health body. So long as authorities are in the dark about the virus, the epidemic will keep growing.

Ebola spreads via direct contact with an infected person’s bodily fluids. Suspected patients must be tested and positive cases isolated. Direct contacts of patients should be identified and tested, too. Health workers need protective equipment to avoid falling sick themselves.

Attempting this in eastern Congo can be like trying to give someone a haircut with toy scissors in a house on fire. Health workers are few in number and poorly paid. Testing kits and isolation facilities are scarce. Bad roads make it difficult to reach patients and bring in supplies; so do the scores of militias that terrorise the region.

The long-suffering population has a deep lack of trust in the Congolese state. Many eastern Congolese believe Ebola is a fiction, concocted by venal bigwigs to embezzle donor funds. On October 24th a machete-wielding mob in eastern Congo killed a nurse whom they accused of spreading Ebola by contaminating water supplies. In September a politician from the ruling party was beaten to death after he went on the radio to urge people to take precautions against Ebola.

The worst Ebola outbreak on record happened between 2014 and 2016 in west Africa, where the UN’s World Health Organisation recorded at least 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths. Haphazard surveillance means it is hard to compare the current epidemic with the one that ended a decade ago. But this outbreak, which involves a rarer strain of Ebola known as Bundibugyo, seems to be spreading and killing more quickly. Mr Kaseya fears that on current trends it “will be the worst Ebola outbreak ever” within another year.

Given the scale of the outbreak in Congo, which has more shared borders than anywhere else in Africa, it is unsurprising that Ebola has been found in nearby countries. Though Uganda officially closed its border with Congo in May, it is a porous frontier. Kenya’s first Ebola patient crossed into Uganda from Congo last month before flying to Nairobi. He subsequently slipped through screening at the airport in Kenya undetected, despite showing symptoms of Ebola on his journey.

The Nigerian case is more troubling. Officials in Uganda claimed at first that the woman had visited eastern Congo. This seems false. She is thought to have been at Uganda’s main airport on the same day as Kenya’s first patient. But there is no evidence yet that they came into contact with one another. All of which raises questions about whether, despite Uganda’s denials, there are active cases in the country. “My biggest concern is that the source of the Nigerian patient’s infection remains unexplained,” says Ahmed Kalebi, a Kenyan pathologist.
Countries such as Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda have relatively strong health systems. They should be able to stop the virus from exploding as it has in Congo.

But there are still three concerns. The first is that Congo is a large country—with an ongoing war in the east involving M23, a Rwandan-backed force. There is a lot of room for further spread. The second is that Ebola could take off in the most fragile of Congo’s bordering states: Burundi, South Sudan and the Central African Republic. The third worry is that the longer the outbreak persists, the greater the secondary effects. In the west African outbreak thousands more babies and mothers died than would have otherwise been the case because of disruptions to health services. Doctors working in Congo say fewer children are being immunised and malaria is on the rise.

The good news is that there are efforts to find an effective vaccine against Bundibugyo. On October 23rd the first participants in clinical trials in eastern Congo received shots of Ervebo, a vaccine that protects against a more common strain. Scientists are also working on a bespoke jab. But it will be months, at best, before a proven vaccine is produced. For many people that will be far too late.

articles.title: Hackers are exploiting Africa’s digital identities
articles.deck: Governments are embracing new databases. So are criminals

paragraphs.text: EARLIER THIS year hackers targeted Senegal’s agency for issuing passports and identity cards. The attackers claim to have stolen sensitive data from the west African country, including biometric information and immigration records. The authorities told citizens that their data were safe. But some of the loot seemingly ended up on the dark web. It was not the only successful recent cyber-attack on the state. In May, criminals targeted the national treasury. Last year hackers demanded a ransom of $10m after breaching the tax authority.

Senegal is not alone. As African governments digitise government services and grow their national-identity databases, they are struggling to protect citizens’ data. Incidents such as the recent discovery of a vulnerability in PHP, a programming language commonly used by governments, show that the problem is not limited to Africa. But the continent has less money and talent to bolster its cyber-security. And as artificial intelligence (AI) expands attackers’ toolkits, African governments will urgently need to find ways to secure their systems.

Their problems often stem from efforts to improve public services. Of the 800m people worldwide who have no legal proof of who they are, more than half live in sub-Saharan Africa. Without a formal identity many find it impossible to join welfare programmes or health-insurance schemes, send children to school, own land, open bank accounts or activate sim cards. Countries like Uganda, where almost 80% of people have a digital ID, can now more easily track their people and close gaps in provision. (Around a decade ago fewer than 10% of Ugandans had some legal proof of their identities.) A digitally savvy state is better equipped to spot fraud, collect taxes and safeguard elections.

Yet governments are failing to secure the growing number of access points for hackers. That is mainly because there are not enough qualified people who can help them do it. Mastercard, the payments firm, reckons that Africa has 200,000 unfilled cyber-security jobs, equivalent to about a quarter of the current workforce. Banking and telecommunications firms snap up the few qualified engineers and security analysts. As ai accelerates, Africa’s skills gap is widening.

Money is another problem. According to a survey by Interpol, nearly all African members cited “resource constraints” as an obstacle to improving cyber-security. Protecting databases is expensive. Software is often installed and managed by foreign firms because there are too few qualified local engineers. Importing these services uses scarce foreign currency. Computers need reliable power, which many African grids do not provide.

Some countries are trying to bolster their defences. In Ghana, firms must report major breaches to the Cyber Security Authority within a day of spotting them or risk fines or the imprisonment of bosses. Kenya has an incident-response centre that regularly publishes reports on cyber threats. But other countries are lagging behind. Only 16 on the continent have ratified the African Union’s Malabo Convention, which is supposed to encourage pan-African digital standards.

In the short term, governments are trying to encourage citizens to be more careful. Ghana’s “Be cyber smart” campaign urges people to protect their passwords, avoid dodgy links and keep private information private. Rosemary Kisembo, who runs Uganda’s identity register, says that “people share more about themselves on Facebook” than with the government, a sign she takes as Ugandans’ lax approach to data security.

The gaps in funding and skills are difficult to close. Wide variation in connectivity, compute capacity and digital literacy among African countries hinders collaboration. But governments could do more to work together. Sharing intelligence about attacks could help them anticipate vulnerabilities. But weak supranational institutions—and national pride—have hampered efforts.

Some countries deny there is an issue. Nigeria’s identity-management body, for example, still claims that its database was not compromised, even though journalists have found national-identification numbers for sale on the black market since 2024. It is hard to solve the problem unless it is identified first.

articles.title: America’s allies oppose more war in Iran. They may not get a say
articles.deck: Economies are shrinking and a deal remains elusive

paragraphs.text: THE DIPLOMATS and military officers gathered last week for the Manama Dialogue, an annual talkfest in Bahrain’s capital, all had the same questions—and no answers. As they nibbled puff pastry at the Ritz-Carlton, their conversations invariably came back to Donald Trump’s threats to resume his war with Iran after the midterm elections. Would he do it, and when? Might the Iranians strike first?

There were almost no Americans on hand to ask: the Trump administration sent only a pair of mid-ranking officials, and both were tight-lipped. To some Gulf officials, the unusually small delegation seemed like a snub. “They could at least try to reassure us,” grumbled one.

Gulf states are reluctant to offer such blunt criticism in public, lest they antagonise the president. But they are unanimous that they do not want another round of fighting—unlike in February, when some were equivocal. This time even the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which has taken the most hawkish stance towards Iran, is urging Mr Trump not to strike. “We in the UAE don’t believe that a military solution is viable,” says Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president.

Behind the scenes, diplomats are scrambling to find a deal. Envoys from Qatar shuttling back and forth to Tehran have encountered two big obstacles, however. One is Mr Trump’s seeming insistence that a new agreement include at least some concessions related to Iran’s nuclear programme. The Iranians refuse to discuss it. Instead they are gloating at Mr Trump’s drubbing in the midterms.

The other is how to sequence an agreement. America and Iran both want to avoid a repeat of the memorandum of understanding, the vague agreement they signed in June and which collapsed within weeks. Each side wants the other to move first. Iran insists that America start by lifting its naval blockade and removing a range of sanctions. Only then will it reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The Americans fear Iran would simply rush to export a glut of stored oil, easing some pressure on its economy, then fail to take reciprocal steps.

Participants in Manama were split on how soon America might act if talks fail to yield a deal. Some suggested Mr Trump may wait several weeks. America is still building up its forces. It has also announced talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on November 10th, a curious thing to do if it were planning to imminently restart a war that would make Abu Dhabi a target.

Citizens and expats alike are nervous: the Gulf has not felt this tense since April, when Mr Trump was threatening to wipe out Iranian civilisation. Some residents are stocking up on food, water and cash. If the war resumes, “you might start to question, why do I stay here?” says Laith Alajlouni of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, a British think-tank.

Gulf states would be less able to defend themselves, having depleted their air-defence interceptors. They would also have smaller fiscal buffers to cushion the economic blow. Saudi Arabia had expected to run a deficit of 3.3% of GDP in 2026; it hit that mark by July and may now exceed 6%. Five of the six Gulf economies are expected to shrink this year. Three will see a double-digit contraction.

The IMF thinks the Gulf could bounce back quickly next year: its latest forecast pencils in 9.1% growth. But that depends on a lasting peace. Some big events are already being scaled back or postponed. The Asian Cup, a football tournament, was meant to start in Saudi Arabia in January. It has been booted to December 2027.

The region will also have fewer escape routes than it did last time. Saudi Arabia was relatively safe earlier this year: Iran attacked it less fiercely than most neighbouring countries. That let Bahrain’s national carrier shift operations to the kingdom. Planes landed in nearby Dammam, and buses carried passengers the rest of the way. Now, though, Dammam’s airport is being targeted by the Houthis, an Iran-backed militia in Yemen. Two people were killed there in a drone attack last month.

Since the midterm elections Mr Trump has sent mixed messages. He told one journalist that he might order a “heavy hit” and another that he was in no rush to do so. Rulers throughout the Gulf would like to believe the second one—but February taught them to beware.

articles.title: Gulf states brace for war with Iran—again
articles.deck: Their air defences are dangerously depleted

paragraphs.text: DRIVE ALONG Bahrain’s King Khalifa causeway into Manama, the capital, and the war damage to America’s main naval hub in the Gulf is apparent: destroyed communication antennae on one side; blackened buildings on the other. Gashes in high-rise buildings are boarded up.

Iran fired more than 700 missiles and attack drones at Bahrain at the height of the American-Israeli war on Iran between February 28th and April 8th. Most were intercepted but some inflicted real damage. Iran hit not only military targets but also a desalination plant, refineries and an aluminium factory. A similar trauma was felt elsewhere in the Gulf (see map).

Now a second round of the war looms. To the east, the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group is sailing to join two others in the Arabian Sea. To the west, an American airlift is ferrying military equipment to bases in Israel and Jordan, including more Patriot air-defence batteries. American strikes against Iranian anti-aircraft missiles on Qeshm island this week were seemingly provoked by threats to American drones and jets, but may also serve to prepare the battlefield.

Gulf states fear that President Donald Trump may lash out abroad after being wounded in the midterm elections at home (see Briefing). They also expect to be the target of Iran’s wrath, as it threatens to respond “without geographical limitations”.

Stocks of Western missile interceptors are severely depleted worldwide. Ukrainian and other systems may help Gulf states reduce the threat from drones, though these are improving fast. Israeli intelligence officials, meanwhile, express surprise at the speed of Iran’s build-up of missile stocks since the ceasefire.

After weeks of air strikes during Israel’s and America’s Operation Epic Fury, many question what can be achieved by more bombing—“a little Epic Fury”, as Mr Trump called it. The pair probably struck all the easy targets and the main nuclear sites at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan were previously bombed in 2025, burying some 400kg of highly enriched uranium.

What remains are mostly hard-to-reach places, such as underground “missile cities” that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has been showing off on television. Entrances to such facilities were bombed in the first round but many seem to have been excavated since. American stocks of the biggest bunker-buster bombs appear to be running low.

Much attention focuses on mysterious work at “Pickaxe Mountain”, possibly another nuclear facility. It is buried so deep in granite that it may be beyond the reach of conventional bombs (raising unsubstantiated claims that Mr Trump might use a nuclear weapon against it). Officials in the United Arab Emirates (uae) say they are “braced for the worst”, and vow to defend their country.

The uae endured the heaviest Iranian fire in the war, facing a total of more than 2,800 Iranian missiles and drones, perhaps because of its close ties with Israel. But it also boasts the region’s most powerful air defences with overlapping layers of interceptors, supplemented by guns on attack helicopters, home-made electronic-warfare gear and perhaps Israeli laser weapons. Saudi Arabia will find it harder to defend its territory, given its larger size and sprawling infrastructure. It also faces threats from both Iran and its Yemeni ally, the Houthi militia.

As America pulls forces and equipment farther from Iran—mainly to Israel and Jordan—the future of its bases in the Gulf is open to question. Increasingly, Gulf leaders are looking for protection elsewhere. Saudi Arabia, for instance, has signed the Mecca pact with Pakistan and Turkey, which have deployed or are thinking of sending forces. What they would do in an actual war remains to be seen.

Deeper integration among Gulf countries would help—not least in setting up joint air defences. But ever-bickering Gulf states have mainly sought national or bilateral security deals rather than collective ones. Gulf states' ability to stand together against the Iran challenge, admit Emirati officials, “has proven hollow”.

articles.title: How the Houthis built their war machine
articles.deck: The rebels in Yemen are outgrowing their dependence on their patron

paragraphs.text: ALI AL-WAZIR is no ordinary businessman. The 47-year-old Yemeni, who is known as “Prince”, plies his trade in Guangzhou in southern China. The bustling port is about 7,000km (4,500 miles) from Yemen. But distance has not prevented Mr Wazir from playing a part in his country’s long civil war. In 2024 he was accused of supplying the Houthis, the Iran-backed rebels that rule much of Yemen, with materials to help them build weapons. America’s Treasury placed him under sanctions. Last year it blacklisted several more Houthi-linked traders for doing the same.

Once dismissed as ragtag insurgents—rebels in flipflops—the Houthis are now one of the most dangerous militias in the Middle East. Since they took control of northern Yemen more than a decade ago, they have built up a formidable arsenal of drones and missiles—aided, in part, by the likes of Mr Wazir. The Houthis’ smuggling networks stretch from the Horn of Africa to China. In recent weeks they have hit Saudi Arabia, which supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government, with one strike after another. At a summit in Tehran last week Saudi Arabia put pressure on Iran to rein in the Houthis but the region is preparing for more war.

The Houthis first got their hands on serious kit in 2014 after they seized Sana’a, Yemen’s capital. A short-lived alliance with Ali Abdullah Saleh, a former president, and his loyalists in the army gave them access to Soviet-style Scud and Tochka missiles. At the same time Iran, which was cultivating the Houthis (also Shia) as part of its “axis of resistance”, increased its support. When Saudi forces intervened in Yemen in 2015, Iran supplied the rebels with ballistic missiles, drones and other heavy weapons. Iranian advisers and operatives from Hizbullah, a militia in Lebanon, taught them how to use them.

Today the Houthis are developing a war machine of their own. On September 21st Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, their leader, boasted that they now build their weapons “from scratch”. That may be bluster but analysts are increasingly convinced that much of the rebels’ arsenal is built inside Yemen. “The speed and ambition of the Houthis’ military production has surprised a lot of observers,” says Fabian Hinz of Conflict Armaments Research (CAR), which tracks the illicit arms trade. While most of the group’s weapons are still based on Iranian designs, some—such as medium-range drones—can be built largely without Iranian parts.

Production mostly happens out of sight, in caves in the Yemeni highlands, making it hard to monitor. Data from The Century Foundation, a think-tank in New York, nevertheless point to a shift in their activities (see chart). During the 2010s most of the shipments that were seized going into Houthi territory contained ready-to-use weapons, such as guns and rockets. Iran was by far the biggest supplier in the mid-2010s. Now most of these consignments contain parts to build weapons, such as motors, wiring and propellers. China has overtaken Iran as the biggest source of such goods.

Lots of these items are “dual-use”, meaning they plausibly have civilian as well as military applications. Houthi smugglers sometimes try to outfox Yemeni authorities by slapping innocuous labels such as “industrial equipment” on drone kits. Other goods seem purpose-made for the arms industry. In October CAR suggested that parts for an Iranian-designed ballistic missile, seized in the government-held port of Aden, were made to order by a Chinese company. Saudi officials have complained to China, to little avail. “China is happy to turn a blind eye to its citizens participating in trade that supports the Houthis’ weapons industry,” says a Western diplomat.

Breaking this supply chain will be hard. American sanctions have achieved little: Houthi businessmen continue to operate in China. The rebels have been under a United Nations’ arms embargo for more than a decade. But the mission that inspects cargo ships sailing to Houthi-held ports is feeble. It reports dodgy vessels to the Saudis and their allies, but has no powers to stop them itself.

Even if it could, much would slip through. Some goods travel overland through the United Arab Emirates and Oman. Others are smuggled via Djibouti and Somalia. Tim Lenderking, America’s envoy for Yemen from 2021 to 2025, says the Houthis move contraband “from big boats, onto small boats, onto tiny boats, onto pack animals and onto people’s backs”. Smugglers hide ammunition in lorries carrying fruit and vegetables. Yemen’s government—a patchwork of squabbling groups—struggles to co-ordinate enforcement. “Different operation rooms are controlled by different factions,” says Baraa Shiban of the Royal United Services Institute, a think-tank in London. “It’s a nightmare.”

Making their own arms helps the Houthis keep fighting when supplies from Iran are disrupted. But the Islamic Republic also benefits from their self-reliance. Under its doctrine of “mosaic defence”, Iran’s regime has tried to make different parts of its armed forces capable of fighting independently. A similar idea underpins its axis of resistance. “Iran has made efforts to enable its allies to produce locally,” says Mr Hinz. Hizbullah has built drones and tried to convert rockets into precision-guided missiles by itself. But the militia has been weakened by Israeli attacks and disruption to its smuggling routes through Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad.

The Houthis are in a better position. While the rebels still get plenty of weapons and intelligence from Iran, they are outgrowing their dependence on the regime. That may explain why the Houthis are unbowed even as the war launched by America and Israel has weakened their patron. The rebels see themselves as more than a mere Iranian proxy but as the real rulers of Yemen. They have sought support from Russia and are fostering connections with armed groups in Africa. The Houthis want to be a “little Iran in their own little neighbourhood,” says Barbara Leaf, a former American diplomat. Their ambition, as well as their firepower, is growing.
