articles.title: Drones don’t just blow up the enemy
articles.deck: They can also pick up on radio transmissions to identify future targets

paragraphs.text: In the David and Goliath war between Ukraine and Russia, drones have proved a great equaliser. Ukraine’s short-range aircraft are cutting Russia’s supply lines to its occupying troops, while long-range versions attack oil refineries, airfields and warehouses as far afield as Siberia.

Not all military drones, however, carry warheads. Many are used instead for spying and target location. A lot of these gather their data at optical or infrared frequencies. But some, involved in the field of signals intelligence, or SIGINT, listen out for radio waves. And within that category are those which seek not to understand what is being broadcast, but merely to identify and locate its source, the better to attack it—a field of endeavour called electronic support measures (ESM).

According to Thomas Withington, an electronic-warfare expert at the Royal United Services Institute, a think-tank, the result has been an arms race in which the radio frequencies used to control drones have migrated ever further up and down the spectrum, in attempts to evade detection. Frequency-hopping radios, which skip from one wavelength to another thousands of times a second, are getting faster, so a transmitter may be visible only momentarily; signals are increasingly disguised to merge into background noise.

Dr Withington notes the advantages drones bring to ESM. A lorry-mounted system with a ten-metre antenna can detect transmitters roughly 13km away. The same receiver on a drone at an altitude of 1,000 metres can see for 130km. Having antennae on drones is also more useful when an attack may come from any direction. It avoids blind spots caused by topography.

The Ukrainians are reluctant to discuss what they are up to. But not all their research is being done in-house. At Eurosatory, a European defence exhibition held in June, Aaronia, a German manufacturer, unveiled a SIGINT electronics package that can be mounted on a drone. The developers say three such drones working in tandem can pinpoint transmitters to within 25 metres from up to 75km away.

At 5kg, Aaronia’s product is inconveniently heavy. Sky Spy, based in Delaware, recently demonstrated Agent 001, a 500-gram electronics package that can be mounted on a small Orqa quadcopter. This proved able to detect, identify and locate “hostile” radios as part of an exercise in Estonia. Agent 001 also has on-board processing, linked to the drone’s camera, so it can move towards a transmitter and capture video for its operator to confirm the identity of the source.

One limitation of small drones, says Dr Withington, is that the amount of processing capacity they can carry is restricted. Such capacity is essential for sifting through signal data. Drone-control signals may, for example, be hidden in Wi-Fi.

New processors and AI software are, however, making small drones vastly more capable. One bit of kit that can be mounted onto a drone, known as Barn Owl, has been developed by NxGenComm of North Carolina. David Gross, NxGenComm’s marketing director, says Barn Owl follows all traffic in the Wi-Fi range, analysing changes to pick out the signatures of concealed military signals. He claims the process is fast enough to keep up with the most nimble frequency-hopping radios, and powerful enough to scan and analyse an 800MHz-wide swathe of radio signals.

Intelligence can go to commanders, or directly to other units. In one proposed set-up, a parliament of Barn Owls would be linked directly to interceptor drones. When they detected an incoming drone, they would launch an interceptor and guide it to the target’s location until it was close enough for visual confirmation by the operator. NxGenComm hopes to deploy Barn Owl to Ukraine in the next few months, and is in discussion with American military customers.

As well as locating enemy drones, ESM can also help identify their control frequencies so that they can be jammed. Both sides get round this by flying some drones via fibre-optic control cables, which unspool as they fly. Such drones, which can carry 50km of fibre, emit no radio signals. Similarly, some AI-enabled drones can operate incommunicado, flying and striking targets without operator input.

In the meantime, however, the vast majority of drones still rely on radio, and the electronic-warfare arms race continues. Falling behind can be disastrous: if an enemy can jam communications and knock drones out of the sky while remaining invisible, heavy losses are sure to result.

articles.title: OpenAI’s approach to mathematics does not add up
articles.deck: Two months after the firm’s initial advances, its lack of transparency is still causing problems

paragraphs.text: On October 29th leading mathematicians gathered at the Royal Society in London to discuss the future of their field. There was plenty of excitement at the progress artificial intelligence is making, leavened with nostalgia for the good old days of early 2026 when human-led mathematics was the only game in town.

Many attendees were also critical of how AI labs have been handling their models’ breakthroughs. In recent months labs have flooded the field with papers that are almost impenetrable to human minds, and kept the details of new results under wraps. Such secrecy, say mathematicians, increases the chance of needless errors and risks creating an illusion of progress. They do not feel the labs are keeping their promises to be more transparent.

Take the announcement by OpenAI, an American lab, on October 26th, of solutions to three more long-standing problems. The first is a proof of the Kakeya conjecture, related to how to rotate an infinitely thin needle while sweeping out as little area as possible. Thus far the conjecture had been found to hold in up to three dimensions. OpenAI said its proof extends it to any number.

The second is a disproof of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), which sets an upper limit on how fast any algorithm can solve a specific problem. The hypothesis had long been assumed to be true, with implications for disciplines ranging from computational biology to database management. A proof that it is false “re-opens questions” about how quickly such tasks could be performed, said OpenAI. For both ETH and the Kakeya conjecture, the lab released the AI’s output so experts can begin working out what these results mean.

When it came to the third of the results, however, a cloak of secrecy descended. It is related to the Yang-Mills existence and mass-gap problem, one of seven landmark riddles known as the Millennium Prize problems. It asks whether a mathematical framework called Yang-Mills theory, which underpins physicists’ understanding of the universe, stands on firm mathematical footing (or, in mathematical jargon, “exists”). For many physicists, the question is of little relevance—the theory already makes predictions that match real-world data, so its truth is assumed. Mathematicians, though, are more pernickety.

OpenAI says its model has proved that Yang-Mills theory exists. But the firm has said little else. Instead, it has chosen to keep the AI’s 1,147-page proof under wraps while a “shepherding committee” of five physicists decides what to do with it. The committee has said that before they release it they “would like to be convinced that it is correct”. Until then, and until those outside the committee are similarly satisfied, there are question marks about how seriously to take their claim.

These worries are not theoretical. Ever since OpenAI released a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem—another of the Millennium Prize problems—on September 8th, mathematicians have been trying to follow its working. They know the proof is worth understanding because it was accompanied by a certificate of logical watertightness known as a Lean formalisation. If a proof translated into Lean code runs without errors, it verifies that the proof contains no inconsistencies.

In a study published online on October 6th, a team led by Anders Hansen, of the University of Cambridge, showed that the proof’s Lean verification does not, in fact, correspond to what is written in the paper. The problem is unlikely to be fatal. Dr Hansen reckons that the Lean code accurately reflects a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, but that its contents differ from those of the accompanying paper. OpenAI, for its part, says it is possible its models came up with two distinct proofs.

Anyone who has spent time navigating a foreign country will know that dodgy translations can cause misunderstandings. The same is true for mathematics. If AI labs do not check that a proof’s Lean code matches the ideas behind it, they risk creating unnecessary confusion. As Kevin Buzzard, a Lean whiz at Imperial College London, put it during his presentation at the Royal Society, the AI labs are doing only one part of the job.

articles.title: Is brown rice really healthier than white rice?
articles.deck: The scientific evidence goes against the grain

paragraphs.text: RICE SUPPLIES nearly a fifth of the world’s calories. Which sort, though, is healthiest? Brown rice becomes white when milling removes its fibrous outer layer (known as the bran), and nutrient-rich seed embryo (the germ), so nutritional lore naturally favours the former. Indeed, some striking findings seem to support that preference. Look closer, though, and the colour of rice may not be what matters most.

Rice is rich in starch, which digestion turns into glucose, or blood sugar. If the body struggles to regulate it, type-2 diabetes can eventually develop. Consider a review of eight observational studies that tracked the diets and health of 577,426 people. Writing in BMJ Open in 2022, the researchers calculated that once daily consumption exceeded about two 158-gram servings of cooked white rice, each additional serving was linked to a 13% higher risk of the disease.

Brown rice, meanwhile, appears to offer some protection. Fibre in the bran slows the breakdown of starch, so glucose enters the bloodstream more gradually. The bran and germ also contain magnesium, B vitamins and other nutrients that may help the body regulate blood sugar. A paper in Archives of Internal Medicine in 2010, included in the 2022 review, analysed three studies that followed 197,228 Americans for 14 to 22 years. Modelling suggested that replacing 50 grams of cooked white rice a day with brown rice was linked to a 16% lower risk of type-2 diabetes.

Correlation, though, is not causation. People who prefer brown rice tend to smoke less, exercise more and eat healthier food overall. Although the authors of the papers from 2022 and 2010 attempted to account for such confounding lifestyle differences, they acknowledged that their findings could still be skewed. So what happens when researchers actually instruct people to eat brown rather than white rice?

Not much. The 2022 review also examined 11 randomised controlled trials involving 1,034 participants. Those assigned to eat brown rice showed no statistically significant improvements in their short- or longer-term control of blood sugar. There was also no clear evidence of improved sensitivity to insulin, which helps cells absorb glucose. Nor did the trials consistently find improved blood pressure.

What matters more for blood sugar than rice’s colour, it turns out, is how much of a starch called amylose it contains. Amylose resists rapid digestion, so it limits spikes in blood sugar. A review of 32 randomised controlled trials published in 2015 identified amylose content—which is largely a function of a rice’s variety—as “the most consistently important” determinant of how sharply rice raises blood sugar.

Processing matters, too. Parboiling—soaking and steaming rice before milling—moves B vitamins from the bran into the grain while making its starch more resistant to digestion. An experiment reported in Nutrition in 2018 found that, among people without diabetes, eating parboiled rather than ordinary white rice reduced the cumulative rise in blood sugar over the following two hours by 38%. It also appeared to have an edge over ordinary brown rice.

A similar trick can be performed at home. Refrigerating cooked rice, whether brown or white, alters some of its starch so that it is digested more slowly. Care, though, is needed: to limit bacterial growth, rice should be cooled within an hour and reheated only once, until steaming hot, within a day.

articles.title: Is childlessness contagious?
articles.deck: A new book offers some surprising reasons people aren’t having children

paragraphs.text: IT’S ALL gone to the dogs. In South Korea sales of buggies for pets have overtaken those for children. Shrines in Japan sometimes bless more canines than babies. Conventional wisdom once held that when a couple got a puppy, they would start to conceive of parenthood—and then start trying to conceive. But a growing number of pet “parents” see four-legged creatures as a permanent substitute for two-legged offspring. Some firms have begun to offer “pawternity” leave, so employees can bond with a new pet or tend to it when it is sick.

Some find nothing cute or cuddly about the trend. Pope Francis warned about a “demographic winter” and frostily decried the choice not to have children as “selfish”. Elon Musk has said falling birth rates are the “biggest danger civilisation faces by far”. The largest 15 countries by GDP are now all below the population replacement rate, including America, China and India. Declining birth rates could cause the world’s population to shrink later this century for the first time since the Black Death killed tens of millions in the 14th century.

Baroness Camilla Cavendish, a columnist for the Financial Times, gives those delaying or forgoing children a name: Generation Maybe. In a fascinating new book, she examines why “what we once thought of as the most profound human instinct, to continue the line, is on the wane.”

The consequences of the baby bust are intuitive: ageing societies will have to rely on a smaller group of youngsters to fuel growth and fund pensions and public services. They are also enormous. Falling birth rates will reshape culture, society and geopolitics. By 2050 Nigeria will overtake America as the third-most-populous country, according to some projections (though such estimates are hotly debated). Low-growth nations could invade one another to expand their numbers and distract from tensions and anxiety at home, Lady Cavendish suggests. She predicts the world will become less peaceful and probably more religious, as “a greater proportion of the planet will live in countries with predominantly Islamic or Christian populations.”

And as more people choose to have just one child, it has sparked a “kin crash” of fewer siblings and other relatives. Fifty years ago the average Canadian 35-year-old would have had 20 living cousins. Today she has about ten, and in 2095 she may have only five. By the end of the century there will be a 38% global drop in the number of living relatives for people aged 65 compared with 1950, according to a study published by America’s National Academy of Sciences. The Beatles’ sombre chorus about “all the lonely people” may be what the future has in store.

What is behind this reverse baby fever? Affordability and housing costs get a lot of attention. Fewer people want to have a baby when they feel like a grown-up child, stuck living with their own parents. One study by Benjamin Couillard at the University of Toronto estimates that about half the recent decline in birth rates in America may be due to housing prices, and that around 13m more children would have been born from 1990 to 2020 if those costs had remained stable. Yet fertility has fallen sharply even in countries where housing is not especially expensive, including Japan.

Opportunity costs may be a bigger factor. Children demand a huge amount of time. As countries grow richer, the alternative uses for that time grow more attractive. And many parents think they have a better shot at winning the educational arms race if they shower Mandarin and violin lessons on one or two kids, rather than stretching their resources over three or four. Academics call this “intensive” parenting; others invoke analogies to helicopters and tigers.

“Social contagion” influences people’s opinions about whether to bear children and how many to have, Lady Cavendish intriguingly argues. TikTok videos exalt the gloriously #Childfree life, which apparently includes mid-afternoon naps, bucket-list travel, big savings and early retirement. (Sorry, exhausted parents, but it’s too late for second thoughts.) Research has shown TV shows, including MTV’s “16 and Pregnant” and Brazil’s telenovelas that feature small (albeit dysfunctional) families, have contributed to falling fertility rates. A growing body of “misery memoirs”, which complain about how hard parenthood and marriage are, acts as a prophylactic, too.

Friends and siblings can strongly influence how many children someone wants. Polish women who move to Britain, for instance, have more babies than their peers back home, “mirroring the household average of their new country, even though it often costs more to raise a child in London than in Warsaw”, Lady Cavendish writes.

Those who think they may like children but are waiting—for the right partner, the right moment, the right bank balance—may be wrongly guided. Lady Cavendish is searing about IVF and egg-freezing; clinics give women a rosier view of their prospect of parenthood than data support. The success rate for frozen embryos varies widely and depends on a woman’s age, but the national average in Britain is under 30%.

Men also face little-discussed problems as they get older. A “spermapocalypse” is quietly occurring, with men’s sperm count having fallen precipitously in many countries, possibly because of exposure to household products. Age degrades sperm quality, too, though even those alert to a ticking biological clock do not always factor in males’ fertility decline.

What can be done to baby-proof the baby bust? Immigration can help, but is often unpopular, and many countries are becoming less welcoming. Efforts to persuade people to have more babies have met little or no success. Campaigns are more likely to vitiate than titillate. Take the “Do it for Denmark” TV adverts (encouraging couples to go on holiday and send proof of conception to win prizes) or a rap in Singapore (“I’m a patriotic husband, you’re my patriotic wife, let’s do our civic duty and manufacture life!”).

Lady Cavendish runs through 11 less cringe-inducing ideas to boost baby-making, which span the sensible (teach both sexes more about the biological clock) to the improbable (rethink the whole education system so people can start families sooner). Some are no-brainers, like trying to make procreation less political and polarising. Other suggestions are brainteasers: for example, should families with children be entitled to more votes? Paul Demeny, a late demographer and economist, proposed that parents should be given a proxy vote for each of their children. This could help counteract older voters’ obvious self-interest in investing more in health care and less in education. But it seems like an unlikely political mantle.

Ultimately child-bearing is a personal choice with public consequences. The pressing question is whether Generation Maybe will become Generation No. For that, demographers and authors will have to wait for the next chapter.

articles.title: What is it like to be a newborn?
articles.deck: Nobody can quite say. But a new book tries to figure it out

paragraphs.text: The naked creature in the incubator measures perhaps 50 centimetres and weighs some 900 grams. It scowls and twitches but cannot smile. Its skin is almost transparent, and its veins close to invisible; it will take a doctor several minutes first to find one and then to draw a few drops of blood. It is probably intubated to help breathing; another tube trickles milk directly to the stomach. If you put tape on this fragile being, you will tear its skin. But if you leave it, it will cry.

Clémentine Goldszal, a French journalist, is consumed by this image and by a single imperative: to find out what birth is like for newborns, and how they experience the multiple medical interventions that may, in a worst case, immediately follow. She would interview them if she could. But of course there is no communication. When her own son Lucien was born, what she took as sweet kittenish sounds turned out to be signs of acute respiratory distress. An apparently lively baby may, in fact, be having convulsions.

She decided to “construct a phenomenology of the newborn” by spending many months as an observer in the neonatal unit of the Necker in Paris. This is a superb hospital, especially for its care of premature babies, rated seventh in the world. Sick babies are rushed there from all over France. Standing in a corner of the incubator rooms, out of the way, she sees nurses ceaselessly watching the beeping monitors, checking on breathing and feeding. In other rooms she watches operations so delicate, performed with miniature instruments, that a margin of error of a millimetre would be a catastrophe.

What she wanted to decipher was the attitude of medical staff to the newborn: whether or not they considered them fully human, individual and even having personalities. She had viewed Lucien as merely “a generic entity” for some weeks, and found it hard to say his name. But at Necker newborn patients were all called by their names and treated tenderly. They were assumed to have agency, if only to close their eyes or poo in their nappies. When those nappies were changed, blankets were put over the incubators to shield their privacy. After all, in French law, they were individuals as soon as they drew breath and no longer occupied their mother’s womb.

And yet without their consent, these babies were invaded. They were injected, intubated, placed among noisy machines and blinded by harsh lights. Tiny catheters were sent in to deliver fluids. In France 94% of babies born between 27 and 31 weeks left the hospital in perfect health. (At 25 weeks, though, the figure fell to 60%.)

These numbers were improving steadily, and had been doing so ever since the days when the only treatment for a struggling newborn was to dangle it by its heels or, in the case of Louis XIII of France, dose it with red wine. Nonetheless, Ms Goldszal worries about the long-term effects of brutal modern procedures, even wondering whether her disabled or confused friends were damaged by them, long before they knew how to complain.

She paints a gripping, vivid picture of life at Necker, especially the nurses, permanently exhausted but perceptive enough to lay a gentle hand on a newborn, turn down the lighting, or rock them. It is the medical setting, among people in scrubs and the tang of sanitiser, that thrills her: she finds herself surrounded at staff meetings by “an entire continent” of words she can’t understand: oesophageal atresia, hypocalcaemia, exomphalos.

Ms Goldszal goes only sketchily into the philosophy of personhood and the difficult legal line between the full-term fetus inside the womb and the newborn outside it. For ideas of ensoulment she has even less time. She envies religious Jews their belief that God breathes life into the fetus at the moment of birth, but she is a modern woman; this is really just “magical thinking”.

All she needs to know she has seen at Necker, and it is “fundamentally prosaic”: new life appears where before there was nothing, and medical ingenuity does its best to ensure that life does not swiftly return to nothing again.

Yet a mystery remains. The last epigram that opens the book comes from J.G. Ballard, an English writer, recording the birth of his daughter: “For the first few seconds I had the sense she was immensely old. She looked like something from Egyptian sculpture, streamlined by time. Within a few seconds she was suddenly very young.” Newborns may seem able to tell us nothing. But perhaps sometimes, for a moment, their eyes and their parents can.

articles.title: What goes on behind the doors of Claridge’s?
articles.deck: A new book gives readers a key card to the storied hotel’s past

paragraphs.text: THINGS CHANGE all the time inside hotels. Guests check in and out; towels and bed sheets are regularly laundered (or so you would hope). Hotels are also forced to accommodate upheavals that take place outside their doors. Two recent books, “The Finest Hotel in Kabul” and “Hotel Exile”, explored the turmoil of the 20th century from the front desks of hotels in Afghanistan and France. Now readers can journey to Claridge’s, one of London’s most prestigious hotels.

Martin Williams, a historian, traces how the hotel has witnessed all manner of political and cultural shifts since 1812. This is a top-down view of history, for Claridge’s clients have always been exceptionally posh. Princes and empresses slept there on visits to Britain; the future George IV, then prince regent, was thought to have slept there with lovers.

In periods of turmoil, such as the revolutions of 1848 and the second world war, European royals and aristocrats ousted from their countries took refuge in Mayfair. Alexander, the crown prince of Yugoslavia, was born in one of its suites in 1945. (Dirt was rumoured to have been spread under the bed so he could say he was born “on Yugoslavian soil”.) Legend holds that a diplomat once telephoned the hotel and asked to speak to the king. “Certainly, sir,” the operator said. “But which one?”

The war years are invariably the most fascinating. Soldiers back from Dunkirk—their uniforms still covered in “salt, sand and sweat”—lunched in the restaurant alongside women in hats. (Like the best hotels, this book pays attention to the details.) American officials moved in to be close to the embassy and were charmed by the hotel’s old-world grandeur. Though Dwight Eisenhower, then commander of American forces in Europe, was not among them: he took offence to his room’s “whorehouse pink” decor.

In the decades since, many notable people have strolled through the lobby. Audrey Hepburn first met William Wyler, the director of “Roman Holiday” (1953), in the hotel; the movie would make her a star and an Oscar winner. In 1974 Agatha Christie made one of her last public appearances at a dinner there, when she celebrated the premiere of the film adaptation of “Murder on the Orient Express”. In 1970 Jackie Kennedy Onassis prompted the hotel to overturn its long-standing policy banning women from wearing trousers.

The trousers tussle notwithstanding, Claridge’s has managed a difficult balance of tradition and innovation over the course of its two centuries. Mr Williams shows how it has adapted time and again to changing social mores and expectations of high-end hospitality. Today it lures foodies and fashionistas. Gordon Ramsay and Noma have had stints in the restaurant; since 2009 the hotel has invited a fashion designer to create its Christmas tree. (This year’s will be unveiled on November 25th, though the designer has yet to be announced.) If you do not feel like shelling out between £1,500 and £60,000 ($2,000-80,000) for a suite, “Claridge’s” offers a sweet (and cheap) escape.

articles.title: Is it time to end the era of remote work?
articles.deck: A new book makes a case for getting out of your tracksuit and into your officewear

paragraphs.text: Those mulling the current AI boom should look back to a kitchen in Google’s office in the early 2000s. Two employees, Noam Shazeer and Georges Harik, began to chat about how computers differentiated between essential and superfluous information. This chance encounter windingly led to the mechanism that underpins large language models.

Had Google allowed remote work, Mr Shazeer and Mr Harik might never have spoken. In-person spitballing has led to ideas ranging from the hugely consequential (IBM’s personal computer) to the hugely entertaining (“Finding Nemo”). That is one reason why bosses often lament the rise of remote work, notes a new book by Natalia Emanuel and Emma Harrington, two economists. In 2019 American workers spent 7% of their paid days working at home. Now it is about a quarter.

Studies suggest that remote work may increase the quantity of output while decreasing its quality. In 2025 a review of return-to-office mandates at large banks found that when firms called analysts back to the office for a few days each week, the accuracy of their earnings forecasts leaped 15% compared with peers at banks that remained fully remote.

What is more, remote work tends to dent the sort of tasks that rarely show up in measures of output. Senior software engineers write more code from the comfort of their homes, but they review junior employees’ work less comprehensively. Lost mentorship and undiscovered ideas can affect the future of a firm.

Such losses may be why the shift has stung new graduates in particular. A new study by Peter John Lambert of the London School of Economics and Yannick Schindler of the University of Oxford suggests remote work, not AI, is to blame for young jobseekers’ woes of late. Jobs done entirely online tend to be susceptible to being done remotely. Firms that are reluctant to let untested employees work away from their boss’s watchful eye may be choosing not to hire them at all.

So why not cancel the corporate Zoom subscription and squeeze back into the cubicle? The authors note that some employees are well-served by remote work: for example, parents and people with disabilities. For most companies a mix is best. To help bosses settle on the right number of days in-office, “In Person” features a “calculator” that asks them to add and subtract days based on the firm’s characteristics. But what executive would not say the stakes of their business are high (add two days), or that innovation is crucial to their firm’s future (add three days)? When it comes to such decisions, psychologists may be more helpful than economists.

Still, many of the book’s points are well-taken. How many days employees spend at the office may be less important than whether they overlap with key colleagues. Hot-desking is a scourge, as would-be collaborators sit together only occasionally. And if bosses want to reap the benefits of in-person culture, they also need to show face. “In Person” should contribute to an ongoing conversation about why remote work has remained so persistent if it comes with so many drawbacks. Watercooler-chat lovers, rejoice.

articles.title: Chinese tech helps repressive African governments crush dissent
articles.deck: A fascinating new book investigates the cause and effects of China’s investment in Africa

paragraphs.text: WHEN CHINA paid $200m to build a new headquarters for the African Union (AU) in Addis Ababa (pictured), it was perceived as an act of great generosity. But five years later technicians noticed something odd. Late every night the servers, which had been provided by China, whirred furiously. Data was being exported to servers in Shanghai, including confidential emails, diplomats’ memos, security-camera footage and more. Algerian and Ethiopian specialists who later swept the building reportedly found microphones hidden under desks and inside walls.

The Chinese government and the companies involved, Huawei and ZTE, all denied any wrongdoing. No surprise there. More dismaying was the public reaction of African leaders, who voiced fury not over the surveillance but towards the reporters who helped expose it. In a gripping new book, Paul Kenyon, a British journalist, argues that China is the latest external power out to gouge the continent while empowering corrupt, local power-brokers.

His broader warning is that much of Africa is being taken over by Chinese tech. Many autocratic governments are using Chinese systems to monitor their people, especially dissidents. That means snooping via mobile-phone networks installed by Chinese firms, for example. Think of the methods of information control in Xinjiang being applied in Zimbabwe, Kenya and beyond. Mr Kenyon, who has a good eye for detail but a tendency to overstate his case, alleges that Chinese engineers in Africa are the “foot soldiers of China’s digital colonialism, enabling totalitarian regimes to prosper in Africa because China wants them to”.

China’s tech is spreading rapidly across Africa thanks partly to generous loans, which make it cheap. Much of it is used to hamper free speech and browsing. A Chinese company, Geedge, exports a version of China’s Great Firewall, for example, so African governments can try to censor what citizens see online.

Nasty regimes are the keenest to learn from China. In Kampala, the hilly capital of Uganda, white poles have been erected; they are topped with some 5,000 cameras that feed images to 83 monitoring centres. This is presented to the public as a measure to cut crime: the monitors use AI, facial recognition and biometric analysis to track individuals. But it is also a tool for a repressive government: Yoweri Museveni, the president, can monitor those who support the opposition.

For years America, Britain and other rich countries have shunned contracts with Huawei and ZTE, citing security risks. No such hesitancy exists in Africa, where few governments could afford to risk damaging relations with a big trading partner. China has also provided loans for countries, including Algeria and Nigeria, to pay for satellites that it built and launched.

In a related corner of the contest for information, Mr Kenyon points to the surging number of Chinese communications staff, whom he calls “propagandists”, setting up in Africa. Xinhua, China’s official state news agency, has around 35 bureaus on the continent, more than any other news firm.

What is the end-game? China is pursuing Africa’s natural resources, including its abundant oil reserves and rare earths. But it is also trying to win political support for its challenge to Western values. China may succeed in creating a “splinternet” in Africa, with digital interaction happening only in tightly monitored spaces.

This would be a “sterile world” with no dissent, Mr Kenyon argues. It would also mark a change from today when, in order to shut up opposition voices, governments sometimes cut off millions of people from online services for months or even years. “China’s African Empire” is a clear-headed warning that, as with the AU building, China is not necessarily the benign partner it claims to be. Sometimes you need to look a gift horse in the mouth.

articles.title: Explaining the popularity of Max Richter’s compositions
articles.deck: The classical composer manages to spin even serious subjects into gold

paragraphs.text: DOES ANY musician get around as much as Max Richter? In April he will be in Las Vegas, providing musical direction for Oprah Winfrey’s “immersive symphony of senses” at the Sphere. He is on screens: his soundtrack for “Hamnet” was nominated for an Academy Award this year. And he may well be in your bedroom: “Sleep”, his eight-and-a-half-hour-long composition, has been streamed more than 2bn times.

But it is probably through “On the Nature of Daylight”, a soulful six-minute composition for string quintet from 2004, that Mr Richter (pictured) has most successfully colonised the consciousness of listeners. It heightens emotions in at least a dozen films and television programmes, including “My Brilliant Friend” and “Arrival”. It transforms millions of commutes into occasions for reverie. Listeners will hear echoes of it on “While the Flood Rages”, a new album.

Achieving such ubiquity would be a feat for any composer. That Mr Richter writes classical music makes it more remarkable. Born in Germany and brought up in Britain, Mr Richter studied at the Royal Academy of Music in London and with Luciano Berio, an Italian modernist. If you do not detect the classical pedigree in Mr Richter’s music, he may point it out to you. In an interview at his studio in the Cotswolds he relocates from the sofa to the piano to demonstrate that a falling sequence of notes from his new album is reminiscent of the music of Johann Sebastian Bach. His record label is Decca, among the most storied in classical music.

But the genre would confine Mr Richter if he did not bend it. Kraftwerk, a German electronic band, is an influence alongside American minimalists such as Philip Glass. The piano in his studio keeps company with banks of vintage synthesisers, giving it the appearance of “mission control”, he jokes. As is fashionable, he deems the conventional distinction between classical music and other sorts to be “bizarre”.

Mr Richter’s medley of influences and instincts have landed him in a musical sweet spot shared with few contemporary composers. Thanks in part to his classical chops, he collaborates with choreographers as well as film directors. “While the Flood Rages” draws from music he wrote for a ballet, “MaddAddam”, which in turn is inspired by a post-apocalyptic trilogy by Margaret Atwood, teller of “The Handmaid’s Tale”. In April the Orchestre de Paris will play the premiere of a cello concerto Mr Richter is writing.

His music has an emotional directness that gives it much wider appeal than that of most living classical composers. Mari Samuelsen, a Norwegian violinist who often performs it, finds it “extremely meditative and cleansing”, both “simple and complex at the same time”. Although film and phone are its natural habitat, Mr Richter’s music also packs concert halls. Audiences tend to be younger than at conventional classical concerts, she says, and more prone to share reactions on social media.

To some listeners the sweet spot is too sweet. Some think his partnerships with brands such as Krug champagne and Christian Dior, a fashion house, are evidence that his art lulls rather than challenges. Alex Ross, a prominent critic, has written that Mr Richter’s pieces “exude a gentle fatalism, a numbed acquiescence” even in the face of “global disaster”. Many deal explicitly with political themes. “Voices”, from 2020, incorporates text from the UN human-rights declaration. “Sleep”, Mr Richter has said, is a “protest” against a “very super-industrialised, intense, mechanised way of living”. “Daylight” comes from an album that opposes America’s war in Iraq. Yet most of the time the strife seems to be happening in the distance.

“While the Flood Rages” considers the aftermath of apocalypse, environmental vandalism and corporate greed. Mr Richter says the music is “more highly coloured” than what he normally composes, echoing the “stylistic omnivorousness” of Ms Atwood’s writing. Synthetic and recorded sounds—of water, of gunfire—suggest a world made strange and threatening. But Mr Richter’s sensibility has the last word. Piano, strings and a church-like choir, sometimes in counterpoint with eerier music, seem to suggest that something good will prevail. The listener, unsettled at first by the album’s dystopian theme, may come away consoled.

That is often the effect of Mr Richter’s music. Rather than depict evil, he imagines alternatives to it. “We’re flooded with negativity, with negative images and negative storytelling,” largely because of social media, he says. “I’m looking to celebrate and elevate the things that are not that, which are ordinary…human qualities which have been with us for ever and will continue to be with us, but are easy to overlook.” While floods rage, Mr Richter offers audiences a life raft. No wonder he’s so in demand.
Correction (November 5th 2026): An earlier version of this story said that “On the Nature of Daylight” could be heard in “Black Mirror”. That was incorrect. Sorry.

articles.title: Dolores Huerta fought for farm-workers’ rights—and kept devastating secrets
articles.deck: The labour activist died on October 28th, aged 96

paragraphs.text: IN LATE November 1986 the United Farm Workers of America (UFW), a labour union, was ready to celebrate. Earlier that month, then-president Ronald Reagan signed into law the Immigration Reform and Control Act, for which the UFW had spent months lobbying. It offered undocumented immigrants long resident in America a path to citizenship, and gave farm workers who could prove 90 days of employment legal permanent residency. It also penalised employers who knowingly hired undocumented workers, whom the union feared would drive down wages and serve as scabs during a strike.

Shortly before a news conference to mark the legislative win, one of the UFW’s founders, César Chávez, told another founder, Dolores Huerta, that she was needed in Florida. A crisis, he said. So of course, she went, because that’s what she did: go where workers needed her. But when she got to Florida, she found there was no crisis. Nobody was expecting her. “They just wanted to get me out of the way so they could take credit for the work,” she said later. “Straight male-chauvinist trick.”

But hardly uncommon, as one fellow activist recalled: “The assumption was that [Chávez] was the leader, and Dolores was the housekeeper of the movement.” In fact, they founded the union together—though unlike him, she had to balance work with raising her 14 children. With his soulful dark eyes, conversational speaking style and love of the microphone, he was the charismatic front man. But she was the union’s chief negotiator. He could make the speeches; there were also boycotts to organise, contracts to negotiate and people who needed help.

Her mother, Alicia, had a similar streak of dogged practicality. After a divorce, Alicia took her three children from New Mexico to Stockton, California, in the Central Valley, California’s agricultural heartland. After stints as a waitress, cannery worker and restaurateur, Alicia ran a 70-room hotel that welcomed migrant workers, often waiving room fees if they were too steep. Alicia, Dolores recalled, “thought she was their mother”, and gave them curfews, made sure they sent money home and didn’t drink away their paychecks, and invited them to dances so they could meet nice girls and settle down—which many did.

From Alicia, who participated in a cannery-workers’ strike in 1938 and joined civic groups in Stockton, Dolores learned about activism, which was nothing more than helping people who needed help, and speaking up for people who could not advocate for themselves. After training as a teacher, she turned to full-time organising in her 20s, when she joined the Community Service Organisation in Stockton. Its founder introduced her to Chávez, and soon afterward the two founded the group that would, after merging with another farm-workers’ group, become the UFW.

From the start, she held her own. As an “experienced lobbyist”, she wrote to Chávez, “I am able to speak on a man-to-man basis with other lobbyists.” Elected officials learned to fear her. She was “indefatigable” and “unorthodox”, recalled one state senator from California. “Dolores will bring in hundreds of people, and they’ll camp outside your office.”

And although sleeping in a Senate hallway sounds uncomfortable, it was nothing compared with what her union members were used to. They worked in the fields for 16 hours a day. There were no toilets: female workers had to squat behind a towel or a blanket. The only drinking water sat baking in a tank under the sun all day. No health care or unemployment insurance, no recourse if the farm owners cheated them.

So she and Chávez got to work. In 1965 their union, which mainly represented Mexican farm workers, joined 2,000 Filipinos on strike at vineyards near Delano, California. Growers hired scabs and refused negotiations, figuring they could force the workers to back down, as they had before.

But times were changing. Strikers drew support from civil-rights activists including Robert F. Kennedy and Martin Luther King junior. They borrowed tactics from the civil-rights movement, calling for boycotts of table grapes. By 1970 the growers had given in, agreeing to raise wages and recognise the union. Membership in the UFW swelled, and five years later California passed a law protecting farm-workers’ rights to unionise, and making migrant workers eligible for health insurance and other benefits.

Chávez became a hero, giving his name to streets, parks and schools across California and beyond, despite whispers about his authoritarian tendencies, his insistence on personal loyalty and subservience. She kept doing the work, campaigning for women’s rights and encouraging them to run for office, picketing and protesting. Age barely slowed her; a policeman broke her ribs and ruptured her spleen during a demonstration when she was almost 60.

But not until this year did Dolores reveal her deepest secret: Chávez, who died in 1993, had raped her in 1966. He had pressed her into sex years earlier. Two of her children were his. She never spoke up because “I didn’t want to hurt the movement.”

A New York Times investigation found that he assaulted and molested multiple women and girls, some as young as 12. Sexism pervaded his union. Liz Sullivan, a UFW organiser who was raped by two men after an organising meeting, recalled that union members berated her and female colleagues who spoke out about the treatment of women. The male executives had no patience for “women’s lib and all that other bullshit”.

In recent months, statues of Chávez have come down and parks renamed. Some blamed Dolores, too, for keeping quiet and dismissing their complaints about being sexually harassed and assaulted by their colleagues. Ms Sullivan took a more charitable view. She urged people to “see her as a human being, in all her beauty and with all her faults, just like the rest of us”.

articles.title: Politics

paragraphs.text: Curfews were imposed in Paris, Lyon and other cities following the worst rioting and looting in France in years. More than 2,000 people were arrested as masked casseurs, or hooligans, targeted shops, businesses and political premises. The roof of the town hall in Limoges, which withstood two world wars, collapsed after it was set on fire. The government admitted the police had lost control of the protests. The French president addressed the nation and said “nothing justifies” the violence. Marine Le Pen, the right-wing front-runner in next year’s presidential election, warned of a threat to democracy and blamed Mr Macron and the left. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the left-wing’s candidate, denied he was stirring up trouble by urging support for the protests.

Widespread looting accompanied similar protests in Italy. The government announced new security steps that allow the police to detain under-18s for 12 hours, among other measures. To prevent further unrest hundreds of soldiers were deployed to Milan, which has borne the brunt of the trouble and saw luxury-goods shops ransacked.

In Albania student-led protests over corruption, poor education and a lack of jobs spread from Tirana to other cities and towns. Riot police used tear-gas and rubber bullets against the demonstrators when they reached the Ministry of Education. Edi Rama said he would not resign as prime minister, and warned that the protesters were endangering Albania’s path to membership of the EU.

Volodymyr Zelensky flew to Oslo for a meeting with Steve Witkoff, Donald Trump’s envoy, amid a deterioration in relations between Ukraine and the White House. Earlier, Mr Trump took another step towards favouring Russia by waiving sanctions mandated by the Graham Act, which he signed into law last month. Mr Zelensky criticised Mr Trump’s waiver, arguing that the act was “supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia”. The Americans described the meeting in Oslo as constructive. Mr Witkoff then flew to St Petersburg for talks with Vladimir Putin. The Kremlin said Mr Putin had agreed to restart three-way peace talks.

At his meeting with Mr Witkoff Mr Putin announced that Stephen Hubbard, an American citizen, had been released from prison. Mr Hubbard, 74, was arrested in 2022. The Russians claim he was manning a checkpoint in Ukraine; his family have rejected accusations that he is a mercenary. His release is another indication of Mr Trump’s closer relations with Moscow. The president had personally called on Mr Putin to set Mr Hubbard free.

Britain said it would deploy fighter jets and a transport aircraft to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom against attacks by the Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran. The jets will help protect infrastructure and residential areas, but will not conduct offensive strikes against the rebels. In Yemen the Houthis fired missiles at a training camp for government forces, killing at least 73 people. The Yemeni government is allied with the Saudis.

Egypt’s president, Abdel-Fattah al-Sisi, also pledged to help the Saudis, and asked parliament to approve the deployment of combat forces. The extent of any Egyptian involvement in the conflict is unclear. Turkey’s parliament was also considering a plan to send military personnel to Saudi Arabia.

More than 80 people were killed in a drone strike near a market in southern Sudan, most of them commuters on their way home from work. The Rapid Support Forces, which controls the area, blamed the strike on the army, which it is fighting in a civil war. Another drone hit a town in a disputed region near the border with South Sudan, killing at least 150 people. Such attacks causing mass civilian casualties have become increasingly common in the three-year conflict.

A former Rwandan soldier and vocal critic of Paul Kagame, Rwanda’s president, was found beheaded near Kampala, the capital of neighbouring Uganda. Robert Kabera, who fled to Uganda in 2020, had recently posted on social media that he feared for his life. He is not the first exiled Rwandan dissident to turn up dead in gruesome circumstances.

Nigeria confirmed its first case of Ebola since the Democratic Republic of Congo announced an outbreak of the disease in May. Authorities said the patient had travelled to Nigeria from Uganda. The Ugandan government said there were currently no active cases of the disease in the country.

America’s State Department reported that 300,000 visas have now been revoked during Donald Trump’s second term, up from the 175,000 that had been tallied up to early August. Announcing the new numbers an official reiterated the administration’s policy: “zero tolerance for foreigners here on visas who break the law”.

A non-binding referendum in Alberta saw more than 75% of voters back an option to remain a province of Canada, rather than start the process of holding a binding referendum on splitting away. Mark Carney hailed the outcome as a victory for “unity”. “Canada is so much greater than the sum of its parts,” he said. However, Albertans did back other measures in the referendum to give the province more control over immigration.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro debated each other ahead of Brazil’s presidential election run-off on October 25th. Polls show the race has narrowed since the first round on October 4th, when Mr Bolsonaro took 47% of the vote to Lula’s 45%.

Marco Rubio, America’s secretary of state, met Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, India’s foreign minister, in Mumbai for talks on finalising a trade deal. The pact has been held up for months because of tensions over American tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. But Mr Rubio now says an agreement is “very, very close”.

More than 9,500 police officers were deployed in Jakarta to deter student-led protests that were called to mark the second anniversary of Prabowo Subianto’s inauguration as Indonesia’s president. The deterrence worked, as few students gathered to demand Mr Prabowo do more to tackle the cost of living and other grievances. The president’s approval rating has plunged since taking office. MSCI, a global index service, warned that it might remove Indonesia’s emerging-market status because of its “market dysfunction”. Downgrading Indonesia would force many tracking funds to sell their Indonesian assets.

Japan’s space agency launched a spacecraft on a five-year mission to collect samples from Phobos, one of two small moons that orbit Mars, the first-ever return journey from the planet’s system. The spacecraft will enter Martian space in August 2027, landing on Phobos at some point in the following years. A rover will use a robotic arm to collect moondust. If all goes well, the spacecraft will depart in 2030 and return to Earth in 2031.

articles.title: Business

paragraphs.text: Elon Musk floated the possibility of merging SpaceX and Tesla. There is a “lot of merit” in combining the companies, he said, and the boards of both have created independent committees to explore their options (as the boss and largest shareholder in both firms Mr Musk is not on the committees). A merger would bring together Mr Musk’s AI ambitions for data centres, driverless cars and robots. SpaceX, meanwhile, reported quarterly revenue of $14.6bn, up by 161% year on year, $7.6bn of which came from AI (which it calls SI, or super intelligence). Mr Musk has pledged to give every child in America one SpaceX share, currently worth nearly $160, next year.

Tesla earlier demonstrated its new Roadster sports car; the demonstration vehicle was modified with SpaceX-derived thrusters and able to flip mid-air and land safely again. The electric-carmaker reported a surprise positive cashflow in its latest earnings.

Market jitters resurfaced about the huge investments being made in AI. CoreWeave, which rents out data-centre capacity, saw its bonds and share price plunge amid worries that it will not be able to service its debt. The sell-off spread to other “neocloud” companies. Meanwhile, the share price of Elice, an AI-infrastructure company, fell by 32% on its first day of trading in South Korea.

Anthropic registered a net loss of more than $80bn in the first half of this year, according to press reports, mostly because of an accounting charge related to bonds that could be eventually converted to shares. The frontier-AI firm is expected to make its stock-market debut in mid-November. Anthropic is to hand over 5% of its shares to a new public-benefit fund it has created to work in AI safety and examine AI’s impact on the jobs market, among other things.

Meta’s third-quarter revenue grew by 26%, year on year, to $64.6bn. The company rolled out its Muse personal AI agent in September. Meanwhile, a court in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn to the state after it was found to have misled users about privacy.
Barclays, a big British bank, revealed that it is cutting 5,000 jobs this year because of efficiencies from adopting AI. Most of the jobs will be among developers and other support services.

Stock in Netflix slid again after the streaming giant reported its slowest sales growth in three years. Revenue grew by 11.8% in the third quarter, year on year, to $12.9bn. It expects even lower growth of 11.5% in the fourth quarter. Media reports of the company’s woes as it struggles with slowing subscriptions read like a Hollywood movie plot, with both the head of film and the head of content summarily dismissed from their positions and the announcement of 1,000 job cuts. Despite massively increasing its spending on content, Netflix is no longer producing a string of hits.
GDP expanded in China by 4.5% during the third quarter, year on year, an improvement on the 4.3% recorded in the second quarter. China’s exports boom is offsetting weak domestic demand.

The riots in France helped push the yield on French ten-year government bonds above 5% for the first time since 2002, as investors bet that budgetary reforms would be delayed. Carrefour, a big supermarket chain, cut its annual profit forecast and blamed the violence, which it thinks will deter shoppers. Insurance losses from the weekend’s unrest are expected to reach €1bn ($1.1bn), exceeding the €700m in losses incurred over a week of rioting in 2023.

The developers of the PHP programming language issued a fix that they urged users to download immediately, after an OpenAI-led consortium discovered two critical vulnerabilities. PHP shores up a large part of the internet, running in the background of websites, hosting platforms and control panels. Some governments, including in Finland and the Netherlands, took some websites offline while they worked on the issue. America’s National Security Agency recommended that systems be taken offline if users couldn’t apply the mitigations. The fix will have alerted criminals to the vulnerability of servers.
Britain’s annual inflation rate jumped to 3.5% in September. Markets are now all but certain that the Bank of England will raise interest rates at its meeting in November.

The British government at last approved the development of the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, the first big endorsement of a fossil-fuel project under Andy Burnham as prime minister. The governing Labour Party has pledged to deliver a net-zero carbon emissions policy. Greens are furious, but Mr Burnham said it would protect jobs. Unions hailed the decision. The government is now under pressure to approve the Rosebank oil project, which environmentalists also vehemently oppose.

UniCredit, Italy’s second-largest bank, won approval from the European Central Bank to take over Commerzbank, a big German lender. Having secured 48% of Commerzbank’s shares, UniCredit thinks it will take control of the bank by the end of the year.

The IPO of Jio Platforms, Mukesh Ambani’s telecoms firm, was fully subscribed just two hours after it opened. The flotation is expected to raise $3.2bn, making it India’s biggest-ever listing. The shares start trading on October 28th.

articles.title: The agony of liberal Europe
articles.deck: Centrist rulers have fallen dangerously short—and are now paying the price

paragraphs.text: “The first steps into the Unrest seem straightforward enough—anger at the fall of real wages, at capitalist aggression, at the unwillingness of Parliament; anger fomented by agitators...reason wars with instinct.” Few of those who mobbed French cities this week would recognise those words. But many would agree with George Dangerfield, the British-American journalist who wrote them. The demonstrators were consumed by rage. Rage at the failure of the state and against the floundering centrist politicians who govern. Rage at high prices and economic dysfunction. And for some, rage against the idea of centrist politics at all.

Dangerfield wrote about “the strange death of liberal England” in the years before the first world war. Some predict a similarly grim fate for liberal Europe today. Arson, mob violence, looting and mass protests show how much citizens despair of their leaders. France has a long tradition of the manif, but the violence unleashed by hooded and masked rioters across the country over the past weekend was unusually severe. Protests also flared in Belgium, Italy and Portugal. In looming elections, first in Spain next month, then in France and Poland next year, voters are poised to punish moderate parties—and in Italy the far right is outflanking the populist Giorgia Meloni, who has governed from the centre. In the wings wait more charismatic figures from the extremes, including Marine Le Pen in France and Alice Weidel in Germany.

Many in America and in Europe say the centre has only itself to blame. Donald Trump crows that Europe is on fire because its leaders spurned his advice, left their borders open and let millions of immigrants rush in each year, from Afghanistan, Algeria and Syria. Those on the MAGA right, such as Elon Musk, say growing Muslim populations pose the greatest threat. Some talk, apocalyptically and absurdly, of “civilisational erasure” or civil war. Even in Germany the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said this week that high rates of migration and a failure to integrate the foreign-born are partly behind the sudden, violent upheaval. So has Hungary’s newish prime minister, Peter Magyar.

Their analysis is either craven or self-serving. Undoubtedly, many European voters also wish to curb immigration and asylum. But when it comes to the violent protests, the diagnosis is plain wrong. Instead the problems facing Europe’s centrists are more complex—and less easy to fix.

Even if some young protesters in France wear Algerian football shirts or chant pro-Palestinian slogans, the upheaval in Europe today is not about race or religion. Over 500,000 people marched in France on Saturday and they were largely unmasked and white. They were fired up, as in other countries, by the cost of living and poor public services. They want more fuel subsidies, more spending on schools, more handouts. Perhaps the largest group are aligned with the populist-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon, an ageing rabble-rouser and one-time Trotskyist, more akin to Bernie Sanders than an emir of ISIS.

Real violence did follow. But blame that on other factors, none to do with race. Mobs struck at public buildings, police cars and more. They also smashed and grabbed from luxury retailers, like Louis Vuitton, and small stores run by immigrants. The police failed to keep order, having earlier been accused of brutality against student protesters. And much of the violence was incited and orchestrated by anarchists, who have a revolutionary political agenda. Typical among them is a man arrested after the burning of a 19th-century town hall in Limoges, a white French citizen in his mid-30s.

Although the critics are wrong, Europe’s centrists do face real problems—and France shows how serious they are. The first is the fiscal bind that makes effective political action so hard. When Emmanuel Macron, the president, faced huge protests by the gilets jaunes in 2018-19, he could deploy billions of euros to placate them. Today, that is no longer possible. France is spending too much and growing too slowly—by just over 1% a year under Mr Macron.

This autumn, lawmakers will struggle to pass a budget that cuts the deficit by a feeble 0.4 percentage points, to an unsustainable 5% of GDP. And still the government may fall. France is so overborrowed, and markets have so little faith in its politicians, that spreads of French government bonds over German ones have soared to levels last seen during the euro crisis.

Instead of rising to this challenge, the centrists seem out of ideas. The Economist once cheered Mr Macron as a bold new standard-bearer for radical centrism. Today, while centrists huddle together for protection, all the energy is at the extremes. Surveys say over 80% of the French are pessimistic about their future, especially about their economy. Mr Merz is deeply unpopular and may be forced from office. His anti-migrant sniping reflects his inability to find the words and ideas to see off Ms Weidel and her party, the Alternative for Germany.

No wonder the centrists face an electoral walloping. Polls show that Pedro Sánchez, the centre-left prime minister in Spain, will probably be turfed out soon to be replaced by a coalition of the centre- and populist right. In France the riots—and the myth that immigrants were to blame—may lift Ms Le Pen of the populist-right National Rally into the presidency in May. Polls show that the violence boosted her this week. While Mr Macron jetted off on a trip to the Gulf, Ms Le Pen gave a presidential-sounding speech calling for public order.

The violence in France should jolt head-in-the-sand centrists to confront the consequences of failure. If their countries descend into strife, they will lose power. If they lose power, the European Union will choke, as the rest of the world races ahead. If bond markets seize up, financial contagion could spread. If EU countries indulge Vladimir Putin of Russia, he will only become more aggressive. Dangerfield was writing about a time when most people were ignorant of the catastrophe that lay ahead. Today’s liberals have no such excuse.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia and the UAE are sowing chaos
articles.deck: Gulf powers should stop fuelling carnage in their backyard

paragraphs.text: Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) could once pose as oases of stability. Now the two Gulf powers are under siege. A hostile Iran has a chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz, through which much of their commerce flows. The Houthis, an Iran-backed militia in Yemen, are lobbing missiles at Saudi airports and pipelines, disrupting trade and travel, and threatening Bab al-Mandab, another vital waterway. America, once the Gulf states’ most reliable ally, is now less willing to guarantee their security, leaving both countries exposed.

Given the scale of the crisis, you might think the Saudis and Emiratis would be marshalling their resources to deal with the problems close to home. Instead, they are tussling for influence farther afield, and recklessly inflaming some of the worst wars in the world.

The conflicts on either side of the Red Sea have complex causes. The Emiratis and Saudis did not start them, and are not the only foreign powers meddling, but they are making them bloodier and harder to end. This is clearest in Sudan, where a mass-raping genocidal militia, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), is fighting the Sudanese army for control of the country. So vile are the RSF that they hunt down and kill doctors, since any doctor can testify to their crimes. Yet the Emiratis arm and support the RSF. (They deny it.) The Saudis back the somewhat less brutal regular army.

In Yemen, where both the Saudis and Emiratis have battled the Houthis, their squabbles have led to an Emirati pullback and allowed the Houthis, a regional menace, to fill the vacuum. The two Gulf states also vie for influence over ports on the Red Sea. Their competing alliances risk further aggravating tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, which are already close to (another) disastrous war.

Little of this makes sense. Granted, the ports of the Horn of Africa could be vital to regional trade, particularly as other routes are under threat. And as America becomes less dependable under President Donald Trump, it is reasonable for both Saudi Arabia and the UAE to develop networks of allies to bolster their own security. But not like this. The two Gulf states’ projections of power seem to owe more to the petulant rivalry between their respective rulers, Muhammad bin Salman and Muhammad bin Zayed, than to any thoughtful strategy. By arming combatants, failing to curb the laundering of war loot and making conflicts more complex, they are likely to prolong them.

The human cost is vast. The wars in Sudan and Yemen have claimed hundreds of thousands of lives, driven nearly 20m people from their homes and pushed millions to the brink of famine. That alone should be ample spur for the Gulf meddlers to change course.

Failing that, they should recognise that their foreign adventurism threatens their own interests. Chaos on either side of the Red Sea imperils trade routes even as the war with Iran buffets the Gulf economies. Also, it is hard to see how hastening the collapse of the gigantic African state in their backyard makes either Gulf power more secure. The barren UAE’s dream of using Sudan as a breadbasket is unlikely to be realised while gunmen are slaughtering Sudanese farmers.

So the Saudis and Emiratis should stop supporting the warring parties in Sudan, especially the RSF, and work together towards a ceasefire. In Yemen they should set aside their rivalry, collaborate to contain the Houthis and try to restore a ceasefire there, too.

More responsible, less incendiary foreign policies from Abu Dhabi and Riyadh would not suddenly make the region calm. But they might make its wars a bit easier to tamp down. And that would ultimately benefit nearly everyone, including the Saudis and Emiratis themselves.

articles.title: Either AI or public debt could crash markets. But probably not both
articles.deck: If AI stocks collapse, bond yields will fall

paragraphs.text: Two SPECTRES stalk financial markets. One is the fear that surging bond yields will make the rich world’s shaky public finances unsustainable, triggering a nasty fiscal crisis. The other is the worry that the revenues from artificial intelligence needed to keep the data-centre boom going will fail to arrive. As we report, that would devastate credit markets and cause a big fall in stocks, too.

The good news is that only an Ichabod Crane would think that both these scenarios could strike at once. Instead, investors must decide which story is scarier. For now, The Economist is more worried about sovereign debt.

For most of the year, concerns about governments have dominated. Between the end of February and the start of October, the yield on 30-year US Treasuries rose by a full percentage point. The Iran war has sent inflation up and forced central banks to raise interest rates. Strong economic growth and the rush to build data centres have caused a scramble for capital in which governments have had to compete with the private sector. In Japan, Britain and especially France, investors have fretted about the ability of governments to service their debts.

In recent weeks, though, the prospect of an end to the AI boom has scared the markets more. The five-year bonds of CoreWeave, a “neocloud” that rents out data centres, trade at a 15% yield, up from 10% in July. The company’s share price has fallen by about a third in the past month. The slowing revenue growth of Anthropic, an AI-model provider, has investors worried that the cash CoreWeave and its peers need may not arrive, or at least not quickly enough to pay their creditors. Interlinked financing means that pain could spread quickly, through both the ai supply chain and the private-credit and insurance firms that hold a lot of data-centre debt.

As a result, many sovereign bonds have rallied. There has been little relief for France, where riots are worsening a political crisis, or Britain, where an upcoming budget makes investors nervous. But yields on ten-year Treasuries are down by a fifth of a point. Investors usually flee to the safety of American bonds in a downturn. Everywhere else, as data-centre investment slowed, an AI crash would ease the scramble for capital. And it would lead central banks to lower interest rates to support growth, thereby making debts easier to service.

Only in a big crash akin to the global financial crisis (GFC) of 2007-09 would the two risks collide. Governments are already sufficiently in the red that a deep recession would, by collapsing tax revenues and increasing welfare spending, make budget deficits look truly terrifying. Long-term bond yields might rise even as short-term interest rates fell—a nasty symptom of fiscal malaise that sometimes strikes emerging markets. It did not happen during the GFC, but the starting-point for debt and deficits today is higher.

Thankfully, there is no reason to expect such a deep crash. True, the history of finance shows that useful new technologies often bring about a boom and bust, and the web of financing behind AI has become complex. But the industry’s interlinkages are better understood than the alphabet-soup of housing-market securities was in 2007. Banks are safer, too. Though they are exposed to ai via their lending to private-credit firms, their balance-sheets are less fragile and better monitored. And backstopping much of the industry is the chipmaker Nvidia, which has an enormous cash pile. Most important, AI assets, though a big slice of many stock indices, are a smaller chunk of household wealth than housing.

So the best comparison for today’s AI vulnerabilities remains the dotcom bubble of the late 1990s. When it burst in 2000, cratering stocks caused only a mild recession. Bond yields came down, too, and underlying productivity growth held up. Such a scenario would hardly solve governments’ long-term budget problems, but it might forestall them. Many economies outside America are less exposed to the AI boom than they are to bond yields; growth falling by less than interest rates would make legacy debts a lighter burden. America’s deficit would grow in a recession, but so would the world’s appetite for Treasuries, because the dollar is the world’s reserve currency.

By contrast, if high interest rates triggered a sovereign-debt blow-up the consequences would be truly grave. If investors lost confidence in Treasuries, it would threaten the dollar’s valuable status as a haven. As France is discovering, trying to close big deficits under duress can lead to political instability. Governments may prefer to inflate away debt than to pay it down. That could imperil the stability on which all investment depends. A run on sovereign debt in a big advanced economy could well leave investors wishing that a dotcom-style ai bust was all they had to worry about.

articles.title: Europe must escape its reliance on American satellites
articles.deck: To do so it will have to drop old habits

paragraphs.text: RECENT DAYS have made clear the folly of relying too much for your national security on a capricious private citizen named Elon Musk. Mr Musk is said to have ordered the partial hobbling of his satellite-internet service inside Ukraine. That had two malign effects. It hampered Ukraine’s already limited ability to defend its cities and civilians from fast and deadly Russian drones. It also made it harder for Ukraine to strike back at Russia’s occupying forces.

If President Donald Trump objected to this egregious favour to the Kremlin, he kept quiet about it. America’s allies, in Europe and elsewhere, may reasonably ask how much they can trust the superpower. If, in the future, they need space-based communications systems to defend themselves against attack, can they be absolutely certain that America will supply them unconditionally? The problem, alas, is that no adequate home-grown alternative exists. Europe talks a good game of trying to achieve “autonomy in space”. But that will take time and money, and also require Europe to cut the waste, infighting and duplication that have weighed down its space efforts.

How to get there? First, Europe must have the launch capacity to put large numbers of satellites into orbit. In this, its record so far is poor. It can lift heavy payloads into space on its Ariane rockets, but nowhere near as cheaply or efficiently as Mr Musk’s company does.

Europe’s rocket programme exemplifies flaws of its space ventures. Delays in developing its heavy-lift launcher, the Ariane 6, left Europe without access to space for almost a year in 2023 and 2024. The European Space Agency (ESA), which funds the programme, is partly to blame. It fails to award contracts to the most innovative or efficient suppliers, instead favouring firms from countries that donate the most funds. The programme is also shielded from market forces, getting roughly €300m ($337m) a year in public subsidies. Small wonder it has been trounced by SpaceX, which last year launched Falcon 9 rockets 165 times, charging private clients $70m a pop, while Ariane charges more than $90m despite those subsidies.

To fix this, the ESA is tentatively copying America’s space agency, NASA, which decades ago encouraged the growth of commercial space firms by switching from “cost-plus” contracts for developing rockets to buying fixed-price launch services, a policy that let Mr Musk’s SpaceX flourish. The agency has awarded contracts to three rocket startups. Mergers, such as the proposed tie-up of three of Europe’s biggest satellite-making businesses, could follow. But can Europe create a firm big enough to compete globally without reducing competition at home?

Europe’s second priority should be to create a rival to Mr Musk’s Starlink, and to do so without policies that drive up prices and stifle innovation. OneWeb, a firm part-owned by the British and French governments, already provides some services similar to Starlink’s. The European Union is going ahead with IRIS2, a €16bn project to deploy 348 satellites to provide secure communications to governments and armed forces. Yet even this suffers from fragmentation and duplication. Germany plans to build a swarm of 100 military-communications satellites at a cost of about €10bn, while France and Britain are investing in their own smaller programmes. It would be wiser for all to pool their demand for satellite services.

Some governments will insist on having such systems under national control. Yet their concerns could be met by building satellites to common standards, so that they are interoperable. Countries or blocs could own these, but by linking them together, all would benefit: larger fleets would mean more resilience and greater coverage. Examples of this are already in orbit, such as small radar satellites built by Iceye, a Finnish firm. It offers customers a “federated model”, in which they can choose how much to share intelligence and co-ordinate where their satellites focus. Such an approach should encourage like-minded middle powers beyond Europe, such as Canada, Japan and South Korea, to co-operate too.

Europe need not stop there. The more it builds up its own space capabilities and shares them with America, the more convincingly it can show that an alliance of democracies is valuable. If so, despite Mr Trump’s instincts, America would have much to lose by holding its allies to ransom.
