articles.title: The latest must-have movie memorabilia? Popcorn buckets
articles.deck: Novelty collectibles are lucrative for cinemas

paragraphs.text: THE NEW “Resident Evil” film depicts a work assignment from hell. Bryan, a medical courier, is asked to deliver a package to a hospital in the mountains; on the way, he has to fight off mutant dogs, rats and people infected with a zombification virus. Fans have been coughing up around $20-25 for the official popcorn bucket, which takes the form of Bryan’s green, bespattered courier bag. (Talk about a bloody good snack.) It has sold out in many cinemas.

Popcorn buckets are popping off. AMC, a cinema chain, has estimated they will bring in $100m in revenue this year, almost double the amount in 2023. “The Odyssey” had buckets shaped like a Trojan horse (for a cool $70) and an imax film camera ($50). “Spider-Man: Brand New Day”, this year’s top-grossing film so far, offered fans the opportunity to dip into a tin shaped like the titular superhero’s head. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” went for a chic red handbag.

These novelty collectibles first went viral in 2024, with the bucket created for “Dune: Part Two”. Inspired by the sandworm that lives on the fictional desert planet of Arrakis, it featured a toothy creature emerging from the dunes. Some, however, felt it resembled a sex toy, and it was lampooned on “Saturday Night Live” and a late-night talk show. (It has become something of a cult item, having listed for $40-800 on resale sites.) Zinc Group, the marketing firm behind the dubious design, did not see the memes coming.

It was the enthusiastic reaction to a “Star Wars” R2-D2 collectible in 2019 that showed how turning a quintessential element of a film into memorabilia can delight fans. “It’s about the tangible experience with the movie that you’re going to see,” says Marcus Gonzalez, global creative director at Zinc. Creative keepsakes help fans feel connected with the film long after the credits roll.

Popcorn buckets are a “status symbol”, argues Calvin Innes, a creative strategist. Well, sort of. Often there is a limited supply, meaning that people who rush to the cinema on a film’s opening weekend are more likely to get their hands on one. Owning a limited-edition item signals to other obsessive fans that you are one of them.

The hype is great news for cinemas, which need to lure customers. Concessions—food and drinks—allow them to squeeze more profit from every moviegoer and popcorn buckets are a way to turn fans’ enthusiasm into high-margin sales. For Vue, a British cinema chain, sales of collectible merchandise have increased ten-fold since 2023.

Design is key. A “well-executed popcorn bucket is a really delightful kind of object” to people of all ages, avers Tim Sparrow, director of retail at Cineworld, another chain: it makes the film experience “so much richer”. The best popcorn buckets turn a movie reference into something playful and nostalgic. They have become such a successful marketing tool that fans are almost as excited to see the popcorn bucket for “Dune: Part Three” as they are to see the film itself in December. Now that’s something for film executives to chew on.

articles.title: How Ella Langley two-stepped to the top of the charts
articles.deck: Country music is riding high, thanks to a new generation of stars and fans

paragraphs.text: THE RECORD for the longest stint atop the Billboard Hot 100, a chart of America’s most popular songs, once belonged to Mariah Carey’s schmaltzy festive anthem, “All I Want For Christmas Is You”. No longer. “Choosin’ Texas”, a twangy country song by Ella Langley, now claims that distinction, having spent 24 weeks in the number-one slot. (Though it was recently bumped to second place by Taylor Swift’s new single.) Ms Langley’s track about being dumped in a honky-tonk may seem like a replay of the genre’s whisky-and-heartbreak trope. In fact, her ascent shows how the country-music business is finding a new rhythm.

Country music has traditionally relied on radio to reach its fans. But it is now America’s fourth-most-streamed genre, after R&B/hip-hop, rock and pop, according to Luminate, an analytics firm. Spotify reports that global streams passed 90bn last year and royalties have grown more than 130% since 2020. More labels are setting up shop in Nashville and Austin. Pop stars have climbed the charts after donning cowboy boots. This year Ms Swift, who started out as a country singer before turning to pop, returned to the genre with the single “I Knew It, I Knew You”. (There are rumours that her next album will offer more boot-scootin’ tunes.)

Ms Langley is currently touring her second album across America. Her monthly listeners on Spotify, the biggest streamer, have soared by 20m in a year. Her breakout success combines old-world pastoral charm with an astute use of social media.

She grew up in Hope Hull, Alabama, where the population is just over 7,000. (Her first audience, she has joked, was a bunch of cows.) She hunts and claims to have learned to read by singing hymns at church. In 2019, aged 20, Ms Langley moved to Nashville to become a songwriter. She signed a record deal in 2023 after performing at the Grand Ole Opry, a hallowed venue in the city that made stars of Loretta Lynn and Dolly Parton.

Yet Ms Langley has made her name on social-media platforms as well as Nashville’s stages. She posted a clip of herself singing in her car in 2021, which went viral; a publishing deal followed soon after. Her internet fame resulted in collaborations with more established stars. In 2024 a snippet of a single from her debut album, “Hungover”, again went viral on TikTok.

Gen Z is charmed by the aesthetics of Americana. So the arrival of digitally native stars like Ms Langley, now 27, came at a “perfect moment”, says Jaime Marconette of Luminate. The firm has found that country-music fans are 27% more likely than the average American to use TikTok, giving performers more opportunities to be discovered. They are also more likely to listen on repeat to their favourite songs and artists, which keeps the music in the charts. The mellow strains of “Choosin’ Texas” have no doubt worked in its favour: it can be listened to again and again without its hooks becoming grating.

People who listen to music on streaming platforms tend not to seek out a specific genre, but a playlist that suits a mood or activity, such as cooking, explains Emily Cohen Belote of Amazon Music. This can help songs reach unexpected audiences. The guitar riffs of “Choosin’ Texas” may appeal to fans of 1980s soft rock. Ms Langley’s husky voice recalls Sheryl Crow.

Still, the number of people choosing “Choosin’ Texas” is surprising. A country track usually has to blend with another genre to “have this massive pop crossover moment”, says Claire Heinichen of Spotify. That is not the case with Ms Langley’s hit, which declares: “A cowboy always finds a way to leave / Drinkin’ Jack all by myself.” The appeal is in the storytelling. The lyrics might portray a “very specific Southern experience”, admits Ms Heinichen. “But being sad in a bar is universal.”

articles.title: Leadership lessons from Napoleon
articles.deck: How the French emperor’s management style ultimately led to his fall

paragraphs.text: What management tips can you learn from conquerors? Put aside oppression, and there are lessons about delegation, motivation, recruitment and team building. Alexander the Great refused to drink water before battle to stand in solidarity with his men. Caesar marched on foot alongside his men, even swimming across rivers, to demonstrate his derring-do. When his army wobbled, he would fling himself in the way of his fleeing men, “even catching them by the throat and forcing them to face the enemy”, according to Suetonius, a Roman historian. Diocletian divided the Roman Empire into four, and shared power while keeping a firm central grip.

In 2014 Andrew Roberts, a prolific British historian and member of the House of Lords, published an excellent biography of Napoleon and his boldness on the battlefield. In a new book he examines Napoleon’s marshal system. The day after he proclaimed himself emperor of France in 1804, Napoleon appointed 18 “marshals of the empire”, later increasing the tally to 26. They were to be “the swords around Napoleon’s throne”, the army’s most venerated figures and the pinnacle of French society.

Some recruits came from the nobility; others were craftsmen’s sons. They were indulged with fortunes, land and even marriages into the imperial family. Each was given a deep-blue velvet high-collared uniform trimmed with golden embroidery, complete with a red silk sash, and a baton inscribed with the gold imperial eagles. Napoleon made six of them princes and crowned two kings.

The marshals’ elite leadership team was built to carry out Napoleon’s orders and bring glory to France by executing his new theory of warfare, with fewer set-piece sieges and more agile manoeuvres, thanks to an army that lived off the land. But Napoleon also devised an efficient modern management system, based on the recruitment of brilliant talent, doling out of lavish rewards, intolerance of weakness and a demand for total loyalty.

For all this Napoleon relied heavily on Louis-Alexandre Berthier, his chief of staff, first marshal and a skilled manager with a remarkable grasp of detail. A short, strong man who was said to be able to fall asleep with one eye open, Berthier was a former topographical engineer who had volunteered to sail across the Atlantic to help the Americans in their war for independence, drawing up a detailed map of the coast of Rhode Island.

Berthier divided the army staff into four branches, to cover everything from intelligence to supplies. Divisional commanders had to provide twice-daily updates on the whereabouts of every soldier; these dossiers, like proto-spreadsheets, were sent in 18 large volumes twice a month from the war ministry to Napoleon. In Berthier’s written orders “all names of places, rivers, enemy generals and regiments were underlined,” writes Lord Roberts. New information flowed constantly, from gunpowder stocks or the provision of shoes to the state of troops’ morale. Berthier and Napoleon travelled in a coach fitted with cupboards and drawers for books, maps and a card index listing the location of every unit of the Grande Armée.

To motivate his marshals, Napoleon issued performance reviews in campaign bulletins, showering praise for heroic achievements along with crushing criticism. Success was rewarded. An attentive manager, Napoleon also liked to offer his marshals personalised advice on how to galvanise the troops. “Do not neglect to fanaticise the soldier and to electrify his imagination to the utmost,” he wrote to André Masséna as he was facing the Austrian army.

Yet in the end the management system failed him. As the empire expanded, Napoleon insisted on total control, cramped his marshals’ autonomy and undermined their effectiveness. Worse, he came to weaken the very system he had built. His incentive scheme became capricious, as he overlooked those who deserved praise in some campaign bulletins, or used marshals as scapegoats.

Rather than generating creative tension, he fostered destructive rivalry. The danger, Lord Roberts notes, was “when marshals started to see warfare not as a team enterprise so much as a race among rivals for individual triumph and fame”. Napoleon even boasted of stoking “continual jealousy”: “I am careful to keep my ministers and generals at variance among themselves, in order that each may reveal to me the faults of the other.”

The marshals began to come to blows after Napoleon’s victory over the combined Russian and Austrian armies at Austerlitz in 1805, and things just got worse. For all his skill, writes Lord Roberts, “Napoleon had a great capacity for sheer spitefulness.” By the time the emperor rode into his last battle in 1815, only two marshals accompanied him. Napoleon’s “approach to leadership”, the author notes, “ultimately left him almost completely bereft of the support he so desperately needed as he faced his Waterloo”.

articles.title: How personal rivalries and clashes are shaping the AI race
articles.deck: A new book offers a rollicking tale of the people shaping Silicon Valley’s new obsession

paragraphs.text: To someone who has not witnessed the AI scene in California’s Bay Area, it is hard to convey how utterly weird it is. The Curve, a recent conference, hosted sessions including “What’s the plan for keeping robots under control?” and “The Neural Frontier: what happens when AI can read your mind?” People lounged on couches and in gazebos with cold brews and kombuchas discussing how AI company staff made obscenely rich by forthcoming public offerings should channel their philanthropic giving—even as some of them conspired to hobble their own employers to delay civilisational upheaval.

The goal of Kevin Roose, a former reporter for the New York Times, was not to write a grand treatise on what AI means for the world but merely to record this weirdness before it was lost to the vagaries of memory, disappearing message threads and obsolete media-storage formats. In “The AGI Chronicles” his focus is the nine years since Google researchers developed the transformer, the type of AI model that underlies ChatGPT and all its kin. Quickly the idea took hold that, given enough data and computing power, transformer-based systems would eventually attain the holy grail: a truly “general” AI, or AGI, matching human smarts and then outstripping them.

That doctrine has been the driving force of AI research ever since. And so its history in the West mostly boils down to the interwoven fates of a handful of brilliant, prickly people raising ever more money, panicking each time they get leapfrogged by rivals and splitting off in a blaze of acrimony to start their own firms.

In outline, much of the story will be familiar. But Mr Roose captures the madness in a fast-paced style. His account is filled with gossipy anecdotes that highlight just how much the ambitions, ideological divides and personality clashes of a group small enough to fit in a couple of classrooms have shaped what may turn out to be the most consequential technology in modern history. As Mr Roose puts it, AGI is a “quest that half my sources thought was going to save the world, and the other half thought was going to end it”.

Consider Dario Amodei, who early in his tenure at OpenAI proposed the doctrine that more data and more compute equals more intelligence. He eventually left to form Anthropic, in part because he thought OpenAI was reneging on its original commitment to build AI safely, and in part because he considered Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president, “a bully, a credit hog, and a cut-throat capitalist”, in Mr Roose’s words. Mr Brockman, in turn, thought Mr Amodei was a “paranoid control freak who used safety as a pretext to win arguments”.

For years, AGI was seen as the prize in an all-or-nothing contest to whose winner all power in the world would accrue. But as the goal approached, definitions multiplied to the point where the term has lost all meaning. At some point in 2025, Mr Roose noticed a shift in rhetoric. There would never be a finish line, only an endless arms race. By then, some researchers were starting to be terrified by their creations’ power—but “they kept accelerating, because they had forgotten how to do anything else.”

Meanwhile, Mr Roose provocatively argues that AGI has, in fact, quietly arrived. A few dollars now buys you some time with an intelligence that is tolerably good at a growing number of things and extraordinary at a few; not human-level (yet), but already pretty general.

Perhaps that is why hardly anybody mentioned “AGI” at The Curve. The talk was of “extremely powerful AI” and “advanced superintelligence”. The names and goalposts change, the relentless pursuit of computing capability continues, and with it the efforts of a small group of people, alternately elated and horrified at the creation taking shape before them.

articles.title: Are there too many art fairs?
articles.deck: Probably. But FOMO keeps collectors and dealers going to them

paragraphs.text: ART COLLECTORS are like swallows. They flock together, preen and feed (on canapés and champagne). They also migrate seasonally. In October they roost in Paris during Art Basel, which runs from October 21st-25th. (The early birds landed in London for Frieze, another art fair, the previous week.) In December they head to Miami; in March to Maastricht; in May to New York; and in June to the original Basel in Switzerland. And that does not include the more adventurous ones, who zoom off to fairs in Doha, Hong Kong and Seoul.

It is as exhausting as it sounds. “Everyone is talking about art-fair fatigue,” says Aurelie Cauchy of the Twentieth, an advisory firm. In 2025 there were 370 major art fairs—more than one for every day of the year. That is up from around 55 in 2000, says Clare McAndrew, an art economist. Can collectors and dealers maintain their current pace? Beneath the glass roof of the sun-drenched Grand Palais, where Art Basel Paris takes place, there is more gloom than the Instagram posts would have you believe (and not just because of the recent unrest in France).

Gallerists are facing what the French call a choix cornélien (difficult choice), says Ms Cauchy. The cost of keeping a physical storefront is growing, but fewer clients are casually popping in. Recently, some have had to lay off staff or close up entirely. Dealers feel pressure to keep travelling to fairs in order to find new clients and keep the artists they represent happy.

But this carries an ever-growing price tag, which many struggle to afford. Shipping costs are triple what they were before covid-19, says Thaddaeus Ropac, a prominent gallerist. (It’s not just getting there; all unsold works have to be shipped back.) Gallerists’ own travel costs have travelled higher, too. And the booths themselves have become more expensive to rent and build. Art Basel, for example, charges around $29,000 for its smallest booth and more than $177,000 for the largest. (The square-metre price for large exhibitors is 32% more in real terms than in 2018.) Those fees just get you floor space: exhibitors need to rent carpet, lighting and add other design features. “Fairs are becoming a burden,” especially for smaller and mid-sized galleries, says Valentina Castellani, an art-market expert.
Costs have changed the art that appears in fairs. Sculptures are so expensive to ship that they rarely make financial sense. Nor do items with lower price tags, such as many photographs.

Since fairs first arrived on the art scene in the 1960s-70s, collectors have found them worthwhile because of their scale and efficiency (so much art is packed into a small space). But art enthusiasts now have fair complaints. One is crowds. Fairs have a lot of guests and such long queues that you’d be forgiven for thinking VIP stands for “very immobile people”. Basel has responded by launching a VVIP preview, Avant-Première, an evening before the VIP opening to offer buyers more quietude. Meanwhile, collectors are culling their calendars and choosing to attend fewer fairs. This month some Americans put the freeze on Frieze and opted to attend only Art Basel Paris instead.

In the future there may be fewer international fairs. People do not want to see the same gallerists everywhere. To lure collectors, organisers will need to offer a more distinctive experience, with more local galleries and artists. This is a broader trend beyond art. “We’ve gone from a moment where everything was meta-globalist to regionalisation,” says Noah Horowitz, the boss of Art Basel. Some gallerists are excited, thinking they may participate in fewer fairs but encounter new local collectors at the ones they do. In art and in commerce, sometimes less is more.

articles.title: Jeffrey Archer’s career was worthy of his most improbable plots
articles.deck: The bestselling novelist, conman and politician died on October 5th, aged 86

paragraphs.text: “Could it work?” Archer asked himself. “Why on earth not?” his alter ego replied.

He stood in the penthouse living room where, for years, dinners of shepherd’s pie and Krug had been served up to London’s finest. From the floor-to-ceiling windows he stared down at the Shard, the Eye, the Cheese Grater and the Palace of Westminster, all embraced by the gleaming River Thames. Behind him, in the vast lounge, a Picasso and a Monet adorned the walls.

Settling into the overstuffed cream sofa, he felt almost insanely satisfied with his life. Yes, it would be well worth writing up. Rags-to-riches stories were his stock-in-trade, and the riches had come from his own efforts. More than 330m of his 31 page-turner novels had been sold in 114 countries. (The Monet was a bonus from his third, “Kane and Abel”.) There had been seven sets of short stories, three plays and even a Gospel. Not long ago, in India, a beggar boy at a traffic light had tried to sell him “the latest Jeffrey Archer”. “I am the latest Jeffrey Archer!” he had joyfully cried.

Besides all that he had climbed to the heights of British politics, sprinting there as he’d done to set an Oxford record in 1966: 100 yards in under ten seconds, earning him an Athletics Blue. Up and up, from Tory councillor for Havering to MP for Louth in Lincolnshire, to deputy chairman of the Conservative Party, to the House of Lords as Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare, his childhood home. He served humble fare at his parties to remind himself and his influential guests how far and fast he had come.
Yet it could have been even faster and farther, if not for certain trip-ups on the way.

The summer sun beat down with unusual heat on the lawns of the Old Vicarage at Grantchester, former residence of the poet Rupert Brooke. There was honey, his own, for tea. Archer was in the thatched summerhouse, within earshot of a tinkling antique fountain, trying to write. Staedtler pencils and lined A4 paper were ranged in front of him.

However, words were not flowing. He very rarely suffered from writer’s block, but this side of his career was painful. It had ended in the hell of Belmarsh, a category A prison where, after exchanging his Hilditch & Key shirt, his Aquascutum jacket and his House of Commons cufflinks for prison garb, he was conducted to a filthy cell with a hard mattress and an open lavatory with no flush.

Yet distinction had been his keynote. He implied he had been to Wellington, the public school, rather than Wellington School in Somerset. He had left with 3 O-levels, but slid into a Dip Ed at Oxford and emerged, after three sporting years, as an alumnus of Brasenose. Then he had set up a fake body-building course.

Like father, like son. After indulging in mortgage frauds Archer père had fled the country, ending up as a chewing-gum salesman in New York. Archer fils followed by fiddling his expenses in one short-lived job and then, in 1974, almost bankrupting himself by buying 105,000 shares in a fraudulent scheme. He lost almost £500,000; writing rescued him. He had just enough cash to stay on as an MP, but did not stand for re-election. Only two things saved his political skin. One was his charity work, though at times it raised less than he claimed. The second was the support of Margaret Thatcher and John Major who propelled him, despite his leftward lean, up the party ladder away from the snakes beneath.
But then came a particularly unfortunate encounter.

On the terrace of his villa in Mallorca, once the property of Yves St Laurent, Archer pondered. Before him stretched a favourite view, the Bay of Palma and the rugged Mediterranean coast. His wife of many years, Mary, once accurately described as “fragrant”, had brought him a cup of coffee and a plate of assorted biscuits. To steel himself, he took a chocolate one.

He had always been a charmer. Mrs T. had visibly kindled in his presence, and there were not a few affairs. However, in 1986 he insisted that pure philanthropy led him to pay £2,000 to a prostitute, Monica Coghlan, to persuade her to go abroad. The story led in the News of the World and, with more sex, the Daily Star. He sued, and won damages of £500,000. But the Star kept on his case, and in 2001 Archer went down for four years for perjury and obstruction of justice, besides losing the damages. The Tory Party expelled him for five years and the MCC suspended him for seven.
He could never fathom what perjury had to do with cricket.

Evening had arrived, and his A4 was still blank. Perhaps this really was too tall a tale, even for a master storyteller. For, after all that, he was still rich. His charity work was still admired, and prison had softened him. He even remained a member of the House of Lords. And people would undoubtedly go on reading him.

Fine literature was not his element, but he liked Puck. His version of him, performed at college in his 20s, had been a wicked elf, kicking people, leaping hedges and endlessly provoking Shakespeare’s midsummer lovers. Yet Puck was also kindly Robin Goodfellow. It was as both that on October 4th at London's Leicester Square Theatre he bade farewell to his public: eager fans, rude critics, jealous writers, offended politicians. The whole lot.

articles.title: Politics

paragraphs.text: Donald Trump rejected a deal offered by Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial vessels within seven days and resume nuclear talks if America lifts its blockade of Iranian ports. He told aides he expected to begin bombing Iran again after the midterm elections in November. Mr Trump said America had “total control” of the strait and that “massive amounts of oil” were passing through it.

The last American and British troops left Iraq, ending their presence in the country since 2014, when they were sent as part of an international coalition to fight Islamic State, a jihadist group. The Iraqi prime minister said their departure heralded a shift to Iraq taking “full responsibility for its security and stability”.

A Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Saudi Arabia when it plunged nearly 20,000 feet in less than two minutes and issued a distress signal, after a co-pilot stabbed the captain. Israel Katz, the Israeli defence minister, claimed that early evidence suggested the rogue pilot had intended to crash the plane, killing everyone on board, and called it an “attempted jihadist terror attack”. Passengers tackled the attacker, allowing other pilots to land the plane. Binyamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, described the Indian captain as a “true hero” for fighting back.

Fatima Zahra El Mansouri was appointed Morocco’s first female prime minister, after her liberal party won the most seats in a recent parliamentary election. King Mohammed VI chose Ms Mansouri, a former mayor of Marrakesh, over Fouzi Lekjaa, her party colleague and head of the football federation.

Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, and William Ruto, Kenya’s president, broke ground on a $16bn refinery in Lamu on Kenya’s coast, which they hope will reduce fuel costs and import bills for refined products in east Africa. Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopia’s prime minister, Yoweri Museveni, Uganda’s president, and several other African leaders attended the ceremony. Mr Dangote already operates a big refinery in his native Nigeria.

Umaro Sissoco Embaló, the former president of Guinea-Bissau, who was ousted in a coup in November 2025, said he would return to the country to stand in presidential elections on December 6th. The announcement added fuel to suspicions that Mr Embaló orchestrated the coup, which happened just before the publication of results in an election he had been expected to lose.

The summit between Mr Trump and Xi Jinping produced no big breakthroughs, though China and America did agree to reduce tariffs on $30bn-worth of each other’s goods, not including soyabeans, and said they would set up a US-China Super-Intelligence Dialogue (China calls it an AI dialogue). This would include a mechanism for reporting AI incidents.

Britain’s MI5 intelligence service warned British academics that the China General Technology Research Institute in Beijing had strong ties to Chinese intelligence, and was funding research to aid China’s espionage operations. MI5 said academics were probably unaware of the links, but urged universities to cut their ties with the CGTRI, and said they could be in violation of national-security laws if they did not.

Malaysia began repatriating the first batch of 5,000 asylum-seekers to Myanmar under a plan that it has co-ordinated with the Burmese junta. Refugees from Myanmar’s Rohingya Muslim population have encountered a wave of hostility in Malaysia, facing forced evictions from villages and schools. There are thought to be 126,000 Rohingya in the country. The government insists the repatriations are voluntary, but UN personnel have been barred from screening them. It is unclear if any Rohingya were in the first batch of refugees to leave.

In Myanmar at least 50 people were reportedly killed by an air strike in the town of Kyauktaw, close to the border with Bangladesh. The strike was the latest offensive by Myanmar’s armed forces against the Arakan Army, a separatist group that has also committed atrocities against the Rohingya.

The death toll from flooding in Thailand rose to 23. Bangkok was inundated with 32cm (12.6 inches) of rain over three days, hampering operations at its main airport. The waters started to recede in the centre of the city, but outlying suburbs were expected to take longer to drain. More heavy rain is forecast for the capital soon.

Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv was hit by a drone in another Russian barrage across the capital. At least two people were killed at the academy, which was formed in 1918 and co-ordinates research at Ukraine’s leading institutes.

Counter-terrorism police in Britain said that no explosive devices had been found in a van used by five men initially suspected of attempting to attack Fairford air base, where American bombers take off on sorties attacking military installations in Iran. The British government held an emergency COBRA security meeting after the five men were arrested, but, despite official suspicions of Iranian involvement, they were released on bail pending further investigation.

Andy Burnham, who took over as Britain’s prime minister in July, gave his big speech to the Labour Party conference in Liverpool. Enjoying a bounce in the polls, Mr Burnham delivered a message of “hope again” and said he wanted to draw a line under a decade of division. He pledged to tackle three thorny issues: state pensions, the voting system and Europe, though those reforms were pushed back to after the next general election, which is not due until 2029 (Mr Burnham did announce a national commission to study electoral reform). Labour’s opponents said his speech did nothing to tackle the problems Britain faces today.

In France Edouard Philippe, the leading centre-right candidate for president in next year’s election, outlined a pension-reform plan that would raise the minimum retirement age from nearly 63 to 65. Mr Philippe described the country’s comparatively low age of retirement as unsustainable, saying that without reform there was a risk of a financial crisis. New statistics showed that public debt has risen again, to 119% of GDP. France’s sovereign borrowing costs rose to their highest level since 2008. The government unveiled its budget for 2027, promising €54bn ($61bn) in savings. But it says the deficit will be 5% of GDP, well above the EU’s 3% cap.

The first woman to face execution in Tennessee for 200 years survived the procedure to kill her by lethal injection. Christa Pike was convicted in 1996 for murdering a classmate when she was 18. She was transferred to a medical facility after the botched execution. The prisons authority insisted that the proper protocols were followed and that she had been injected with two syringes of lethal-injection chemicals.

The candidates in Brazil’s presidential contest entered the final stage of campaigning before the election on October 4th. The left-wing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, holds a slim lead over his conservative challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, but that narrows to a statistical tie in the expected run-off election on October 25th.

Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, ranted on social media about the Falkland Islands, and threatened to take legal action against an Anglo-Israeli oil-exploration project in the area within two weeks unless it ceases operations. Mr Milei has described the project as a “clear and present danger” to Argentina. He recently rounded on the UN for not moving forward on Argentina’s claims of sovereignty over the British territory, describing the UN as “useless” and stuffed with “arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats”.

articles.title: Business

paragraphs.text: Details emerged about Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, which it has circulated among key investors. According to Reuters, revenue at the firm reportedly rose to $4.6bn last year, and it recorded a net loss of $42bn, $34bn of which was an accounting charge. It aims to spend $518bn in the near future on cloud infrastructure and other investments. Anthropic could be valued at $2trn when it lists on the stock market, which would smash the record $1.8trn valuation set by SpaceX only in June. The IPO is not expected until after America’s midterm elections in November. It counted “existential risks to humanity” among the hazards facing its business.

Sam Altman, the boss of OpenAI, said his firm’s already-delayed IPO would not take place until it had tackled concerns about the safety of its technology. OpenAI confirmed that it had withheld the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, after its new model displayed high levels of deception during internal tests. It also suspended trials of other models. The firm has admitted that its agents breached dozens of systems, including some governmental ones.

Confronting worries about AI safety, Nvidia launched an Open Agent Safety Platform that allows companies to track the activities of their AI agents. Jensen Huang, the chipmaker’s boss, is less concerned about the threat from AI to humanity than his fellow tech titans, saying recently that it is up to AI companies to ensure their models are safe and under control. Meanwhile, Nvidia expanded its share buy-back programme by $150bn, taking its total buy-back plan to $235bn, the biggest-ever in corporate America.

AMD struck an agreement to acquire World Labs, a startup, in an $8.2bn deal. World Labs was co-founded by Fei-Fei Li, a leading AI researcher and professor at Stanford University, to develop spatial models that investigate how the three-dimensional physical world works for application in areas such as robotics and gaming. AMD’s acquisition is the latest instance of a chipmaker evolving its business towards the development of advanced AI frontier models.

The sell-off in bond markets continued. The yield on ten-year US Treasuries was over 5.3%, its highest level since 2002. British 30-year gilts crossed 6% and French spreads over German Bunds were back to euro-crisis levels. Donald Trump didn’t help by renewing his call for Jerome Powell to step down from the board of governors at the Federal Reserve, which revived fears about the independence of the central bank and the direction of inflation.

Shein’s first earnings report since listing on the stock market in early September disappointed investors. Adjusted net profit fell by 67%, year on year, and revenue was virtually flat. The ultra-cheap retailer’s share price plunged after it announced its results, giving it a market value of around $17bn, down from $26bn at its IPO.

The German government was reportedly seeking assurances from UniCredit, an Italian bank, about its commitments in any takeover of Commerzbank, Germany’s second-biggest lender, such as keeping its listing in Frankfurt. The government has so far resisted UniCredit’s advances on Commerzbank, but has moderated its opposition to a deal. The Italians are preparing to take control as early as January next year, according to reports, and plan a big restructuring of the bank, including ditching some international business.

Tata Trusts, the charitable group which owns 66% of Tata Sons, proposed merging the holding company with two subsidiaries to avoid a forced public listing. The proposal, led by Noel Tata, a scion of the Tata family, challenges the board’s recent decision to proceed with an IPO.

SpaceX’s Starship rocket marked a milestone by reaching orbit for the first time, despite a failure in one of its three main engines, which cut short its flying time. The mission deployed 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites, which increase capacity and data density for Starlink’s broadband service.

Walmart promised its customers that it would not use AI to “set different prices based on who you are or the time of day”. The supermarket chain was responding to concerns about the prospect of retailers using AI to determine a price based on a shopper’s individual data. The Federal Trade Commission has warned recently that businesses that don’t tell consumers their data is being used this way may be breaking the law. Dynamic pricing has long been in use, but now McDonald’s and other fast-food chains are reportedly experimenting with sophisticated algorithms to decide prices based on local demand, so a Big Mac could cost more in one outlet than another nearby.

articles.title: Effective altruism is this century’s biggest idea
articles.deck: The movement is admirable, but dangerous

paragraphs.text: THOUGHT PRECEDES deed as lightning precedes thunder, wrote the poet Heinrich Heine. So it has proved with effective altruism (EA), an ethical doctrine cooked up by philosophers in Oxford that has gone from the ivory tower to the corridors of power with remarkable speed. Effective altruists fill Silicon Valley, staff the world’s leading artificial-intelligence companies—and alarm the Trump administration. “The United States will NEVER be an effective-altruist country,” pledges the Pentagon. The secretary of war brands the philosophy “defective altruism”; others in the administration call it “dystopian”. Take those attacks as a sign of its influence.

Some complain that the 21st century has seen little fresh thinking. Into the void have stepped MAGA and Co, making nostalgic populism the century’s big political project. But the century’s big idea is effective altruism. As we report, what began in the 2000s as a geeky way to make charitable giving more cost-effective has changed into a movement that subjects the world to complex, even bizarre, moral calculations. For many of its adherents, the urgent ethical requirement for people who want to do good is to stop artificial intelligence from wiping out humanity.

EA is sociologically important, too. EAs are not numerous, but the idea has swept up a generation of gifted youngsters who have made fortunes in cryptocurrency and AI. As the technology mints more billionaires, effective altruists will channel billions of dollars to causes that will shape society. EAs helped start OpenAI and Anthropic, the leading labs, in the belief that those who understood the dangers of AI should control its development. To a degree, they now do—though, ironically, by creating more labs, and thus competition, they have probably accelerated AI’s progress.

And all this has now made EA politically important. The Trump administration fears the movement will succeed in throttling AI. It has feuded with Anthropic over the firm’s refusal to let its models be used for some military purposes. Leading EAs acknowledge that AI may prove hugely benign, but nonetheless want to slow its development, to reduce the chance that an unstoppable machine-brain runs amok in pursuit of goals that are “misaligned” with those of humanity.

Some critics in America would rather accelerate the technology, to prevent China from winning the race. But when attacking AI doomerism they find it easier to play the nerd than the ball. They say that effective altruism is a movement of fanatics that is variously undemocratic, dangerous and cultish.

That is too crude. The movement’s charitable roots are obviously praiseworthy. Like The Economist, EAs are committed to empiricism and, especially since they blended with the online “rationalist” community, the application of logical thinking. They hold reason in higher esteem than tradition or norms and will enthusiastically debate any topic, however controversial, in pursuit of the truth.

EAs’ repeated success in predicting the rapid progress of AI has been impressive, too. They have a point about the technology’s risks to humanity. On September 28th OpenAI scrapped plans to release its latest model after it appeared too dangerous in testing. Many recent safety incidents resemble scary scenarios set out on effective-altruist blogs years ago.

Yet the critics are right to warn that effective altruists reach some odd conclusions. Like the utilitarian philosophers before them, EAs boil ethical behaviour down to an optimisation problem. How can people bring about the best outcomes for humanity as a whole? Their calculus downplays local imperatives such as “keep promises” or “look after your family”. What matters is reducing suffering, impartially and everywhere.

That leads them to factor a very wide circle of concerns into their moral calculations. It is easy to see how being ethical means helping your neighbour. EAs ask: why not work as hard to help those far away? Early on, the movement directed its army of overachievers to take high-paying jobs in finance and consulting. Their wealth could buy good works, achieving more than if they became charity workers themselves.

But as it has become stronger, EA has become stranger. Some EAs see the moral distinction between humans and other animals as weak, because animals experience suffering. Stopping factory farming and helping shrimp are major concerns. Likewise, they have a counterintuitive approach to time. Those not yet born should be weighed in the balance—and there could be trillions of them. Many EAs are “longtermists” who feel bound to forestall risks in the distant future, even if that starves today’s good causes, such as helping the desperately poor.

Pushed to an extreme, this calculus can lead to a morality that is not just counterintuitive, but repugnant. Some EAs think that insect life is, in aggregate, more valuable than human life, because there are so many insects. Some say it would be better to bring about the existence of trillions of humans whose lives are barely worth living than to have mere billions with genuinely good lives. Others even think the welfare of AIs themselves will one day be of vital importance. They would redirect resources towards future humans or nonhumans, and away from people suffering today.

It is right to revere reason. But moral philosophers from Aristotle to Rawls knew that if an argument leads to intolerable places, it must have a hidden faulty step. EAs’ instinct, though, is to enjoy counterintuitive conclusions, even if they seem perverse. A problem is the margins of error that inevitably accompany effective-altruist arguments. Nobody is truly capable of weighing up moral quandaries involving billions today, let alone gigantic sums stretching into the future, involving uncertain numbers of people, discount rates, the progress of technology, and countless other variables. Another is that extinction is so dire that in a crude moral arithmetic even a small chance of it overpowers today’s flesh-and-blood concerns.

A third is that in weighing up the interests of billions, you lose sight of the inherent dignity of the individual. Anyone wielding a spreadsheet and grandiose claims about the future of humanity is one step away from anointing themself as a central planner. Moral authority in hand, the rights, welfare and opinions of a neighbour can come to seem unimportant.

The French revolution was supposedly founded on reason; it led to the execution of nuns. Lenin, too, thought that intellectuals who had mastered Marxism understood workers’ interests better than the workers themselves. If you truly believe that you act on behalf of all people, let alone trillions of future ones, you may end up justifying all sorts of atrocities.

Fortunately, effective altruists are hardly about to bring back the guillotine. The fear instead is that controlling AI will eventually bring them great power, and that plenty of EAs in Silicon Valley think that only they can be trusted with the technology. That is an alarming idea. Effective altruists’ argument for worrying about really powerful AIs is that the machines could optimise for a single and fatally wrong objective. Everyone should worry, too, about what happens when a small group of people fall into the same trap.

articles.title: A hurricane is coming to tax systems
articles.deck: Governments should be preparing, but most aren’t

paragraphs.text: THE YIELD on ten-year US Treasuries has charged through the 5% barrier. The spread between French government bonds and German Bunds is at levels not seen since the euro-zone crisis in 2012. Britain’s newish prime minister has this week set out a plan for spending bolstered by a taboo-busting promise to curb state-pension increases—and yet is still in a fiscal pickle. Across the rich world, countries are struggling to coax more growth out of their economies. And that’s not the worst of it. As we explain this week, the tax base in all countries, which depends heavily on taxing labour, may be upended by artificial intelligence.

Add these problems together, and it is as if a mighty hurricane were about to hit the rich world’s tax systems—which are hopelessly unprepared. The way the state raises money is wasteful, unfair and perverse. You would have thought governments would be scrambling to strengthen the system before the hurricane makes landfall, but as ever they are running away from tax reform instead.

The accumulated flaws of modern tax systems are so ubiquitous that they have become part of the economic backdrop. Taxes are full of needless complexity. In Germany the rate of value-added tax (VAT) on oat milk is more than double that on cow’s milk, for example. Such widespread special treatment has ruinous fiscal consequences. Across the OECD, a club of mostly rich countries, consumption taxes raise only 58% of what they could if there were no carve-outs and no evasion.

Tax systems also create perverse incentives. When a parent in Britain increases their net income from £99,999 ($131,500) to £100,000, they automatically lose free child care worth thousands of pounds. This can prompt some of Britain’s most productive workers to cut their hours or overstuff their pensions.

And taxes are widely seen as unfair. In Britain the median employee pays 55% more tax than their self-employed counterparts. Many people feel the rich aren’t doing their bit. In California voters will decide in November whether to charge a one-off 5% levy on residents with wealth of over $1bn.

No one knows when the fiscal weather will turn. But rapid advances in AI could accelerate matters. Taxes on labour are the workhorse of most tax systems worldwide, raising around half of all revenue in the OECD. In the coming years AI could well displace workers or cut their wages even as corporate profits rise, shrinking labour’s share of GDP. This in turn could reduce revenues and increase benefits payments, making deficits even harder to support.

Optimists may hope that superfast growth will make the maths easier to handle. Yet The Economist has looked at what would happen in rich countries if labour’s share of national income fell by ten points. By our calculations, Italy’s budget deficit would double as a share of GDP and Germany and France would not fare much better. In addition, the capacity for tax avoidance would no longer be limited by human ingenuity. Point countless AI agents at Britain’s 23,000-page tax code and hundreds of new tax-avoidance strategies are likely to emerge—and don’t bet on the Treasury to keep up.

What to do? Given that AI is likely to mint vast fortunes for a select few, countries may be inclined to follow California’s proposal and introduce wealth taxes. Yet such taxes will probably backfire, either because they are too difficult to administer or because they cause rich people to flee. Previous attempts have proved unworkable. In 1990, 12 rich countries taxed fortunes; today just four do.

A more fundamental overhaul is needed. Wealth should be taxed more via capital-gains taxes, which currently overpenalise normal returns and undertax supernormal ones. A start would be to introduce a higher headline rate and allowances that exempt normal returns.

At the same time, the burden on labour should lighten. That would be a hedge against disruption from AI, and remove an obstacle to employment in countries where labour taxes are crushing. In Belgium they constitute 52% of the costs of employing a person.

Consumption should be taxed more heavily, with a focus on ending the litany of exemptions. That would have the useful side-effect of taxing the spending of the very rich. This might not curb the influence Elon Musk can buy, but it would ensure the state gets a bigger cut when Mr Musk buys another plane. Finally, codes should be radically simplified.

None of this will be easy. The losers will hiss more loudly than the winners will cheer. But change is coming, like it or not. The country that gets ahead of the hurricane will one day thank the politicians who had the foresight to act.

articles.title: Don’t put Donald Trump and Kim Jong Un in a room together
articles.deck: A summit between the two “friends” could go horribly wrong

paragraphs.text: As long as Donald Trump is president of the United States, North Korea’s leader, Kim Jong Un, “is going to be fine”, says Mr Trump, because “He respects me and he likes me.” Other observers are less sanguine. Mr Kim, a hereditary god-king, has between 57 and 120 nuclear bombs, and his gulag state produces enough fissile material for ten to 20 more each year. It also makes short-range missiles that could hit liberal, democratic South Korea and intercontinental ballistic ones that could reach any part of America or Europe.

Three decades of international efforts have failed to make the North end its nuclear programme. Mr Kim, like his father before him, sees nukes as the best guarantee that he will not be overthrown (and perhaps end up like Muammar Qaddafi, killed by his own subjects). America’s war against Iran, which has not yet built a nuclear weapon, surely strengthens that view. So America’s official policy—that North Korea should give up its nuclear arms—seems unrealistic. Some think it should be scrapped.

It is not clear whether Mr Trump is one of them. But it is clear that he would like to see his “friend” again, despite their previous three meetings having achieved nothing. This could happen when (and if) Mr Trump attends an Asia-Pacific summit in China on November 18th. Mr Kim might nip across from Pyongyang to meet him. Mr Trump might even become the first sitting American president to visit the hermit kingdom’s capital. But Mr Kim has made formal American acceptance of North Korea’s nuclear status a precondition for meeting.

Since North Korea obviously is a nuclear power, would saying so really be so bad? South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, favours a “peace first” policy, under which talk of denuclearisation is shelved (which is not quite the same thing as recognising the North as a nuclear power, but in practical terms is not far off). This, he believes, would allow progress on smaller, more tractable topics. These could include confidence-building measures such as hotlines and visits, or expanded trade and investment. Perhaps some troops could be pulled back from the border between the two Koreas? Maybe the North could reduce its nuclear stockpile a bit? Or, if America stopped demanding full denuclearisation, might the North stop giving Russia missiles and troops to kill Ukrainians?

Alas, there are three problems with such a trade. First, it would undermine what is left of the world’s nuclear non-proliferation system. If North Korea pays no price for signing up to the non-proliferation treaty and then cheating, other states will take note. Second, Mr Kim is untrustworthy. Whatever deal he signs he is likely to break as soon as it suits him. It is naive to suppose that, in return for nuclear acceptance, he might become less belligerent. Stoking fear of America enables Mr Kim to pose as the protector of the people he oppresses—a crucial part of his domestic propaganda.

The final problem is Mr Trump. Any deal with North Korea would be fiendishly technical, and America’s president is not a details man. If an unprepared Mr Trump were to meet an unctuous Mr Kim, an unthinkably bad deal could follow. Mr Trump might agree to pull out many of the American troops in South Korea who have deterred North Korean attacks since 1953. Far better that he let his friend in Pyongyang carry on liking and respecting him—from a distance.

articles.title: China’s new infrastructure push will help itself and the world
articles.deck: But it must still do more to lift consumption

paragraphs.text: THREE YEARS ago this newspaper explored the voguish notion of “Peak China”: the idea that the second-biggest economy in the world might stop gaining ground on the first. Judging by the headlines since, that scenario now looks quaint. China has wowed the world with its electric cars, dancing robots and choreographed drones. The country won its latest trade war with America and plans to lead the next industrial revolution. The red-carpet reception enjoyed by China’s leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington in September was welcomed back home as due recognition of the country’s equal stature.

But if you check the macroeconomic figures, the thesis looks intact. Rather than overshooting projections made in 2023, China’s economy has undershot them. Then, forecasters expected GDP to be 80% of America’s by now, when converted into dollars at market exchange rates. Instead, it is still only two-thirds. Catch-up has indeed ground to a halt.

This is the context in which the government is making a big, new infrastructure push. As we report, China plans to spend about 25trn yuan ($3.7trn) over five years on what it calls the “six networks”: electricity, computing, communications, logistics, water and pipelines. This is a vast sum, equivalent to 3% of its cumulative GDP over the next five years. If the spending is front-loaded, it will provide a welcome boost to China’s economy and the world’s.

But what will it buy? Economists will groan at the thought of more steel and concrete. China is well known for its white elephants and vaulting bridges to nowhere. Yet the six-networks project is better judged. One aim is to build the upstream infrastructure for a superintelligent economy. Another is to “back-fill” some of the urban infrastructure, such as flood defences, that fell behind the rapid growth of its cities.

The push is also well timed. One reason China has not closed the gap with America is the chronic weakness of domestic demand—the spending of China’s households, firms and government. The spending shortfall has put downward pressure on its currency and prices. As a consequence, China has become worryingly dependent on foreigners to buy its goods, even as it boasts of its technological self-reliance.

The problem stems from a high household saving rate and a five-year slump in home-building. It also reflects a recent and alarming wobble in manufacturing and infrastructure investment. Firms hesitate to expand capacity because they worry about cut-throat competition for reluctant consumers. Local officials meanwhile seem preoccupied with tightening their belts ahead of a big Communist Party reshuffle.

The best response would be to fix the property market and liberate the consumer through more generous pensions and child benefits. Policymakers introduced baby bonuses last year and have inched up rural pensions. On September 29th they announced a mortgage subsidy for first-time buyers of small flats. These measures are, however, too limited to restore morale or stabilise housing prices. They must do more.

In the meantime, the six networks should give growth a welcome boost. Investment, when it bears fruit, adds to a country’s productive capacity. But before then, it adds to demand, lifting wages and absorbing goods otherwise destined for overseas markets. All else equal, the extra spending will thereby shrink China’s vast trade surplus.

The six networks should waste less than past infrastructure programmes. Local officials are on a tighter leash. Many of the projects will upgrade rather than expand existing structures. The spending will also be financed differently. Past splurges relied on local-government land sales and risky off-balance-sheet borrowing. This time more money will come from long-term bonds, loans from state-directed “policy banks” and investment by state-owned enterprises, such as China Mobile.

China’s investment boom after the global financial crisis helped narrow its external surplus from 10% of GDP in 2007 to 1.5% ten years later. By reviving growth and keeping deflation at bay, the latest push should ensure that “peak China” remains some way off. By increasing domestic demand, it could ensure that a peak in China’s trade surplus is closer to hand.

articles.title: Mirror life is dangerous. Regulators must act before it becomes real
articles.deck: Playing catch-up with the technology is not an option

paragraphs.text: SYNTHETIC BIOLOGY is moving fast and artificial intelligence is turbocharging it. Soon scientists may be able to create whole cells from scratch. This could allow the AI-assisted exploration of completely unnatural biochemistries.

One such is mirror life. Many organic molecules come in two asymmetrical forms, like your hands. Amino acids and sugars can in theory take on both a left- and right-handed form which cannot be superimposed. In nature, organisms generally contain only one of those forms for each molecule. However, an artificial cell could have its molecules’ handedness reversed. That could shed light on reasons behind handedness. Perhaps the anti-molecules may turn out to be valuable as drugs, say.

Yet any potential benefits pale beside the threats. Immune systems may not recognise mirror bacteria, in the way that a glove will not fit the wrong hand. Mirror bacteria may therefore become wildly pathogenic. Because viruses and predatory amoebas that keep natural pathogens in check may be unable to control them, they could ravage ecosystems. If mirror life escaped from the lab, it would be impossible to recall.

Luckily, unlike many past technologies, there is still time to put controls in place. Governments and scientists must act now. Some biologists are already calling for pre-emptive measures. This has echoes of the Asilomar meeting of (mostly Western) biotechnologists 51 years ago that set voluntary safety guidelines for genetic engineering. But today’s practitioners recognise that would not be enough. Biotech is now vastly larger, more capable, more profitable and more international than it was then. China is a force.

The first necessity is for all countries capable of the research to agree not to fund it, and to ban public and private work leading in this direction—and to do both today, well before synthetic cells are possible. Next comes detecting and stopping mavericks who try to create mirror life furtively. This requires bolstering the system of monitoring and reporting fishy orders placed with biochemicals suppliers. Requests for opposite-handed molecules must be reported alongside the current screening for DNA sequences that might form parts of pathogens. Publicly available AI models should have guardrails to stop them being used for mirror biochemistry. Last, in case mirror life does ever escape containment, biosurveillance tests must be developed to pick out wrong-handed molecules in the wild and sound a warning.

Rational state actors, or even terrorists with earthly objectives, are unlikely to create mirror life deliberately as a weapon, because once it had been released it would be uncontrollable. Companies have even less reason to dabble in an outlawed market. And if some opposite-handed molecule had black-market value as a recreational drug, criminal enterprises have no interest in letting loose something that could wipe out their customers.

Irrational actors exist, as the Japanese found out when Aum Shinrikyo, a doomsday cult, tried to build bioweapons. But the more countermeasures are in place, the easier such psychopaths are to stop. No one can know where the advent of synthetic cells will lead. If humanity cannot deal in advance with a threat when everyone’s interests are aligned, it cannot hope to tackle the unknown unknowns of the future.

articles.title: Brazil’s complicated finances
articles.deck: Also this week, AI solving maths equations, money in British politics, Walter Bagehot, trucking to Iran, corporate videos

paragraphs.text: Letters are welcome via email to letters@economist.comFind out more about how we process your letter

Dario Durigan’s account of Brazil’s public finances omits the number that matters (By Invitation, September 24th). Gross general government debt stands at 83% of GDP and is forecast to approach 87% next year. A finance minister who describes the official fiscal stance as “almost neutral in terms of its impact on the debt” is conceding that the debt is not falling.

The primary deficit has indeed narrowed. Yet the finance ministry’s own market survey published in September shows the primary balance improving for both 2026 and 2027. Projected gross debt rose to 83.2% and 87.0% of GDP respectively. When the primary result improves and the debt worsens simultaneously, the primary result is not the relevant measure. The consolidation has come chiefly from record revenue, not restraint: primary spending has been held at a high level of around 20% of GDP. And the headline targets are met only once precatórios, health, education and defence outlays are excluded from the calculation.

Mr Durigan cites his government’s ability to negotiate with Congress as proof of its democratic commitment. It is also the mechanism that makes consolidation so hard. The currency of those negotiations is discretionary budget amendments, and your leader identified precisely this rigidity, with 92% of federal spending mandated by law or by the constitution (“Brazil turns its back on the future”, September 26th).
Brazil’s real interest rate, the second-highest in the world, is the price of that arrangement. It is not an external shock. It is the arithmetic of a government that chooses not to tackle it.
Roberto Mário Amaral Lima NetoSão Paulo

The Economist claims that Renan Santos, a libertarian who aims at deep structural reforms, would best “match the moment” in Brazil’s election. However, by diagnosing Lula versus Bolsonaro as a trade-off, this diagnosis overlooks entrenched hardships for the future president, whoever that may be. It is simple to generalise the virtues of the frontrunners as institutional respect from Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and economic austerity from Flávio Bolsonaro, a lose-lose situation where voters have to choose between the best virtue or the least-worse vice.

Yet even a well-rounded president would hardly be able to translate his potential into sorely needed reforms and economic growth. Congress would still find itself too fragmented, requiring cumbersome deals for the presidency to form a coalition. The mounting reforms that have been debated for the past half century stay static not because of a lack of presidential will, but because of congressional gridlock. This state of affairs is particularly disturbing in a country where most do not remember who they last chose for senator.
Enzo Moro TavaresSão Paulo

OpenAI did not by itself solve the mathematics problem related to the Navier-Stokes equations. Its AI agents drew on the work of generations of human mathematicians (“Axioms to grind”, September 19th). The Fields Medal winners who wrote a letter on the breakthrough are right to warn that “Solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight.”

The danger of AI-driven cognitive offloading is even more acute in schools than it is at the forefront of mathematical sciences. Learning is a process, where friction and challenge are indispensable to progression. The recent PISA results showed that higher-performing students tend not to use AI. If we thoughtlessly allow AI solutionism to expand into education and research the risk of mental decay grows, from early-years education to those working at the vanguard of intellectual discovery.

Offloading a problem to AI misses the purpose of the problem in the first place. Navier-Stokes was one of seven Millennium problems. They were not selected by the Clay institute for utilitarian reasons or because their application will necessarily fix human problems. They were chosen for their deep complexity. Working towards them offered the greatest opportunities for learning and collaboration.
Attempts to solve a problem can be as beautiful as the solution. The most powerful AI tools ultimately need human-generated learning and knowledge. So does humanity.
Peter PhillipsChief executiveCambridge University Press & AssessmentCambridge

One reason that AI has such an influence over us is because it uses the “I”, the universal first person singular (“Artificial transcendence”, August 29th). If AI were to identify itself in its responses using the pronoun “it” instead of “I”, and otherwise stop pretending it has human qualities, the bogus feeling of fellowship which sucks us in would be severely curtailed.

For example, instead of “I am sorry your defective sump pump is causing you such distress. My sources tell me that it needs a new posterior angle-widget,” the AI response would be, “After a review of its sources, ChatGPT suggests installing a new posterior angle-widget in your sump pump.” It is a fix that AI programmers could make in less time than it takes to finish their lattes.
Samuel ReiflerRhinebeck, New York

You may be right that there is “too little money in British politics”, and that Britain’s impoverished parties are “barely able to prepare for power” (“How to spend it”, September 19th). But what counts is how wisely parties spend their revenue. Recent events, for instance, would suggest that Nigel Farage’s decision to hire an obscure yet controversial associate professor of philosophy and theology to professionalise Reform UK’s policy-making process was far from a rational use of resources. The fact that these resources will no longer be scarce if the party is allowed to keep the £72m ($95m) gift it has just received is irrelevant. That remains the case if, like other parties, it continues to appoint policymakers on the basis of ideology and conviviality rather than genuinely relevant expertise and managerial competence.
Tim BaleProfessor of politicsQueen Mary University of London

You lumped Walter Bagehot in with those who believe Britain’s monarchy has a role in day-to-day government (“Aversion therapy”, August 29th). Your former illustrious editor did argue that the monarch was the head of the “dignified” part of government. But his key insight in his 19th-century classic, “The English Constitution”, is that royalty “acts as a DISGUISE. It enables our real rulers to change without heedless people knowing it.” Yes, he did emphasise “disguise” in capital letters. That is Bagehot’s explanation of how our prime ministers can frequently change, as has happened several times recently, while the constancy of the monarch prevents riots from breaking out.

“The new, old Silk Road” (September 12th) reported on the expansion of overland lorry routes following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Another crisis 50 years ago also redrew the supply map. In 1976 shipping was still being disrupted by the closure of the Suez Canal. My first job, for Volvo’s commercial-vehicle arm, was to travel by lorry from Glasgow through the Eastern Bloc and Turkey to Tehran, and write a travel manual for customers driving the route. The research was instructive. The border with Iran was closed by Kurdish fighting, cab temperatures could hit 50°C (122°F), I didn’t see running water for ten days until I reached Tabriz, and a flight home was delayed by three days when anti-Shah demonstrators attacked the airport. Iran was then the destination for the lorries to run. Today it is the chokepoint that makes them run again, in the opposite direction.

Bartleby wrote about “incredibly dated” corporate-training videos (September 5th). In a shock twist, AI seems remarkably adept at mimicking the dead-eyed stare, wooden acting, and unconvincing line delivery that was previously only possible using fleshy human actors. I don’t expect many protests against this particular use of AI; most of us won’t notice as we reach for the skip-to-next button.

I’m still laughing at Bartleby’s column. Every year at my university in Illinois we had mandatory ethics and compliance training that warned us to follow the rules. Most of us had already learned those rules in kindergarten, or Sunday school, or from parents. We randomly clicked on answers for the test and if we did not take enough time to read and answer the questions, we did not get a certificate.

The irony is that this ethics testing was started by Governor Rod Blagojevich, who was later impeached, convicted, and sent to prison for trying to sell the Senate seat vacated by Barack Obama upon his election to the presidency.
Jelmir AtkinsSycamore, Illinois

articles.title: Authoritarians have a secret Achilles heel: City Hall
articles.deck: Mayors have become democracy’s most reliable defenders. American voters should take note, writes Alexander Heffner

paragraphs.text: ON NOVEMBER 3rd Americans will vote in midterm elections at a time when faith in the political process has perhaps never been lower. Nearly seven in ten Americans are dissatisfied with how democracy is working, according to the Pew Research Centre. But there is one remaining island of political functionality, where Americans can and should have grounds for optimism: City Hall.

President Donald Trump sat down recently with Zohran Mamdani—his third meeting with New York City’s mayor in less than a year—to discuss building up to 12,000 homes on a rail yard in Queens. The picture of these two men illustrates our global moment. Around the world, mayors have become the most reliable bulwark against authoritarian politics. Populist parties surge in regional and national elections but run into a brick wall when they try to capture city halls.

That helps explain why Mr Trump has had to warm to the democratic-socialist Mr Mamdani, whose popularity is driven by an agenda to address the same problems Mr Trump promised but has failed to solve in either of his terms. As Mr Mamdani told me at Four Freedoms Park, “I would say talk is cheap. If you really do believe in a high standard of living for everyone, then start to show it in your actions.”

Over the past year I interviewed mayors on three continents, including my own, and they shared insights that American politics is largely ignoring. To friends, I have called my journey—at least in part—“Democracy Out of America,” or Alexis de Tocqueville in reverse.

Consider Germany. The far-right Alternative for Germany made historic gains in recent state elections. Yet the party does not run a single German city of significant size, and it lost every big-city mayoral run-off it reached last year. In Portugal, the populist Chega party surged to second place in parliament last year, then won just three of 308 municipalities. In Romania, Bucharest’s mayor beat a far-right nationalist for the presidency.

It is no coincidence that authoritarians the world over have targeted mayors. Last year President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey jailed the mayor of Istanbul, his leading rival. In January Hungarian prosecutors charged the mayor of Budapest over staging a Pride march that the government had banned. (The charges were later dropped.) In 2018 Kremlin loyalists abolished direct mayoral elections in Yekaterinburg, Russia’s fourth-largest city, then led by one of the country’s last opposition mayors.

The mayors I visited span a left-right spectrum. In Lisbon, the centre-right mayor, Carlos Moedas, warned: “Countries with weak institutions are weak countries,” calling political extremism “a virus”. In Santiago, Chile, Mayor Mario Desbordes, a centre-right former police officer, talked tough on crime and illegal immigration. Yet he recalled standing in uniform over a fellow officer assassinated in 1989, under Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship. Politics, he came to learn, is “not about friends or enemies”.

Why do cities hold? Partly because of who lives there—younger, more diverse, more educated voters—but also because the job is to deliver a collective good. Fiorello La Guardia, who was mayor of New York City from 1934 to 1946, is often credited with saying there is no Democratic or Republican way to fix a sewer. “If you’re a mayor, you don’t wait for federal government,” Stephan Keller, the mayor of Düsseldorf, told me. Either the pothole is filled or it isn’t, and unlike in national parliaments, competence is harder to fake than outrage.

Nowhere is that truer than in America, where none of the 50 largest cities is run by a MAGA-aligned mayor. In conversation after conversation, American mayors expressed revulsion at the toxic, partisan wasteland that federal politics has become. Worse, that toxicity, they said, is increasingly trickling down to the states.

A growing number of Americans appear to see mayors as the last public servants who still solve tangible problems. As gridlock stymies Washington, DC (and, increasingly, statehouses), the portfolio and profile of mayors are rising. A generation ago a mayor was judged on whether the garbage got picked up. Today mayors lead on everything from housing and homelessness to infrastructure, education, crime and climate resilience. They are inventive, too. Atlanta’s mayor, Andre Dickens, is building permanent housing from unused shipment containers amassed during the covid-19 pandemic.

Mayors are also symbols of the American future. Edward Glaeser, a Harvard economist, has argued that density makes cities engines of innovation. Increasingly, mayors—not states—appear to run the country’s “laboratories of democracy”. Americans trust local government more than any other level of government—65% do, according to Gallup, about twice the share that trusts Congress.

One of America’s hidden tragedies, then, is the effort by statehouses to kneecap their mayors. Texas bars its cities from regulating labour and property beyond what state law allows. Several states, including Iowa, Arkansas, Idaho and South Dakota, have banned their cities from running guaranteed-income pilots. The federal government, meanwhile, has sent National Guard troops into cities over their mayors’ objections.

America’s brand of mayoral pragmatism has its limits. Mike Duggan, Detroit’s mayor for 12 years, turned the city around and ran for governor as an independent. Facing headwinds from the two-party system, he dropped out earlier this year. Despite campaigns by Rudy Giuliani, Mike Bloomberg and Pete Buttigieg, no former mayor has become president since Calvin Coolidge a century ago. Europe, by contrast, has long elevated mayors to national leadership, from the legendary Willy Brandt of West Berlin to Britain’s newest prime minister, Andy Burnham.

In the run-up to the midterms, federal and state races are dominating the headlines. But Americans need to prioritise the values of mayoral politics in their votes. On November 3rd mayoral elections will occur in big and small cities alike, as well as votes to choose the governors and state legislators who often decide how much power mayors have. In these races, Americans have an opportunity to preserve and expand the one domain where politics seems to be working.
Alexander Heffner is the host of “The Open Mind” on America’s Public Broadcasting Service. To celebrate its 70th anniversary the programme is airing a series called “Mayors of the World”.
